11933-a-narrative-of-a-nine-months-resid:
Augustus Earle, draughtsman to His Majesty's surveying ship Beagle, spent nine months in New Zealand in 1827 and published this account in 1909. An illustration of a New Zealand war speech, drawn from his own sketch, fronts a narrative written by an artist-traveller rather than a settler.

Earle describes Maori meetings of ceremony, where a song of welcome could last half an hour amid copious tears. Evening scenes in a village where many inhabitants, fed by slaves or lying flat, seemed struck by sudden disease. His observations mix admiration, misunderstanding, and vivid detail, preserving an outsider's view of New Zealand society before large-scale colonization.
18345-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Number 315 of the Scientific American Supplement, dated January 14, 1882, gathers practical articles for engineers, mechanics, and inventors. The supplement, founded with Scientific American in 1845, cost five dollars a year alone and seven with the parent paper. Its table of contents runs from engineering and mechanics through electricity and magnetism to other useful arts.

Engineering pieces treat a watchman's detector, a canal boat propelled by air, head linings of passenger cars, an improved mortar mixer, and practical notes on plumbing by J. P. Davies, with figures on pipe bending and soldering. Electrical pieces give the Pacinotti machine of 1860, the Elias motor of 1842, Bjerknes's experiments, and Leo Daft on the arc electric light. Readers get an inventor's weekly: new devices, explained with figures, for the workshop and the street.
18763-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
This December 30, 1882 issue, number 365 of volume 14, is the Scientific American Supplement, priced at five dollars a year. Its engineering pages cover Louis Favre, builder of the St. Gothard Tunnel, with a portrait and Turin monument, plus Captain Eads's plan for a new harbor at Vera Cruz. Flour making, lift hammers, and hydraulic tests on the Ganges Canal also appear.

Other sections treat aerated drink machines, fusel oil, silicon, metallic thorium, and an obituary of chemist Friedrich Wohler. John Tyndall writes on atoms and ether waves, while Richard Owen discusses the Neanderthal skull. The issue is a rich snapshot of late Victorian science and craft.
22487-journal-of-a-young-lady-of-virgini:
Journal of a Young Lady of Virginia, 1782, preserves a girl's diary of revolutionary years. Lucy, the young writer, records reading, visits, and walks in a clear hand. One morning's entry shows her daily pleasures plainly.

She spent the morning in reading, much to her satisfaction. Old Mrs. Gordon came to spend the day at the house. Lucy Gordon and she returned from walking out together with delight. They walked to a narrow river they only call a river. Its banks are beautiful, covered with moss and wild flowers. All that a romantic mind could form, she writes. Such entries give social history a young woman's fresh, exact voice.
2700-medical-essays-1842-1882:
Oliver Wendell Holmes gathers forty years of medical essays in this volume, from 1842 to 1882, with prefaces old and new. Homoeopathy and its kindred delusions, the contagiousness of puerperal fever, and currents and counter currents in medical science lead the set.

Border lines of knowledge, scholastic and bedside teaching, and the medical profession in Massachusetts follow, with notes on young practitioners, libraries, and early teachers. Holmes writes as a reformer with wit, fighting quackery and defending honest doubt. The essays remain a landmark of American medical thought. Holmes's Boston voice, witty and humane, runs through them all.
27177-the-lost-ten-tribes-and-1882:
Reverend Joseph Wild's The Lost Ten Tribes, and 1882, printed in London in 1880, gathers twenty discourses chosen from 130 given to his Brooklyn congregation over three years. Wild, pastor of Union Congregational Church, Brooklyn, arranged them to lean on one another into a continuous argument.

The book opens with a plate of the Great Seal of the United States, adopted in 1782. It turns to prophecy's image of massive proportions: a head of fine gold, breast and arms of mixed composition. Wild reads the lost tribes into the nations of his day, with 1882 as a prophetic marker.
4833-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
Between 1580 and 1582 the Dutch cause faces isolation, and John Lothrop Motley follows Orange through sieges, bans, and embassies. La Noue sits captive, Hohenlo blunders in the north, and Philip publishes a ban against the prince, answered by Orange's famous Apology defending his life and cause.

Holland and Zealand offer Orange the sovereignty, an embassy goes to Anjou, and the siege of Steenwyk ends with Renneberg's death. Motley also tracks Granvelle's plotting and the arrival of the Duchess of Parma. The volume captures a leader under a death sentence, turning personal danger into a public argument for the revolt's legitimacy.
5249-travels-in-england-in-1782:
Charles P. Moritz's Travels in England in 1782 records a German visitor's journey, chiefly on foot, through several parts of England, described in letters to a friend. Translated from the German and published in 1795, the account shows England about a hundred years before its Cassell reissue, seven years before the French Revolution.

Moritz writes of roads, inns, towns, and the people he meets, with the fresh eye of a foreigner walking rather than riding. The book offers a vivid, ground-level portrait of Georgian England, and it remains a favourite among travel writing that lets readers see a familiar country as a stranger saw it.
8452-scientific-american-supplement-no-3:
December 16, 1882, brought readers the New York canals, their past, their size, and their trade. Cottrau's engine for steep grades, Bachmann's steam drier, and Parmelee's auto sprinkler shared the pages with a tool for drawing lines that meet, and a heater that cleans feed water. Paper making down east got a full write-up too.

Dye tests on yarns, gas cleaning, fake ivory, and creosote flaws filled the chemistry pages. The power pages took up Thomson's pile and Siemens's work. With canals, dyes, and power in one issue, the magazine shows an industrial nation at work, in plain, illustrated detail.
8483-scientific-american-supplement-no-3:
March 18, 1882, brought engineers tools for boiler makers, with drills and rollers for boiler plate, and Colonel Maitland on modern guns. His piece covers rifled cannon, built guns, steel castings, breech loading, and how much harm guns can do. Shaw's new kind of engine, Siemens on gas motors, and the Bazin dredge fill the rest of the power pages.

The chemistry pages take up drugs that widen the pupil, atropine and its kin, tests for morphia, and how to gauge manganese. Guns, engines, and lab tests in one issue show a magazine that served both works and war. For modern readers, it is a clear, illustrated record of 1882 craft.
8504-scientific-american-supplement-no-3:
November 11, 1882, brought engineers a hydraulic filtering press for treating oleaginous seeds, detailed in fifteen figures, and Laurent and Collot's automatic injection pump, in six. An improved one-ton bucket dredger, a history of the fire extinguisher, and how to tow a boat filled the engineering pages. Railways of Europe and America, locomotive painting, crackle glass, and how marbles are made fill them too.

Technology and chemistry covered drawing room photography, and a new method of preparing photographic gelatine emulsion by precipitation of bromide of silver. Taylor's freezing microtome and Vincent's chloride of methyl ice machine, in ten figures, complete the picture. The issue shows the Supplement's workshop range, from oil seeds to ice machines, illustrated for practical readers.
8559-scientific-american-supplement-no-3:
November 25, 1882, brought engineers Gjers's soaking pits for steel ingots, on rolling ingots with their own initial heat, with six figures, and Clemandot's tempering by compression. Economical steam power, Mississippi River improvements near St. Louis, Bunte's burette for furnace gases, the Universal gas engine, and a gas furnace for baking refractory products filled the engineering pages.

Fans, coal refuse fuel, hank sizing machines, coke breakers, and printing machinery added workshop variety, while chemistry covered pure water apparatus and more. The Supplement's range shows a magazine serving steel, steam, and print alike. For modern readers, it is a detailed record of 1882 industry, illustrated and practical.
8687-scientific-american-supplement-no-3:
Scientific American Supplement number 362, dated December 9, 1882, leads with recent improvements in textile machinery. Harris's revolving ring spinning frame, a new electric stop motion, and a new positive motion loom take pride of place. Six figures, followed by spinning without a mule, new binding machines, flumes and their construction, and Chuwab's rolling mill for dressing and rounding. The Supplement cost five dollars a year, seven with the main journal.

Practical detail rules: diagrams, measurements, and workshop description, aimed at engineers, mill owners, and inventors. The textile articles show an industry mechanizing fast, with electricity beginning to guard and drive the looms. For historians of industry, this issue is a precise snapshot of the mill floor in 1882. For general readers it shows how a popular science paper taught working technology to a wide audience.
8717-scientific-american-supplement-no-3:
Scientific American Supplement number 344, dated August 5, 1882, opens with the Panama Canal. In an article by Manuel Eissler tracing Spanish discoveries in Central America, early explorations, Nicaragua projects, and the Panama railway. Engineering and mechanics fill the front of the issue: an improved averaging machine, Borsig's compound beam engine with four figures. Power hammers with a movable fulcrum by Daniel Longworth.

The Supplement, five dollars a year alone and seven with the main journal, served readers who wanted working detail behind the news. Diagrams, figures, and practical description dominate, rather than theory alone. This issue gives a fine snapshot of 1882 technology in progress, when the canal was still a scheme of surveys and railways, and steam power ruled the workshop. Historians of technology will find it a rich primary source.
a-narrative-of-a-nine-months-residence-i: Augustus Earle, draughtsman to a surveying ship, recounts nine months in New Zealand in 1827, after a roving early life that carried him through the Mediterranean and up Mount Etna. The narrative records the people, warfare, and daily life he observed there, illustrated from his own sketches, including a war speech scene. Its value lies in an artist's eye for ceremony and character in a country still little known to English readers.
an-account-of-some-experiments-on-mercur:
An Account of Some Experiments on Mercury, Silver and Gold was printed in 1782 by James Price. The experiments were made at Guildford in May of that year, in Price's own laboratory. Before the account stands an abridgement of Boyle's account of a degradation of gold, setting Price's work beside a famous earlier case.

Price's pamphlet belongs to the last chapter of public transmutation claims in England. He reported experiments on the three noble metals at a time when chemistry was separating itself from alchemy, and such claims drew the Royal Society's attention. The short quarto preserves his report as he made it, with the Boyle preface he used to support it.
arxiv-2509-00082:
Sukriti Manna, Constantine M Megaridis, and Subramanian KRS Sankaranarayanan present a phase-field model for two-phase flows in 2025. Two-phase flows mix fluids such as oil and water or liquid and vapor. A phase field tracks the blurry border between phases, which lets a model follow splits, merges, and bubbles without sharp edge tracking.

The joint Cahn-Hilliard and Navier-Stokes equations govern the border and the flow. The pair is hard to solve: one part has higher-order terms and strong curves, and each part feeds back on the other. Shifts in density and thickness add strain. Their projection-based method aims to keep mass and stability while handling sharp contrasts. Such flows drive boiling, coating, and microfluidic tools.
arxiv-2509-00182:
Uwe D. Hanebeck, working alone, proposes a particle filter in 2025 that never degenerates, built on a generalized Cramér distance. Particle filters track a hidden state in high dimensions with a set of sample points. Classic filters can degenerate, meaning nearly all points lose weight and the estimate collapses.

His filter uses deterministic low-discrepancy point sets, which spread points evenly by design. In the update step, a likelihood is eased in over artificial time by homotopy continuation. A Newton flow then moves points smoothly from prior to posterior, guided by a closed-form distance that ignores point order. The filter needs only a prior set and a likelihood, and can replace classic filters directly.
arxiv-2509-00282:
V. Hnizdo and G. Vaman derive new distributional Laplacians in 2025 for an inverse hyperbolic sine function and a related logarithm function. A Laplacian sums the second rates of change of a function across space directions. A distributional Laplacian extends that operation to functions with sharp points, where ordinary derivatives break down, by treating them in a generalized sense.

The method used for the first result is then applied to a classic problem in electromagnetism. It yields the gauge transformation function for a uniformly moving point charge in the Coulomb gauge, a standard choice that fixes the form of the potentials. Exact distributional results support careful field calculations where point charges create singular behavior.
arxiv-2509-00482:
Saksorn Ruangtanusak, with two co-authors, Pittawat Taveekitworachai and Kunat Pipatanakul, reports on role-play agents for a dialogue challenge held in 2025. Their agent is a large language model with tools, playing a set persona, a fixed character, while it must also call the right functions.

The team compares four prompting plans, from basic role prompts to automatic prompt tuning. Their rule-based role prompting, built on character cards and strict rules for function calls, scores best, beating a zero-shot baseline, meaning a start with no examples. Ruangtanusak and his co-authors share their best prompts and tuning tool, arguing that clear rules beat more complex tuning for this task.
arxiv-2509-00982:
Lead author Mateusz Wilinski and one co-author wrote this 2025 research paper on machine learning for stock markets. It asks whether a generative model can learn to copy how real trading agents behave. The data at the centre are limit order book records, where each investor can be told apart.

The team adapts a state-space design to build their generative system and trains it on synthetic data from a varied agent-based setup. They then check how well the trained system predicts what investors do. Its forecast spread across parts of investor behaviour is set against the known truth built into the synthetic data.
arxiv-2509-01082:
Writing programs that model chance is hard, because a small code flaw can break the statistics behind them. Madhav Kanda, Shubham Ugare, and Sasa Misailovic present RefineStat, a tool that helps small language models write such programs correctly. It draws on the fixing habits that skilled human coders use when they debug.

RefineStat first enforces rules so the code uses valid chance distributions and well-formed settings. When checks on trust or soundness fail, it resamples the prior or likelihood parts, the pieces that state early beliefs and how data arise. Tests on several coding tasks show the output was sound and often matched programs from much larger closed models.
arxiv-2509-01982:
Amit Pradhan, Pratik Mullick, and Parongama Sen study how contrarians affect opinion spread in a weighted voter model. In the q-voter model, a group of neighbors influences one agent, with weights set by a bias parameter. Contrarians always oppose the prevailing push, whether the group agrees or splits. The authors add a tunable share of such agents to the system.

Mean field math and Monte Carlo simulations map the final opinion states. Simple phase lines split regions of positive and negative majorities. Small contrarian shares cannot overturn the built in bias. Larger shares push the system toward balanced coexistence, though bias blocks exact parity. Timing analysis shows how fast opinions settle in each regime. Structured dissent thus preserves diversity without full deadlock.
arxiv-2509-02082:
Xia'an Du, Junjie Qi, Hua Jiang, and X C Xie engineer domain walls in graphene Josephson junctions to steer supercurrents. Domain walls in graphene host topological kink states that carry current along the wall. Josephson junctions pass supercurrent between superconductors, and both technologies are now fabricable. Combining them, however, remains largely unexplored in theory and practice.

Three strategies are proposed and analyzed in transport calculations. Adding walls morphs the interference pattern from one classic form to another, matching recent experiments. Asymmetric wall layouts under a field yield an ideal Josephson diode with one way supercurrent. Crossing walls split supercurrent among leads with ratios tuned by angle, field, and phase. The platform suits sensitive magnetometry and next generation quantum devices.
arxiv-2509-02182:
Shyma Alhuwaider leads four co-authors in a track based test set for test time tuning and a memory trick to match. Test time tuning tweaks a model post launch as new data drift in form. Old test sets stress drift but treat each shot as lone, which misses time links in real streams. Their set draws shots from tracklets, short tracked clips of one object from a tracking set.

Shots in a row show the same object by build, so time links are real. Wide tests show where live tuning ways fail when time links are strong. A foe based memory start trick then lifts memory based ways by a lot on the set. The work pushes tuning work toward true stream terms. Hand held and car cam scenes drove the design from the start.
arxiv-2509-02282:
Pedro Fontanarrosa and Chris P Barnes probe truth and doubt in physics led nets that infer microbe web dynamics. Such nets pull clear link terms from noisy microbe time data. Hands on users face a pile of knobs, from loss weights to train plans, with thin help. Doubt bars are scarce in most work of this kind. Their two part study uses a six type Lotka-Volterra model with a known step input.

Part one sweeps truth knobs and finds plain term scaling gives the top gains. Tune work and smart point picks match on pair link error in the tests. Part two grades deep groups and dropout for doubt bars on forecasts. Groups give the best growth rate truth, while dropout gives bars. Code, marks, and plots are shared as base lines.
arxiv-2509-02482:
Francesco Denti and three co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on tissue analysis. It works with multiomics imaging data. Mass spectrometry imaging maps molecules across a tissue slice. New workflows repeat the scan on one section for lipids, peptides, and sugars.

Repeated rounds share one pixel grid, but the data are huge and structured. Their Poseidon model does nested biclustering. It groups pixels into tissue regions and clusters molecular signals inside each class at once. A spatial extension uses hidden Markov random fields. Those fields favor neighbor pixels agreeing with each other. Fast variational inference keeps the method scalable. Simulations check the approach. A kidney cancer case study shows clear tissue splits and candidate biomarkers.
arxiv-2509-02782:
Václav Sobotka, Lucas Kletzander, Nysret Musliu, and Hana Rudová wrote a 2025 optimisation paper on cross-domain hyper-heuristics, methods that choose among simple search heuristics to solve varied problems. Most research tunes how heuristics get selected; this paper instead studies what the heuristic set contains.

Three transformation principles are analysed: which solutions get accepted, how often heuristics repeat, and how much of a solution each perturbative step changes. With the right transformation, even a trivial random selector beat all published rivals on three hard real-world domains and found eleven solutions better than any previously known. Against a famous competition winner, the same recipe stayed competitive. Adding the transformations to recent methods improved them too, often while simplifying their designs.
arxiv-2509-02882:
Caleb Marshall wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on the Favard length of certain fractal sets. Favard length measures, on average, how long the shadows of a set are when light shines from every direction. The sets here are product Cantor sets, built by repeatedly removing middle pieces along each coordinate with rational rules.

Marshall proves stronger upper bounds on how thick small neighborhoods of these sets can be, in every dimension from two upward. His proof mixes estimates for small values, sets of large values, and a sharpened counting argument on symbolic pieces. For the classic four-corner Cantor set, the bound improves to a new power law. Special planar examples reach even stronger exponents when their defining polynomials avoid zeros on a key circle.
arxiv-2509-02982:
Hritik Arasu and Faisal R Jahangiri presented a 2025 method called StableSleep for adjusting sleep staging models at the bedside. Sleep staging sorts a night's brain waves into stages, yet models often slip when a new patient's signals differ from training data. Their recipe adapts a model while it runs, without needing the original training data.

The recipe pairs entropy minimization, which pushes the model toward confident calls, with refreshed normalization statistics drawn from the live signal. Two safety rails guard the process: a gate pauses updates on shaky stretches, and a slow-moving average can pull the model back if it drifts. Tested on a public sleep dataset, it beat the frozen model at low delay and small memory cost.
arxiv-2509-03482:
Jamison Sloan and eight co-authors report a 2025 research paper on controlling quantum noise in light that travels through many modes at once. Multimode systems can beat single-mode ones, but nonlinear interactions between modes build up noise. That noise caps how well optical devices can perform.

Shaping the incoming wavefront, the pattern of the light's surface, lets the team focus a bright spot whose brightness barely fluctuates. In a multimode fibre, noise falls well below what simple dimming achieves, approaching the basic quantum limit set by shot noise. The shaped input separates output fluctuations from laser fluctuations at the source. A new theory and simulation framework backs the result, pointing toward quieter nonlinear optical technologies.
arxiv-2509-03582:
Measuring cosmic shear across the largest lensing dataset assembled so far is what D. Anbajagane and eighty co-authors do in a 2025 research paper. Cosmic shear is the slight distortion of distant galaxy shapes by gravity from matter in between. Their data combine the DECADE project surveys with Dark Energy Survey Year 3 results, covering 270 million galaxies.

Within the standard cosmological model, their fitted values agree with Planck satellite results to within about two standard deviations. Extending the model to dark energy that changes over time brings only small gains over supernova and sound-wave measurements. Six models for how ordinary matter reshapes small-scale structure give consistent answers once prior ranges are wide enough. Standard scale cuts leave a small residual bias, which fuller modelling does not remove. Extra non-lensing data will be needed to unlock the full statistical power.
arxiv-2509-03982:
In a 2025 mathematics paper, Yasuhiro Wakabayashi examines pointed stable curves carrying dormant higher-level opers, and on the shape of their moduli space. An oper is a flat bundle carrying differential-operator structure, and dormant means its curvature-like data vanishes. The moduli space organises such curve-and-bundle pairs into one object.

A Hitchin-Mochizuki morphism is introduced on these spaces, defined through characteristic polynomials of the opers' p-power curvatures, turning bundle data into polynomial invariants. The machinery aims at a theorem: this moduli space, for dormant rank-two opers of the higher-level type, is irreducible. Irreducibility means the space cannot be split into components, so any two such objects connect through a continuous family. Results of this shape underpin counting arguments in the area, since enumerative formulas presuppose a connected space. The work extends the dormant oper programme that links bundles, curves, and characteristic-p geometry.
arxiv-2509-04082:
Yu Qiu and one co-author, Renyue Cen, study how giant radio jets from black holes affect nearby galaxies in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Some huge black holes blast out jets that inflate lobes of magnetized gas far into space. Using large computer simulations of the evolving universe, the authors add jet energy around the time black hole growth peaked. Galaxies near those jets then pull in less fresh gas afterward.

Less gas means fewer raw materials for new stars. In the most strongly magnetized areas, the gas share inside galaxy halos dropped by roughly an eighth to a sixth. The authors argue future universe simulations should include this outside, preventive effect from active black holes.
arxiv-2509-04282:
Amelia J Cordwell and three co-authors test how faithfully flat simulations capture planets carving gaps in gas discs in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Young planets orbit inside discs of gas and dust, and their gravity opens gaps and twists flows. Real discs are three-dimensional, but most studies flatten them for speed. A fudge factor called a smoothing length softens the planet's gravity in flat models, with rival values proposed for different purposes.

The team re-derived the flat flow equations and ran large suites of both flat and full simulations for comparison. A Bessel-type potential, a formula built from special functions, matched best. Even so, total torque scaling stayed off, and gap-based planet masses may be underestimated twofold.
arxiv-2509-04482:
Ravi Shankar and six co-authors teach a medical question-answering system when to stay silent in a 2025 research paper. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in fetched documents, but in women's health a wrong answer can cause real harm. Their energy-based model builds a smooth energy landscape over millions of guideline-derived questions, scoring each new query by how well it fits. Low-fit questions trigger abstention instead of a risky guess.

Against a calibrated probability baseline and a nearest-neighbor heuristic, the energy approach won clearly on hard cases, questions close to the guidelines yet subtly off. False alarms at high sensitivity dropped notably. Easy cases tied across methods. Ablations credit the energy scoring head itself for the robustness.
arxiv-2509-04582:
Jingyi Lu and one co-author, Kai Han, rethink drag-based photo editing as warping plus inpainting in a 2025 research paper. Dragging points in an image should pull features naturally, but current methods steer generative latent spaces, giving imprecise, slow edits tied to one model. Their framework, Inpaint4Drag, treats image regions as elastic material: a bidirectional warp deforms pixels in real time, then an inpainting model fills the gaps. Any inpainting engine plugs in without architectural changes, inheriting future improvements automatically.

Warp previews take about a hundredth of a second and inpainting a third of a second at standard resolution, versus minutes for rivals. Extensive experiments show better visual quality and control. Interactive editing becomes genuinely responsive.
arxiv-2509-04682:
Underwater sound monitoring fails in noisy, shifting conditions more often than standard tests reveal. Nicholas R. Rasmussen, lead author with three co-authors, present a framework meant to expose those failures in a 2025 paper. GetNetUPAM uses nested cross-validation arranged in site and year blocks, so each test fold reflects a distinct environment.

The nested stage measures model stability rather than tuning for inflated scores. With it, they test a network with attention for spectrograms of varying size. Attention acts as a learned noise filter. The goal is more honest estimates of how marine bioacoustic systems will perform when deployed.
arxiv-2509-04782:
Classical statistical patterns can strengthen a modern forecasting transformer. Jiajun Song and one co-author propose VARMAformer in a 2025 time series paper. Recent transformer designs drop self-attention for speed and accuracy, but they can miss fine local patterns that vector autoregressive moving average models capture well.

Their architecture adds a feature extractor inspired by that classical model, working at patch level. A second mechanism uses a temporal gate to make attention queries more aware of context. Together the parts capture global long-range links and local statistical structure. Extensive benchmark experiments show consistent gains over leading methods.
arxiv-2509-04982:
Short texts give sentiment classifiers little context. Their labels are often skewed, and the mood they record is a matter of taste. Julius Neumann, lead author with three co-authors, study how to tune small transformer models for multi-label sentiment analysis in a 2025 paper. They test BERT-style models below a billion parameters under those constraints.

Three factors are tested: more domain pretraining, generative data augmentation, and classification head design. Added data improves results in their experiments. More pretraining on that data can add noise instead of accuracy. Head changes give only small benefits. The findings offer practical guidance for teams building sentiment models on limited resources.
arxiv-2509-05082:
A young star with a disputed planet shows dramatic radio flares in a 2025 astronomy paper by Rachel A. Osten and one co-author. They monitored the star V830 Tau for eight days at microwave frequencies with a radio interferometer. Earlier brief observations had hinted at a bright, variable source.

The new data confirm brightness changes larger than a factor of five, with a long-lived flare spanning several days. The authors discuss whether magnetic interaction between the star and its putative planet could power such a flare. They draw on monitoring of active binary systems for comparison, and note that repeating flares near the orbital period would support the idea.
arxiv-2509-05782: A famous open conjecture about which shapes admit a basis of pure tones is taken up again by Mihail N. Kolountzakis in a solo 2025 paper in harmonic analysis. Fuglede's conjecture asks which bodies in Euclidean space admit an orthogonal basis of exponentials for their L2 space, a basis like the tones that build any signal on an interval. Kolountzakis reads part of Fuglede's original 1974 paper, where the conjecture was posed, and what that source in fact showed.
arxiv-2509-05882:
How the training alignment of a language model changes its behavior as a group collaborator is studied in a 2025 paper by Abhijnan Nath and two co-authors. Models are increasingly placed inside multi-party workflows beside people and other AI systems. Alignment methods, though, are usually tuned for a single user in short exchanges.

The test uses intervention agents that join group dialogues not to answer, but to slow the group down and prompt reflection before decisions. Through roleplay simulations, the authors compare alignment methods inside long collaborative tasks and track belief alignment and coordination. Theory based on a modified-action model explains why single-user tuning misses multi-party dynamics. An agent robust to having its actions modified supported correct outcomes far better than standard baselines.
arxiv-2509-06082:
Sharper scans of tiny specimens come from teaching an optimizer where the edges are, in a 2025 paper led by Anuraag Mishra with four co-authors. Tomographic reconstruction rebuilds a three-dimensional object from projections, but standard methods blur the sharp boundaries between homogeneous material phases. The team trains a neural network to spot edges inside small image patches.

Those edge predictions are then woven into a mathematical optimization model: reconstructions are favored when they agree with the learned edges, yet the raw data can still overrule them. On experimental datasets, interface sharpness and material homogeneity improve clearly over benchmark algorithms. The hybrid design shows how learned knowledge and hard data checks can cooperate in scientific imaging.
arxiv-2509-06682:
Farm vehicles that must cover fields while obstacles keep moving are guided by Sajad Ahmadi and two co-authors in a 2025 robotics paper. Coverage control spreads a fleet of off-road ground vehicles over an area. Standard methods assume a fixed world, but real fields have moving machinery and uneven, muddy ground.

The proposed system adds drones overhead to spot obstacles and judge terrain in real time. The field becomes a weighted directed graph, and the weights update continuously as drone observations arrive. Space is divided with Voronoi partitions, which assign each vehicle its nearest region, and paths are chosen by cost. Simulations show better path planning, lower travel costs, and coverage that holds up despite moving obstacles and soft terrain. The design aims at practical farming fleets rather than laboratory conditions.
arxiv-2509-06782:
Robots that learn goals from logged data alone get a physics-based nudge from Vittorio Giammarino and two co-authors in a 2025 reinforcement learning paper. Offline goal-based learning suits steering and movement, where live trial and error is costly or unsafe. Sparse data coverage and long time spans make the learning shaky.

The authors add a regularizer to value learning derived from the Eikonal equation, a formula describing how travel cost grows with distance. Unlike plain penalties used just to steady training, this one comes from continuous-time optimal control and pushes the learned value function to match true cost-to-go geometry. It plugs into current temporal-difference methods. Combined with a hierarchical implicit Q-learning algorithm, the regularized version improved results and reach, with the largest gains when separate data segments must be stitched together and in large steering tasks.
arxiv-2509-06982:
Xiaomeng Hu and 4 co-authors propose CARE, a way to keep language model output safe while it is being generated, in a 2025 paper. Models used in everyday products can produce harmful text partway through an answer. Older fixes applied during generation often made answers safer but much worse, or left quality intact at the cost of safety.

CARE combines three tools. A separate guard model watches the text as it forms and spots risky content early. A rollback step, backed by a stored buffer of recent tokens, can undo unsafe output before the user notices a problem. The model also writes short critiques of what it just produced, and those notes are fed back in to steer what comes next. Together, the parts aim for timely, precise action and a better balance between safety and quality.
arxiv-2509-07282:
Jeff Shen and 1 co-author introduce ALICE in 2025, a neural system that cracks substitution ciphers and shows its work. A substitution cipher swaps each letter for another, giving an astronomical number of possible keys. Solvers must pick the right mapping without ever seeing the key, which makes cryptograms a clean test of neural reasoning and generalization.

ALICE is a simple encoder-only Transformer, the attention-based architecture behind most modern AI models. It sets new records for both accuracy and speed on the task, and, surprisingly, it handles unseen ciphers after training on only about 1500 of them. A special decoding head exposes the letter mapping it has learned, so researchers can read it directly. Probing tests show early layers lean on letter frequency, like human solvers, while later layers build word shapes.
arxiv-2509-07382:
Some diffusion equations spread material so fast that standard math tools strain to describe them. Yi C. Huang and Xinhang Tong study ultrafast diffusion in a 2025 research paper. They prove that solutions settle toward equilibrium, the balanced end state, at an exponential rate. Their proof is deliberately simple.

The argument uses the Poincaré inequality directly, a classic tool linking a function's spread to its gradient. It avoids the optimal transport machinery used in an earlier one-dimensional result. That earlier work also had to exclude Gaussian weights. Huang and Tong remove both limits, extending exponential convergence to Gaussian measures in higher dimensions. A cleaner proof that covers more cases helps analysts apply the result to a wider family of equations.
arxiv-2509-07782:
Hugo Blanc and 2 co-authors speed up Gaussian-based rendering for novel view synthesis in a 2025 paper. Novel view synthesis rebuilds a scene so it can be viewed from new camera angles. RayGauss represents a scene with irregular elliptical basis functions. It renders by volume ray casting. It reaches top quality on synthetic and indoor scenes. Its cost blocks real-time use on real-world scenes, though.

RayGaussX adds several accelerations. It skips empty space, samples in an adaptive way, and improves ray coherence. Scale regularization cuts false intersections. A new densification rule improves the density layout in distant regions. Training runs 5 to 12 times faster. Rendering runs 50 to 80 times faster on real-world datasets. Visual quality improves by up to 0.56 dB in PSNR. Real-time, high-quality view synthesis brings interactive scene capture closer to practice.
arxiv-2509-08082:
Benjamin Cahen builds symbol rules for a group that mixes shifts with the Heisenberg group, in a solo 2025 maths paper. The Heisenberg group sits at the heart of quantum mechanics. The wider group adds plain shifts in space. Cahen builds its main representations on Fock space, a standard home for quantum states, by growing the known Heisenberg ones.

Two rules then turn operators into functions, called symbols. One is the Berezin rule. The other is the complex Weyl rule. Both are shown to respect the group's action. Cahen also gives plain formulas for the symbols of the group operators themselves. Symbol rules let analysts treat operators like functions. Extending them to richer groups widens that handy trade.
arxiv-2509-08182:
Faruk Alpay and 1 co-author give XML prompting a formal logic treatment in a 2025 paper on human-AI interaction. Tagging prompts with XML structure steers language models toward parseable, schema-following outputs in production systems. Practice has outrun theory: nobody had said precisely what a structured prompt protocol converges to, or when it stabilises.

XML trees form a complete lattice under a refinement order, and monotone prompt-to-prompt operators then have least fixed points that describe steady-state protocols. Under a task-aware distance on trees, convergence guarantees follow. Grammar-constrained decoding, fixed-point semantics, and interaction loops are unified in one account. Formal footing matters as prompts become interfaces between people, models, and software that must agree on meaning.
arxiv-2509-08782:
Mah Jan Dorazahi and 3 co-authors study safety and privacy views of Pakistani Facebook matrimony group users in a 2025 paper. Dating apps face censorship in Pakistan, so marriage groups act as an alternative space. Members often share photos, addresses, and phone numbers there.

Twenty-three interviews explore how users judge risk, trust, and personal sharing. Many share little information due to high concern, which then breeds mistrust between potential partners. Fears include fake profiles, theft of identity, harassment, and social judgment. Cultural norms shape much of this behavior. The authors suggest stronger checks by admins, clearer rules, and features that limit downloads.
arxiv-2509-08982:
Karim Slimani and 2 co-authors present iMatcher for point cloud registration in a 2025 paper. Registration aligns two three-dimensional point clouds of the same scene. Matching points correctly is the core step, and errors there spoil the whole alignment.

A local graph module first scores possible matches. A repositioning step refines scores using nearest neighbors in both directions. Paired features then pass through global consistency learning to give a matching probability for each point. Tests cover outdoor driving data, indoor scans, pose estimation, and partial matching. Inlier ratios reach the mid ninety percent range outdoors. The method is fully differentiable and beats prior approaches.
arxiv-2509-09182:
Poulami Paul and 1 co-author define new past entropy measures based on quantiles in a 2025 paper. Past entropy gauges doubt about how long a system has been idle or has lived in the past. A fractional form of this gauge came out in 2021, with a time based version.

The new measures use quantiles, cut points that split a distribution at set shares. Closed form results are worked out for many lifetime laws, some with no explicit distribution form. Bounds, monotone traits, and order rules are checked. A data based estimator is built and tested by simulation for bias and error. A test on the logistic map shows the gauge tracks shifts from order to chaos.
arxiv-2509-09682:
Maxim Zhelnin and 10 co-authors speed up training for sequential recommendation models in a 2025 paper aimed at shops with huge catalogues. Transformer recommenders must be retrained often as tastes shift, yet scoring every item with cross-entropy loss makes memory swell with catalogue size, batch size, and sequence length together. Sampling fewer negatives saves memory but dulls quality, while sampling more quickly overflows a typical industrial graphics card.

Their CCE approach reimplements the sampled loss so the graphics processor does far less wasted work. Training ran up to twice as fast while using notably less memory. The practical point is headroom: shops can afford larger batches and richer negative samples, the very settings their experiments show improve the model most.
arxiv-2509-09782:
Roshini Pulishetty and 10 co-authors tackle a deployment headache in 2025: with many language models on offer, which one should answer each question? Models differ wildly in price and skill, and sending every query to the biggest system wastes money. Their router uses a single cross-attention head to read a query and a candidate model together, learning their fit directly.

Tested on RouterBench, a broad public suite of model pools and domains, the router forecasts both answer quality and generation cost for each pairing. Quality gains over rival routers reached several percent, helped by an exponential reward rule that keeps the quality-versus-price balance steady across user tastes. The design stays light and carries well into new subject areas.
arxiv-2509-09982:
Stav Armoni-Friedmann and 2 co-authors grade explanation tools for AI in a 2025 paper where the right answer about importance can be computed exactly. Judging an explanation is usually guesswork, since nobody knows which inputs truly drove a prediction. Their test bed sidesteps that fog: models predict values of Boolean formulas, and actual causality supplies a formal yardstick for how much each variable should matter.

Leading black-box explainers are scored against that yardstick, and the authors add a new tool, B-ReX, grown from an earlier system called ReX. On a large suite of random ten-variable formulas B-ReX tracked the causal truth far more closely than its rivals, with a small average divergence. The study gives the explanation field a rare ground truth to argue from.
arxiv-2509-10082:
Weitao Tang and 7 co-authors present a deep learning system for fetal sleep staging in a 2025 paper. It is the first such system built for the fetal brain signal. Electrodes on the brains of unborn lambs record the signal. Humans find those patterns slow and hard to score. Yet fetal sleep states could flag poor brain growth. Such growth is linked to low oxygen or stunted growth before birth. Recordings came from twenty-four late-gestation sheep.

A compact network was first built for adult sleep scoring. The team retrained it across the species gap. A step that evens out the spectrum helped bridge that gap. Plain transfer did poorly on its own. Full fine-tuning with the spectrum step did best. It beat the baselines tried on accuracy. The authors call the system FetalSleepNet. They present it as a first step toward tracked fetal brain health.
arxiv-2509-10182:
How few arrows can a hard-to-color directed graph have? Tapas Das and three co-authors take up that question in this 2025 graph theory paper. They work with pushable coloring. In that scheme, an oriented graph may be recolored after flipping some of its vertices. A graph is pushably 3-critical when it resists such coloring, yet every smaller piece of it does not.

Apart from four exceptions, the authors prove a tight lower bound on the arcs of any such graph. They also list the critical examples that meet a related degree limit. One payoff is broad. Wide classes of sparse oriented graphs need a pushable coloring number of at most three. Planar graphs with enough girth are among them. Their results sharpen several earlier bounds. They also add a map into a small six-vertex target graph.
arxiv-2509-10382:
Shrinking a proof into the Fibonacci number system is Milan Rosko's solo 2025 contribution, a pairing function he calls carryless pairing. A pairing map squeezes two natural numbers into one code that can later be split again. Rosko's version places the Zeckendorf digits of the two inputs into separate bands, divided by a marker computed from the first input.

Because the bands never touch, the combined digit pattern has no consecutive ones, so every code is already in normal Zeckendorf form. Encoding and decoding then run on set operations over digit positions alone, with no multiplication, factoring, or digit shuffling. The map is one-to-one but does not hit every number, and membership in its image can be decided by the same machinery. The main theorems are machine-checked in the Rocq proof assistant.
arxiv-2509-10582:
Namrata Srivastava and 5 co-authors present LearnLens, a dashboard that helps teachers read open-ended student work, in this 2025 paper. In exploratory science classes, students explore simulations and answer in their own words, which makes their thinking hard for a teacher to survey in time to act on it.

LearnLens processes those open responses and shows sample answers, word clouds, charts, and AI-written summaries of class thinking. It was shaped by teacher input during training sessions and built into a middle school Earth science course. Interviews with teachers, reported in the paper, point to good usability and to real potential for adjusting lessons mid-stream as patterns in student understanding appear.
arxiv-2509-10782:
The same global teaching question, viewed through equality, occupies Ruiwei Xiao and six co-authors in this companion 2025 study. They interviewed thirty K-12 teachers in three countries: Taiwan, South Africa, and the United States. Their question is simple to state. Will generative AI in education narrow the gaps between students, or widen them?

Teachers actively frame their AI use as equality work. They ease pre-existing disadvantages where they can. They try not to create new ones. Yet systemic barriers keep defeating individual effort. Infrastructure is unequal. Professional training is thin. Social norms can be restrictive. In response, teachers articulate visions of what genuinely inclusive AI education would require. The study centers practitioners' experience and hopes, not platform promises. It maps the daily reality of classroom AI. It also maps the systemic changes teachers themselves say must come with it.
arxiv-2509-10882:
Yuping Wu and thirteen co-authors generate synthetic clinical notes that privacy law can live with, in this 2025 paper. Hospitals cannot train models freely on real patient narratives. Differentially private synthetic text promises an escape, with formal guarantees. The language of clinics has defeated most attempts, though, due to its detail and length.

Their method, Term2Note, splits content from form. It builds note content section by section, conditioned on medical terms. The terms and the notes are privatized under separate budgets. A private quality maximizer polishes the output. The notes matched real ones in their stats. Models trained on them did about as well as models trained on real data. Existing private generation baselines were beaten on both fidelity and utility, with no assumptions about label distributions.
arxiv-2509-11582: Hinnerk Schulz-Hildebrandt describes a new color illusion in a 2025 paper. Purple structures in the image look purple exactly where the viewer is looking, at the point of fixation. Identical purple structures around that point are instead perceived shifted toward blue. As viewing distance grows, more of the surrounding structures revert to appearing purple. The short report documents the effect and how it depends on both fixation and distance.
arxiv-2509-11682:
Sricheta Karmakar, Alexander A. Mushtukov, and Matthew Middleton model super-bright X-ray pulsars from varied angles. This 2025 astrophysics paper treats neutron stars feeding past a critical rate. Radiation blows outflows off the disc. The outflows form a cavity. Its walls reprocess the pulsar's X-rays before escape.

A simple geometric model and Monte Carlo runs do the work. Only reprocessed light from the walls is counted. The direct beam is set aside. The spectrum hardens or softens mainly with viewing angle. Hot wall zones near the disc plane swing in and out of sight. The soft flux barely changes with tilt. The pattern is a testable prediction. Highly variable ultraluminous sources may just be precessing toward and away from us.
arxiv-2509-12082:
Finding hydrogen galaxies inside a terabyte of simulated radio sky is the contest D. Cornu and ten co-authors recount winning in 2025. Their method, YOLO-CIANNA, adapts a well-known object detection network into three dimensions for the SKA Science Data Challenge 2.

The team reworked the regression-based detection formalism and built an end-to-end 3D convolutional backbone, then ran the full pipeline on the challenge's simulated spectral cubes. The updated method lifts the original winning MINERVA score by about a tenth. It reaches detection purity above ninety percent. It also confirms nearly half again as many sources as classical tools, with best-in-class measurement accuracy. It chews through the whole cube in half an hour on one graphics card. That speed is a hopeful sign for real SKA data.
arxiv-2509-12282:
Writing a good review paper eats weeks of expert time. Sasi Kiran Gaddipati and three co-authors present AIssistant in 2025. It is an open-source framework for joint work. Language model agents and human researchers draft reviews and perspective pieces together. The machine does not work alone.

Two multi-agent systems split the labor. One runs the research workflow. The other runs the writing workflow. Scholarly search tools are attached. Human checkpoints run throughout. Expert reviewers and model judges both scored the output. The strongest scores came from a top reasoning model paired with literature search. A user survey reported time savings of roughly two thirds.
arxiv-2509-12382:
Anu Pradhan and 3 co-authors ask whether a large language model can judge legal document recommendations in a 2025 paper. Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation systems, which search before answering, is a bottleneck, especially where quality has high stakes. Standard metrics miss nuanced quality in specialized domains like legal research.

The authors test LLM-as-a-judge for that setting, focusing on which agreement measures best capture alignment with human assessments and how to compare competing systems soundly. They find standard agreement statistics can mislead when score distributions are skewed, as they often are for AI systems. Other measures, including Gwet's AC2 and rank correlations, emerged as more robust for selecting a judge. Statistical comparison methods such as the Wilcoxon test are also discussed.
arxiv-2509-12482:
Millimeter-wave radar is cheap and tough. It is blind to darkness and fog. But its angular resolution is poor. That flaw is worst in the single-chip units used in cars and rooms. Tianshu Huang and six co-authors aim to give radar a foundation model in 2025. They train a general transformer on raw radar data, at unusual scale.

Their dataset holds about a million samples. The samples span twenty-nine hours. The model is the Generalizable Radar Transformer. It predicts three-dimensional occupancy and semantic labels. The quality is one once reserved for far sharper sensors. Raw data beats the usual compressed forms by a wide margin. That margin is worth ten times the data. Accuracy also grows steadily as data scales.
arxiv-2509-12982:
Erblin Isaku, Hassan Sartaj and six co-authors catch odd robot acts with a digital twin in 2025. Self-tuning robots in messy places must spot acts that fall outside trained norms. Twins that mirror the robot offer a way to flag such acts early.

Their ODiSAR twin uses a transformer to forecast robot states. Miss size and dropout spread are joined to score doubt. A reason layer links flags to the states that drove them. Twins for an office robot and a ship both flagged odd acts well. Top scores reach near the best mark, with clear reasons to guide self-tuning.
arxiv-2509-13182:
Ali Ghojavand, Cem Sevik and Milorad Milosevic tune in 2025 the electric output of atom-thin nickel halide sheets with strain. In rest form these sheets hold swirled spins that break symmetry. That break creates in-plane charge shift on its own.

Stretch in one or two axes shifts output via two paths. Tensor parts change directly, and spin wave pitch shifts too. Far-neighbor spin pairs matter much: under strain they can match or top near pairs. Total shift can thus be dialed with care. The dual path opens design for thin strain devices that mix magnetism and charge.
arxiv-2509-13282:
Ali Salamatian, Amirhossein Abaskohi and four co-authors align chart reading in vision-language models with human gaze in 2025. Charts carry much public data, yet models stare at wrong zones and err. Human gaze during chart tasks was not mapped at scale.

ChartGaze records eye tracks on chart reasoning tasks. Model focus diverges from human focus in set ways, which hurts scores and clarity. A gaze-guided fix aligns cross focus with fixations. Scores rise by up to a few points across models. Focus match also improves. Human gaze proves a cheap guide for chart models.
arxiv-2509-13582:
Sungwoo Jeong, Alex Townsend, and Christopher Wang prove convergence results in a 2025 numerical analysis paper. Their subject is pivoted Cholesky factorization. The method builds a low-rank approximation of a kernel matrix. It works by repeatedly picking the largest remaining diagonal entry. Such approximations power Gaussian process regression and fast solvers. But theory lagged practice for rough kernels.

For kernels that are merely Lipschitz continuous, the least smooth case, the error shrinks at a clean rate. The rate depends on how well the chosen points fill the domain. With one more derivative of smoothness on a convex domain, the rate improves further. Earlier proofs needed smoother or shift-invariant kernels. The new results close a real gap and link the method to greedy interpolation.
arxiv-2509-14082:
Valerii Serpiva and five co-authors train drones inside generated video in a 2025 robotics paper. FlightDiffusion is a diffusion model framework. It produces realistic first-person drone footage from a single starting frame. It also produces the action sequences that would generate the footage. A drone can learn navigation from synthetic experience instead of costly real flights.

The generated flight paths proved physically plausible and flyable. Position and orientation errors against reference paths were small. Policies trained on this synthetic data planned smoother routes. They stayed robust in simulation and adapted to unseen conditions. Tests found no significant gap between simulated and real flight success rates. That indicates strong sim-to-real transfer. The released datasets give other aerial robotics groups a reusable training resource.
arxiv-2509-14482:
Mark G Orr, writing alone in 2025, studies how people predict how long an event will last in real time, in a real world setting. Duration judgement guides planning, yet the psychology behind on the fly prediction is thin. The data context here offers unusually rich, linked judgements.

Provisional findings suggest the existing theoretical mechanism is incomplete in two ways. It cannot support adaptive responses when duration judgements depend on each other. It also cannot integrate fresh information that arrives mid event. Orr points to specific directions for future research that could repair both gaps. The contribution is deliberately theoretical: better mechanisms for how a running estimate updates as an event unfolds and new evidence lands.
arxiv-2509-14782:
G. Lacedelli and a large international team report two strikingly similar planet systems in a 2025 astronomy paper. Each system orbits a cool M dwarf star, TOI-521 and TOI-912, and each hosts a sub-Neptune, a planet type missing from our own Solar System. Both candidates were first spotted by the TESS space telescope and followed up under the THIRSTEE program.

The team combined light curves, ground-based photometry, and radial velocity data from three spectrographs to pin down orbits, masses, and radii. The two planets turn out nearly identical in size and mass, each about twice Earth's radius and about five times its mass. One system shows an extra non-transiting candidate on a wider orbit. The second planet appears to follow an unusually eccentric path, which makes the pair a useful test for formation theories.
arxiv-2509-14882:
Issa Sugiura, Shuhei Kurita, Yusuke Oda, and Ryuichiro Higashinaka present Llama-Mimi in a 2025 speech technology paper. Speech language models work on tokenized speech that must carry both meaning and sound quality. The Mimi audio codec produces several token levels at each time step, and earlier systems needed layered architectures to handle them.

Llama-Mimi instead flattens all token levels into one long sequence and models it with a single Transformer decoder, borrowing the simple design trend from text models. The flattened model beats a hierarchical baseline on most tasks in the team's evaluation. It also achieves the best acoustic consistency, meaning generated speech keeps a stable sound character. Models, code, and speech samples are released publicly for others to test.
arxiv-2509-15282:
G. Nashed derives fresh black hole solutions in f(R) gravity in a solo 2025 paper. In f(R) gravity, the curvature term of the classic action is swapped for a broad function. No cosmic constant is put in by hand at the start. Working with two space dims and one time dim, Nashed builds charged and uncharged cases under matched and unmatched metric forms.

By their dials, the cases act at large range like anti-de Sitter or de Sitter space. Next to the classic BTZ hole of standard gravity, these cases carry strong spacetime singularities shown by their curvature values. The f(R) functions at work turn out to be polynomials. Stability is argued two ways: a plus heat capacity for heat stability, and a plus second derivative of the function for soundness.
arxiv-2509-15482:
Vaibhav Mishra and William Lotter compare six large models built for pathology, the study of tissue under a microscope. Such models promise help on many medical tasks. Most past checks graded what the models can do, not how they store what they learn. The pair look inside, using tools first made for brain science.

They feed the models stained tissue patches from a cancer atlas and compare their inner patterns. Two models stand apart as the most distinct, while a third sits closest to the rest on average. Models trained the same way did not always match inside. All models leaned hard on which slide a patch came from, and stain fixes lowered that lean.
arxiv-2509-15982:
Some diffusion equations spread along curved directions set by vector fields, a setting tied to Carnot groups in geometry. Giulio Pecorella and Annalaura Rebucci study how smooth the solutions of such equations must be. They first build a basic solution kernel with a classic approximation method and pin down its main traits.

With mean value formulas in hand, they prove a maximum principle for these equations. They also prove a Harnack bound, which says values at nearby points cannot differ too wildly. The proofs lean on the natural distance that the vector fields define. Such bounds are core tools for this branch of analysis.
arxiv-2509-16082:
Starlight that passes through a planet's air can reveal what gases that air holds. Amélie Gressier and twenty-six co-authors report Webb telescope data for HAT-P-26 b, a warm planet about six times wider than Earth. From one transit, they detect water vapor and carbon dioxide with high trust, plus sulfur dioxide.

The sulfur gas links this cooler world to hotter giant planets where it was seen before, a sign of light-driven chemistry at work. Measures of carbon, oxygen, and sulfur point to air richer in heavy elements than the Sun's. The sulfur amount also tracks that richness across eleven giant planets.
arxiv-2509-16182:
Judging emotion from speech is hard when a model trained on one voice set is tested on another. Orchid Chetia Phukan and six co-authors ask whether benchmarks for this task have missed the best kind of pre-trained model. Since emotion is a side channel of speech, they argue models trained for such side traits should shine here.

Their tests compare models trained for language, for many tongues, for speaker identity, and for side traits. The side-trait model came out on top, as they had guessed. The result warns that past rankings may be skewed, and it guides fairer tests of emotion tools.
arxiv-2509-16382:
Sorting thyroid scan images into cancer classes leans on texture, since the gland sits amid dense, noisy anatomy. Saurabh Saini and three co-authors build a computer-aided system around a new texture descriptor that blends local cosine features with a binary pattern method known for noise resistance. A nonlinear classifier then makes the final call in two stages: first benign versus malignant, then finer risk grades.

On the only two public thyroid data sets, accuracy neared total in the first stage and stayed very high in the second. The staged design mirrors how clinicians grade risk, which eases adoption.
arxiv-2509-16482:
A line of robots that follows a leader like a conga line needs steady spacing without rigid timing. Pranav Tiwari and Soumyodipta Nath update each follower's target from the leader's travel distance, not from the clock, which avoids the sync drift of timed paths. The scheme assumes a shared position reference, as indoor tracking systems provide.

Simulations with wheeled and four-legged robots showed accurate path tracking and stable gaps between agents. The line settled into place within a fraction of a second in both cases. Simple spatial rules may scale better than strict schedules for indoor fleets.
arxiv-2509-16582:
Antonio Scardace and co-authors raise a privacy risk in brain scan AI in a 2025 paper. Models that make fake brain scans can help research. Yet they can also memorize real scans from training. That could leak private patient data. The team set out to detect when a model has memorized a scan.

They propose a new score that compares made scans with real ones in a deep way. In tests, it beat the best prior scores by a wide margin on a key measure. The team share their code and data in public. Hospitals and labs could use such a check before sharing a trained model. The work links model safety with patient trust.
arxiv-2509-16782:
Yassine Sekhmani and co-authors test a modified gravity model against black hole photos in a 2025 paper. Their model adds a two-form field that breaks a local symmetry on its own. It also adds a conformal electric sector. The team build spinning, charged hole solutions in this setting.

They compare predicted shadow sizes with telescope measures for two famous holes. One is in the galaxy M87, the other at our galaxy's center. Modest values of an effective charge fit the images well. Large values fit worse and worse. The bounds narrow where such gravity tweaks can hide, using real sky data.
arxiv-2509-16882:
Junzhuo Li, Bo Wang, Xiuze Zhou, and Xuming Hu adapt expert-mix models across domains without forgetting in a 2025 paper. Such models route each task to a few expert parts. Tuning them for many domains at once often erases past domains. Past fixes cost too much or needed a run per domain.

Their method gives experts dynamic, separate roles per domain. Tests cover six domains, from math and code to law. One unified model matched models tuned for a single domain each. Forgetting fell by a large share versus full tuning. Training also finished much faster. One model that keeps many skills could serve varied users at lower cost.
arxiv-2509-16982:
Wei Su reviews how space weather affects space-based gravitational wave detectors in a 2025 paper. Such detectors measure tiny shifts between free test masses with lasers. Plasma and magnetic fields between the Sun and Earth add noise to those measures. Laser light itself picks up noise as it travels. Magnetic fields can also push the test masses.

Su surveys studies of both noise types. A method called time-delay interferometry suppresses the laser noise. The review frames open questions for heliophysics raised by these detectors. Planned missions need this noise map to reach their design sensitivity for faint cosmic waves.
arxiv-2509-17182:
Sam Jacob Jacob, Markus Mrosek, Carsten Othmer, and Harald Köstler tackle slow car aerodynamics testing in a 2025 arXiv paper. Designers need drag values and full airflow fields to shape a car, but fine simulations are slow and costly. Stand-in models can help, yet they strain to reach high resolution in three dimensions with little training data.

Their recipe, called PMRT, trains the stand-in model on a shifting mix of low and high resolution data. Training starts with mostly coarse batches and leans toward fine ones over time. One model learned from five data sets made by distinct solvers, including real-world data. On a car benchmark, it matched known scores while training in a day on one high-end GPU, far cheaper than the fine-only route.
arxiv-2509-17582:
Vassil Atanassov, Wanming Yu, Siddhant Gangapurwala, James Wilson, and Ioannis Havoutis teach a four-legged robot a general skill layer. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that quadruped control is often learned end to end for one task at a time. Each new task then demands fresh reward design and tuning, a slow and fiddly loop that blocks scaling.

Their policy, GeCCo, sits below any planner and tracks arbitrary contact points the planner requests. Deep reinforcement learning trains that one low-level policy to hold contacts steady under dynamic uncertainty and planner mismatch. Planners of any breed, handcrafted, learned, or optimization-based, can then be composed and swapped with no retraining. The team tests one generalist policy across many gaits and manipulation tasks in a shared frame. The pitch is a stable border between planning and control for legged machines.
arxiv-2509-17782:
Nik Weaver sets out what it means for a quantum graph to have no triangles. His 2025 maths paper works with operator systems, which act as the quantum form of graphs. He gives two forms of the idea: plain triangle-free, and a stronger form.

Weaver works through cases that meet each form and cases that do not. For the strong form, he gives a full account of which systems count. Sharp lines like that help sort a new field. The paper lays base terms that later work on quantum graphs can build on.
arxiv-2509-17982:
Akilan Rajamani and 3 co-authors show that an even mix beats a weighted mix for quantum chemistry sums. Their 2025 letter deals with excited states of molecules, which drive how light changes matter. Quantum solvers for such states rest on a group form of the classic lowest-energy rule.

Two group styles are compared head to head. In the weighted style, states count by set weights. In the equi style, states count the same. Tests lead the team to back the equi style as the way to go. The claim rests on cost weighed against how close the sums land.
arxiv-2509-18182:
Isabelle Tingzon, Yoji Toriumi, and Caroline Gevaert use AI on satellite images to map roof traits in a small island state. Their 2025 study uses Saint Vincent and the Grenadines as its case. Roof pitch and material help guess storm, flood, and slide damage, but such data are scarce in many island states.

Two routes face off: broad geo base models with plain classifiers, and tuned deep nets. Extra training data from nearby island states is also tested for its lift. Top models scored high on both pitch and material sorts. The work pairs the tools with local skill building for island staff.
arxiv-2509-18282:
Jesse Zhang and 8 co-authors let a vision-language model point a robot hand where it counts. Their 2025 method, PEEK, deals with a snag in robot policy learning: one policy must learn where to look, what to do, and how to move, all at once. The first two parts can be offloaded, they argue.

A tuned vision model marks two things on the robot's view: the path the hand should take, and the zones that matter for the task. Those marks work with any policy form. An auto-tag pipe built training data across many robot sets. Real tests gave large zero-shot gains for both big and small policies.
arxiv-2509-18382:
Language models that think step by step get better as they think longer, but long thinking costs a lot of compute. Adarsha Balaji and four co-authors ask what those cost cuts do to safety. Their 2025 paper tests two ways to rein in reasoning models: capping how long they may reason, and shrinking the model with quantization.

One approach retrains the model with rewards tied to a set reasoning length. The other compresses model weights so more thinking fits in a fixed compute budget. The team then studies the trade-off between saved compute and safe behavior. Their setup frames safety as a thing that can be spent down when budgets shrink. The paper maps that trade-off rather than naming one best setting. Results guide labs that must run reasoning models on tight hardware.
arxiv-2509-18482:
Quantum computers are held back by gate errors, and some of that error comes from noisy control electronics. Yuanzheng Paul Tan and seven co-authors study that noise for superconducting qubits in this 2025 paper. Qubits are steered by shaped pulses, and flaws in those pulses lower how faithfully gates act. The team asks how gate quality depends on the signal-to-noise ratio of the controls.

They build a model of how control noise interacts with a qubit. From that model, they derive a method to characterize the noise in a qubit's control setup. The method gives labs a way to measure a hidden error source directly. Knowing which part of the error budget comes from electronics guides fixes. Cleaner control signals should raise gate fidelity on near-term devices. The work targets the noisy mid-scale quantum machines in use today.
arxiv-2509-18782:
Train delays do not fall in a tidy bell curve; long delays bunch far more than chance suggests. Tommaso Rondini, Gregorio Berselli, Mirko Degli Esposti, and Armando Bazzani trace that pattern to hierarchy in this 2025 paper. Their model layers agents on a multi-level graph with simple priority rules. High-speed trains outrank local ones when paths conflict.

Random wobbles in travel time, drawn from real data, feed the model. Local trains then show far more big delays than high-speed ones. A queue-based model, tuned on Italian data, reproduces the observed power-law exponent for local delays. Policy leaves fingerprints: refund thresholds cut the Italian curves at thirty and sixty minutes. German data, lacking such priority-change rules, shows no such cuts. Simple rules on a layered network, the authors argue, can breed complex delay statistics.
arxiv-2509-18882:
Proteins do their jobs by binding other molecules, and a binding at one site can change binding far away. Naoto Morikawa proposes a simple mathematical model of that coupling in this 2025 paper. The coupling, called allosteric regulation, has resisted a clean mechanism since its discovery in 1961. His model starts from electron delocalization, a core idea of quantum chemistry.

The geometry is a quantized form of differential geometry, built from discrete simplex shapes. In that frame, interactions are defined so that allosteric coupling follows directly from the definition. Morikawa stresses that no background in the source fields is required to follow the paper. He hopes the model gives mathematicians an entry point into chemistry and molecular biology. It is a proposal, offered as a starting point rather than a settled theory. Its test will be whether working scientists find it fruitful.
arxiv-2509-19082:
Alexey Nekrasov and four co-authors report how a small fix lifted a video segmentation model to third place in the LSVOS 2025 MeViS challenge. The base model, Sa2VA, finds and outlines objects in video from written descriptions, and it leads several benchmarks. The team found it was held back by a mismatch: steps used in training did not line up with steps used at test time.

Their improved version, Sa2VA-i, aligns training and inference and reuses the same model weights. Scores rose across four video benchmarks, with the largest gain on MeViS itself. Strikingly, a one-billion-parameter version with the fix matched the original model many times its size on that benchmark. The authors share code and updated models, arguing that plain implementation details can matter as much as new architectures.
arxiv-2509-19182:
Biomedical data portals are powerful but hard to search, and plain chatbots throw away the value of charts and filters. Devin Lange and nine co-authors build YAC, short for Yet Another Chatbot, to join both styles. A user types a request in natural language, and a team of cooperating AI agents turns it into structured output. That output renders as linked interactive charts with filters applied, which the user can then adjust directly with widgets.

The system also writes structured text that states the user's intent, flags the system's limits, and explains data points through live links. Domain experts tried the prototype in a user study, showing where it needs improvement. The authors reflect on the design choices behind mixing conversation with direct manipulation. Their aim is data discovery that keeps the strengths of visual exploration.
arxiv-2509-19282:
Ask an image generator to follow a layout of boxes, and it copes until the boxes overlap heavily. Bingnan Li and nine co-authors study that failure. Dense overlaps hurt in two ways: large shared regions, and overlapping objects that look nearly alike. Their analysis shows existing benchmarks mostly contain easy, low-overlap layouts, so models look better than they are. They define a score that measures how complex a layout's overlaps are.

Their new benchmark, OverLayBench, balances cases across overlap levels with high-quality annotations. Scores on it expose how sharply quality drops as overlap grows. As a first step toward a fix, the team fine-tunes a model on a curated dataset of amodal masks, which show each object's full shape even where hidden. The work lays groundwork for layout-following generators that survive realistic, crowded scenes.
arxiv-2509-19982:
Two cosmic mysteries, dark matter and the excess of matter over antimatter, might share one mechanism. Subhojit Roy revisits a Higgs-portal model with a complex singlet that splits into two nearly equal states. The pair annihilate together to set today's dark matter amount. A feeble direct coupling lets the survivor dodge detection experiments.

The same setup supports a strong first-order electroweak phase transition. Present-day annihilation into Higgs pairs could explain the galactic center gamma-ray excess. Roy adds a CP-violating top quark operator, and the framework then also generates the baryon asymmetry through electroweak baryogenesis. Two-step cosmological history completes the story. One minimal model addressing three puzzles at once is worth the scrutiny this paper gives it.
arxiv-2509-20082:
Maksim Surov wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on robot control. It deals with robots that have fewer controls than motions, called underactuated robots. Such robots often need to repeat a periodic motion, like a walking cycle. The paper tackles two goals at once: keeping that motion stable and keeping its timing in sync.

The approach builds on transverse linearization, a classic way to study motion near a repeating path. Surov extends it to track timing drift as part of the dynamics. He then stabilizes the system with a mix of time-varying optimal control and sliding-mode control. Both central and shared control setups were tested in hardware. The experiments used a group of six Butterfly robots. Results confirm the method works on real machines, not only in theory.
arxiv-2509-20382:
A heartbeat can serve as a password, and Dilli Hang Rai and Sabin Kafley test that idea under attack in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their authentication model pairs a lightweight image network with a recurrent unit, sized for wearable devices. Heartbeat biometrics promise security that is hard to copy. Spoofing and privacy risks, though, shadow the approach.

The team simulated wearable conditions with added noise and custom preprocessing. Four public heartbeat datasets were used, and accuracy stayed high across all of them. Federated training, which keeps raw data on device, was part of the evaluation. Adversarial examples told a darker story: crafted attacks crashed accuracy dramatically. The paper argues that secure deployment needs both federated methods and far more diverse wearable datasets.
arxiv-2509-20682:
Data augmentation helps speech deepfake detectors handle new voices and attacks, but it can also disturb training. Duc-Tuan Truong and five co-authors study that side effect in a 2025 paper accepted for ICASSP 2026. The problem is gradient misalignment between original and altered speech.

When the two versions push the model in conflicting directions, training can settle in a worse spot. The authors build a dual-path framework that runs each utterance in original and augmented form side by side. It then compares the two gradient directions and aligns them to cut conflicts. Experiments reported in the paper show more robust detection. The work matters as fake speech grows harder to catch.
arxiv-2509-20882:
