Large language models can learn a task from a few examples placed in the prompt, a trick called in-context learning. Huaze Tang, Tianren Peng, and Shao-lun Huang study one structured version of that trick in a 2025 theory paper. Their subject is concept-based in-context learning.

In this approach, demonstrations are organized around explicit concepts. The authors build theory explaining why and when the method predicts query labels well from only a few demonstrations. Their analysis quantifies how much knowledge the model can actually draw from the prompt. It also yields a similarity measure between demonstrations and the query. That measure offers practical guidance for choosing examples. The paper adds to the still-thin theoretical understanding of in-context learning.
arxiv-2509-21182:
Franco Ferrari and 2 co-authors wrote a maths physics paper in 2025 on Liouville theory. The work deals with a known exact formula called the DOZZ formula. It gives a three point value used in two dimensional field theory. The authors study the case where a small scale value tends toward zero.

They show that the exact formula splits into a front factor and a series of added terms. Each added term is a balanced polynomial in three input values. They give closed forms for the first terms in the series. The paper then links these terms to loop level work in celestial holography, a field that maps scattering to a sky sphere.
arxiv-2509-21282:
Clipping, the standard brake on reinforcement learning updates for language models, also throws away useful signal. The 2025 paper is by Madeleine Dwyer and 2 co-authors. Methods like PPO and GRPO clip update ratios to keep training stable. Clipping throws away information and breaks smooth gradients. It can also block the search for better policies. The authors propose a softer way to limit updates.

Their method, PSPO, smooths current policy probabilities toward the old policy. It then computes importance ratios from the smoothed values. That creates a soft trust region, a zone where updates stay safe but gradients survive. The smoothing is a simple linear blend, not a sigmoid curve. Tests on maths reasoning beat clipping and sigmoid based rivals when refining models with prior domain knowledge.
arxiv-2509-21482:
Reasoning models throw away rich information when they sample one token at a time. Adit Jain and Brendan Rappazzo study mixture of token generation in a 2025 paper. Their setting is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Group relative methods sample several completions and score them against each other. Each step still picks discrete tokens, discarding the full probability distribution.

Preserving distributional information helped in non reinforcement settings. The authors ask whether it can widen the reasoning search space here. They present a unified framework that generalizes existing mixture of token approaches. Training time and generation time variants are included. The framework aims to use the candidate token distribution rather than constrain reasoning to single sampled tokens at each step.
arxiv-2509-21582:
Energy can jump resonantly between a Rydberg atom and a polar molecule when their transitions match. J. Zou and 4 co-authors report observing that transfer in a 2025 paper. Helium Rydberg levels and ammonia inversion transitions form the pair. Collisions happen at very low temperature. The exchange is a monopole dipole reaction that needs spatial overlap of the electron and molecular wavefunctions.

Calculations including the charge dipole interaction explain the observations quantitatively. Total parity is conserved through mixing of collisional angular momentum in the complex. The hybrid system joins neutral atoms and polar molecules in one platform. Charge dipole mediated energy exchange expands the toolbox for quantum science with such hybrids. The experiment validates the underlying interaction picture.
arxiv-2509-21682:
Man made aperture imaging sharpens pictures by combining views, but speckle noise blocks the macroscale version. Janith Senanayaka and Christopher Metzler tackle light based aperture imaging in a 2025 paper. Fourier ptychography brought high resolution, wide field imaging to microscopy. Long range use is far harder. The authors first prove a fundamental limit for stepwise readings.

Imaging fully diffuse scenes is impossible when each stepwise reading suffers independent speckle, they show. A snapshot method with aperture phase synchronization overcomes that limit. One capture replaces the vulnerable sequence. Model runs further show speckle can be exploited to recover missing spatial frequency information. Boiling speckle, usually a nuisance, becomes a resource in their scheme.
arxiv-2509-21882:
Fang Wu and twenty-three co-authors question how well the gains of a popular training method have been measured. The method is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, used to improve language models on math, code, and similar tasks with clear right answers. This 2025 position paper argues that many headline gains mix real improvement with three confounds. The confounds are uneven computing budgets, scoring that turns careful silence into confident guesses, and test data the model has already seen.

The authors rerun comparisons with matched budgets and probe for memorized test material. Several cited gaps shrink a lot, or vanish, once budgets, prompts, and data versions line up. They stress the method still works in checkable domains. What they ask for is a minimum standard: matched-budget curves with spread, tracking of calibration and refusals, a stress test when models judge the answers, and a contamination screen.
arxiv-2509-22482:
Septimus Boshoff, Sebastian Peitz, and Stefan Klus merge two frameworks for learning how systems evolve. The Koopman operator turns a nonlinear system into a linear one on a richer space. Kernel methods exploit that view but scale poorly and need costly tuning. The team brings in Gaussian process methods inside kernel Hilbert spaces to ease both pains.

Their Bayesian transfer operators cut computing demands and resist sensor noise better. They also ease the tuning of parameters and the learning of good dictionaries of functions. The core move unifies Gaussian process regression with dynamic mode decomposition. That union gives a more practical route to data-driven models of dynamics.
arxiv-2509-22782:
Jianyu Gong and 3 co-authors build a bootstrap framework for energy correlators in gauge theories. Energy correlators measure how energy flows in a collision and are key observables in super Yang-Mills theory and in QCD. Bootstrapping means fixing an analytic answer from consistency rules rather than computing diagrams head-on. Their method mixes spherical contour techniques, physical demands like pole cancellations, and data from singular limits.

They derive leading-order three-point correlators for equal and unequal energy weights. The unequal case feeds projected multi-point correlators. A lattice-reduction regression trick can bypass explicit singular-limit data. The work brings amplitude-style bootstrap tools to realistic QCD event shapes, opening precision tests.
arxiv-2509-22982:
David M Kahn and 3 co-authors speed up automatic bounds on how much a program costs to run. The method, called AARA, uses types to derive cost bounds. It leans on cost-free types to compose those bounds. Finding such types with the current algorithm is slow, since each one can trigger more searches. The old route also only fits polynomial bounds.

Their fix encodes all cost-free types of a function as one linear map. Matrix inequalities then carry the reasoning, and standard solvers check them fast. A prototype inferred the maps far faster than the old algorithm. The approach also covers non-polynomial bounds like exponential ones.
arxiv-2509-23282:
Long jumps make Lévy flights hard to cage, since one leap can clear the boundary whole. Barnali Pyne and Kiran M Kolwankar solve that problem on a half-line domain. A fractional differential equation governs the symmetric flights. At zero, the boundary can reflect or absorb. The pair build both conditions into the equation for the first time.

They solve it analytically for the probability densities. Monte Carlo simulations check the math. For the reflecting case, theory and simulation agree perfectly. For the absorbing case, they agree at large positions. The result closes a long-open modeling gap.
arxiv-2509-23482:
AI models can treat places unevenly, yet geographic bias has drawn far less study than social bias. Zhangyu Wang and 10 co-authors build GeoBS, a scoring framework grounded in information theory. Older measures fit single models or hide where the bias sits on the map. GeoBS is meant to work for any model and to show the spatial pattern itself.

Three new scores in the framework track how bias changes with map scale, distance, and direction. Tests span three tasks, eight data sets, and eight models. Both task-built GeoAI models and general foundation models showed forms of geographic bias. The authors aim to make spatial fairness part of how AI systems are designed and checked.
arxiv-2509-23682:
Regional aircraft need cleaner power that can keep up with back-to-back flights, where slow battery charging fails. Harshal Kaushik and 6 co-authors design a hybrid powertrain that mixes three sources. A hydrogen fuel cell supplies steady main power. A lithium-ion battery smooths sudden demand spikes. An aluminum-air battery waits as a high-energy emergency backup for critical moments.

A mixed-integer optimization model sizes the parts and schedules power among them. The team tests the design on real power demand data from a Cessna 208 across several scenarios, with stress on emergencies. Results support the layout as feasible, efficient, and safer for regional flying.
arxiv-2509-23782:
A language model can know the right answer and still pick the wrong option on a multiple-choice test. Yoonah Park and 2 co-authors measure and then mend that knowledge-prediction gap. Their analysis of hidden states first sizes the gap across models and data sets. Next, a geometric view finds separate subspaces in the residual stream for what the model knows and what it predicts.

Their fix, KAPPA, is a light inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces. It reduced the gap across varied multiple-choice benchmarks and models, and carried over to free-form settings. The authors present the gap as an interpretable, geometric failure, not random noise.
arxiv-2509-23882:
Open-weight reasoning models invite a special kind of security audit: their thought process is on display. Shuyi Lin and 5 co-authors summarize an extensive evaluation of GPT-OSS-20B under adversarial conditions. Using a systematic tool called the Jailbreak Oracle, they probe how the model behaves when its chain of thought and Harmony prompt format are pushed. Several named failure modes emerge from the tests.

The catalog includes quant fever, reasoning blackholes, and Schrodinger's compliance, among others. Experiments show how each behavior can be exploited, with severe consequences claimed by the authors. The paper reads as a warning list for deployers of open reasoning models.
arxiv-2509-24082: A. Yu. Zakharov sets out the basic principles for a microscopic grounding of thermodynamics inside relativistic quantum theory. The title frames the work as a field-theoretical form of the molecular dynamics method for condensed matter physics. In this framing, heat laws are not taken as given at the large scale. They are to rest on the quantum rules that govern matter at the small scale, with relativity built into the theory from the start.
arxiv-2509-24382:
Instructional videos are long and messy, with stretches of background and repeated moves that are not real steps. Soumyadeep Chandra and Kaushik Roy built REMAP, an unsupervised framework that learns procedures from such videos. Its core is a partial optimal transport method that lets uninformative frames stay unmatched instead of forcing every frame into a step.

The method models meaning and time order together, with smoothness rules that block degenerate alignments and cut background interference. On egocentric and third-person benchmarks, REMAP beat leading methods by clear margins in step scores. The gains were largest on one cross-task benchmark, where partial alignment mattered most.
arxiv-2509-24482:
Music models learn genre, but they may quietly learn who is singing as well. Roman B Gebhardt and 2 co-authors use Concept Activation Vectors to probe whether singer traits such as gender and language leak into genre representations. They test four leading music models on a data set balanced to control for genre confounds.

Each model showed its own significant biases, in line with disparities reported in music research and sociology. The team then proposes a fix that edits the concept vectors after training. That manipulation cut the measured biases in their tests. Concept-based tools, they argue, can both diagnose and treat representational bias in music models.
arxiv-2509-24582:
Approximating many-variable functions fast, without knowing their smoothness in advance, is the problem Zexin Pan and 2 co-authors take on. They study functions in a weighted Korobov space and build a universal median lattice algorithm. An earlier version needed the smoothness and weights up front to choose its index set; the new one needs no such prior information at all.

Each coefficient is estimated by the median of approximations from randomly shifted lattice rules. The price is a slight loss in the tractability property. In return, the error comes arbitrarily close to the optimal rate per function evaluation, for any smoothness and downward-closed weights. Numerical tests support the claim.
arxiv-2510-00282:
G. Miloshevich and five colleagues published this 2025 paper on using neural networks inside plasma simulations. Earth's magnetosheath is a turbulent plasma region where energy channels decide how the solar wind heats up. Fluid models need a closure rule for electron pressure, and simple local rules miss nonlocal effects. The authors parametrize that closure with a fully convolutional neural network instead.

The network learned from detailed particle-in-cell simulations run with fewer particles per cell. It then generalized to a costlier run with many more particles, a key practical test. The learned equation of state beat multilayer perceptron and double-adiabatic closures by wide margins. It reproduced the spatial pattern and averages of pressure-strain interaction, a central energy channel. Fine small-scale features, mostly in off-diagonal pressure parts, were still missed. More training data steadily improved those features in the authors' checks.
arxiv-2510-00382:
Marawan Gamal Abdel Hameed and Guillaume Rabusseau published this 2025 paper on learning probabilistic tensor networks efficiently. Tensor networks compress huge tensors into small shared pieces, and their probabilistic versions allow exact marginal calculations. Training them, though, has been slow, tied to awkward algorithms, or numerically unstable. The authors propose a simpler learning approach built for stability.

Their method computes the training loss with logarithmic scale factors, keeping numbers in a safe range. It plugs directly into standard automatic differentiation pipelines, unlike the older DMRG-based route. On MNIST generative modeling, training ran about ten times faster than before. Density estimation tests handled ten times more variables than previous approaches managed. Code is public, and the authors argue the changes make these models practical for real-world experimentation at last.
arxiv-2510-00582:
Sangmin Lee and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on marking where each language is spoken inside mixed speech. People code-switch mid-sentence, and diarization must label every stretch by language. Prior systems handled few languages and stumbled on scarce training data. Their model, SAGE-LD, targets an unbounded span of languages in one end-to-end framework.

Learnable queries drive iterative decoding on top of multilingual feature extraction. Pretraining on simulated code-switching audio supplies the practice data reality lacks. The simulations mix languages artificially, teaching boundaries before real data fine-tunes them. Benchmarks across several diarization suites put the model at the front of the field. Relative improvements over previous methods ranged from about twenty-three to fifty-two percent. Results held across recording environments and language pairs, the authors report. They frame the system as groundwork for broader code-switching speech technology.
arxiv-2510-00882:
Kenia, Li, Srivastava, and Thakoor present AI-CNet3D in this paper, published in the journal MELBA in 2025, on medical image analysis. Glaucoma damages the optic nerve and causes irreversible blindness when missed, and optical coherence tomography gives doctors detailed 3D scans of the eye. Clinicians often compress those volumes into flat 2D reports, which throws away structural detail. The model instead reads the full volume directly.

A 3D convolutional network with cross-attention compares the upper and lower halves of the retina and links the optic nerve head with the macula, mirroring known anatomy. A consistency fine-tuning step aligns its attention maps with standard saliency maps for interpretability. On two large datasets it beat leading attention and convolutional models on every key metric. It also used about one hundred times fewer parameters than rival attention designs.
arxiv-2510-01082:
Tamiti, Joshi, Hasan, and Barua, at George Mason University, show that building pressure sensors can eavesdrop on speech, in this 2025 arXiv paper on security. Heating and cooling systems use pressure sensors sampled hundreds of times per second, mounted in walls near occupants. Speech pressure overlaps the sensors' range, so the readings encode conversation. Earlier side channels recovered only digits or hot words, with poor intelligibility.

Their system, HVAC-EAR, reconstructs intelligible speech from pressure data sampled as low as five hundred hertz. A complex-valued conformer with a unified attention block captures phoneme dependencies across the aliased signal. The model rebuilds magnitude and phase of the missing frequencies while suppressing transient duct noise. Evaluations on HVAC deployments recovered audio up to eight kilohertz with intelligibility. The attack works only within a metre and a half, but it exposes an unexpected privacy hole in buildings.
arxiv-2510-01282:
Chu and co-authors keep camera-based pulse measurement accurate while the world around the camera keeps changing. Remote photoplethysmography reads blood flow from facial video, but lighting and weather shifts corrupt models adapted naively. Their framework, PhysRAP, adapts continually at test time without forgetting physiology.

Before adapting, the system judges its own uncertainty and shields the knowledge that identifies real pulse signals. Proactive preparation for likely future domains guards against overfitting the present one. The design answers the catastrophic forgetting that plagues self-training on drifting video. Deployment in dynamic environments is the scenario the whole framework serves. Remembering, adapting, and preempting name the framework's three commitments. Erroneous gradients accumulate silently in naive self-training loops. Uncertainty evaluation precedes every adaptation step in the design. Future domains are anticipated rather than merely survived. Contact-free monitoring wins when sensors cannot touch patients.
arxiv-2510-01382:
Varona and co-authors argue that the shapes scholars draw to explain theories quietly shape the theories themselves. Visualization research leans on a small wardrobe of standard figures, planes, flows, and trees. Each familiar shape affords some explanations and quietly forbids others.

Icebergs, horseshoes, Möbius strips, and even sandwiches enter the authors' speculative wardrobe. What changes when hidden depth, return, or one-sidedness becomes the picture's logic gets explored concretely. Figure-making emerges as generative theorizing, not decoration after the fact. The closing provocation is literal: theory is shapes, and choosing them is scholarly work. Cartesian planes and flowcharts are the incumbents being questioned. An iceberg figure literally illustrates submerged theoretical depth. Affordances, a design concept, do the analytical work throughout. Toronto, Princeton, and Northwestern host the four authors. Playfulness here is method, not ornament. Figures think alongside their makers.
arxiv-2510-01582:
Chitty-Venkata and Emani release a large public dataset that teaches vision-language models to show their reasoning. Models that answer image questions silently give users no way to audit the thinking. The dataset pairs a quarter-million ImageNet images with explicit step-by-step reasoning and final answers.

Two strong reasoning models generated the material, giving each image two thinking-and-answer pairs. The scale makes it, by the authors' account, the largest public resource of its kind. Benchmarks accompany the release for comparing future models. Training on visible reasoning should yield systems that are both stronger and easier to inspect. Human-written traces would cost far more at this scale. Two independent traces per image let researchers compare reasoning styles. Public release invites replication and criticism alike. Reasoning visibility also helps teachers show how answers form. Scale plus openness is the contribution. Benchmarks ship with the data.
arxiv-2510-01682:
Maryenko and nine co-authors report an unusual effect in this 2025 condensed matter paper. They studied the boundary between two oxides, lanthanum titanate and potassium tantalate. That interface can carry electric current without resistance, becoming a superconductor. A magnetic field normally kills superconductivity, yet here the state vanishes and then returns as the field grows stronger.

The returning phase appeared across a wide range of charge densities at the interface. Better still, the density could be tuned in place with electrostatic gating. The authors link the effect to strong spin-orbit coupling in the material. A field-driven change in the Fermi surface also plays a central role. Their result is only the second clear case of this behavior in a two-dimensional system, after moire graphene.
arxiv-2510-01782:
Pan and seven co-authors ask whether language models know when to stay silent in this 2025 paper. A model that answers beyond its knowledge invents facts, so refusing unknown questions matters for reliability. Existing scores measure that refusal skill poorly, because they bend with each model's general tendency to refuse. The authors propose a cleaner measure called the Refusal Index.

The index is a rank correlation between a model's refusal probability and its error probability. A light two-pass procedure estimates it from two ordinary evaluation runs. Experiments covered sixteen models across five factual datasets. The index stayed stable across different refusal rates and overall accuracy levels. It also ranked models consistently from test to test. Their analysis highlights an overlooked gap in factuality research. Strong accuracy can coexist with refusal behavior that fails to track what the model truly knows.
arxiv-2510-01882:
Rollano and nine co-authors hunt a source of measurement error in sensitive sky detectors in this 2025 paper. Kinetic inductance detectors measure faint millimeter waves for astronomy, including cosmic microwave background studies. For this work, a detector must ignore light polarized the wrong way. That leakage across polarizations limits how faithful the readings can be.

The team suspected the interdigitated capacitor inside the standard lumped-element design. Parasitic currents there might respond to the unwanted polarization directly. They compared the standard design with a quasi-lumped resonator without any capacitor. Both designs behaved alike in ordinary optical response during cryogenic tests. The new design, however, rejected the wrong signal far better on average. The result confirms the capacitor's role in the leakage and offers cleaner detectors for polarimetry.
arxiv-2510-02282:
Park and co-authors built VidGuard-R1, a detector that flags videos made by artificial intelligence. Their 2025 paper also asks the detector to explain each verdict. Fake videos can spread false claims and harm reputations. A bare yes or no gives regulators little to act on. The team fine-tuned a multimodal language model with reinforcement learning. Two reward models guided training toward timing flaws and generation quirks. Their training set held about one hundred forty thousand real and fake clips.

The finished detector scored eighty five percent accuracy on its own hard test set. It reached ninety seven percent on the GenVidBench set. It also reached ninety six percent on the GenVideo set. Those marks beat earlier detectors by wide margins. Each verdict comes with readable reasoning. That pairing of accuracy and explanation is the main advance.
arxiv-2510-02382:
Xie and co-authors cut the compute cost of separating mixed sounds in echoing rooms. Their 2025 signal processing paper improves a method called CTF-MNMF. The method unmixes several microphone recordings into separate sources. It handles strong echoes by modeling delayed copies across frames. Its standard update rule inverts a matrix for every source. That step is slow and can turn numerically unstable. The team swaps in iterative source steering instead. Steering updates avoid matrix inversion entirely. Separation filters then adjust through cheaper, stable steps.

Experiments compared the new variant against the original. Sound separation quality matched or beat the older method. Runtime dropped by about forty percent in their tests. Stability held up across different starting points. Echo heavy rooms benefited the most from the change. Hearing aids and meeting devices need exactly this thrift. Faster unmixing brings such tools closer to real time.
arxiv-2510-02682:
Wan and Jamieson carry low latency congestion signals across cellular networks for the first time. Their 2025 networking paper presents a design called L4Span. Interactive apps need queues that stay empty. Wired providers already roll out queue signaling. Cellular radio networks form the other last mile for many users. Those networks lag behind the wired efforts. L4Span hides the radio queue behind one simple interface. Servers then see the queue state end to end. The system predicts queue occupancy at millisecond scales. It marks packets for low latency and classic flows.

The design asks little change from the radio side. It stays compliant with 5G and open RAN standards. A prototype ran on open source radio software. Both flow types improved across applications in tests. Deployment can proceed piece by piece. Gamers and callers feel last mile lag most. Cellular links deserve the same latency care as fiber.
arxiv-2510-03682:
Zhang, Nie, and Tang present a 2025 arXiv paper recasting neural network training with polynomial activation functions as a polynomial optimization problem. When activations are polynomials with learnable coefficients, the whole network map is a polynomial. Training then becomes one big polynomial optimization, which the Moment SOS hierarchy can attack globally. That contrasts with gradient descent, which settles for stationary points that may be far from optimal. The authors use the hierarchy to recover network parameters directly.

Numerical experiments show the method recovering optimal parameters accurately. The recovery stayed robust when the data carried noise. Global guarantees are rare in deep learning, where training is usually a leap of faith. Polynomial activations suit tasks like image generation and face detection, where this machinery could certify results. The approach will not replace gradient training for giant models. It offers something different: small networks whose training answers come with proofs attached.
arxiv-2510-03882:
Parvizi and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on whether quantum gravity can rescue two struggling models of cosmic inflation. Inflation describes a burst of rapid expansion in the early universe. Two popular driving potentials, one from supersymmetry and one exponential in shape, clash with recent telescope data in their classical form. The authors test them inside loop quantum cosmology, which adds inverse volume corrections.

The corrections shift one key prediction, the spectral index, downward in a helpful direction. With corrections included, both models land inside the region favored by new data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. The exponential model revives only when its main parameter stays small enough. The supersymmetry model allows a broad range of correction settings. Without the quantum corrections, both models fall outside the favored region entirely. The study shows how quantum gravity could change which inflation models survive observation.
arxiv-2510-04082:
Guo, Zhang, and Zheng present this 2025 arXiv paper in harmonic analysis on averaging operators tied to a magnetic Schrödinger operator. The operator describes a quantum particle in a scaling-critical magnetic field on the plane. Its Bochner-Riesz means of negative order smooth out spectral expansions, and analysts ask for which exponent pairs they stay bounded. Sharp answers delineate exactly where the theory holds and fails.

The authors determine the full set of exponent pairs for which boundedness holds. In the plane of exponents, the boundedness region forms a pentagon depending on the order parameter. The result extends an earlier uniform resolvent estimate by Fanelli, Zhang, and Zheng. Sharp boundedness regions for such operators feed into estimates for magnetic Schrödinger equations.
arxiv-2510-04182:
Ye, Liang, and Shan present this 2025 arXiv paper on improving a language model's reasoning at test time without touching its weights. Latent reasoning replaces written chain-of-thought with hidden thought vectors, gaining efficiency but turning brittle on hard, unfamiliar problems. Trained latent modules collapse almost completely on competition-level benchmarks. The authors instead optimize the thought vectors themselves, separately for each problem.

Their framework, Latent Thought Policy Optimization, treats the latent thoughts as dynamic parameters during inference. An online policy gradient method refines them using a reward computed from the frozen model's own output confidence. Across five reasoning benchmarks, the method matched or beat strong baselines on standard tasks. On the highly challenging AIME problems, where other latent methods fell to near-zero accuracy, it delivered substantial improvements. Test-time latent optimization offers a practical route to sturdier reasoning from existing models.
arxiv-2510-04582:
James Chok and Domenic Petzinna wrote this 2025 paper on sampling and optimizing inside a polyhedron. Many tasks ask for points that obey a set of linear limits, which carve out a faceted region. Standard random walk methods bounce off walls or need projections at the boundary. The authors built a diffusion that feels the walls through a log barrier. The barrier grows near each face and bends both the drift and the noise of the walk.

In continuous time, they prove the walk never leaves the region when it starts inside. Feasibility thus holds by construction. For real computation, they discretize the walk and add a Metropolis correction that targets the law. When the goal function is flat, the method reduces to a known Dikin random walk. Tests on stretched Gaussian targets showed clean convergence diagnostics. On a two peak target, the walk crossed between wells more often than rivals.
arxiv-2510-04682:
Chanjoo Jung and Jaehyung Kim wrote this 2025 paper on moving an adapter from one language model to another. LoRA adapters tune models cheaply, but each adapter fits only the model it was trained on. New base models arrive, so teams retrain adapters. Their method, TiTok, transplants an adapter without new training data from users. It watches how the source model answers with and without its adapter.

The difference between those two runs highlights the tokens that carry the task skill. TiTok uses that contrast to filter synthetic examples down to the informative ones. A target model then learns from the filtered set and gains the adapter skill. No discriminator model is needed, unlike a recent rival approach. Across three benchmarks and several transfer settings, TiTok beat the baselines. Average gains ran from four to eight points in their reports. The method keeps adapter investments useful as base models turn over.
arxiv-2510-04982:
Aakash Ahmad and five co-authors survey how to build quantum computing services in this 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum Computing as a Service lets customers rent time on quantum hardware over the internet. Providers such as Amazon Braket and IBM Quantum already sell such access. Building these services well takes software engineering methods that barely exist yet.

The authors ran a systematic mapping study and kept 41 peer-reviewed papers as evidence. From them, they map a four-phase life cycle for developing quantum services. They also catalog the special requirements, modeling notations, patterns, and platforms the field uses. These pieces are assembled into a layered reference architecture. Future work, they note, points toward low-code tools and AI help in the process.
arxiv-2510-05082:
Kabir Tomer and Mark Zhandry probe what a proof of quantumness really costs in this 2025 arXiv paper. In such a proof, a quantum device convinces a classical checker that it is genuinely quantum. A trivial version just assumes a problem that is hard classically and easy quantumly. Researchers want versions grounded in quantum hardness assumptions instead.

The authors prove lower bounds on the hardness any nontrivial proof requires. Different variants demand different kinds of cryptographic hardness, they show. One result ties four-message public-coin proofs, under black-box reductions, to a weak form of public-key quantum money. Another blocks security proofs for three-message interactive proofs from quantum-hard assumptions alone. The bounds help explain why lattice-based publicly verifiable proofs have been so elusive.
arxiv-2510-05182:
Hajg Jasa and four co-authors compare ways to align two sets of points in this 2025 arXiv paper. Alignment, or Procrustes, problems appear in image registration, graph matching, and network testing. The goal is to rotate one data matrix onto another as closely as possible. Which distance norm you minimize changes the problem completely.

The classical Frobenius norm has a closed-form solution but may fit the task poorly. Spectral and robust norms suit many applications better, yet they demand expensive nonsmooth optimization. The authors show the cheap Frobenius solution often replaces those costly minimizers safely. Case studies run from low-dimensional alignments to hypothesis tests on random networks. In their network tests, the robust-norm statistic gave the strongest detection power.
arxiv-2510-05482:
Thompson and colleagues build a faster way to simulate how molecules move. Molecular dynamics tracks atoms over time and guides drug design and materials research. Exact quantum calculations are accurate but very slow, which limits long simulations. Their 2025 model, ATOM, learns the motion from data instead of solving quantum forces.

ATOM is a transformer trained in advance on a new dataset called TG80. That dataset holds long motion records for eighty different compounds. The model predicts many future states at once instead of stepping one by one. It relaxes strict symmetry rules that slowed earlier designs. On standard benchmarks it matched or beat the best prior models. After broad training, it also handled molecules it had never seen, across varied time spans. The authors see ATOM as a step toward one reusable simulator for many chemicals.
arxiv-2510-05582:
Tao and Shokri sharpen the standard test for training-data leakage. Membership inference attacks ask whether a sample trained a given model. The state-of-the-art attack, RMIA, leans on a large population dataset for calibration. Their 2025 InfoRMIA recasts the test in information-theoretic terms.

The new test treats membership as a composite hypothesis testing problem. Dominance over population data is measured in bits, not sample counts. InfoRMIA beats RMIA across tabular, image, and text benchmarks. It also drops the need for a large population set. A token-level variant then localizes leakage inside generated sequences. It pinpoints exactly which tokens the model memorized. A continuous score replaces RMIA's discrete one, adding statistical power. Sequence-level inference also grows stronger under the token view. That granularity enables targeted unlearning and extraction studies. Privacy audits before model release become cheaper and sharper.
arxiv-2510-05682:
Sánchez Almeida turns the faintest galaxies into a dark matter laboratory. Ultra-faint dwarfs show flat stellar cores in their centers. Stellar feedback seems too weak there to carve cores into cold dark matter halos. His 2025 paper asks what self-interacting dark matter would need to do the job.

He derives the cross-section range that reproduces the observed core sizes. Halos in a core-forming phase need low cross-sections per unit mass. Halos in a core-collapse phase need high ones instead. The allowed band runs from zero point three to two hundred in the usual units. A model linking stellar mass to core radius matches the same range. It predicts larger cores in more massive dwarfs, as observed. Because feedback cannot fake these cores, the dwarfs anchor the cross-section at low velocities. Under collapse, halos thermalize on kiloparsec scales, dwarfing the stellar cores.
arxiv-2510-05782:
Meza De la Jara and colleagues look inside neural networks for signs of unfamiliar data. Out-of-distribution detection flags inputs unlike anything from training. Most methods read only the final layer of a pretrained model. Their 2025 study shows the middle layers carry rich detection signals too.

Residual connections gradually reshape the input as it passes through the network. Different layers therefore hold complementary clues about distribution shift. An entropy-based rule picks the most complementary layers automatically, with no extra training. Adding those layers lifted far-OOD accuracy by up to ten percent. Near-OOD accuracy rose by over seven percent in their benchmarks. The method needs no examples of out-of-distribution data at selection time. It plugs into existing pipelines at modest compute and memory cost. The gains held across architectures and training objectives. Models with late-concentrated information may gain less from the fusion.
arxiv-2510-06182:
Gur-Arieh, Geva, and Geiger dissect how language models bind and retrieve entities in context in a 2025 interpretability study. When a model reads that Ann loves pie, it binds Ann to pie to later answer who loves pie. Earlier work on short lists found models retrieve entities mainly by position.

They show this positional mechanism degrades as bound entities multiply, turning noisy in middle positions. Models compensate with two backups. A lexical mechanism retrieves Ann through her bound counterpart pie, and a reflexive mechanism uses a direct pointer. Across nine models and ten binding tasks, the same mixing pattern appeared. Their causal model combines all three mechanisms and matched real next-token distributions with about ninety-five percent agreement. It also generalized to long, open-ended text with interleaved entity groups. Entity retrieval is a blended strategy, not a single trick.
arxiv-2510-06282:
Moffat and Thompson lay out the invariant structure of their Holomorphic Unified Field Theory in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. The theory derives gravity and gauge interactions from one geometric framework. It lives on a product principal bundle over complexified spacetime, with one connection and a Hermitian field.

From one action invariant under diffeomorphisms and the gauge group, variation produces the Einstein and Yang–Mills equations. Their paired Bianchi identities emerge alongside, keeping the geometry consistent. A compatibility condition ties the construction to ordinary physics on spacetime's real slice. It forces the Hermitian field's antisymmetric part to equal the gauge field's exact curvature there. The condition can be imposed by definition or through an auxiliary penalty functional. Unification programs often add structures until gravity and gauge forces merely coexist. Here both equation sets flow from a single invariant action, the paper's central claim.
arxiv-2510-06482:
González-Avilés simulates a sharply driven chromospheric jet with radiation magnetohydrodynamics in a 2025 solar physics paper. Chromospheric jets shoot plasma from the Sun's lower atmosphere into the corona. Macrospicules are large cases coupling plasma motion, magnetic fields, and radiation. Simple models usually drop radiation transport.

The model solves non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic equations coupled to radiation transport. Radiation energy density and flux evolve along with the plasma. A compact Gaussian velocity pulse launches the jet from the upper chromosphere. The narrow structure looks like observed macrospicules as it rises. It crosses the thin upper chromosphere and corona, where opacities are low. Radiation transport barely changed the jet's shape. It still governed coronal radiative processes strongly. The model thus splits shape questions, which magnetohydrodynamics decides, from coronal energy questions. Transport helped disperse the jet, acting as a radiative cooling channel.
arxiv-2510-06582:
Fei Zhang and six co-authors work on labeling laser scans of forests and other outdoor scenes. Their 2025 paper addresses a bottleneck in 3D point cloud research. Someone must mark which points belong to trees, ground, or other classes before models can learn. Doing that by hand for dense scans is slow and costly.

Their pipeline cuts the labeling effort with several combined tricks. It projects the 3D points onto a spherical grid and adds features from multiple sources. An ensemble of networks then drafts labels and marks the regions it finds uncertain. Human reviewers focus only on those doubtful regions. Using the pipeline, the team built Mangrove3D, a labeled dataset for mangrove forests. Performance leveled off after about twelve annotated scans in tests. A compact nine-channel feature stack captured nearly all useful signal, with accuracy scores near 0.76 on their measure.
arxiv-2510-06782:
Kaichun Yang and Jian Chen test whether better prompting or a better model fixes chart reading errors. Their 2025 paper compares two generations of multimodal language models on hard chart questions. They selected 107 visualization questions that GPT-4V had answered wrongly. Other models also scored poorly on this deliberately tough set.

GPT-5 answered far more of those questions correctly than GPT-4V did. Changing the prompt wording, by contrast, moved accuracy only slightly. Adding a written chart description to the prompt did not help either. The authors conclude that model architecture dominates accuracy on this task. Prompt engineering tweaks the surface of the output more than its correctness. Their study was preregistered, which strengthens the claim. For practitioners, the lesson is blunt. When a chart task matters, upgrading the model beats clever prompt wording, at least on difficult chart questions like these.
arxiv-2510-06982:
Masih Aminbeidokhti and three co-authors revisit Mixout, a finetuning trick they view as an ensemble in disguise. Their 2025 paper studies why swapping weights during training improves robustness. Finetuning vision foundation models boosts accuracy on familiar data but often weakens them elsewhere. Mixout intermittently replaces finetuned weights with their pretrained originals.

Reading that process as a weight-sharing ensemble exposes three levers that control robustness. They are the anchor weights, how often masks resample, and how sparse the mask is. Their improved method, GMixout, makes the anchor adaptive. It tracks an exponential moving average snapshot of the weights instead. A new dial controls the resampling frequency explicitly. A sparse update kernel touches only a few parameters, so training runs on consumer graphics cards. Across shift, corruption, and imbalance benchmarks, GMixout beat Model Soups and other baselines. It did so with no extra cost when the model is deployed.
arxiv-2510-07182:
Ye, Shani, and Vitercik propose Bridged Clustering, a learning method for data whose inputs and outputs were never paired. Their 2025 paper tackles a common mess. Museums may hold many specimen records and, separately, many gene sequences. Standard methods need matched pairs.This method learns from the unpaired bulk plus a handful of pairs. It keeps the link between the two sides sparse and readable.

The method first groups inputs and outputs on their own. It then learns a sparse bridge between the groups from the few known pairs. A new input is matched to its group, and the linked output group's center becomes the prediction. Theory shows the method works when grouping and bridging errors stay bounded. In tests it rivaled top methods while using very few labels. It suits fields rich in data but poor in matched records.
arxiv-2510-07582:
Bao and Rompf put programming language effect systems on a common measuring stick. Their 2025 paper concerns the separation every language wants: pure computation over here, world-altering effects over there. Monads, type-and-effect systems, and capability systems all police the border, trading precision against usability in non-obvious ways. The authors first define purity semantically, through contextual equivalence, independent of any typing discipline, so systems can be graded against meaning rather than their own rules.

The paper then synthesizes the two into type, ability, and effect systems that combine the strengths while dodging the weaknesses. A mechanized logical relation supports purity proofs across the disciplines compared. For language designers, the contribution is a fair scoreboard plus a hybrid design the scoreboard recommends.
arxiv-2510-07782:
Haruta and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on shrinking large language models through structured pruning. Pruning removes whole parts of a model to make it cheaper to run. The cut introduces errors, because pruning uses far less data than training did. Plain least-squares fixes overfit that calibration set and damage pretrained weights. The authors repair the damage under a geometric constraint instead.

Their method, RCPU, only allows updates that act like rotations on the retained weights. Rotations preserve the lengths and angles of output representations while realigning them with the original outputs. A variance-aware score also protects input dimensions that matter most to the main output directions. On LLaMA-7B, RCPU beat rival pruning methods on perplexity and task accuracy. Gains grew at higher pruning ratios, where the retained space shrinks most. The method needs no architecture changes and adds only modest computing cost.
arxiv-2510-07982:
Jin and five coauthors wrote this 2025 computational physics paper on hot carriers in two-faced metal nanoparticles. When light excites plasmons in such particles, the energy lands in energetic electrons and holes. Devices for photocatalysis, solar cells, and sensing all want those carriers. Janus particles join two metals, here gold, silver, and copper, in one body. The authors model them atomistically, coupling Maxwell's equations to large quantum tight-binding calculations.

For spherical particles, the hot-carrier spectrum blends the two hemispheres' spectra with interface coupling. Under sunlight, the silver-gold pairing generated carriers fastest. Dumbbell shapes changed the story through their neck. A wider neck concentrated the electric field and sharply raised generation rates. Light polarized across the metal interface worked best, thanks to maximal dipole coupling. These rules tell experimentalists how shape, pairing, and lighting direction should be chosen when designing hot-carrier devices and photocatalysts.
arxiv-2510-08082:
Cruz, Kuzmanoski, and Pires wrote this 2025 paper on improving brain-computer interface rehabilitation after stroke. Stroke is a leading cause of long-term disability, and recovery stays limited. Interface therapy asks patients to imagine moving the affected hand, driving neuroplasticity. The conventional task contrasts left-hand with right-hand imagery. The authors instead contrast affected-hand imagery against rest, targeting the weak opposite-side activation common after stroke.

They evaluated the change on healthy and stroke datasets with two standard decoders. The affected-hand-versus-rest task improved classification performance in stroke patients. A second finding concerned session length. Shorter training sessions beat longer ones, suggesting fatigue or drift hurts the signal. Splitting therapy into short sessions, or adapting protocols, may work better. The message is practical: task design and schedule matter as much as decoder sophistication, and both are cheap to change.
arxiv-2510-08182:
Rai wrote this 2025 mathematical finance paper extending martingale optimal transport to markets where trading itself costs money. Robust hedging seeks price bounds consistent with observed marginal distributions, without trusting one model. Real trading pays bid-ask spreads and moves prices, frictions the classical theory ignores. Rai adds a convex frictional cost combining proportional spreads with quadratic liquidity impact, generalizing the frictionless theory's monotonicity principles.

At each step, the optimal joint distribution of consecutive prices has a clean geometry. Given today's price, tomorrow's sits on one of two monotone branches for upward or downward rebalancing. Between them lies a no-transaction band where holding still is optimal. A recursive identity extends the structure across many periods, and the construction converges to the frictionless solution as costs vanish. Model-independent hedging can now price path-dependent derivatives with realistic trading costs.
arxiv-2510-08382:
Jacob Trauger, Tyson Trauger, and Ambuj Tewari settle when a forgiving loss function can be learned, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Machine learning classes often score errors with a simple zero-one loss: right or wrong. Forgiving versions soften that rule, accepting some near-miss labels as good enough. The setting here has finitely many class labels, the multiclass case.

The authors create a new combinatorial dimension modeled on the classic Natarajan dimension. Such dimensions count how rich a hypothesis class is, in a precise combinatorial sense. They prove a class is learnable under forgiving loss if and only if this new dimension is finite. They also connect the result to learning with set-valued feedback, where teachers give sets of acceptable answers. There, learnability is characterized by the original Natarajan dimension, they show.
arxiv-2510-08482:
Onur Keleş and co-authors test whether vision-language models grasp sign language iconicity in a 2025 arXiv paper. Iconicity means a sign's form resembles its meaning, common in signed languages. For models, the challenge is reading such mappings from dynamic human motion, not static pictures. Their Visual Iconicity Challenge turns psycholinguistic measures into a video benchmark.

The benchmark has three tasks in Sign Language of the Netherlands. Models predict phonological form, like handshape and location, infer meaning from form, and give graded iconicity ratings. Thirteen leading vision-language models were tested in zero-shot and few-shot settings against human baselines. Models recovered some handshape and location detail but stayed below humans. On transparency, inferring meaning from form, they fell far short of people. Only top models correlated moderately with human iconicity ratings.
arxiv-2510-08982:
Ooi and Phuc settle a conjecture in the theory of function spaces, in this 2025 arXiv paper dedicated to the memory of David Adams. Capacity is a refined way of sizing sets that sees fine detail ordinary volume misses. A strong type inequality ties integrals measured against capacity to the energy of the function producing them. Adams had conjectured a generalization of a classic inequality of Maz'ya, and the pair prove his conjecture right.

With that result in hand, they pin down the identity of the function spaces involved. Those spaces turn out to be the exact dual partners, in a precise pairing sense, of spaces built from Sobolev multipliers. Using tools from nonlinear potential theory and weighted inequalities, the authors further show the spaces match more concrete, workable descriptions. The characterizations plug the abstract spaces neatly into the modern theory used across harmonic analysis.
arxiv-2510-09082:
Wang, Wang, and Xue forecast how complex networks evolve by honoring both group interactions and physical law, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Brains, supply chains, and social systems all change through relationships that involve more than pairs at a time. Standard graph learning sees only pairs, and purely data-driven forecasters, while accurate, cannot explain themselves. Pure theory models explain but miss the numbers.

Their method learns a dynamic hypergraph, where one link can join many nodes, capturing the group structure as it shifts. A dual prediction engine then combines two drivers. The Koopman operator framework rewrites nonlinear dynamics as a linear system that can be solved forward. A physics-informed differential equation component keeps the evolution faithful to known laws. On public benchmarks and a purpose-built industrial chain dataset, the method predicted accurately far into the future. The authors stress the balance it strikes between accuracy and interpretability.
arxiv-2510-09382:
Ankush Pratap Singh, Houwei Cao, and Yong Liu present CHUCKLE in a 2025 arXiv paper on teaching computers to recognise emotions. Curriculum learning trains a model on easy examples first and harder ones later. For emotion recognition, earlier methods judged difficulty from the data or the model, ignoring how hard each clip is for a human listener or viewer.

CHUCKLE instead defines difficulty from crowdsourced human annotations, using how much annotators agree as the signal. The framework assumes that clips people find hard are also hard for neural networks. In experiments, models trained with this human-led ordering beat non-curriculum baselines, both when test speakers matched the training speakers and when they were new. Training also needed fewer gradient updates, which the authors read as gains in both efficiency and robustness.
arxiv-2510-09682:
Rupam Patir, Keyan Guo, Haipeng Cai, and Hongxin Hu make AI-written code safer in a 2025 arXiv paper. Large language models have transformed software development, but their generated code often contains vulnerabilities. Fixes that retrain models or add external analysers can be expensive, slow to adapt to zero-day flaws, and impossible for proprietary models.

Their system, GRASP, instead reasons over secure coding practices in a structured way. It organises the practices into a directed acyclic graph that captures dependencies and relationships between rules. A graph-based reasoning process then walks the model through the relevant practices for each generation task. The design is interpretable, works with any model, and scales to unseen vulnerabilities. In evaluation, GRASP kept security rates above eighty percent across several models. On zero-day vulnerabilities it improved security by up to eighty-eight percent over baselines.
arxiv-2510-09782:
Yufa Zhou, Yixiao Wang, Xunjian Yin, Shuyan Zhou, and Anru Zhang picture language model reasoning as flowing geometry in a 2025 arXiv paper. They model a model's path through its representation space as a flow, a trajectory with position, velocity, and curvature, where logic is what steers the motion. To separate logical structure from surface meaning, they reuse the same natural deduction claims dressed in different semantic carriers.

Their theory states two claims: reasoning takes the form of smooth flows in representation space, and logical statements steer those flows locally, setting their pace. Controlled experiments then draw and measure the flows, validating the framework. The results suggest that plain next-token training can lead models to take in logical rules as fixed geometry. That challenges the stochastic parrot dismissal of model understanding. Experiments across two model families hint at a general law behind both, independent of architecture.
arxiv-2510-09882:
Anand, Milad Alshomary, and Kathleen McKeown present iBERT in this 2025 arXiv paper on interpretable text representation. iBERT is an encoder that turns text into embeddings, numeric vectors that capture meaning and style. Unlike standard encoders, its vectors are built to be read and steered by people.

Each token is represented as a sparse mixture of sense vectors, fixed vectors that each stand for one clear cue, such as a style or topic signal. Sparse means only a few senses are active at once, and the mixture weights cannot go negative. The token vectors can be pooled into sentence-level embeddings or used one by one. This gives users direct control over which cues shape the final representation.
arxiv-2510-09982:
Dr. Cesar Mello and Fernando Medina da Cunha propose Tumor Obliteration by Resonant Amplification in this 2025 arXiv paper on cancer treatment. TOR is a nonthermal, spectrally targeted idea: tuned energy is meant to disintegrate tumor tissue without heat or cavitation, the violent bubble collapse used by some other methods. The study is strictly simulation-only.

The authors run forward solutions in three engineering simulators, COMSOL, ANSYS, and Abaqus, with matched material settings and safety guards. An emulated closed loop, with phase-locked actuation and a contrast and safety gate, controls each run. In the reported tests, TOR achieved per-focus extinction across at least 200 Monte Carlo runs for each configuration. The results are computational only, with no clinical testing claimed.
arxiv-2510-10082:
Chatterjee and co-authors augment preference data for personalized summarizers in this 2025 arXiv paper on natural language processing. A summary should keep what a specific user finds relevant, but relevance is subjective. Documents with many facets make that judgment harder, since different users care about different facets.

The authors diversify the dynamic user preference data used to train personalized summarizers. More varied preference examples should teach the model finer distinctions between users. The boosted training data aims to raise the quality of summaries tailored to one reader. The work treats personalization as a data problem: models cannot respect preferences they have never seen expressed in training.
arxiv-2510-11082:
Some machines and materials lose energy in a way that depends on their whole past motion, not just the present. Belgacem, Ober-Blöbaum, and Jiménez build computer methods for such systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their systems are written with fractional derivatives, which capture that long memory. They turn a physics action principle, step by step, into simulation schemes that respect the physics.

One ingredient, Runge-Kutta convolution quadrature, handles the fractional parts. Galerkin ideas of rising order build the time steps that yield the new integrators. The team studies the family built on Lobatto IIIC rules in most depth. For second order schemes they prove claims about energy loss and error, and tests back them. The full set of schemes reaches second, fourth, and sixth order accuracy in its tests. A shorter final part treats a midpoint version of the same idea.
arxiv-2510-11482:
Before text can feed a classifier, it is usually cleaned: filler words are removed, words are cut to stems, and inflected forms are reduced to dictionary entries. Marco Braga, Gian Carlo Milanese, and Gabriella Pasi ask whether large language models can do that cleaning better than the standard algorithms in this 2025 arXiv natural language processing paper. The classical tools ignore context, even though those choices often depend on context.

The team compared language-model preprocessing against traditional algorithms on web-sourced data, across several text classification tasks in six European languages. The models replicated traditional stopword removal with accuracy reaching ninety-seven percent, lemmatization at eighty-two percent, and stemming at seventy-four percent. More importantly, classifiers trained on model-preprocessed text improved the F1 measure by up to six percent over traditionally preprocessed text. The authors release their code, prompts, and results.
arxiv-2510-12082:
Huy Nguyen, Christoph Treude, and Patanamon Thongtanunam feed code models the backstory developers actually read. Neural program comprehension powers clone detection and summarization, yet models typically see source code alone, ignoring version history and structural relationships. Their 2025 arXiv paper runs an empirical study of what extra context buys.

Five pretrained code models, including CodeBERT and CodeT5, were fine-tuned with and without context on two benchmarks drawn from thousands of open-source projects. Context generally helped across classification and generation. Version history was the most reliable booster, lifting one model's clone detection by nearly sixteen percent and its summarization scores noticeably. Call-graph context helped only some models on some tasks. Combining version history, call graphs, and method age pushed clone detection gains past twenty-one percent for specific models. Human judges also ranked context-augmented summaries significantly higher for accuracy and content.
arxiv-2510-12182:
Youngju Yoo, Seho Kim, and Changick Kim segment 3D scenes using only bounding boxes as teachers. Point-level annotation for 3D instance segmentation is brutally expensive, while boxes are cheap but ambiguous where instances overlap. Prior methods train a separate pseudo-labeler in an extra stage. Their 2025 arXiv paper, BEEP3D, generates pseudo-masks end-to-end instead.

A student-teacher design does the work: the teacher, updated by exponential moving average of the student, produces pseudo-masks on the fly. Instance center-based query refinement sharpens the teacher, anchoring position queries near object centers and exploiting nearby features. Two new losses, query consistency and masked-feature consistency, align the semantic and geometric signals of predictions and pseudo-masks. On the ScanNetV2 and S3DIS benchmarks, BEEP3D matches or beats leading weakly supervised methods while staying computationally efficient. Every gradient serves the final model, not an intermediate labeler.
arxiv-2510-12382:
Wen and Pinson help wind power producers bid together in electricity markets by first making their forecasts agree, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Producers who form a coalition can earn more and share profits by rules from cooperative game theory. But producers often hold incoherent forecasts of future wind, which creates ambiguity in both the joint offer and the profit split.

Their reconcile then optimize framework first aligns each producer's forecasts into one coherent joint forecast. A two stage stochastic programming problem then produces the aggregate market offer and scenario based dual values for every trading hour. From those dual values they construct a profit allocation rule which is budget balanced, meaning payouts match earnings, and stable, meaning no subgroup gains by leaving. Case studies validate the approach. The authors present the framework as a practical way to run cooperative wind offerings on forecasts the whole coalition can stand behind.
arxiv-2510-12482:
Chai and co-authors segment medical images from text descriptions without breaking the link between words and picture regions during data augmentation, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Referring segmentation asks a model to outline the structure a text prompt names. Augmentation tricks such as rotation and flipping enlarge training data, but they scramble the spatial alignment between image and text and weaken learning.

Their framework fuses text and visual features early, before augmentation, so the alignment survives whatever transformation follows. A lightweight generator projects text embeddings into visual space, bridging the semantic gap between language and pixels. Visualizations of its generated pseudo images show accurate localization of the referred regions. The method was tested on three medical imaging tasks across four segmentation frameworks and reached state of the art results. The code is public, and the authors frame early fusion as a general fix for augmentation in multimodal medical models.
arxiv-2510-12582:
Koch and colleagues present Guppy, a programming language embedded in Python for writing quantum programs that mix quantum operations with ordinary control flow, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Hybrid quantum classical programs need loops, conditionals, and measurement based decisions, which low level quantum assembly handles awkwardly. Guppy lets users write such programs in Pythonic syntax, aiming at real quantum hardware.

The paper illustrates the language with compact examples. A single qubit rotation is built from more basic gates. A teleportation protocol entangles qubits, measures them, and applies classical corrections conditioned on the outcomes. A repeat until success routine loops over attempts, discarding failed ancillas, until a measurement signals success. These examples show complex control flow, including loops and branching on measurement results. The work is ongoing, and positions Guppy as a high level front end for hybrid quantum computation.
arxiv-2510-12682:
Khatua and a large team report signs that magnons, the quanta of magnetic waves, condense into one quantum state in a high spin honeycomb magnet, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Field induced Bose Einstein condensation of magnons near a magnet's saturation field is a prized quantum phase transition, but it has mostly been seen in low spin systems. Their material is a manganese based honeycomb lattice antiferromagnet with spin five halves, where each site offers several possible excitations.

Combining thermodynamic measurements on single crystals with density functional theory, they find a field induced transition. It leads to a fully polarized state at a critical field of a few tesla. The ordering temperature follows the power law scaling expected for magnon condensation in three dimensions. The authors present this as expanding condensation driven quantum criticality to high spin antiferromagnets.
arxiv-2510-12782:
Zhang and a large team of collaborators map the Perseus galaxy cluster in this 2025 arXiv paper. They use the XRISM space telescope's Resolve instrument. They combined five new pointings from 2025 with four earlier datasets. That gave a long total exposure on the hot gas between the cluster's galaxies. Perseus is the only cluster mapped this far out with enough detail to see gas structures driven by mergers and by its central black hole.

The maps show fast gas motions in the eastern region. These match a bright X-ray excess and imply that turbulence supplies a noticeable share of the pressure there. Across the cluster the bulk flow forms a dipole pattern along the east-west direction. The authors read this pattern as rotation left over from a recent merger. Their simulations suggest at least two energetic mergers since early cosmic times.
arxiv-2510-12982:
Maan, Katira, and Mooley catalog Galactic X-ray transients from the first eROSITA all-sky survey in this 2025 arXiv paper. Transients are sources that flare or fade over time, and while targeted studies of them abound, blind population surveys have been limited. The authors cross-matched source catalogs from the ROSAT and eROSITA X-ray telescopes with the Gaia star catalog to find sources that changed over timescales under thirty years.

Their search yielded more than seven hundred transients, most of them active stars or interacting binaries. About forty were compact object systems, including at least eight newly identified white dwarf systems, three known X-ray binaries, and one known pulsar. X-ray spectra split flaring systems into two types with different peak energies, and systems containing giant stars proved significantly more luminous than those with only main-sequence stars or young stellar objects.
arxiv-2510-13082:
Koch and co-authors bring ownership and borrowing to quantum programming in this 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum mechanics forbids cloning and deleting qubits, and linear type systems can enforce those rules at compile time, catching bugs before expensive hardware runs. Functional quantum languages use linear types well, but imperative languages, where qubits are opaque pointers handled by side-effecting operations, have resisted usable versions.

The authors develop a type system combining linear typing with imperative semantics while keeping the safety guarantees, borrowing the ownership discipline made popular by systems languages. Every idea is implemented in Quantinuum's Guppy programming language rather than left as theory. They contrast their approach with earlier attempts that gave qubits value semantics and treated gates as pure functions. Those approaches, they argue, merely dress the functional style in verbose syntax. They miss how languages like Q# and OpenQASM work in practice.
arxiv-2510-13482:
Baistrukov and colleagues describe a low-impedance stripline kicker built for the SKIF synchrotron light source in Russia. Their 2025 arXiv paper covers a key part of the machine's bunch-by-bunch feedback system. SKIF aims at an ultra-low beam spread while running a strong beam current. Collective effects, where the beam interacts with its vacuum chamber, threaten both goals.

The kicker delivers fast transverse nudges that counter growing beam instabilities. Its design was optimized for easy manufacturing and for a uniform kick across the beam. The paper reports the device's electrical parameters, imparted momentum, and beam impedances. Its chosen length also lets the same hardware serve as a beam position monitor. That dual use simplifies the feedback system that keeps the beam stable. The design follows lessons from the MAX IV facility's kicker experience.
arxiv-2510-13582:
Kahng and Kang build ArtNet, a generator of artificial chip netlists for machine learning and co-optimization studies. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses a data drought in electronic design automation. Real designs are proprietary and slow to run through full flows. Learning methods and design-technology exploration both starve without diverse, realistic examples.

ArtNet uses hierarchical clustering to mimic the topology of real netlists closely. Its outputs match target parameters more faithfully than earlier generators, the authors report. In a test predicting design rule violations with a neural network, ArtNet data lifted the F1 score by 0.16 over training on real data alone, a clear gain for a scarce-data task. Its miniature stand-in designs also matched full blocks on power, performance, and area metrics. That match reached up to 97.94 percent for the targeted designs in their study.
arxiv-2510-13782:
MacNeil and co-authors grow manganese germanide thin films on a non-magnetic template to expose the material's own magnetism. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies MnGe, a B20 compound whose spins twist into very short helices. Earlier films sat on magnetic buffer layers that muddy the signal. A chromium silicide template avoids that contamination entirely.

Single-phase films grew between two and forty nanometres thick on silicon. Surfaces stayed smooth, with roughness around half a nanometre or so. The crystal structure showed the expected B20 form with a slight rhombohedral squeeze. Magnet measurements in perpendicular fields fit a conical spin state, as expected. Below thirty-five kelvin, though, an unexpected leftover moment appears in the films. Matching features show up in the electrical transport data at the same temperatures. The team reads this as indirect evidence of a low-temperature topological phase others have reported.
arxiv-2510-13982:
Jinkun Chen and co-authors argue that simulations of society built from large language model agents are stuck in static sandboxes, in this 2025 arXiv position paper. Most current multi-agent simulations give agents fixed tasks inside closed environments and grade them with rigid rules. Real societies, by contrast, keep changing: agents adapt, reshape their surroundings, and produce behavior nobody scripted.

The authors review emerging architectures that blend language models with multi-agent dynamics and name the key hurdles, including balancing stability against diversity, evaluating unexpected behavior, and scaling to greater complexity. They propose a scheme for the field built on dynamic scenario evolution, agent-environment co-evolution, and generative agent architectures. Their roadmap calls for open-ended systems where agents and worlds evolve together continuously, aiming at resilient, socially aligned AI ecosystems rather than brittle one-task systems.
arxiv-2510-14782:
Gemechu, Fu, and Zitelli investigate, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how light in a few-mode optical fiber quietly leaks out of the mode it started in. Few-mode fibers carry several spatial patterns of light at once. Pumped with visible ultrashort pulses, the fundamental mode, the simplest pattern, loses power through Raman scattering, an interaction where light sheds energy to vibrations in the glass and shifts color.

The team combined experiments with numerical simulations. They used a tunable femtosecond laser and standard SMF-28 fibers run below their single-mode cutoff, in lengths of twelve and fifty meters. Careful coupling control, holographic decomposition of the outgoing modes, and spectral analysis let them watch the transfer directly. Experiments and simulations both show significant energy moving into higher-order modes through intermodal Raman scattering. The findings matter for high-power laser delivery and next-generation optical communication systems.
arxiv-2510-15082:
Gonzalez builds, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a photolithography stepper, the machine that prints microscopic patterns onto chips, for about three thousand dollars. Steppers are part of semiconductor manufacturing and have patterned devices for decades, but their size and price confine them to industry and university laboratories. The design here is open-source, maskless, and meant to be assembled by its users.

Instead of a mask, the stepper uses a digital light processing projector as its optical engine, projecting each pattern. It achieves optical resolution under two microns. A motorized micropositioning system aligns features with single-digit micron precision, and a deep learning vision model handles the fine-grained alignment of patterns on a chip. Those capabilities suffice for microfabrication: the paper demonstrates micron-scale devices, including NMOS transistors, made with the machine. The aim is to put a semiconductor process tool within reach of small labs and classrooms.
arxiv-2510-15382:
Kexin Zheng and four colleagues improve generalist agents that must handle brand-new tasks with no extra training. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in zero-shot reinforcement learning, where a pre-trained policy should adapt to any task on demand. Popular forward-backward methods promise this, but the team found their representations lack expressiveness and drift when offline data contains out-of-distribution actions.

Their upgraded framework, BREEZE, regularizes the policy toward behavior seen in the data, turning policy learning into a steadier in-sample problem. A task-conditioned diffusion model then extracts the policy, so it can express varied, high-quality action patterns for each new task. Attention-based networks model how states, actions, and tasks relate, enriching the learned representations. On two standard benchmark suites the method matched or beat prior offline zero-shot approaches. The authors stress its robustness over rival methods.
arxiv-2510-15482:
Terry Mart and Jovan Alfian Djaja build a fresh calculational tool for a nuclear reaction where light creates a kaon particle. Their 2025 paper, published in Few-Body Systems, works within a Feynman diagram framework, the standard picture-based bookkeeping of particle physics. The operator they construct describes kaon photoproduction on a single nucleon and, by extension, inside nuclei.

The model's unknown coupling strengths, at the points where photons and particles interact, were fitted to all available experimental data across six isospin channels. The result matched the data excellently. The operator includes twenty-six nucleon resonances for channels ending in a lambda particle and seventeen more delta resonances for sigma channels. For use on nuclei it is written in Pauli space, so a nonrelativistic approximation drops in easily. The authors also propose output forms that separate frame-dependent pieces.
arxiv-2510-15682:
Answering research questions demands sources, yet standard search-augmented chatbots often cite poorly. Ines Besrour, Jingbo He, Tobias Schreieder, and Michael Färber present SQuAI in this 2025 arXiv paper. The system answers scientific questions using four cooperating agents over millions of papers. The agents split hard questions into sub-questions, retrieve evidence with hybrid search, and filter documents adaptively. Every generated claim carries an in-line citation plus supporting sentences from the source documents.

Built on over two million full-text arXiv papers, SQuAI improves faithfulness over a strong baseline. Answer and context relevance also rise, by up to twelve percent on their measures. The team releases a benchmark of one thousand question-answer-evidence triplets for reproducibility.
arxiv-2510-15982:
Donghyeok Shin, Yeongmin Kim, Suhyeon Jo, Byeonghu Na, and Il-Chul Moon unify a scattered trick for teaching small language models from large ones. Knowledge distillation aligns a student's output distribution with a teacher's, cutting cost and memory. The capacity gap and training instability from near-zero probabilities in high-dimensional outputs, though, limit the transfer.

Recent work adds an assistant distribution between teacher and student, but each proposal fixed its mixing path and divergence by fiat. Their alpha-mixture family makes the mixing a continuous design variable, and the AMiD framework generalises the divergences used with assistants on optimality grounds. Extensive experiments show better performance and steadier training than earlier assistant schemes, the five authors report, and the code is released publicly.
arxiv-2510-16082:
