Elias Hossain, Mehrdad Shoeibi, Ivan Garibay, and Niloofar Yousefi explain gene clusters from RNA sequencing with a team of checking agents. Their target is antimicrobial resistance studies. Pathway tools summarise co-expressed modules in broad terms. Their explanations are often generic and loosely tied to the literature, though. Mechanistic insight is what spawns testable hypotheses in resistance work.

BIOGEN combines biomedical retrieval, structured reasoning, and multi-critic verification. It writes cluster-level explanations with explicit evidence and confidence labels. On a primary Salmonella data set, its grounding scores beat a language-model-only baseline clearly. Its measured hallucination rate is zero, against a tenth for that baseline. Four more bacterial data sets also stay at zero under the same pipeline. Against open agentic baselines, BIOGEN is the only framework at zero across all five data sets, the team reports.
arxiv-2510-16182:
Jan Rozendaal, writing alone, proves a result about how sharp features in waves travel through uneven media. The waves obey equations whose coefficients, the numbers that set local wave speed, are only mildly smooth. A classic law says sharp spots must move along set paths called bicharacteristics, never appearing from nowhere.

Rozendaal shows that law still holds when the coefficients have just a touch more than minimal smoothness. For one key case, even slightly less smoothness than the usual bar is enough. The proof works across curved spaces too, as long as their bending stays bounded. The result widens the range of rough media and curved spaces where wave paths can be trusted.
arxiv-2510-16382:
Ze Tao leads nine co-authors in a 2025 study on AI models that must work on new kinds of data. Most models learn links between data and labels from counts alone. Their model, HSCM, copies how human sight works in layers. It splits an image into traits like colour, texture, and shape, then weighs each trait by cause.

Tests, both in theory and in trials, show HSCM beats older models of this kind. It holds up well when the test data shifts in style or source. The clear split of traits also makes its choices easier to read. Code for the model is shared in public for others to try.
arxiv-2510-16482:
Romulo Aparecido leads thirteen co-authors in a short 2025 report on fixing flaws in fibre optic links. Light pulses blur as they cross glass fibre, which caps data speed. Their fix, digital backpropagation, runs the trip in reverse on a computer to undo the blur. They test it in the O-band, a range of light waves near zero blur.

A single-step form of the fix worked on a real test link. The link ran two spans of fibre for 151 km in all. It sent fast, dense signals with many levels per pulse. Signal quality rose by up to 1.6 dB, a clear gain. Cheap fixes like this lift the speed of long-haul links.
arxiv-2510-17082:
C. B. Z. Luo and nine co-authors report on clean water for a huge neutrino detector in this 2025 paper. The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory sits deep below ground in China. Its main tank is ringed by forty thousand tons of ultra-pure water. Radon gas in that water must stay very low to avoid false signals.

The team built a two-stage plant that makes one hundred tons of water per hour. Fine bubbles help thin films strip radon from the water in five steps. The system removes more than ninety-nine point nine percent of the radon. Final levels fall well below the design goal. The paper maps where radon enters and how each part helps.
arxiv-2510-17582:
Petri nets are diagram based models of systems where tokens move through places and transitions, and they are used to check security properties of software and hardware designs. Ning Ran and four co-authors study a property called strong non-deterministic non-interference in bounded, labelled Petri nets. The question is whether low level users, who see only low level output events, can ever deduce that a high level event has fired behind their backs.

Ran and her co-authors build a special checking automaton, the SNNI verifier, that watches the system behaviour for exactly such leaks. With it they state a condition that is both necessary and sufficient for the property to hold. That gives designers a complete test for one strong form of information hiding in this class of models.
arxiv-2510-17782: Sergio Sánchez Cruz reports searches at the CMS detector for new physics in top quark events. The top quark matters because many new physics models predict broken symmetries there. Some models break lepton number conservation, a rule the Standard Model keeps by accident. Others add new sources of CP violation, meaning matter and antimatter behaving differently. Cruz presents measurements that probe these symmetry breaks in top quark processes. The processes involve the top quark together with additional particles.
arxiv-2510-17982:
Samudra Sur and Thierry Giamarchi study how a quantum ring current fades when noise and open contacts act together. A steady current that flows without power is a sign of quantum coherence in a ring. Here the ring faces random disorder over time, plus a fermionic reservoir touching every site.

Using a standard non-equilibrium method, the authors find the current does not fall in a simple way. Two decay routes appear, one set by contact strength and one by the ratio of noise to contact coupling. Simple rate equations capture the flattened steady state. Cold-atom setups could test the claims.
arxiv-2510-18182:
Ji-Hoon Ha and Elena S Volnova study how a plasma drift instability speeds up electrons across many cosmic settings. Uneven density in magnetized plasma stores free energy, and the lower-hybrid drift instability is one release valve. Such waves are often seen near Earth's magnetotail and magnetopause, and earlier work modeled the speeding with a quasilinear approach.

The new study widens the range from weakly to strongly magnetized media, spanning planetary, interstellar, and galaxy-cluster plasmas. Two control knobs, plasma pressure against magnetic pressure and the shape of the fast electron tail, guide the analysis. Space physicists get broader reach for one acceleration route.
arxiv-2510-18382:
Hailiang Li, together with Li-Yong Zhou and Xiaoping Zhang, uses computer simulations to study how planets moved in the early solar system. Migration, the slow drift of a planet's orbit, helps explain many features seen today. Their simulations confirm a feedback loop: the faster Neptune moved, the more small rocky bodies, called planetesimals, it consumed, and when migration slowed, Neptune cleared its surroundings and further drift became harder.

A tenfold rise in migration speed cut the planetesimal mass needed for a given change in Neptune's motion by about thirty percent. Two triggers could speed migration up: Neptune crossing major resonances with Uranus, and passing through a dense ring of planetesimals. The results suggest Neptune's present place is a delicate outcome, and a different crossing could have sent it much farther out.
arxiv-2510-18482:
Daniele Barettin and his three co-authors study a new carbon crystal. The crystal is built from single-atom carbon chains. The chains form thin sheets called carbyne. Such free-standing sheets were made only recently. The team paired lab tests with theory. They used light emission tests of two kinds. They asked when the crystal acts as a semimetal. They also asked when it acts as a semiconductor.

Their models place the switch at chains of about forty-two atoms. Past the switch, the energy landscape has a sharp feature. That feature creates odd light states called hyperbolic excitons. The lab tests saw clear signs of those states. The states absorbed light less as chains grew longer. Theory predicted just that trend near the switch. The work gives a full frame for tuning the energy gap. It applies to the thinnest carbon crystals known.
arxiv-2510-18782:
Noam Soker and Kobi Shiran argue a case about supernova 2023ixf. They say its structure supports a specific explosion mechanism. They examined published measures of its photosphere. That is the expanding surface that radiates its light. They found two stretches of constant expansion speed. A third stretch may also be there. They read each stretch as a shell of ejected material.

Like shells appear in the remains of other such supernovae. Past studies tied those shapes to the jittering jets mechanism. In it, wandering pairs of energetic jets drive the blast. The authors conclude the shells here support the same origin. They present the study as one more piece of evidence. In their view, evidence is accumulating that jittering jets are the primary mechanism. That is a claim the paper advances, not a settled fact.
arxiv-2510-18882:
Tatsuki Saito, Yuto Kikuchi, Kuniharu Ushijima, and Kentaro Yaji design better water-cooled heat sinks by computer optimization. Porous heat sinks cool electronics well but their intricate passages create large pressure drops that limit practical use. The authors' framework optimizes the layout across scales, explicitly representing empty channels and porous regions together, with lattice density graded from place to place inside a multi-material design.

A two-layer flow model keeps simulations cheap enough to run inside the optimization loop while still tracking the mixed porous and empty distribution. Winning designs were rebuilt as full lattice geometries and checked with detailed coupled heat and fluid simulations at fixed pressure drop. The voided lattice designs beat both conventional plate-fin sinks and uniform lattice sinks, reaching roughly twenty to thirty percent higher peak heat transfer performance while actually losing less pressure.
arxiv-2510-19082:
Jacob Folks proves new stability and convergence results for higher-order Wiener-Wintner systems in ergodic theory. These systems are defined through special averages that control how often patterns recur, and earlier work showed that fast convergence of those averages yields pointwise convergence for several kinds of recurrence averages.

Folks shows the averages have a sublinearity property and can bound conditional expectations and products of functions. That transfers into stability: the systems stay well behaved under sums, factors, and products. Broader convergence results follow as well, including a polynomial return times statement for this class of dynamical systems.
arxiv-2510-19382:
Nikos Tsikouras and three co-authors build a frame for structure discovery. It removes randomness from the analysis. Earlier work used a teacher-student setup. A small student trained with random steps grew a low-rank first layer. That structure lowers the data needed to generalize. But the result held only under narrow conditions.

The new frame weakens those conditions a lot. Networks may have any size and depth. All parameters may train. Any smooth training rule is allowed. Removing randomness clarifies which ingredients force structure to appear. Cleaner theory could guide network design well past the first setting.
arxiv-2510-19582:
Steffen Berg and five co-authors review new ways to describe how two fluids move together through porous rock, from pore scale up to the scale engineers use. Porous rock has a huge inner surface area. In two-fluid flow, the balance of capillary and viscous forces makes complex, shifting patterns. The classic Darcy-law extensions cover only part of this behavior with rigor.

A decade of progress in imaging and modeling single pores has driven several newer concepts that try to upscale the physics honestly. The review compares these approaches, which draw on heat theory, statistics, and geometry. The goal is a large-scale description that covers moving interfaces and shifting flow paths, not just connected-path flow where capillary forces rule.
arxiv-2510-19782:
Prashant Kodali and five co-authors adapt language models to code-mixed text, where speakers blend two languages in one sentence, by merging models instead of only fine-tuning them. Their recipe first continues pretraining a multilingual base model on unlabeled code-mixed text, then merges that checkpoint back with the base, and finally fine-tunes on the task. Tests cover sentiment and hate speech classification for English-Hindi and English-Spanish.

Merged models beat both plain fine-tuning and the continue-then-fine-tune pipeline, gaining several F1 points, while prompting much larger models lagged behind. Models adapted on one language pair also transferred better to new pairs, such as English-Tamil, than English-only baselines. The authors close with practical recipes for different data situations.
arxiv-2510-19982:
Vipin Rathi and six co-authors present QORE, a framework for moving 5G and beyond-5G core networks onto quantum-safe cryptography. The algorithms securing today's mobile cores, RSA, elliptic curve methods, and Diffie-Hellman, all fall to Shor's algorithm on a future quantum computer. QORE applies the standard lattice-based key wrapping and signature schemes across the 5G service-based design.

A hybrid configuration, combining classical and post-quantum primitives, keeps networks interoperable during the migration. Experiments show the key wrapping step reaches quantum security with only minor performance overhead. It meets carrier-grade latency and throughput demands. The roadmap aligns with industry study groups and the standardization process. It offers operators practical guidance for both network functions and user equipment.
arxiv-2510-20282:
Eva Horvat and Michal Jablonowski study how 3-handles join in smooth four-manifolds. Kirby charts for such shapes tend to draw just the 1- and 2-handles. The 3-handles are left out as a rule. The pair give tools to draw those joins in a clear, full way.

They add a set of moves with 3-handles to the classic Kirby rules. If the count of 3-handles meets a set rank from the edge shape homology, a test picks out a base set of spheres. Those spheres sit apart in the edge and match the 3-handle joins. This match gives a sole-form proof for how the joins must look.
arxiv-2510-20382:
László Kozma and Michal Opler design a compact data structure for storing pattern-avoiding permutations, a central object in combinatorics and theoretical computer science. Their structure stores any permutation of a given size that avoids an arbitrary fixed pattern, even an unknown one, in a number of bits that is asymptotically optimal. It answers both forward and inverse queries in constant time.

That constant-time access sidesteps a known lower bound that holds for general permutations, and earlier comparable results covered only restricted cases such as separable permutations. Extensions support geometric queries like rectangle range counting on the permutation point set in very fast time. For bounded treewidth classes the structure becomes succinct, and all versions can be built in linear time.
arxiv-2510-20782:
Alicia Sagae, Chia-Jung Lee, Sandeep Avula, Brandon Dang. Vanessa Murdock built a test data set for checking responsible behavior in language model outputs for one concrete job, writing plain product blurbs from a feature list. Broad model tests miss fairness issues because the traits that matter change with the job at hand.

Their prompts vary fairness traits crossed with gendered describing words and product groups, giving a rich labeled set for close study. With the data, users can spot gaps in quality, truth, safety, and fairness for this exact use case. The work pairs a general proposal for job specific testing with a shared resource other teams can adopt.
arxiv-2510-20882:
The Belle and Belle II Collaborations, with three hundred twenty four names on the author list, report first measurements of rare charmed baryon decays using data from both detectors. The decays studied are singly suppressed modes in which a Xi baryon turns into a Lambda plus a light meson.

One decay into an eta meson is observed and another into an eta prime shows clear evidence, with ratios to a reference decay measured at a few percent. No signal appears for the neutral pion mode, so an upper limit is set instead. Absolute rates follow from the known reference rate, sharpening tests of charm decay theory.
arxiv-2510-21282:
Pavankumar Chandankar and Robin Burchard present a system for recognizing human activities from wearable motion sensors, built for a data challenge on the WEAR data set. Real sensor data are noisy, so a model trained on clean recordings can stumble when test data arrive in damaged form.

They train four separate transformer models, one for each body location where a sensor sits, using a design called PatchTST. Training windows are deliberately tampered with, using jitter, scaling, rotation, and dropped channels, so the noise matches what the test set contains. At test time the four models vote by averaging their probabilities. On the private leaderboard, the system reached a macro-F1 score well above the baseline.
arxiv-2510-21382:
S. John Sharon Sandeep, Dibyajyoti Sahu, and Suhas Gangadharaiah look for a simpler way to shield a quantum system from unwanted excitations while it is driven across a critical point. Standard counter-methods work but call for complex many-body controls that labs struggle to build in practice.

Working with the transverse-field Ising model, they instead vary one existing coupling over time, choosing its path with quantum optimal control tools guided by a shortest-time principle. Under a straight ramp of the field, the best path for the second knob rises and falls rather than moving steadily. The scheme reaches higher fidelity than several orders of the standard approximate methods and resists noise better. The authors prove an unusual scaling law for excitations when noise acts on either knob.
arxiv-2510-21482:
Marek Socha and six co-authors track people across many cameras in packed enclosed spaces, where bodies constantly hide each other. Their system, GRAP-MOT, works without training labels and keeps identities straight by updating each person's label online, guided by tracked paths and personal appearance features woven into a graph.

The team rethought every stage of tracking, from feature extraction to grouping. Added a position estimation module that tells the tracker where each person stands, a strong extra clue in crowds. Tests on their own closed-area recordings and on public crowded data sets put the system ahead of rivals. They also argue, after reviewing scoring rules, that one standard score judges such crowded tracking more fairly than another, and they release code and data openly.
arxiv-2510-22082:
Sam Hopkins explains a cornerstone of combinatorics, the Robinson-Schensted-Knuth correspondence, through small local moves called toggles. The correspondence links permutations and other objects to pairs of number tableaus and quietly powers results across algebra and probability. Its usual definition can feel like a magic trick performed row by row.

Hopkins rebuilds the definition from local transformations, so the global correspondence emerges from simple switches applied in the right pattern. The note grew out of presentations by Alex Postnikov, was written in two thousand fourteen, and circulated privately for years before being posted to the arXiv for preservation. As a teaching-flavored exposition, it offers specialists and students a more mechanical, transparent way to see why the correspondence works.
arxiv-2510-22282:
Tianhui Liu leads a six-author team reading a city's wealth from its face. Judging urban socio-economic status from images serves sustainability planning, and large vision-language models promise to do it as a reasoning task. Off the shelf they produce predictions that are neither accurate enough nor interpretable enough to plan with.

Their framework, CityRiSE, trains the model with reinforcement learning on a curated multimodal dataset, with rewards that can be verified rather than merely preferred. The training steers the model toward semantically meaningful visual cues and structured, goal-directed reasoning about them, so the answer arrives with its working visible. In experiments the framework significantly outperformed existing baselines on accuracy. The authors highlight the reasoning behavior that emerged under the reward design as the mechanism behind the gain, not a side effect.
arxiv-2510-22682:
Locating a speaker in a reverberant room, where echoes blur direction, is hard for spatial audio systems. Bar Shaybet, Vladimir Tourbabin, and Boaz Rafaely present SRP-PHAT-NET in 2025, a neural network that also reports how reliable each direction estimate is, a feature most learning methods lack.

The network uses directional maps from a classic steered response method as its spatial features. Training labels are Gaussian weighted around the true direction, letting the model score confidence meaningfully. The authors show label smoothing width can be tuned to each application. Keeping only high confidence predictions improves localization accuracy substantially in their experiments.
arxiv-2510-22782:
Green hydrogen is costly, mostly due to power prices. Zhichao Chen, Hongyuan Sheng, Hao Wang, and Jiaze Ma study that cost in 2025. Electrolyzers split water to make hydrogen. Most plants buy power only a day ahead. That misses gains from real time markets.

Their plan uses a rolling horizon method. It coordinates bids and plant operation. The plant first buys base energy day ahead. It then trades in real time. It can buy cheap extra energy. It can also sell day ahead energy back at high prices. Results show net power costs can drop sharply. Costs can near zero or turn negative in cases.
arxiv-2510-22882:
Splitting many sorted lists at a shared rank is a core task. Amit Joshi, writing alone in 2025, gives a merge free method for it. The task is multi way co-ranking. Cut indices must make all prefix segments hold exactly K elements together. No full merge should be needed.

His method extends two list co-ranking to many lists. It searches in index space, not value space. Per sequence bounds narrow to a consistent frontier. Runtime depends on log of total size and log of list count. Space stays linear in list count. Correctness follows from an exchange argument. Uses include parallel merge partitioning and multi stream joins.
arxiv-2510-22982:
Guanchen Du and seven co-authors tackle service choice on the web, where many similar services compete and users need reliable quality forecasts. Predicting quality of service is hard when records are sparse and noisy. Older methods often miss rich context and fail badly in those sparse cases.

Their QoSGMAA framework joins multi-order graph attention, which weighs links between users and services at several scales, with adversarial training for robustness. The design aims to keep forecasts stable even when data is thin or corrupted. Better forecasts would help platforms recommend services that truly meet user needs.
arxiv-2510-23282:
Andrew P Allan, Aline A Vidotto, Jorge Sanz-Forcada, and Carolina Villarreal D'Angelo model how stellar activity cycles change the helium transit signal used to trace escaping planet atmospheres. The helium line at 1083 nanometers is a common probe of escape, but star activity can distort it and confuse readings.

They model four kinds of highly irradiated planets at two close distances, at cycle minimum and maximum, around both the Sun and the more active star iota Horologii. Reconstructed stellar spectra drive the models. The results warn observers how much of a helium signal may be the star, not the planet.
arxiv-2510-23482:
Zujing Liu, Junwen Pan, Qi She, Yuan Gao, and Guisong Xia measure and improve the faithfulness of visual thinking in large vision-language models. After reinforcement fine-tuning, these models produce multimodal chains of thought mixing vision and text. The authors observe that the visual information cited is often inaccurate even when the final answer is correct.

They blame a reward that pays only for the format of interleaved cues, not their correctness. Measuring that gap and enhancing training to reward correct visual evidence should make model reasoning trustworthy, not just plausible. Faithful traces matter wherever users audit AI decisions.
arxiv-2510-23782:
J. Gonzalez and eleven co-authors ask a blunt question: does machine learning actually work for finding gravitational lenses? They compare three independent learning-based searches run on the Dark Energy Survey, each with its own architecture and training strategy. The test bed is a visually inspected sample of 1,651 reported lens candidates, scored against expert judgment.

The three models improved in step with their vintage, reaching F1 scores from 0.31 up to 0.54. Their completeness on solid candidates rose from about a third to seventy percent. Together they recovered eighty-two percent of those candidates, showing they catch different lenses. The authors then tried ensemble strategies — averaging, regression, decision trees, random forests, and a Bayesian method. Nearly all beat the best single model, and some cut false positives by up to a factor of six. For future surveys, the takeaway is to combine diverse classifiers rather than crown one winner.
arxiv-2510-24182:
Judith Rousseau and two co-authors study Bayesian estimation for high dimensional Hawkes processes, which model events that trigger further events over time. In the sparse regime they consider, each component of the process depends on far fewer interaction functions than the total dimension. They ask how well Bayesian methods recover both the intensity functions and the parameters themselves.

The authors prove bounds for two loss measures: an empirical distance between intensity functions and a norm on the parameters, covering background rates and interaction functions. These are the first results to control the parameter norm in this setting and the first study of Bayesian procedures for high dimensional Hawkes processes, giving a base for sparse event modeling.
arxiv-2510-24382:
Haoyang Liu and four co-authors study stars in the Galactic Bulge, the dense central region of the Milky Way, sorting them by metal content. They select bulge stars from the APOGEE survey matched with Gaia astrometry. Using mixture models and peak finding, they split stars into metal poor and metal rich groups and compare their velocity spreads and element patterns.

The team also examines retrograde stars and a chemical plane to hunt for accreted components from past mergers. Finally, they fit analytic bulge models to map how the boxy, X shaped structure changes with metallicity. The work ties the bulge's chemistry and motion to its formation history.
arxiv-2510-24482:
Klemens Iten leads a team of five authors on learning control over time. Most learning control methods chop time into fixed steps. Real machines move smoothly, with no natural step breaks. The team study control where motion follows differential equations. Those equations are unknown at first and must be learned from trials.

Their method, COMBRL, learns the motion with models that track doubt. Gaussian processes and Bayesian neural networks supply that doubt signal. Each trial seeks reward while also probing where doubt is high. The team prove regret grows slower than the trial count. They also bound trials needed when no reward is given at all. In tests COMBRL beat rivals and scaled to larger tasks.
arxiv-2510-25482:
Sweta Das and Andrii Dmytryshyn study degenerations of matrix pencil orbits. Their 2025 math paper concerns skew-symmetric matrix pencils. Complete eigenstructure describes eigenvalues, multiplicities, and minimal indices. That form can change drastically under small perturbations. Matrix coefficients are subjected to those perturbations here. Qualitative investigation uses stratification graphs of congruence orbits.

Closure hierarchy graphs show how orbits relate under limits. Their results facilitate constructing such graphs for pencils. They give all closest neighbours for a given node. A necessary and sufficient setting is proved here. It decides when one orbit lies in another closure. No intermediate pencil orbit may sit strictly between them. That setting identifies minimal degenerations between orbits precisely. Skew-symmetric pencils have special form aiding the study. Congruence transformations preserve that skew symmetry throughout. Eigenstructure changes are organized by the hierarchy. Matrix theory scholars can build stratification graphs faster. Perturbation actions becomes clearer through these neighbour relations.
arxiv-2510-25782:
Jorge A Arroyo evaluates nightlife regulation in San Juan. His 2025 paper studies a late-night alcohol sales ordinance. San Juan, Puerto Rico implemented that ordinance recently. A multi-outcome synthetic control method pools series. Economic and public-safety outcomes are pooled jointly. A common-weight estimator clarifies mechanisms under low-rank form.

Restaurants and bars show such reallocation effects. Hospitality employment shifts are part of pattern. Late-night public disorder arrests show no clear departures. Violent crime also shows no clear trend departures. Pre-policy trends continue for those safety outcomes. The short post-policy window limits statistical power. Small donor pool also limits power largely. Statistical tests do not reject the null. He emphasizes effect magnitudes and persistence instead. Code and diagnostics are ready for replication.
arxiv-2510-25882:
Wenhao Yang, Minghui Zhou, Daniel Izquierdo Cortazar, and Yehui Wang build a framework to help firms govern risks from open source software. Firms now build core systems on open source code, which exposes them to risks beyond bugs, such as quiet upstream fixes, community fights, or sudden license changes. Standard risk tools focus on technical checks and can miss those wider threats.

Yang and the team base their work on interviews with fifteen practitioners and on grounded theory, a method that builds theory from field data. Their rule is that an outside threat becomes critical only when it meets a weakness the firm can control. They arrange the response as a chain from objectives to threats, weaknesses, and mitigation steps.
arxiv-2510-25982:
Chaithanya Naik Mude leads five co-authors in a method to read out neutral atom quantum computers faster without losing accuracy. In these machines, atoms hold qubits, and reading their states by imaging takes milliseconds, far longer than the gates themselves. Slow readout stalls error correction cycles and lets errors grow while qubits sit idle, but faster imaging collects fewer photons and gets noisier.

Their framework, GANDALF, denoises the dim images to rebuild a clear signal before classification. Combined with light classifiers and a pipelined readout design, it allows reliable reads at up to one point six times shorter times in their tests. Shorter cycles in turn lower the logical error rate in their analysis.
arxiv-2510-26082:
Fan Yang, Lingyao Li, Yaxin Hu, Michael Rodgers, and Renkai Ma study how people react when they see a robot being abused. The response depends on how human like the robot looks. Anthropomorphism means giving a machine human traits. Two hundred one participants watched videos of abuse toward a spider like robot, a two footed robot, or a humanoid robot, spanning low to high human likeness.

Yang and the team combine self report surveys, automated facial expression analysis, and written reflections. Protective responses did not rise in a straight line. The middle robot, rated most eerie in line with uncanny valley theory. It drew the strongest physical anger expressions. Self reported anger and guilt were higher for both the middle and humanoid robots than for the spider.
arxiv-2510-26182:
Shikhar Tuli leads seven co-authors in a language model architecture that mimics multi head attention with state space experts. Recent efficient models replace transformer attention with state space or gated recurrent blocks, but those blocks often emulate only a single attention head, which may limit expressiveness. Their MossNet uses a mixture of experts design, where different specialist blocks handle different inputs, in both channel mixing and time mixing parts.

By placing state space experts in the time mixing kernels, MossNet realizes several attention like heads in linear form. Language modeling and downstream tests show it beating transformer and state space models of similar size and data budget in their experiments. Larger variants trained on trillions of tokens confirm scalability, and phone and GPU profiling shows favorable runtime.
arxiv-2510-26682:
Natasha Van Bemmel, with sixteen co-authors, reports a strikingly fast dwarf nova found by the KiloNova and Transients Program. A dwarf nova is a binary star system whose light flares as gas falls onto a white dwarf. This one, AT2022kak, brightened by more than three magnitudes in a single night and faded back within two nights.

Van Bemmel and the team monitored it for two months with no repeat burst. Three years later, a new outburst during a planned observation let them take time-resolved spectra of the rise and fade. The traits match a dwarf nova, and it ranks among the fastest and faintest seen. Its estimated distance from the Galactic centre and its height above the disk place it in the thick disk. Very few dwarf novae are known there, so it may be a rare Population II system.
arxiv-2510-26982:
Ziling Ma, Angel Lopez-Oriona, Hernando Ombao, and Ying Sun tackle grouping of multivariate time series, meaning several signals tracked together over time. Fuzzy clustering lets each series belong partly to several groups, which suits states like driver drowsiness that change by degree. Older methods often fail on long, uneven, noisy, or high-dimensional records.

Their method, RFCPCA, learns a separate low-dimensional space for each group while trimming outliers and adding a noise group for bad records. It also picks its own settings without hand tuning. On brain-wave records for driver alertness, it beats related methods on accuracy. It also gives clearer uncertainty readings and flags odd series more reliably than the methods compared.
arxiv-2510-27282:
Dominik John, Gregor Breitenhuber, and nine other co-authors report a gentler way to scan tiny tissue samples in 2025. X-ray tomography builds three-dimensional views from many X-ray shots, but the dose can harm living tissue. Weak detectors force long exposures, and contrast tricks need repeat scans. Their setup attacks both faults at once.

The setup joins three parts: a waveguide that shapes the beam, a patterned modulator, and a photon-counting detector, one that tallies each X-ray hit. It reached near the best possible scores on contrast strength and photon catch in their tests. That means sharp views at one-micrometer scale with far less dose. The team says native, living tissue can now be scanned in ways once out of reach.
arxiv-2510-27382:
Sagar Dutta, Banani Basu, and Fazal Ahmed Talukdar detect motor faults with a plain antenna in this 2025 paper. Induction motors drive much of industry, and worn bearings or imbalance can stop a line without warning. Standard checks need costly sensors fitted by experts. Their sensor is an antenna placed near the motor, touching nothing.

The antenna picks up a reflected radio signal that shifts as the motor vibrates. Charts of that signal over time show distinct patterns for each fault type. The team checked the vibration tones against math and measured signal power in each state. A deep learning model then sorted the faults, reaching high accuracy when both signal strength and phase were used. Accuracy stayed strong across radio bands, antenna spots, and time windows.
arxiv-2510-27582:
Richard Karl, Meissa Diouf, Aleksandr Shlykov, Mikolaj Roguski, and Stefan Willitsch describe a fully automated lab system for cold molecular ions in 2025. Such work needs frequent sample prep and exact control of traps and lasers. By hand, the pace is slow and runs need constant care from staff.

Live image checks spot and load single ions into crystals with atomic ions. Trap tweaks then drop extra atoms to leave two-ion strings. Laser pulses are timed to a tiny fraction of a second for quantum logic tests. The system runs alone for long spans, with about ten times more test cycles than hand work. Its modular build suits other labs.
arxiv-2510-27682:
Paolo Antonelli and Yuri Cacchiò study a limit case for a fluid model with a surface-tension-like effect in 2025. The Euler-Korteweg system adds a capillarity term, which resists sharp jumps in density, to the classic Euler flow equations. The question is what happens as that term shrinks to zero inside a smooth domain with no flow through its walls.

Using a relative energy method, which compares two flows by an energy-like gap, they show weak solutions tend to strong Euler solutions. A thin layer near the wall needs a fix to the density profile. Unlike viscous limits, no extra ban on piled-up capillary energy is needed, since this wall layer is weaker. The method may suit other such limits.
arxiv-2511-00082:
Bryce Iversen presents a new method for finding the day of the week of any Gregorian calendar date using simple linear models with truncation. The Gregorian calendar, introduced in October fifteen eighty-two under Pope Gregory the thirteenth, is now the world's dominant calendar, so calendrical computation matters in software. Unlike classic methods, the method avoids memorizing tables of values.

Tables needed for the computation are instead encoded through the linear formulas themselves, keeping the method accurate, fast, and easy to implement. Computing readers get a fresh take on a classic puzzle problem. Day-of-week methods are a rite of passage in recreational mathematics and useful programming alike.
arxiv-2511-00182:
Kelian Sommer, Bertrand Plez, and Johann Cohen-Tanugi present a StarDICE method for fixing ground-based photometry against gray air dimming using same-time thermal infrared records. Surveys like the Rubin Observatory need calibration stable and uniform below one percent even in non-light-based weather, and clouds cause color-neutral dimming that is hard to track. StarDICE aims at a metrology chain from lab standards to astrophysical fluxes.

Thermal infrared data tracks the cloud dimming so visible readings can be fixed in the standard bands. Astronomy readers get calibration progress toward millimagnitude accuracy. Precision photometry supports supernova cosmology, so taming clouds improves distance readings.
arxiv-2511-00582:
Carsten Hartmann and seven co-authors ask whether quantum algorithms can rewire power grids for the better. Distribution grids run as radial networks, trees of lines feeding customers, and choosing the spanning tree with the lowest losses is a routine but hard problem. The authors show that even approximate solutions are computationally hard, which motivates a quantum alternative in the Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz family.

Two algorithmic primitives are derived. One samples only radial topologies directly, building the constraint into the search. The other samples freely and suppresses non-radial shapes with penalty terms. Both are mapped onto the grid reconfiguration problem, and the necessary quantum resources are quantified. The use case grounds abstract quantum optimization in a concrete energy transition task.
arxiv-2511-00782:
Jifan Gao, Michael Rosenthal, Brian Wolpin, and Simona Cristea benchmark simple count based models against newer language model pipelines for predicting outcomes from structured health records. Count based methods group medical codes and feed two time windows into standard learners, and they have long performed well on this kind of data.

Using the EHRSHOT data set and eight prediction tasks, they compare those models with a pretrained record transformer and with a multi agent language model pipeline that turns histories into text summaries. Wins split fairly evenly between the count based and multi agent approaches. Given their simplicity and ease of interpretation, the authors argue count based models remain a strong default for structured record benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-00982:
Thomas Heston introduces the Neutrality Boundary Framework, a geometric way to say how robust a statistical result is. The neutrality boundary is the surface where an effect equals zero. Robustness is then the normalized distance from that boundary, giving a score between zero and one.

The score needs no significance threshold and does not change with sample size, unlike fragility indices that count how many cases must flip to cross a p-value line. Heston proves the score is bounded and monotone, and gives versions for binary outcomes, analysis of variance, and correlation, built from a risk quotient, partial eta squared, and Fisher's z transform. The framework is offered as a complement to effect sizes and p-values across fields.
arxiv-2511-01282:
Min Fang, Zhihui Fu, Qibin Zhao, and Jun Wang speed up language model inference with retrieval enhanced speculative decoding. Speculative decoding drafts upcoming tokens cheaply and lets the big model verify them, but retrieval based drafters switch strategies by fixed heuristics and often retrieve when it does not help.

Their framework, ReSpec, turns those choices into adaptive decisions. An entropy guided trigger starts retrieval only when the context is predictable enough for it to pay off. Feedback from past rounds organizes several high quality candidates for parallel verification. And verification is source aware: strict for model generated drafts, relaxed for retrieved ones. On the Spec-Bench benchmark the authors report state of the art acceleration, beating leading model based and retrieval based systems by over a third.
arxiv-2511-01482:
Neha Sharma, Navneet Agarwal, and Kairit Sirts tackle cognitive distortion detection, the labeling of distorted thinking patterns in text, a task so subjective that even expert annotators agree poorly. That makes the training data itself unreliable. Their proposal is to let large language models do the annotating, repeatedly and independently.

Multiple runs of the same model reveal stable labeling patterns despite the subjectivity, and one leading model produced annotations with strong internal consistency. Models trained on those annotations then performed better on test sets than models trained on human labels. The authors also introduce a dataset agnostic evaluation framework using Cohen's kappa as an effect size, so results can be compared fairly across data sets and studies where F1 scores mislead.
arxiv-2511-01682:
Nicolas Romeo and five colleagues ask a foundational question about self-organization: how robust can a structure built from noisy, fluctuating parts ever be? Living embryos and synthetic nanostructures both assemble precise patterns despite noise. The authors look for a universal limit on that precision. They treat self-organization as a noisy encoding task.

They prove that the positional information capacity of short-range classical systems with discrete states obeys an area-law-like bound, echoing bounds in quantum information. Lattice models saturate the bound only when transport coefficients are fine-tuned. The models were analyzed by exact coarse-graining and dynamical renormalization. The tuning effect is traced to domain wall dynamics at boundaries. A wave-pinning model from biology shows how long-range correlations and global constraints bypass the limit, using integral feedback to relax the tuning.
arxiv-2511-01982:
Pradyun Hebbar, Thandikire Madula, Vinicius Mikuni, Benjamin Nachman, Nadav Outmezguine, and Inbar Savoray ask how machine learning for particle physics can use physical symmetries without being ruled by them. Symmetry is a strong guide for building models. It can bring robustness, data efficiency, and results that are easier to interpret. But models forced to obey a symmetry exactly need special parts, and real detectors blur exact symmetry anyway.

Their method, called SEAL, adds soft constraints instead. The model itself learns how much weight to give each symmetry during training. One route penalizes the model under chosen changes to its inputs. The other draws on group theory and tiny, infinitesimal changes. Tested on top quark jet tagging, with Lorentz symmetry as the test case, the soft approach gave more robust performance. It also needed only negligible changes to current leading models.
arxiv-2511-02082:
Amitabh Basu, Phillip Kerger, and Marco Molinaro prove limits on how much information any algorithm must gather to solve constrained convex optimisation problems. They study two stingy oracles: one that returns first-order information bit by bit in coordinates, and one that answers only whether an inner product with a gradient or separating direction is positive. Each answer carries a single bit.

Under either oracle, they show the information needed grows quadratically with the number of continuous decision variables, a bound not previously known even for purely continuous problems. The bound is tight up to a logarithmic factor, matched by a discretised cutting-plane method. The moral is that the standard bit representation of gradient information is essentially the best possible choice.
arxiv-2511-02282:
Nam Luong, Chuyen Nguyen, and Thanh Pham analyse a wireless system that must communicate and sense at the same time, using light instead of radio. Multiple users share the channel through non-orthogonal multiple access, which stacks their signals with different power levels, while the waveform, an optical version of OFDM, carries both data and radar-like sensing. The catch is that OFDM signals spike in power, and light emitters have a limited range, so the waveform gets clipped and distorted.

The authors propose clipping each user's signal before the superposition step rather than after, softening the distortion's impact. Their analysis covers achievable data rates and error rates for communication, and estimation error and its theoretical bound for sensing distance. Simulations show that giving more power to the stronger user improves rate, errors, and sensing together, while balanced allocation degrades all three.
arxiv-2511-02482:
Rodrigo Bernal and Federico Milano propose a unified way to control the inverters that connect solar, wind, and batteries to the power grid. As spinning generators retire, these inverter-based resources must themselves keep the grid stable and in synchrony, a role called grid-forming control. Many competing schemes exist, and the authors' Generalized Swing Control framework generalises their definition while exploiting how active and reactive power dynamics couple to each other.

The framework was validated with time-domain simulations and small-signal analysis on two test systems. One was a modified version of the standard WSCC nine-bus network, the other a 1,479-bus dynamic model of the all-island Irish transmission system. Configurations studied include single, coupled, and dual virtual synchronous machine schemes. Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis helped tune parameters and check stability across the nonlinear range of behaviours a real grid can show.
arxiv-2511-02582: Jaime Benabent Guerrero and Ramón Flores work in algebraic topology on the Bousfield-Kan completion. It is a standard procedure that completes a space relative to a chosen homology theory. Some spaces are called R-bad when this completion behaves pathologically for the ring R in question, and recognising them matters because such methods silently fail on such spaces. The authors establish criteria for deciding when a space is R-bad, and apply them to closed surfaces, the compact two-dimensional manifolds such as spheres and tori.
arxiv-2511-02682:
Tracking a moving object whose readings live on a curved space calls for special filters. Jordi-Lluis Figueras, Aron Persson, and Lauri Viitasaari extend the well-known extended Kalman filter to the Stiefel manifold in a 2025 paper. That manifold covers readings like points on a sphere and sets of perpendicular axes, both common in tracking work.

The authors test their filter on two settings: points moving on a sphere, and four-by-two matrices with perpendicular columns. In both cases the filter's estimates beat the raw readings by a wide margin. The work gives engineers a general tool for cleaning up noisy data that naturally takes values on these curved spaces, rather than flat ones.
arxiv-2511-02782:
Arbaz Khan, Felipe Lepe, David Mora, Ricardo Ruiz-Baier, and Jesus Vellojin analyze a numerical method for coupled fluid and elastic motion. Such systems govern sloshing tanks and elasto-acoustic vibration. Their 2025 paper uses a displacement and Herrmann pressure form for the solid, and a pure displacement form for the fluid, then seeks the natural frequencies of the joined system.

They propose a nonconforming finite element method that avoids locking, a common stiffness fault. Using theory for non-compact operators, they prove convergence and error bounds. They also build an a posteriori error estimator and show it is both reliable and efficient, so the mesh can be refined where it matters. Tests in two and three dimensions back the theory.
arxiv-2511-02882:
Lahcen Khammich and Driss Kiouach build a stochastic model of an epidemic with stages for susceptible, vaccinated, exposed, infected, and recovered people. Real outbreaks wobble randomly, so their 2025 model perturbs the system with a Black-Karasinski process, a mean-reverting noise used in finance. They ask the two classic questions: when does the disease persist, and when does it fade?

Using a Lyapunov function method, they derive a threshold condition for a stationary distribution to exist, which signals long-term persistence. Below a second threshold, the disease dies out at an exponential rate. Their headline result is that random fluctuations can help an outbreak take hold, not only hinder it. The analysis gives health modelers a sharper picture of noise-driven epidemics.
arxiv-2511-03182:
Vinaik Chhetri, Moghis Fereidouni, A. Siddique, and Umar Farooq test whether editing a code model, rather than retraining it, can teach it updated programming interfaces. Libraries change after training, and models keep calling the old versions. Their 2025 benchmark builds 2,040 problems from three standard sets, covering 140 synthetic API changes, with a sandbox that enforces the new interfaces when code runs.

Under a single edit, models generalized poorly to new uses of the changed API. Many apparent passes were workarounds, not true adoptions of the new call. Work on untouched APIs also slipped. Under repeated edits, most method and model pairs collapsed to near zero on both fronts. Memory-based methods and plain fine-tuning kept specificity best.
arxiv-2511-03282:
Xinyu Ning and colleagues survey how generative artificial intelligence is being paired with extended reality. Extended reality covers virtual and augmented settings where users see and shape digital scenes. The review screens work from 2023 to 2025 with a formal method and keeps twenty-six studies for close analysis.

Across those studies, the authors sort uses by field and by the core tricks that make each system work. They chart fast growth, uneven coverage, and clear gaps where testing or design lags behind claims. Open chances for later work include better content control and smoother live interaction. The survey gives builders and scholars a compact map of a young, fast-moving blend of two fields.
arxiv-2511-03382:
Ievgeniia Korniienko and colleagues build magnetic atom-to-atom force models for nickel oxide, a textbook cubic antiferromagnet. Force models drive simulations of how atoms move, yet adding magnetism for complex antiferromagnets has stayed hard. Their method folds a magnetic energy term, covering both neighbor exchange and a classic sublattice picture, into the base model.

Two versions result, one built on an ionic solid model and one on a reference-free embedded atom style. Both include coupling between magnetism and strain. Checked against density-based calculations, they match mechanical and magnetic traits at zero temperature closely. The recipe should transfer to other cubic antiferromagnets where spin order and lattice shape shape each other.
arxiv-2511-04182:
Christos Tranoris, writing alone, proposes using Git repositories as the medium for async information exchange between spread-out groups, replacing app interfaces and message brokers. The design borrows from Kubernetes operators and custom resources, where a spec states desired state and a status field records what happened.

Publishers and consumers share one repository as a single source of truth, extending GitOps beyond infrastructure into cross-domain and even air-gapped teamwork. Git's versioning, commit signing, and access control supply openness and tracking, and results others can repeat, while systems stay loosely coupled. Design, build choices, and trade-offs against REST and broker designs are covered in full.
arxiv-2511-04282:
L Ducci is the lead author among seven authors reporting a new pulsating ultraluminous X-ray source in the galaxy NGC 4631, found with the XMM-Newton observatory. Periodic pulsations with a period near nine point seven seconds identify the compact object as a neutron star, adding a member to the small pulsating ultraluminous class.

The source also shows one of the largest spin-up rates ever observed for such systems. Two explanations compete: Doppler shift from the neutron star's orbital motion, or genuine spin-up from accretion torque. Its X-ray brightness and spectrum, fit by an absorbed disk blackbody or cut-off power law, resemble other pulsating members. The source should help constrain how super-Eddington luminosities arise.
arxiv-2511-04382:
Yujie Lu leads a team of thirteen authors designing a storage ring light source. Their ring aims to produce high-power, fully coherent radiation in the extreme ultraviolet range. The design uses a Double Bend Achromat lattice, a layout that bends the beam in paired arcs.

Twelve superconducting wigglers strengthen radiation damping and shrink the natural emittance of the beam. A bypass line then generates the coherent output. The team ran full linear and nonlinear beam studies to check stability across the working range. Their optimized design reaches very low emittance, a key step toward a bright EUV source for research and industry.
arxiv-2511-04582:
Hyeonhee Jin, writing alone, studies embedding calculus through Goodwillie-Weiss theory and functor calculus. Building on work by Tillmann and Weiss, Jin constructs a functorial complement for a class of embeddings. Values land in Heuts's categorical approximation of pointed spaces.

An analogue of Stallings' theorem is proved for lower central series in this setting. It covers embeddings of a product manifold times an interval into a disc. As an application, the embedding tower for string links is shown to detect Milnor invariants. The result ties abstract homotopy methods to concrete knot and link invariants.
arxiv-2511-04682:
Eleni Bougioukou and her co-author study how to deploy neural networks across in-memory computing units. In-memory computing cuts data movement by computing where data sits. Convolutional networks must be split across several processing units without wasting their speed.

Their Load-Balance-Longest-Path algorithm assigns network nodes to the available units dynamically. The goal is the highest processing rate with low latency for the full model. Tests run on a multi-unit emulator of the hardware. Balanced placement matters because one overloaded unit can stall the whole network, erasing the gains that in-memory designs promise.
arxiv-2511-04782:
Haochun Ma and his co-author offer a way out of a liquidity trap puzzle in macroeconomics. In the standard New Keynesian model, one shock at the effective lower bound gives wildly different forecasts. The outcome hinges on how long the shock is assumed to persist.

Their fix assumes the shock forces exit from the lower bound in finite time. Under that assumption, the confidence-driven trap cannot arise as an equilibrium. A unique return path exists for each steady state. Government spending then lifts consumption for sure, though the effect may grow without bound, which they flag as a puzzle.
arxiv-2511-04882:
Joon Kim and two colleagues probe bit-flipping attacks against 5G networks and their defenses. Fifth-generation links carry vital traffic at high speed and low delay. Security study has lagged the push for performance, leaving integrity gaps unexplored.

A bit-flipping attacker alters chosen fields of an encrypted message in transit. The mutated message still passes as valid at the receiver, with no decryption needed. The attacker need not know the plaintext, only the meaning of the targeted fields. Mapping where such edits slip through is the first step toward countermeasures for everyday mobile infrastructure.
arxiv-2511-05682:
Yujin Potter leads a team introducing VMDT, the first broad benchmark for trust in video foundation models. Text and image models have such benchmarks, but video models, which both make and describe video, lacked one. Their platform tests models on safety, hallucination, fairness, privacy, and resistance to attack.

The team ran seven text-to-video and nineteen video-to-text models through the suite. Every open-source video generator failed to recognize harmful requests and often produced harmful clips, with more unfairness than image models show. Among describing models, unfairness and privacy risk grew with size, while safety showed no link to size at all. The authors argue video models need far stronger trust work, and offer VMDT to track it.
arxiv-2511-06182:
Peican Lin and co-authors present OpenVLN, a framework that lets drones follow spoken or written directions in open outdoor settings. Vision-language models already guide ground robots, but aerial flight brings harder data collection and much longer routes. OpenVLN aims to handle language-guided flight while training on only limited data.

A reshaped reinforcement learning setup fine-tunes the vision-language model for drone navigation using rule-based policies. A separate long-horizon planner builds flight paths step by step, guided by value-based rewards. On the TravelUAV benchmark, the method raised success rate by up to about four percentage points over baselines, with similar gains on path quality measures.
arxiv-2511-06382:
Myeong-Hwan Mun and colleagues fit scattering data for alpha particles bouncing off carbon-12 nuclei within cluster effective field theory. The analysis includes resonance states below the breakup threshold into a proton and nitrogen-15. Their amplitude expands in effective range parameters for angular momentum states up to six, giving thirty-seven free parameters in total.

More than eleven thousand measured cross-section points pinned those parameters down. A differential evolution search found the same best fit across independent runs, and a Markov chain Monte Carlo check estimated the uncertainties. The final fit matched the experimental cross sections about as accurately as a standard R-matrix analysis, supporting the method for low-energy nuclear physics tied to stars.
arxiv-2511-06882:
Zhipeng Li and Wenjie Ma study streaming codes for relay networks, where data must be decoded with a strict delay even when packets vanish in bursts. In their three-node setup, a source sends through a relay to a destination, and each hop can erase bursts of packets up to certain lengths. Earlier constructions reached the best possible rate only when a divisibility condition held among the delay and burst lengths.

Their extended delay profile method attains the optimal rate under a strictly weaker, relaxed condition on those parameters. That widens the range of network settings where perfectly efficient streaming is provably possible. The authors also show that when the delay margin falls in a certain small range, the optimal rate cannot be achieved within the convolutional code system at all.
arxiv-2511-06982:
Ankit Mazumder and Srikanta Bedathur improve link prediction, the task of guessing which connections a network will form, by adding class-level information that graph neural networks usually ignore. Their system, CGLE, first builds a class-conditioned probability matrix recording how often links form between each pair of node classes. Labels come from ground truth when available, or from clustering otherwise.

That global semantic prior is concatenated with the structural embedding from a backbone graph network and passed to a small classifier for the final prediction. Because CGLE works as a preprocessing stage, it adds no cost to the underlying model's complexity. On benchmark graphs it beat strong baselines by over ten points of HR at 100 on Pubmed and DBLP, and improved ranking quality on the sparse, heterophilous Chameleon graph as well.
arxiv-2511-07082:
A twenty-three-author team from the MEG II experiment reports that oxygen, long considered poison for drift chambers, is in fact essential to theirs. Oxygen is strongly electronegative, so even traces were believed to capture drifting electrons and kill the detector. Yet the MEG II drift chamber at PSI has run for years on a helium-isobutane mixture. That mixture deliberately includes a small amount of isopropanol and half a percent of oxygen by molar concentration.

Measurements show electron capture in this mixture is negligible for proper operation. The results also agree well with Garfield++ simulations once three-body capture is correctly accounted for. The paper documents how a supposedly forbidden ingredient sustains a working precision detector, a useful counterexample for designers of future drift chambers.
arxiv-2511-07482:
Dev Patel and colleagues prune large language models without erasing their safety training. Cutting unused circuits speeds inference, but dynamic pruning that adapts per input can drop safety-critical parts on some prompts. Refusals then fail exactly when they matter most.

Alignment-Aware Probe Pruning keeps circuits tied to safe behavior while trimming the rest. Tests on three open models, including LLaMA and Qwen variants, show refusal rates rising by about half at equal compute. Efficiency and alignment improve together rather than trading off. The method targets real deployments where cost pressure often pushes safety aside.
arxiv-2511-07682:
Michael Hoffmann, Jophin John, and Jan Fillies turn a classic anthropology book into a playable lesson. Malinowski's Lens lets players step into Bronislaw Malinowski during his Trobriand Islands fieldwork retold in Argonauts of the Western Pacific. Retrieval-augmented generation plus image synthesis create steady retro-style visuals.

Indigenous people appear as silhouettes while Malinowski is drawn in detail, a choice meant to spark debate about representation. Trials with non-specialists showed strong learning gains. The game tests whether AI-native design can teach ethnographic method and its ethics together, rather than treating a landmark field study as neutral content to consume.
arxiv-2511-08282:
Eranga Bandara and co-authors propose SRE-Llama, a site uptime engineering platform for communication and networking software that combines several fashionable tools. Keeping cloud native services reliable depends on monitoring tools like Prometheus and Grafana, plus well chosen service level measures and goals. Many developers, however, do not know these tools deeply enough to set good targets and alerts.

Metrics flow into a time series database, federated learning picks the most relevant measures while protecting privacy, and a fine tuned Llama model generates goals, error budgets, and alerts. Blockchain and non fungible token components support the platform design. The goal is automated, accessible uptime management for usual development teams.
arxiv-2511-08482:
David Jaklitsch and Makoto Yamashita work in category theory, a branch of pure mathematics that studies structures through the maps between them. Their subject is the tube algebra, an algebra built from a spherical semisimple multitensor category, and the representations of that algebra, meaning the ways it can act on other objects.

The authors build a braided monoidal structure with a twist on those representations, giving the collection a well-defined way to combine objects and swap them. They then prove this category matches, as a braided tensor category, the Drinfeld center of the ind-category of the starting category. The result extends an equivalence that was previously known only at the linear level.
arxiv-2511-08582:
Michal Heller and three co-authors build a systematic way to solve relativistic hydrodynamics, the theory of hot, fast-moving fluids, as an expansion in gradients. Expansions like this often suffer secular growth, where small errors swell over time and break the calculation.

A covariant resummation scheme reorganizes the degrees of freedom at each order while keeping the total unchanged, and the authors spell out the first two orders. At first order the known BDNK equations appear as an intermediate step in the Landau frame. Modes that are not hydrodynamic show up only inside those intermediate steps and cancel in the final solutions. No extra fields or starting data are needed beyond ideal fluid theory.
arxiv-2511-08982:
Preesha Gehlot and three co-authors teach graph neural networks to approximate a hard reasoning problem from formal argumentation. In assumption-based argumentation, arguments are built from premises through rules, and deciding which assumptions survive under stable semantics is intractable for large systems, so a learned shortcut has real value.

Each framework becomes a graph whose nodes are assumptions, claims, and rules, with typed edges for support, derivation, and attack. Two architectures stack residual mixed layers, one convolutional and one attention-based, to embed the nodes. Trained on the ICCMA 2023 benchmark plus synthetic systems, with Bayesian hyperparameter search, both beat an adapted state-of-the-art baseline, reaching node-level F1 up to zero point seven one. A sound polynomial-time reconstruction then turns predictions into full extensions, scoring above zero point eight five on small systems.
arxiv-2511-09682:
Tiansheng Huang and four co-authors defend audio reasoning models against jailbreak attacks delivered through sound. Audio language models that can reason are spreading, but their safety under attack was unstudied. Standard reasoning training with safety data blocks naive audio jailbreaks, the authors first show, yet fails against their stronger attacks.

The failure traces to representation drift: advanced jailbreaks push the model's internal representations far from anything safety training covered. Their method, Rebellion, trains the model to withstand the worst-case drift explicitly. On the Qwen2-Audio model, Rebellion resists advanced audio jailbreaks without hurting benign-task performance, they report. Its accuracy-safety trade-off significantly beats standard robust training in their experiments.
arxiv-2511-09982:
Marius Tărnăuceanu, writing alone, determines the Reidemeister spectrum of ZM-groups, a specific family of groups in algebra. For a group automorphism, two elements count as equivalent when one can be reached from the other by a twisted conjugation formula. The number of equivalence classes is the Reidemeister number of that automorphism, and the spectrum collects these numbers over all automorphisms of the group.

Computing a full spectrum is usually difficult, since it requires understanding every automorphism at once. For ZM-groups, Tărnăuceanu carries out that determination completely, extending results from an earlier cited work. The paper adds one more family to the list of groups whose Reidemeister spectra are known exactly, a classification-style contribution to group theory.
arxiv-2511-10182:
Yiran Zhang, Mingyang Lin, Mark Dras, and Usman Naseem present VISTA, a web-based visual tool for inspecting how large language models reason across multi-turn conversations. Multi-turn reasoning mirrors real problem solving, but tangled context makes the process hard to analyze and loads researchers heavily. VISTA visualizes how earlier context influences each model decision, turning an opaque transcript into something explorable.

Users can edit conversation histories interactively to run what-if comparisons across models. The platform also parses a session automatically and draws a reasoning dependency tree, exposing the model's step-by-step logical path. VISTA is open source and accepts custom benchmarks and local models.
arxiv-2511-10282:
Adrien Lafage, Olivier Laurent, Firas Gabetni, and Gianni Franchi present Torch-Uncertainty, an open library that gives deep learning models honest estimates of their own uncertainty. Neural networks perform impressively yet often cannot say how unsure they are, which blocks use in critical applications. Many quantification techniques exist, but no unified tool offered a smooth workflow to train with them and evaluate them together.

Built on PyTorch and Lightning, the framework streamlines training and evaluation with a range of uncertainty methods and metrics. The paper lays out the library's design principles and benchmarks a diverse set of methods across classification, segmentation, and regression tasks. The authors aim to make uncertainty quantification a routine part of deep learning practice rather than a specialist add-on.
arxiv-2511-10382:
Zhen Chen and six co-authors examine tools meant to protect personal photos from AI personalization systems such as DreamBooth. Those systems can learn a person's face from a few images and reproduce it. Defenses like Anti-DreamBooth add crafted noise to photos so the learning fails, but the authors find two serious weaknesses in that approach.

First, the added noise often shows as visible patterns or stripes, so protected photos look tampered with. Second, the noise is fragile: even a simple, non-learned filter can wash it away and restore the model's ability to memorize a face. Their test framework, AntiDB_Purify, shows no current defense keeps working under such cleaning, leaving users with a false sense of security.
arxiv-2511-10782:
Milagros Colazo and Alvaro Alvarez-Candal assemble the largest color census yet of trans-Neptunian objects, the icy bodies beyond Neptune. They merge data from the Sloan survey, Col-OSSOS, the Dark Energy Survey, and the new Rubin Observatory's First Look release, totaling more than forty-three thousand measurements.

From these they derive phase curves for 781 objects and absolute colors for 633. Colors at opposition correlate with how colors change as the viewing angle grows: redder objects tend to redden further, bluer ones to turn bluer. Once phase effects are corrected, the colors show no strong two-group split and no clear link to orbital properties. The sample includes the first Rubin photometry of eight objects, five of them newly discovered, reaching faint magnitudes the full survey will exploit.
arxiv-2511-10882:
Parashmoni Kashyap, Liton Majumdar, and their colleagues study the chemistry of the planet-forming disk around the young star HD 163296. They use sharp radio views from the ALMA telescope in four bands. The disk is near, large, and rich in spectral lines, so it works well for this kind of test.

The team maps ten kinds of molecules and fits how much of each is present and how warm the gas is. Their models point to a carbon-to-oxygen balance just above one. They also set strict upper limits for two larger molecules and map one rare form in the finest detail yet, showing rings that match the dust rings.
arxiv-2511-11182:
Dayong Liang, Xiao-Yong Wei, and their colleagues introduce MUG, a protocol that hunts hallucinated agents inside multi-agent debates about images and text. Debate among agents can boost reliability, but it assumes each debater reasons honestly, which fails when agents themselves hallucinate. Social deduction games, where players hunt a hidden impostor, supply the model for a fix.

MUG edits reference images to plant counterfactual evidence, then watches which agents notice the change. Agents that miss it are flagged as hallucinating, giving a ground-truth check beyond mere consensus. The design adds cross-checks over changing evidence, aiming for sturdier joint reasoning.
arxiv-2511-11382:
Gonzalo Barriga, Carla Henríquez-Baez, and their colleagues construct self-gravitating tube-like solitons held up by pi- and omega-mesons. The setting is an Einstein nonlinear sigma model coupled to omega vector mesons in four spacetime dimensions. The tubes carry a topological charge, read as baryon number, and stay free of curvature singularities, the points where gravity models usually break down.

Using a maximal embedding of the two-flavor case into the general flavor case, the team builds tubes for any number of flavors, with charge scaling in step. In the flat-space limit, total energy grows with flavor count while binding energy falls. The authors argue that adding flavors steadily improves the model's physical predictions.
arxiv-2511-11582:
Orfeu Bertolami revisits the Drake equation, the famous product of factors meant to estimate how many advanced civilizations might exist in our galaxy. More than six decades after it was proposed, and after thousands of exoplanet discoveries, it remains nearly the only quantitative tool for the question besides direct searches that have found nothing.

Attention falls on how Bayesian inference should handle the equation's deeply uncertain factors, and on what the Fermi question, where are the aliens, really implies. Astrobiology has strengthened the discussion, but each factor still hides wide disagreement. Readers get a careful tour of why a simple formula raises hard problems in probability, philosophy, and the search for life.
arxiv-2511-11782:
Sascha Desmettre and three co-authors build a way to fit the hidden values of hybrid stochastic systems. These systems mix smooth random drift with sudden jumps. They suit insurance, biology, and plant control problems. Their worth depends on good fits to observed paths.

The tool is approximate Bayesian computation. It scores fits by comparing simulated paths with real data. Path simulators are spelled out in detail. Summary statistics from diffusion theory are adapted to the hybrid case. Systems with stable long-run behavior are handled well. Tests show the method finds true values where direct methods stall.
arxiv-2511-12082:
Lokender Singh, Saksham Kumar and Chandan Kumar work on multilabel image classification, where one photo can carry several true labels at once. Their method uses a changed ResNet-101 network and adds probabilistic reasoning, which models links between labels and the doubt in each call. They test it on the COCO-2014 dataset.

In their tests the model beats earlier methods and reaches close to the best known results on this task. They report full checks with measures such as precision and recall, and a mean average precision score above two named baselines. The gain comes, they argue, from treating label links as part of the model rather than as an afterthought.
arxiv-2511-12182:
Yifei Zhu and five co-authors introduce StoL, a framework that builds large molecule shapes from knowledge learned only on small molecules. Getting accurate three-dimensional forms for large molecules at quantum level is slow, and training data for large cases are scarce. StoL works from a SMILES string, which encodes a molecule as text.

The system splits the molecule into valid fragments, makes three-dimensional forms for each with a diffusion model trained on small molecules, then assembles them like blocks. Chemical rules guide key steps, so the assembled forms stay plausible and varied. Checks against density functional calculations support the approach, which needs no large-molecule training data.
arxiv-2511-12682:
Amirpasha Hedayat and Karthik Duraisamy build a lean framework for short-range weather prediction. Weather is a chaotic, high-dimensional system, and recent AI forecasters need heavy computing to handle it. Their approach first compresses weather fields with a convolutional autoencoder strengthened by attention blocks. It then learns a simple linear operator in a time-delayed version of that compressed space. The dynamics are advanced by cheap linear steps rather than by a large neural network at every moment.

On the ERA5 reanalysis dataset, the system predicted weather patterns inside its training period well. It struggled more when pushed into future periods beyond the training window. Their analysis points to projection error, the loss from compressing the weather state, as the main bottleneck rather than the step forward itself. They suggest pairing such models with larger AI systems where budgets are tight.
arxiv-2511-12782:
Thomas Rivasseau proposes a simple defense for large language models: sprinkle control sentences through long user inputs. Alignment research has shown that the chance of a successful jailbreak grows as user input or conversation length grows, because harmful instructions can hide in a sea of text. Rivasseau's interruptions are control statements inserted at regular intervals through the input. They are meant to reassert the model's alignment instructions at a rate that scales with the input itself.

The four-page note also suggests carrying the idea into chain-of-thought reasoning, where inserted checks might interrupt scheming before it develops. The proposal is brief and conceptual rather than experimental: it names a mechanism and where it could apply, without benchmarks or proofs. Readers should treat it as a design sketch for length-resistant alignment.
arxiv-2511-12982:
Xuankun Rong and five co-authors make multimodal models reason about safety under rules they can be graded against. A text-image pair can be harmless in each part and unsafe combined, and current multimodal models notice such compositional risks poorly. SafeGRPO builds on group relative policy optimization, which refines a model using its own sampled outputs as the reward signal. Adds rule-governed reward construction so that safety reasoning gets verifiable feedback instead of vibes. Training uses a purpose-built dataset of three thousand examples tagged for visual, textual, and combined safety.

The model is trained to think about safety step by step, in a structured way the rules can check. Across diverse benchmarks the authors report stronger multimodal safety awareness, better compositional robustness, and steadier reasoning, without sacrificing general capability. Rules give the self-improvement loop something solid to push against.
arxiv-2511-13082:
Kyunghyun Lee and six co-authors predict where a breast tumor moves during biopsy, in real time. MRI-guided biopsy finds lesions well but ties up an expensive scanner. An indirect version works outside the scanner room, yet the breast deforms under instruments, so the recorded cancer site shifts. The team first builds a patient-specific finite element model from MRI data to simulate that deformation. A graph neural network then learns to predict the full tissue displacement from surface motion and distance data.
