On phantom and real patient data, predicted cancer positions landed within a fifth of a millimeter of the truth, and the predicted regions overlapped the real ones almost completely. The network also ran more than four thousand times faster than the finite element simulation it learned from, .
arxiv-2511-13182:
Mihai Nadas and Laura Diosan test how well large language models restore Romanian diacritics. Romanian text often loses its accent marks in digital form, and putting them back correctly matters for search, translation, and reading. The authors assembled a comprehensive corpus and tried models from several families: OpenAI's GPT-3.5, GPT-4. GPT-4o, Google's Gemini 1.0 Pro, Meta's Llama 2 and Llama 3, Mixtral, airoboros, and a Romanian-tuned RoLlama model. Each was tested under prompt templates ranging from zero-shot to complex multi-shot instructions.

GPT-4o restored diacritics with high accuracy, consistently beating a neutral echo baseline. Other models, including the Llama family, varied much more. The authors conclude that model architecture, training data, and prompt design all shape performance on this task. For builders of NLP tools for diacritic-rich languages, the study maps which general models can be trusted with the detail work and where specialized effort is still needed.
arxiv-2511-13282:
Kaiwen Wang and 4 co-authors address the recovery of 3D body meshes for many people from a single photo. Training data for wild scenes is scarce, and older labeling methods treated each person alone. That habit produced crowds with clashing depths and scales inside one image.

Their Depth-conditioned Translation Optimization step refines all crowd placements at once, using height priors and depth cues in a principled framework. Applied to a large dataset, it yields over half a million scene-consistent images. A second network then predicts mesh and camera values in true metric scale, reaching top results on depth reasoning and mesh recovery tests.
arxiv-2511-13582:
Alfonso Cevallos, Robert Hambrock, and Alistair Stewart introduce the Merkle Mountain Belt, a commitment structure for ordered lists aimed at blockchain light clients. A light client, such as a phone wallet, must check single items against a public commitment without downloading the whole list. Older structures each miss one key trait: compact first sync, cheap frequent resync, or constant-time updates.

The Mountain Belt is the first structure to be succinct, incremental, and optimally additive at once, and a variant stays usable while out of sync. Its slightly unbalanced shape gives newer items shorter proofs than older ones. In systems where queries favor recent data, that tilt lowers the average cost for light clients.
arxiv-2511-13682:
Pierre-Luc Thériault and 6 co-authors engineer molecules to boost the second-order nonlinear response of evaporated organic films. Such films orient themselves during vapor deposition, avoiding the poling step that complicates photonics production. Starting from a donor-acceptor base molecule, they made four variants aimed at stronger molecular response or better self-orientation.

The winning change locks an internal bridge, raising both the molecular response and the favorable orientation by cutting harmful electrostatic clashes during deposition. The best film doubled the parent material's response at telecom wavelengths. Careful analysis showed better orientation, not raw molecular strength alone, drove most of the gain, a design lesson for future nonlinear films.
arxiv-2511-13882:
A. F. Kemper and 26 co-authors survey a hybrid style of quantum computing that mixes two kinds of quantum units. Most machines use discrete-variable qubits, but continuous-variable modes, which behave more like waves, can be added alongside them. The authors set out when this combined approach helps and what it is good for.

The guide walks through candidate uses in physics, chemistry, and computer science, and explains the gains the hybrid modes can bring, such as richer native operations. It also covers the algorithmic and software questions the new style raises. The paper serves as an entry point for researchers weighing whether hybrid machines fit their problems.
arxiv-2511-13982:
Francesco Navarra, Ayesha Asloob Qureshi, and Giancarlo Rinaldo study rook polynomials, counting functions for placing chess rooks on a board so that no two share a row or column. A variant called the switching rook polynomial is conjectured to match an algebraic invariant of a ring built from the board's cells. Whether it reads the same forwards and backwards matters, because that symmetry signals a Gorenstein ring.

The authors define a new property of cell collections, domino-stability, and prove the switching rook polynomial is palindromic exactly when the collection has that property. The equivalence gives fresh insight into which algebras built from polyominoes and other cell shapes are Gorenstein.
arxiv-2511-14282:
Vincent-Daniel Yun, Junhyuk Jo, and Sunwoo Lee train neural networks that survive aggressive pruning. Cutting a trained model down in one shot, without retraining, often wrecks accuracy because standard training spreads importance across many weights. Their weight concentration regularizer instead pushes energy into a small set of parameters during training and drives the rest toward zero.

Magnitude pruning then removes mostly weights that contribute almost nothing. Earlier regularizers either shrank all weights evenly or produced scale-invariant sparsity; this one explicitly concentrates. The authors supply a convergence analysis and test the method on language model fine-tuning, image classification, and medical segmentation, finding consistent gains in pruning robustness across architectures.
arxiv-2511-14382:
Eknath Ghate explains, in lecture-note form, how the mod p reduction of semi-stable Galois representations can be completely determined. The setting is the local Langlands correspondence, which matches representations of the p-adic Galois group with objects on the automorphic side. Ghate begins with an Iwahori-theoretic reformulation of the mod p correspondence and the classical functional analysis behind the attached Banach spaces.

He then sketches how to reduce a lattice inside the Banach space attached to a two-dimensional semi-stable representation. Combined with the mod p correspondence, that fixes the reduction. It covers a full range of weights and all values of the L-invariant. The notes, summarizing joint work with Anand Chitrao, stress motivation over completeness.
arxiv-2511-14482:
Tim Schwabe and Maribel Acosta propose a gradient based method for ordering joins in database queries. Join order strongly affects how fast a query runs, yet finding the best order is a hard search problem. Classic methods search over discrete tree plans with a cost model. That search forces trade offs between speed and plan quality.

When the cost model can be differentiated, plans can be relaxed into a soft matrix form. Gradient search can then move through that relaxed space toward low cost plans. Using a graph neural network as the cost model, the method finds plans as good as or better than discrete search. Its run time also scales more favorably.
arxiv-2511-14582:
Keda Tao and five co-authors present OmniZip, a method to speed up models that jointly process audio and video. Long token sequences make such omnimodal models costly to run. Past compression methods treated each modality separately. OmniZip instead lets audio guide how video tokens are pruned, without any retraining.

It first finds salient audio tokens and scores each time group by information density. Video tokens are then compressed with an interleaved space and time scheme. Cross modal similarity keeps audio anchored cues in view. Broad tests show faster inference with strong understanding retained. The training free design makes the method easy to add to existing large models.
arxiv-2511-14682:
Vaskar Chakma, MD Jaheid Hasan Nerab, and four co-authors test whether machine learning can flag smoking-related health decline early. Smoking harms the heart, liver, kidneys, and metabolism, yet routine screening often misses the first warning signs. The team compares three prediction methods on health screening records from more than fifty-five thousand people.

The study weighs Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM models using body measures, blood tests, and personal background data. The authors stress clear, explainable results that clinics could actually use, rather than chasing a novel algorithm. Their comparison shows which approach best picks out people at high risk, which could help doctors act before late-stage disease sets in.
arxiv-2511-14782:
S H Wassegh presents an observable for the laser ranging instrument aboard the GRACE-FO satellites, a pair of spacecraft that measure Earth's gravity by tracking the distance between them with great precision. Standard ranging analysis needs the two spacecraft clocks synchronised, and low-level systematics can hide in the data. Wassegh's observable is built from successive differences of pulse intervals in one-way ranging, a construction that suppresses first-order Doppler effects and cancels static and slow biases without any clock synchronisation.

Applied to instrument data from four seasonal stretches of 2019, the method reveals a stable, narrow modulation at exactly the orbital frequency. Its amplitude and phase stay consistent across all sets, pointing to a deterministic origin inside the mission itself. Synthetic signal injections, shuffle tests, and comparison with the microwave ranging system confirm the detection independently.
arxiv-2511-14882:
Michael T. Goodrich, Songyu Liu, and Ioannis Panageas study how to rebuild a hidden weighted network by asking questions about it. The learner knows the nodes but not the links or their weights, and an oracle answers queries such as shortest path lengths. Rebuilding the full graph exactly is the goal, a problem also known as graph reconstruction.

The authors show that simple shortest-path questions alone cannot always pin the graph down. They then design combined queries, bundling two or three simple ones, that do recover the graph with far fewer questions than the number of possible links. Efficient reconstruction matters wherever networks must be inferred indirectly, from road systems to molecular structures.
arxiv-2511-15182:
Subhashis Hazarika and four co-authors present SWR-Viz, an interactive visual analytics approach for ship weather routing. Fast, lower emission shipping needs good outlooks and adaptive routes. Operational use lags due to forecast delays and the need for human judgment under changing seas. Their system couples a physics based neural wave forecast with an established routing engine.

Near term outlooks are generated directly from current settings, with assimilation of sparse observations. Interactive emissions analytics support rapid what if route exploration. Tests along Japan coast and Gulf of Mexico corridors show stable outlooks and realistic routes. Expert feedback praises usability and voyage isolation tools. The approach aims to bring advanced routing into daily maritime practice.
arxiv-2511-15282:
Ninell Oldenburg, Ruchira Dhar, and Anders Søgaard argue that AI research is quietly split by two rival pictures of what intelligence is. One picture, realism, treats intelligence as a single universal capacity that any system can be measured against. The other, pluralism, sees many context-bound capacities that no single scale can capture.

Tracing current debates, the authors show these hidden commitments steer the field in concrete ways. They shape how models are selected, how benchmarks are designed, and how results are validated, and they change what counts as evidence in the first place. Naming the split, the paper suggests, would let researchers argue about the real disagreement instead of talking past each other.
arxiv-2511-15482:
Ainara Saiz-Pérez, Christian M. Fromm, Yosuke Mizuno, Matthias Kadler, Karl Mannheim, and Ziri Younsi investigate why the glowing ring around the black hole in galaxy M87 looks bigger at lower radio frequency. Recent images show the ring at a lower frequency about half again as large as the ring seen at a higher frequency. The team asks what role fast, hot electrons play in that change.

They run three-dimensional simulations of gas swirling into the black hole, then compute the radio glow from both thermal and faster electrons. The lower frequency ring is always larger, due to stronger self-absorption and mixed glow from the disk and jet base. Results match the observed size well.
arxiv-2511-15582:
O. Moreno Segura, Y. Pavlyukh, and R. Tuovinen map when a fast approximation for electron motion stays stable. Predicting real-time dynamics in correlated materials is costly with exact two-time methods. The Generalized Kadanoff-Baym Ansatz offers propagation that grows only linearly with time, but it can behave in uncontrolled ways, so users need to know its safe range.

The test system is a Holstein dimer, a minimal model of electrons coupled to vibrations. With a consistent treatment of that coupling, the authors chart regions where the approximation is stable and where it fails. Failures trace to changes in ground-state solutions, and attaching electronic leads can damp or partly cure the instability, giving practical checks for future simulations.
arxiv-2511-15682:
Akshay Gaikwad, Manuel Sebastian Torres, and Anton Frisk Kockum speed up quantum measurement tomography. That task learns exactly what a quantum detector measures from lab data. A detector is described by a set of measurement operators. Estimating them by standard methods can be slow. Their method borrows mini-batch stochastic gradient descent, a workhorse of machine learning that updates estimates from small data samples at a time.

Two parameter schemes keep the rebuilt operators valid, meaning positive and complete. One works on a special curved space of matrices. The other rescales eigenvalues of Hermitian operators. Two loss types are tested. In simulations for both discrete and continuous systems, the new methods ran at much lower cost than leading methods.
arxiv-2511-15782:
Martyna Chruślińska, Mirko Curti, and five co-authors separate the cosmic history of oxygen and iron production. Stars forge oxygen and iron on different timescales, so their ratio varies widely between stellar populations. The two elements also play different roles: oxygen mainly sets how gas cools, while iron shapes stellar atmospheres and the light stars emit, yet observations of distant galaxies usually measure oxygen alone.

Using an observed link between the oxygen-to-iron ratio and how fast a galaxy forms stars relative to its mass, they derive separate star formation histories for each element. Most cosmic stellar mass formed at non-solar ratios, and average iron metallicity runs well below oxygen metallicity, with the gap growing toward earlier cosmic times.
arxiv-2511-15882:
Sida Chen, Jessica K. Barrett, and three co-authors improve how biomarker variability is modeled when forecasting disease outcomes. A biomarker is a measurable sign in the body, like a blood level. Interest is growing in how much it wiggles over time, not just its level, as a sign of risk. One view measures the roughness of the hidden biomarker path, but judging it needs joint models of repeated measures and event times.

The path shape is key and hard to set. The authors compare three Bayesian semiparametric methods inside joint models. Two are new: one uses penalized splines, the other uses functional principal components. Tests show better inference and forecasts, and a cystic fibrosis registry shows the methods at work.
arxiv-2511-16082:
Colin Burke and three co-authors test whether local analogs of distant Little Red Dots vary in brightness over decades. Little Red Dots are compact red sources seen in the early universe. Three nearby metal poor dwarf active galaxies resemble them closely. Long photometric and spectroscopic records spanning about twenty years let the team measure true variability.

Optical continuum variability is extremely low, below a few percent for all three objects. Broad hydrogen emission shows the same quiet behavior in multi epoch spectra. Normal dwarf active galaxies and quasars vary far more strongly. Structure functions lack the usual active galaxy pattern entirely. The stillness constrains what powers Little Red Dots and warns against assuming standard accretion variability.
arxiv-2511-16282:
Gergely Dinya and four co-authors present a system that builds three-dimensional maps with object meaning attached, fast enough for near real-time use such as helping a person navigate. Their pipeline rests on VGGT, a transformer that infers scene geometry from images, but VGGT alone uses too much memory for a continuous video stream.

The system processes images in a sliding window and aligns the local submaps into one growing map. It reuses the VGGT tracking head to lift two-dimensional instance masks into three-dimensional objects. It stores timestamps and object identities so changes in a room can be spotted later. Tests on standard benchmarks and on custom assistive navigation data show the approach holds up in real-world scenes while staying memory efficient.
arxiv-2511-16482:
Poushali Sengupta, Yan Zhang, Frank Eliassen, and Sabita Maharjan introduce ExCIR, an explainable AI method that says which input features drive a model's output while taking links between features seriously. Standard global attribution tools are often costly, unstable when inputs correlate, and hard to scale to large mixed datasets.

ExCIR scores features by sign-aligned co-movement with the output after robust centering, and a lightweight transfer protocol reproduces full-model rankings from a fraction of the data. A groupwise version, BlockCIR, scores clusters of correlated features together, avoiding double counting among near-duplicates. Across text, tabular, signal, and image data, the rankings matched known baselines and the full model while running faster, offering practical explanations for deployed systems.
arxiv-2511-16882:
Tim Menzies and six co-authors release MOOT, a repository of more than a hundred and twenty real multi-objective optimization tasks from software engineering. In these tasks, decisions trade off speed against cost, security against usability, accuracy against interpretability. Researchers have long tested methods on toy problems or a handful of examples.

The tasks cover software configuration, cloud tuning, project health, process modeling, and hyperparameter optimization, with sample scripts that load the data and generate baselines in one step. The authors are explicit that the novelty is infrastructural, curated data and research enablement rather than new algorithms. With MOOT, studies of stability, sample efficiency, failure modes, and cross-domain generality can run across the whole collection. That makes software engineering optimization research harder to fool and easier to reproduce.
arxiv-2511-17082:
Anna A. Taranenko extends a classic test from the algebra of latin squares to higher dimensions. A latin square is a grid where each symbol appears once per row and column. A famous criterion says such a square comes from a group table exactly when all its quadrangles agree. Reformulated geometrically, the most group-like squares contain the most octahedra, a link found by Gowers and Long.

Taranenko states a multidimensional version of the condition for latin hypercubes, using small submatrices rebuilt from a handful of entries, and in terms of cuboctahedra, the higher-dimensional shapes that replace octahedra. She shows the most associative multidimensional quasigroups have tables whose every flat slice is group-like. Lower bounds on cuboctahedra counts, plus computations, round out the picture for these structures.
arxiv-2511-17282:
Chuancheng Shi and 11 co-authors document a cultural blind spot in text-to-image models. Asked in different languages for culturally specific scenes, current models often return culturally neutral or English-biased pictures, even though language carries cultural connotations that the image should reflect. Studying two representative multilingual models, the authors find the problem is not missing knowledge: the cultural information is present in the network but too weakly activated.

A probing method locates the culture-sensitive signal in a small set of neurons within a few layers. Two fixes follow from that map. One amplifies those neurons at inference time, with no retraining; the other fine-tunes only the culturally relevant layers. On their CultureBench benchmark, both strategies improved cultural consistency over strong baselines while preserving image fidelity and diversity.
arxiv-2511-17382:
Patricia Ribes-Metidieri, Ivan Agullo, and Béatrice Bonga challenge a received conclusion about entanglement in de Sitter space, the rapidly expanding spacetime of cosmology. Entropy-based studies of patches, and studies of Fourier modes, had suggested that curvature enhances entanglement. The authors take a fully local approach instead, examining pairs of field modes confined to compact regions inside the cosmological patch. The approach is framed through a metric and complex structure that the Bunch-Davies vacuum induces on phase space.

They find curvature raises links between local modes but, against intuition, lowers their entanglement. Their methods also map how the entanglement is spread in space, showing that even a tiny cosmological constant alters the vacuum's entanglement structure in kind. Properly interpreted, they argue, the results agree with the older entropy studies. The distinction matters for entanglement between observables created during cosmic inflation.
arxiv-2511-17582:
Jie Ou and three co-authors make lightweight fine-tuning of large models pay attention to which tokens deserve adaptation. Parameter-efficient methods update a small low-rank patch instead of the whole model, but they apply the same static update to every token, wasting capacity on trivial content and under-adapting the informative parts. GateRA adds adaptive gating to the update path, so each token's update strength is modulated: well-modeled inputs keep the pretrained knowledge, hard cases get the capacity.

Visualizations show the gates behaving differently across generation phases, suppressing redundant early tokens and emphasizing decoding. An entropy-based penalty pushes gate decisions toward confident, near-binary choices, giving sparse, interpretable adaptation without hard thresholds. Theory shows the gating softens into a gradient-masking effect over the adaptation path. On commonsense reasoning benchmarks, GateRA matched or beat prior efficient fine-tuning methods.
arxiv-2511-17982:
Jiayi Luo and six co-authors attack graph foundation models, models pre trained on varied graph data and adapted to new tasks, by planting a hidden backdoor. A backdoor is hard here because the attacker does not know the downstream task, triggers must hide across domains, and fine tuning may erase them.

Their attack links a trigger to prototype embeddings without label knowledge, generates a custom trigger per node, and anchors the backdoor in parameters that fine tuning barely changes. Extensive experiments show the attack stays effective, stealthy, and persistent, exposing a real security risk.
arxiv-2511-18082:
Wencheng Ye and five co-authors shrink vision language action models, which let robots act from images and instructions but run too slowly for handy manipulation. Earlier compression focused on vision and language links, not on the action predictions that matter most at run time.

Their ActDistill method distills a trained teacher into a light student guided by action structure, modeled as a graph of how predictions evolve. A dynamic router picks computation paths per input, and extra graph parts are removed at inference. On embodied benchmarks the student matches or beats full models with over half the computation removed.
arxiv-2511-18182:
Lee Ackerman proposes that the workflow itself is the medium in human-AI co-creation, and builds a framework called the Creative Intelligence Loop around that claim. The loop gives dynamic teamwork between a person and several AI collaborators a disciplined structure, while the human stays the final judge of ethics and creative integrity. Ackerman demonstrates the approach through the making of two graphic novellas, a subjective field with no objective score to lean on.

The process surfaced familiar hazards: AI skill that is strong in patches and weak in others, a tendency to flatter, and scarce human attention for feedback. Working through them produced a multi-sided critique system and refined teaming habits. The paper offers those lessons as guidance for responsible creative partnerships with AI.
arxiv-2511-18582:
David Almog shows that worry about how one looks can block good use of AI help at work. In a field experiment on a large online labor market, he hired hundreds of United States based remote workers for an image sorting job with AI advice on hand. Pay hopes rested on an evaluator's view of their work.

Workers took the AI advice less when their reliance was visible to the evaluator, and task scores fell in a clear way. The gap held though workers knew the evaluator was told to grade accuracy on that same AI aided task. Praise for past strong work did not close the gap. Image concerns, the study finds, are hard to soothe and cost real output.
arxiv-2511-18682:
Xiang Gao, Xinmu Wang, Zhou Zhao, Junqi Huang, and Xianfeng David Gu unwrap phase maps for structured light 3D scans in a staged graph cut flow. Scanners project striped light and read phase wrapped to a circle; the true phase needs an unknown whole count of turns per pixel. Noise, blocked zones, and bent shapes make that count hard to guess.

Their method leans on an invariance tied to smooth surface warps, framed by diffeomorphisms. A hierarchy of graph cuts then picks the counts with both speed and care, where past tools traded one for the other. Clean phase feeds depth builds for faces and bodies in motion. Uses span virtual scenes, digital humans, and medical imaging.
arxiv-2511-18782:
Lukas Twist and Jie M. Zhang ask if a plain language summary of buggy code helps a language model fix it. Model code often holds small flaws with large effects. Their test is prompt only: a model first sums up the faulty code, then drafts a repair guided by that summary.

Trials span eight models and two repair sets, known bugs and models' own failed attempts. Summaries that name the error and its cause do best, fixing up to about two thirds of unseen errors and beating direct repair by a small margin on average. Gains stay modest and vary by model. A summary alone does not crack hard self repair. The study prices a cheap diagnostic step with care.
arxiv-2511-18882:
Ayca Duran, Christoph Waibel, Bernd Bickel, Iro Armeni, and Arno Schlueter build a pipeline for judging which building facades could carry solar panels. Panels built into facades could decarbonise dense cities where roofs are too small and ground arrays impossible, yet automated planning tools for facades lag far behind those for roofs. Their pipeline first segments a facade image into its architectural parts using a fine-tuned segmentation model trained on a standard facade data set.

Those part labels are then converted into facade-level suitability masks and panel layouts that respect real module sizes and clearances. Applied to several hundred facades of known size across ten cities, the method finds significant installable potential. The work gives planners a detailed, automatic first pass at a resource that simpler tools overlook.
arxiv-2511-18982:
Raz Kupferman, Cy Maor, and David Padilla-Garza lower bound the bending energy of a surface placed in three dimensional space without stretching. The energy, the squared norm of the second fundamental form, matches the Willmore functional. It spikes when curvature piles up in a small zone, as at a cone tip.

One new bound ties the energy to the surface's Gaussian curvature. A second ties it to a Burgers vector, a measure of non flatness linked to torsion. For cones the bounds give the optimal blowup rate as curvature concentrates. For pairs of opposite curvature lumps, dipoles, the Burgers bound gives the optimal rate by system size. Non Euclidean elasticity, where cones and dipoles rule, drives the work.
arxiv-2511-19182:
Hao Wu and Liping Wang present one framework for decentralized optimization, where networked agents jointly minimize a sum of functions without a central coordinator. The functions may be nonconvex, meaning they can have many local dips, and the network is fixed and connected. Many known methods, including gradient tracking and quasi-Newton schemes, fit inside their unified algorithm.

The authors give a single convergence analysis covering both the plain nonconvex case and the stronger Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz condition. New quasi-Newton methods fall out of the framework as special cases. In numerical tests those new methods run very efficiently compared with leading decentralized algorithms.
arxiv-2511-20282:
Da Silva counts how often a family of conic curves has rational solutions. His 2025 paper studies conics with polynomial coefficients. Each conic mixes three squared variables with polynomial weights. The weights depend on many further variables. Whether a rational point exists varies across the family.

An asymptotic formula counts the solvable cases. Parameters of bounded height are tallied precisely. The result matches two standing conjectures in the area. Loughran-Smeets and Loughran-Rome-Sofos both predicted this behavior. The proof leans on a recent circle method advance. Destagnol, Lyczak, and Sofos supplied that key input. Arithmetic functions are averaged over many-variable polynomials. A simpler diagonal conic family is analyzed first. Its coefficients range over arithmetic progressions. Solubility proportions there feed the main count. Analytic number theory gains a sharp family census. Rational point statistics grow more predictable. The circle method stretches to broader polynomial families.
arxiv-2511-20682:
Ioannis Contopoulos, Jérôme Pétri, and Ioannis Dimitropoulos build in 2025 a first-principles route to pulsar radiation. Pulsars are the remains of massive stars, and most of their hardest radiation is thought to come from the equatorial current sheet. That sheet is a layer of electric current around the star's equator. The team distrusts recent particle-in-cell simulations run at unrealistic settings.

Their method first fixes the sheet's shape and field with a steady solution. It then adds extra field parts that appear once dissipation is allowed, and follows the particles they accelerate. About 6 percent of particle pairs meander across the sheet, gaining energy at each crossing. The other 94 percent stay trapped and accelerate in its midplane. The resulting sky maps match a simpler split-monopole model. The authors argue the sheet stays stable because a sideways magnetic component, born of global reconnection, holds it together.
arxiv-2511-20782:
Russel Arbore, Alvin Cheung, and Max Willsey fix in 2025 a blind spot in equality saturation, a compiler technique that rewrites programs non-destructively inside an e-graph holding many equivalent versions at once. Its analysis, e-class analysis, is pessimistic: it assumes the worst about cycles, failing on cyclic code in SSA form, the representation modern compilers use. Optimistic analyses exist elsewhere, but the ill-formed graphs poison them.

The authors design an abstract interpretation algorithm that analyses cycles while staying sound on ill-formed graphs, unifying optimistic analysis with rewriting. They give SSA a new semantics suited to e-graphs and build a prototype optimiser in Rust. On example programs needing both rewriting and optimistic analysis, it succeeds where clang and gcc fall short. The result points to optimisers that reason about loops as confidently as they rewrite expressions.
arxiv-2511-21182:
Avik Kumar Das and five coauthors track a distant blazar across 16 years of telescope data in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The target, TXS 0518+211, is a galaxy whose narrow jet points almost straight at Earth, brightening its glow. The team combined gamma-ray records from Fermi-LAT with optical, ultraviolet, and X-ray light curves from the Swift observatory.

Das and his coauthors split the record into 11 activity epochs and found the X-ray light varied most strongly in every one of them. Links between the bands were only weak to moderate, with correlation coefficients from 0.29 to 0.58 across the epoch pairs. One epoch held an orphan flare, an X-ray surge to about 2.4 times the average level, with no matching rise in optical or ultraviolet light. A two-zone leptonic model, where electrons in two jet regions make the light, fit the full spectrum best.
arxiv-2511-21482:
Shalmali Bandyopadhyay, Briceyda Delgado, Nsoki Mavinga, and Maria Onydio prove that certain coupled reaction systems actually have solutions, in a 2025 analysis paper. Each system pairs two elliptic equations, the kind describing steady diffusion with reactions. The pair is coupled twice over: inside the region, and again in the boundary rules on its edge. Such systems model chemical reactions and interacting species that live in thin boundary layers.

The response rules are quasimonotone, a structured halfway house to full monotone behavior. When extra order conditions hold, Bandyopadhyay and her coauthors iterate between a subsolution and a supersolution, a lower and upper fence. The process traps smallest and largest weak solutions between the fences. When those conditions fail, existence still follows from explicit growth limits on the response rules. Worked examples show the theorems biting on realistic systems, assuring modelers that the steady states they compute are real.
arxiv-2511-22182:
Baker, Pervez, Hawkey, and colleagues pattern perovskite color converters for augmented and virtual reality microdisplays. MicroLED screens promise the needed brightness, but making red, green, and blue at resolutions beyond 5,000 pixels per inch, where a full color pixel spans five micrometers, is the bottleneck. Perovskite nanocrystals absorb blue light far more strongly than quantum dots. Their optical density per micrometer is over twice that of cadmium-based dots and five times that of indium phosphide, letting two-to-three-micrometer layers convert color cleanly without extra filters.

The team demonstrates three patterning routes: lift-off, simple but limited to thin layers around half to one micrometer. A perovskite-loaded negative photoresist is mechanically robust but has about 25 percent lower optical density and undercut risks. Dry etching with chlorine plasma is scalable but has poor etch contrast. Together the results argue perovskites are robust, versatile converter materials for high-resolution microdisplays.
arxiv-2511-22382:
Behnke, Gattinger, Wang, and Ghosh compare two compact ways of representing knowledge states for computer checking. Dynamic Epistemic Logic describes how knowledge changes after events such as private announcements, but standard models list every possible world, which explodes in size. Two compact alternatives exist: symbolic structures built from binary decision diagrams, a data structure compressing sets, and succinct models written as mental programs, a small language for agents' reasoning.

The team settles the cost of checking formulas symbolically: model checking for dynamic epistemic logic on these structures is PSPACE-complete. Even plain epistemic logic without dynamics is already PSPACE-complete there, matching the known cost for mental programs. They also give direct translations between the representations. Both can produce exponentially large outputs, and for the direction from mental programs to decision diagrams they prove no smaller translation exists, with the same behaviour conjectured in reverse.
arxiv-2511-22482:
Gonçalves, Cavalin, and Pinhanez investigate a puzzling gap in machine translation for endangered Indigenous languages. Fine-tuning a pre-trained model on a small dataset is the standard recipe for such ultra-low resource languages. Two related Brazilian languages, Guarani Mbya and Nheengatu, were translated with the same method and similar data. Earlier work reported SacreBLEU scores of about 12 and 38 respectively, a huge difference with no clear explanation.

The team systematically varied the suspected causes: data cleaning, pre-trained model limits, model size, and training data size, in both directions. None explained the gap; model size made no difference, and data size had limited impact. The best results came from the smaller NLLB model, though with wide variation. They conclude that structural differences between the languages, such as predominant word order, likely drive the difference, meaning some language classes need new techniques rather than more fine-tuning.
arxiv-2511-23182:
Furuta and colleagues show how the early universe could in principle have manufactured primordial black holes plentiful enough to be the dark matter, using a twist on multi-field inflation. As the inflating fields pass a symmetry breaking point, a partner field's mass squared turns negative instead of merely vanishing. This triggers a tachyonic resonance that strongly amplifies curvature ripples on small scales while leaving the large scales we observe untouched.

Those amplified ripples collapse into black holes in the asteroid-mass window, from about 10^17 to 10^23 grams. In that window, observations still allow such holes to make up all of the cold dark matter in their benchmarks. The same ripples induce gravitational waves in the deci-hertz band targeted by the future LISA, DECIGO, and BBO interferometers in space. And black hole binaries formed later add merger signals that resonant-cavity experiments could also catch.
arxiv-2512-00082:
Judging how visually complex a web page looks is a task people do at a glance. Divendar Murtadak and Yoon Kim test whether multimodal language models can do it reliably, in a 2025 case study. Their test pages are Amazon search results pages, rated against judgments from human experts.

The authors compare diagnostic prompting with standard prompting based on gestalt principles. Diagnostic prompting improved how well the model matched human complexity judgments in their tests. The study matters for design and retail research, where automated page assessment could speed up work that now needs human raters. Design teams routinely face this judgment when they compare page layouts.
arxiv-2512-00182:
Jayce Getz and co-authors develop a new function space for harmonic analysis on reductive groups in 2025. The space is named in the title after a representation of the group's Langlands dual. Suitable assumptions on that representation shape the whole construction.

Spaces of test functions control which integrals and transforms are well behaved in the Langlands program. That program is a vast web of conjectures linking number theory and representation theory. A well-chosen Schwartz space can make trace formulas and period integrals work more smoothly. The work is deep pure mathematics for specialists in automorphic forms. The assumptions on the representation decide which groups and fields the theory covers.
arxiv-2512-00482:
Speech enhancement models are usually judged only by how clean their output sounds. Yair Amar, Amir Ivry, and Israel Cohen instead probe the internal representations of an enhancement model in 2025. They use MUSE, a transformer-convolutional model trained on the VoiceBank DEMAND corpus.

Activations are analyzed across the encoder, latent space, decoder, and refinement blocks while input noise levels sweep widely. Watching representations change with noise reveals whether the model organizes sounds sensibly or relies on brittle shortcuts. Such probing helps engineers build hearing and communication tools that degrade gracefully in real-world noise. VoiceBank DEMAND is a standard noisy-speech corpus, which makes the probing comparable to other work.
arxiv-2512-00782:
Aviv Aroch, Shimshon Kallush, and Ronnie Kosloff work on controlling noisy quantum gates in a 2025 paper. Quantum systems pick up noise from their surroundings and from imperfect control fields. That noise lowers the fidelity of gates, the basic operations of a quantum computer.

The team uses optimal control, which shapes control pulses carefully to hit a target despite the noise. Their setting is a multilevel system, where each unit holds more than the usual two states, and the noise is thermal. Better pulses for noisy multilevel systems could make quantum hardware more reliable without new materials.
arxiv-2512-00982:
Christoph Pütz classifies certain power series in a 2025 math paper. A Laurent series is like a power series that also allows negative powers. Pütz studies those that converge on the unit circle over a non-Archimedean local field, a number system measured by a prime-like valuation rather than size.

He fully classifies the series that send infinitely many roots of unity to roots of unity. Roots of unity are the special points that multiply back to one after fixed steps. For series over fields of positive characteristic, he proves effective bounds on how many such roots can occur. Classification results pin down rare, rigid behavior.
arxiv-2512-01082:
Praphull Kumar, Dean Townsley, and Hunter Anz study vibrating white dwarf stars in a 2025 astronomy paper. White dwarfs are the final fate of most stars in our galaxy, so they trace stellar history well. Some white dwarfs pull matter from a companion star in cataclysmic variable systems.

A subset of those systems undergo dwarf novae outbursts, episodes of rapid mass transfer and brightening. The authors relate major physical parameters of these accreting white dwarfs to their normal mode frequencies. Those frequencies are the tones at which the star naturally oscillates, set by parameters like mass and temperature. Those frequencies, if observed, could reveal the star's hidden properties.
arxiv-2512-01182:
Yuri Shimane, Karl Berntorp, Stefano Di Cairano, and Avishai Weiss build a navigation pipeline for lunar orbits in a 2025 paper. Near-rectilinear halo orbits are large, elongated loops around the Moon, planned as parking orbits for lunar stations. Staying on one takes careful navigation and station-keeping in a high-fidelity model of real gravitational dynamics.

Their pipeline generates synthetic camera images and feeds them to a horizon-based optical navigation algorithm. An extended Kalman filter turns those sightings into a state estimate, and a controller keeps the spacecraft near its reference orbit. Self-reliant navigation reduces dependence on Earth tracking.
arxiv-2512-01282:
Jiahao Yuan and co-authors work on chat tools that give kind, helpful replies. Good support needs more than soft words. A tool should know who the user is and what that user feels over time. Many past tools lose track of the user and give vague replies.

The team built Kardia-R1 to fix that gap. It trains a language model to think step by step about a user's state. A judge based on clear rules scores each reply for care and fit. Strong scores guide the model to learn. The goal is support that feels both warm and well aimed.
arxiv-2512-01582:
Junran Peng and co-authors release RoleMotion, a large set of human motion data. It holds role-play and task motions fit to set scenes. Past text-motion sets were built from scattered parts. Their clips were isolated and not tied to real social acts.

RoleMotion ties motions to scenes and roles in fine detail. Each clip is labeled for its role and goal. Models trained on it can make motion that fits a scene, not just a prompt. That helps animation, games, and robot training where acts must suit the place.
arxiv-2512-01682: Guilherme Seidyo Imai Aldeia completed a thesis in Santo Andre in November 2025 on current challenges in symbolic regression. Fabricio Olivetti de Franca supervised the work. Symbolic regression searches for short math formulas that fit a data set. It does not fit a fixed model form. The thesis covers four open problems in that search. They are how to optimize candidate formulas, how to select among them, how to simplify them, and how to benchmark methods fairly.
arxiv-2512-01782:
Chenhao Sun, Yuhao Mao, and Martin Vechev improve randomized smoothing beyond one global noise level. Smoothing certifies that a network resists small attacks. Noise size sets a trade-off. Small noise certifies small radii well, large noise certifies large radii well. One variance cannot do both.

Their dual method uses two noise scales at once. That split aims for high accuracy at both small and large radii. Certified defenses matter for vision systems in safety roles. Dual smoothing could widen the certified range without a matching loss in clean accuracy. Dual scales compose at inference, so one deployed net carries both certificates without doubling its size or its serving cost.
arxiv-2512-01882:
Self-driving cars must fuse camera images, laser scans, and heading data into split-second decisions, and the computing budget on board is tight. A 2025 paper by Aref Ghoreishee and four co-authors proposes a new spiking architecture for this multi-modal decision-making, built around reinforcement learning from end to end.

Their perception module uses cross-attention transformers to merge the different sensor streams. Transformers are powerful but costly, which limits their use on small edge hardware in vehicles. Spiking networks, which compute with brief pulses like real neurons, promise a cheaper route. The work tests whether that promise can meet the demands of driving decisions.
arxiv-2512-02182:
Checking cheap measures against true ones costs money. So studies check a small subset of patients with the costly test. Sarah Lotspeich and Cole Manschot build a 2025 plan for this two-phase check. It works across several models at once and stays easy to grasp, with help from principal components.

In phase one, cheap facts are gathered for all in the study. In phase two, a subset gets the costly, more exact checks. The hard part is to pick and weigh that subset so the fix serves many models, not just one. Good design saves funds in large health data banks, where no one can test all with care.
arxiv-2512-02282:
Chat systems now talk with folks in deep distress. A careless reply in a crisis chat can do real harm. Han Luo and Guy Laban built DialogGuard in 2025. The tool grades the safety of model replies in such raw, touchy talks.

It grades five grave risks. They are leaks of private facts, biased or unfair acts, sly steering of the user, harm to the mind, and insults. A team of agents shares the grading, since one pass can miss much. Checks of this sort must come first, before chat tools are let near crisis help lines.
arxiv-2512-02482:
Vishwesh Nath and colleagues at NVIDIA and Northwell Health build tools for seeing inside the body during surgery. Small scope surgery needs fast, accurate 3D views of soft tissue that bends and shifts. Recent Gaussian splatting methods render such scenes in real time, which suits live use in an operating room.

Many of those methods rest on code that firms cannot use in products, which blocks real deployment. The team's G-SHARP pipeline is built to be commercially usable from the start. Fast, lawful, and accurate tissue views could help surgeons work with more confidence during delicate procedures. In time, such views could cut risk when a cut must be placed with great care.
arxiv-2512-02682:
P. Bisconti and four co-authors warn that AI safety tools built for one model fail when models talk to each other. Current practice guards single agents with prompts, fine tuning, and moderation layers. Those layers constrain one model's behavior but leave group dynamics ungoverned.

The 2025 study builds a taxonomy of risks that arise in model to model interaction. New failure modes can emerge from feedback loops, imitation, and shared blind spots between agents. A shared risk map gives regulators and builders a starting point for governing multi agent systems before they scale further. Two safe bots can still make an unsafe pair, and that is the gap this map tries to name first.
arxiv-2512-02782:
Hu Cang and Yuan Wang ask whether quantum spacetime itself would blur gravitational waves as they cross the universe. Microscopic curvature fluctuations, if real, should leave a mark on long traveling waves. The authors build a gauge invariant framework, free of coordinate artifacts, for that cumulative effect.

Working from the Riemann tensor's two point function, they use the extreme slowness of cosmic expansion versus wave frequency. Phase diffusion emerges as the unique leading imprint, not fading or mode mixing. A clear, falsifiable target helps future detectors test quantum gravity ideas with real data. A phase drift is a faint mark, but faint marks are what the next wave of gear is built to catch in flight.
arxiv-2512-02882:
Youkang Wang and five co-authors spend a language model's test time budget where it counts most. Test time policy optimization lets a model adapt to shifted tasks using feedback from its own trial answers. Common methods estimate rewards by majority vote over a fixed number of rollouts, wasting compute.

OptPO allocates rollouts adaptively, giving more trials where the reward is still uncertain. That principled budgeting trims substantial redundancy, the authors argue. Smarter allocation could make self improving inference cheaper, helping deployed models adapt without retraining or human labels. Trials cost time and coin, so a plan that spends them where doubt is thick is a plan that pays for its own keep.
arxiv-2512-02982:
Xiang Xu and six co-authors model moving 3D worlds from LiDAR sequences while tracking where the model is unsure. Dynamic scene modeling underpins 4D worlds for autonomous driving and embodied AI. Existing generative frameworks treat every region alike, ignoring how uncertainty varies across a real scene.

Uniform generation leaves artifacts in complex or ambiguous regions, hurting realism and temporal stability. U4D makes generation uncertainty aware, spending care where the scene is hardest. Worlds that know their own weak spots are safer to train and test driving systems inside. Marks of doubt on the map warn the car where to slow. A plain map with no doubt marks can not serve that use at all in fog or glare.
arxiv-2512-03082:
Large language models can favor their own past choices. Nan Zhuang and five co-authors study that flaw, called choice-supportive bias, in this 2025 work. When a model judges options, it may back the one it picked before, which can skew fair decisions.

Most past fixes target bias about social groups, not this kind of thinking bias. The authors build a method based on how reasons depend on each other. Their aim is to make model judgments more even and fair. Fair judging matters as these models help with hiring, grading, and other key choices. For model evaluators, the work shows that bias can hide in choices, not just in data about people.
arxiv-2512-03482:
Special wave functions on exotic surfaces hide number patterns. Jiaqi Hou studies Kakeya-Nikodym norms of Maass forms in this 2025 work. The setting is a compact arithmetic complex hyperbolic surface, with a Hecke-Maass form of large spectral parameter.

Hou applies the amplification method to bound the norm. The result gains a power saving over the trivial bound. Such bounds show how evenly wave functions spread. They connect analysis, geometry, and number theory in the study of quantum chaos on arithmetic spaces. Amplification boosts a chosen form's signal, a standard trick with delicate tuning.
arxiv-2512-03582:
Propaganda works through stories, not just slogans. This 2025 study proposes fine-grained narrative classification in biased news articles. Narratives organize persuasive techniques into coherent stories that assign blame and build identification with a camp.

The authors also explore article-bias classification as a precursor task. Sorting narratives at a fine grain could help analysts track how biased outlets frame events. Such tools may support media literacy and research on polarization. They must be used with care to avoid labeling disputes. Bias classification first helps sort articles before the harder narrative labels are applied, giving the pipeline a staged path to fine detail.
arxiv-2512-03782: Marco Adamo Seveso develops an explicit p-adic integration theory in this short 2025 number theory note. The setting is the Igusa towers built over Siegel modular varieties, families of spaces that organise modular forms of higher genus. P-adic integration assigns sizes to sets in the p-adic world, where distance is measured by divisibility by a prime. Seveso states that the theory he builds has applications to explicit reciprocity laws, a central theme in modern number theory.
arxiv-2512-04882:
Rahul Barthwal, Firas Dhaouadi, and Christian Rohde build approximation systems that tame dispersive wave equations by rewriting them as hyperbolic ones. Dispersive equations, where waves of different lengths travel at different speeds, resist standard solvers. Their 2025 arXiv paper constructs a first-order, strictly hyperbolic stand-in for purely dispersive problems with nonlinear fluxes. A unique symmetrizer, valid for any smooth flux, gives local well-posedness of smooth solutions.

Under stronger flux conditions, the hyperbolic system gains a strictly convex entropy that mirrors the original equation's energy. For equations that also diffuse, the team uses a viscoelastic damped system that respects the same entropy. That pairing yields global well-posedness for the mixed approximation. Relative entropy methods then prove the approximations converge to the true solutions. Reliable stand-ins open dispersive flows, from water waves to plasmas, to mature hyperbolic solvers.
arxiv-2512-04982:
Mostafa Behtouei, Carlos Salgado Lopez, and Giancarlo Gatti build a new mathematical frame for laser-plasma wakefield acceleration, a method that surfs electrons on waves in ionized gas to speed them up. Inside a narrow discharge tube, an intense laser pulse and the plasma answer each other in tangled ways, and the usual descriptions can be hard to steer or simplify. The authors recast the whole system with operators, the workhorse objects of quantum-style mathematics.

Four operators carry the story: one for the laser's crosswise modes, one for the plasma's nonlinear reply, one for its ringing, and one for the push of the light itself. In the gentle regime the modes stay separate and stable; stronger action mixes them, which is where energy passes into the wake. The frame also plugs into neural operator methods, pointing toward fast simplified models for planning and controlling future accelerator experiments.
arxiv-2512-05282:
Armand Ley studies what entropic regularization selects in optimal transport on a line. Optimal transport asks for the cheapest way to reshape one distribution into another. Adding an entropy penalty smooths the problem and makes it computable. But as the penalty shrinks, which optimal plan the smoothed solutions approach is subtle, when the cost is plain distance and the optimal plan is not unique. Outside discrete settings and unique-plan cases, existence and characterization were largely open.

Ley proposes a natural candidate for the limiting object and proves convergence to it when the two distributions share no common mass. For arbitrary distributions, he shows every limit point of the smoothed minimizers obeys a structural condition called weak multiplicativity. The candidate rests on a decomposition theorem for transport plans he flags as independently interesting, and the paper complements earlier work by Di Marino and Louet.
arxiv-2512-05482:
Mai Tsujimoto hunts the rare objects that self-driving systems need to see and least often do. Detectors trained on point clouds stumble on uncommon categories — construction vehicles, motorcycles, barriers — because labelled examples are scarce. Tsujimoto's cross-modal framework uses a vision-language model to mine driving scenes for exactly those rarities. It turns image understanding into training data for the three-dimensional detector.

The pipeline blends object detection, semantic feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, and outlier detection from two matching methods. Concept-based filtering keeps the catch meaningful and easy to check. Because it labels concepts on its own, the burden collapses to the valuable samples. On a standard driving dataset, detectors trained with the mined data beat those trained on the same amount of random data. The biggest gains land on hard cases like trailers and bicycles. It is a data-picking strategy for safety-critical perception.
arxiv-2512-06682:
Boyang Xu and four co authors build a decision framework that runs machines and schedules their upkeep from the same live signals. Factories watch their equipment with many sensors, but folding all those streams into one good call on when to run hard and when to service is hard. The true wear state of a machine is never seen directly; sensors give a noisy window on it.

Their model treats the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process, the standard frame for acting under hidden state. From the live degradation signals it derives joint policies for production capacity and preventive maintenance, with limits that keep wear in bounds. They test it on bearing wear data and on a NASA data set of aircraft turbofan engines. The framework improved performance in both cases, showing a systematic way to let real time wear data steer operations and maintenance together.
arxiv-2512-06982:
Yu Yu, Qian Xie, Nairen Cao, and Li Jin address a design chore in reinforcement learning: building the encoder that turns many kinds of input into one useful picture of the world. An agent may juggle sensor readings, signals over time, camera views, and written instructions at once. Hand-designing a module for each source, plus a module that fuses them, is slow. Automated architecture search exists, but standard versions ignore handy clues from the modules' own outputs.

The team hands the search to a large language model acting as a design agent. The model uses its prior knowledge plus signals about how well each candidate part represents its source. In a mixed traffic control task, the pipeline found better encoders than traditional search while testing fewer candidates. It also beat an earlier language-model framework called GENIUS, suggesting guided search can save costly trials.
arxiv-2512-07082:
Yuan-Ting Zhong and co-authors build TRACE, a detector for the moment a data stream changes its character. Streaming optimization, where decisions must track live data, breaks when the underlying pattern drifts, and the drift times are rarely known in advance. Older detectors assume tidy settings: fixed intervals between drifts or full sight of the environment. TRACE instead learns what drift looks like in general, then recognizes it in new streams.

Statistical features are first extracted from the stream by a principled tokenization, turning stretches of data into a sequence a model can read. An attention-based sequence learner then spots drift patterns across time scales. Plugged into a streaming optimizer, the detector lets the search adapt when the world shifts. Across diverse benchmarks, TRACE generalized to unseen data sets better than rivals and stayed robust under varied conditions.
arxiv-2512-07682:
Manika Bag wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on controlling how two phases separate. The Cahn-Hilliard equation describes that separation, here in a higher-order, sixth-order form. A Brinkman equation for fluid flow is coupled to it.

The coupled system includes a source term for mass exchange between phases. The flow equation carries a forcing term that is not divergence-free. That forcing serves as the distributed control the author can dial. Mobility and viscosity are held constant through the analysis. The nonlinearity takes the classic double-well shape, smoothed for the proofs. The goal is an optimal control that steers the mixture at least cost. The cost functional includes an absolute-value term that promotes sparse controls.  Bag derives the first-order conditions that any optimal control must obey. Both cases get full treatment.
arxiv-2512-07982: Eunice Sukarto, a mathematician working in homotopy theory, posted a short paper on arXiv in December 2025. Her topic is the rational form of a classifying space for real special unitary groups, with a two element symmetry acting on it. It grows out of a motivic homotopy problem raised by Asok, Fasel, and Hopkins. Sukarto describes that homotopy type using equivariant Eilenberg MacLane spaces, standard building blocks in algebraic topology. That gives specialists a concrete way to compute with a space that had been hard to pin down.
arxiv-2512-08082:
Vala Vakilian, Zimeng Wang, Ankit Singh Rawat, and Christos Thrampoulidis, machine learning researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They test a simple hypothesis about natural language: for most text, only a short recent stretch of context is needed to predict what comes next. They call this short context dominance, and they measure it using large language models as statistical oracles.

Across long documents, most sequences needed only the last ninety six tokens or fewer to match full context predictions. The team then builds a practical proxy that flags the minority of sequences where distant context truly matters, without knowing the next token. A simple threshold on that proxy separates long context cases from short ones well. Finally, they design a decoding method that boosts tokens tied to distant context, reducing the bias short context creates. Across question answering tasks and model designs, that fix improved performance.
arxiv-2512-08182:
Yongda Wang and Shifeng Xiong, statisticians in China, posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025 about empirical likelihood with massive data. Empirical likelihood is a flexible way to do inference without assuming a distribution, but with huge datasets it becomes painfully heavy. Their grouped method cuts that cost by treating blocks of data as units.

The method splits the observations into far fewer groups and gives every point in a group the same probability weight. Only the group weights must then be estimated, shrinking the optimization problem by orders of magnitude. The authors prove the grouped version keeps the same first order accuracy as the standard method for estimating equations and two sample mean problems. A distributed version spreads the work across servers. In tests, it matched the standard accuracy while running far faster, handling a billion data points in tens of seconds on one ordinary computer.
arxiv-2512-08582:
The CMS Collaboration, one of the two big detector teams at the Large Hadron Collider, posted a measurement paper on arXiv in December 2025. It measures how often proton collisions produce a Z boson together with a photon, using data the CMS detector gathered in 2022 at a record collision energy. Events were kept when they showed an electron or muon pair matching a Z boson, plus an isolated photon.

The measured rate matched the standard model prediction closely, well inside the uncertainties. Beyond a headline number, the result probes how force carriers interact with each other. Certain three way couplings among neutral bosons are forbidden in the simplest picture, and any sign of them would mean new physics. Using a modern effective theory framework, the team set the first constraints on those couplings from this channel. Precision measurements of clean processes remain sharp tools for cornering new physics.
arxiv-2512-08782:
Roopak Surendran presents a machine learning method to detect malicious smart contracts on the Ethereum blockchain before they are deployed. Harmful contracts in the Solidity language can exploit flaws such as reentrancy or bad randomness to drain funds or block service. Finding them early can prevent those attacks.

The method analyzes the operation codes of the virtual machine that runs the contracts. Opcode counts are balanced with a synthetic oversampling method, then turned into binary features through an entropy based binning step. A classifier trained on those features detects almost all malicious contracts with a very low false positive rate. An explanation tool is added to show, for each flagged contract, which opcode features drove the decision. That transparency helps reviewers trust and audit the automated verdicts.
arxiv-2512-08882:
Mohamed Elmahallawy and Asma Jodeiri Akbarfam propose OrbitChain, a blockchain backed method for federated learning across satellite networks run by many vendors. Low Earth orbit satellites now produce huge data for tasks such as disaster detection, border monitoring, and climate study. Federated learning lets vendors train a joint model without sharing raw data, but slow links and trust problems remain.

Biased or falsified updates can enter through cyberattacks on satellite links, and intermittent connectivity slows convergence. OrbitChain offloads consensus to high altitude platforms with more compute power. It also records a transparent, auditable history for each model update from other orbits and vendors. Manipulated or incomplete contributions are blocked from the global aggregation step. Studies show lower overhead, better privacy and security, and improved model accuracy. The ledger finalizes many blocks with sub second latency, and convergence time falls sharply on real satellite data.
arxiv-2512-08982:
Jian Xu and coauthors present Consist Retinex, a one step method for enhancing low light images. Generative approaches can give high quality results, but they rely on repeated sampling and are hard to deploy when latency is strict. Consistency models allow one step restoration, yet direct use for Retinex enhancement is unstable.

Their system first uses a transformer decomposition network to obtain paired reflectance and illumination maps. Two conditional consistency models are then trained with a dual objective that joins trajectory consistency with alignment to ground truth components. A noise emphasized sampling rule concentrates supervision near the inference endpoint while keeping full noise coverage. Theory gives an endpoint error bound and explains why the two signals complement each other. Tests on paired and unpaired low light benchmarks show leading scores under one step inference, at lower cost.
arxiv-2512-09182:
Hunjae Lee studies failure modes of transformer models through the lens of graph neural network theory. Decoder only transformers dominate language models, yet they show surprising failures. The article argues that much of deep learning is about learnable mixing and propagation of information, so failures are best read as bottlenecks in that propagation.

Graph network theory already has a rich account of such bottlenecks and of theoretical failure modes. Lee makes the case that many issues known for graph networks also affect transformers. The causal nature of decoder only models adds its own geometry to information flow, producing predictable and potentially severe failure modes. Existing fixes in transformer research are often ad hoc and driven by intuition. The article unifies many of them under the graph based perspective, explaining why each works and what problem it truly solves. That framing can guide more targeted improvements to transformer design.
arxiv-2512-09882:
Justin W. Lin leads a large team in the first head to head test of AI agents against human professionals at live penetration testing. Ten cybersecurity professionals, six existing AI agents, and the authors' new agent scaffold, ARTEMIS, all attacked the same large university network of about eight thousand hosts. ARTEMIS is a multi agent system that can spawn sub agents and sorts found vulnerabilities automatically.

ARTEMIS placed second overall. It found nine valid vulnerabilities with a high valid submission rate, beating nine of the ten humans. Older scaffolds lagged behind most human participants. The agents shone at systematic enumeration, parallel attacks, and cost, with some variants running far cheaper per hour than professionals. But gaps remain: the agents produced more false positives than humans and struggled with tasks needing a graphical interface.
arxiv-2512-10182:
Tsuyoshi Kato, Daisuke Kishimoto, and Mitsunobu Tsutaya extend fixed point theory to infinite, noncompact spaces. Classical Lefschetz theory counts fixed points of maps on compact manifolds and obstructs vector fields. Many natural spaces, covering spaces and infinite complexes among them, are not compact. The authors work on complete Riemannian manifolds of bounded geometry with uniformly continuous maps. They define a uniform Lefschetz class for such a map. It vanishes exactly when the map can be deformed evenly to one with no fixed points at all, including at infinity.

A companion class obstructs nonvanishing vector fields; both vanish on their own on nonamenable spaces. For covering spaces of closed manifolds, a Lefschetz-Hopf style formula gives the class, and a Poincaré-Hopf theorem follows. The key new tool is a uniform bounded cohomology with the traits topology needs: homotopy invariance, excision, and Poincaré duality.
arxiv-2512-10582:
Tobias Rohe and co-authors argue that quantum circuits should be shaped by the problem they solve, not pulled from a generic shelf. Much quantum computing work reuses one-size-fits-all circuit layouts. And the authors test whether baking in geometric prior knowledge helps a hybrid quantum generative adversarial network that must produce graphs obeying geometric rules.

Their test bed is generating constrained complete graphs on four nodes, judged by how well outputs match the target distribution and respect rules such as the triangle and Ptolemaic inequalities. A portfolio of entanglement layouts and loss designs was compared. The circuit whose topology mirrored the triangle rule achieved the best geometric validity among quantum models and matched a classical GAN. Gate choices, variance control, and output scaling each shifted the balance between geometric consistency and statistical accuracy.
arxiv-2512-10782:
Alon Hever and co-authors hunt for undiscovered crystals by borrowing the shapes of neighbours. Their scheme adapts known structure types from compounds of nearby elements, reasoning that a stable arrangement for one element's compound often suits its neighbours in the table too. They show the search on the binary selenide and sulfide families, a key class of semiconductors.

The directed search predicts ten compounds missing from the inorganic crystal structure database. Comparing against wider searches that borrow structures from more distant elements shows the near-neighbour screen is relatively efficient, finding candidates without trawling the whole table. The authors propose the approach as a general heuristic rule: when prospecting for new stable compounds in other families, raid the neighbours' structures first. It is a simple scheme, aimed at guiding expensive stability checks toward promising ground.
arxiv-2512-11182:
Niranjana Shankarappa and colleagues use the Parker Solar Probe's full mission data to trace where small ion scale waves in the solar wind get their energy. These circularly polarised waves are common close to the Sun and mark where plasma instabilities and turbulence exchange energy. The team surveyed waves across many solar encounters and compared them with the measured shapes of proton distributions.

Left handed waves appeared often, and more frequently nearer the Sun, matching long storms of ion cyclotron waves running alongside the magnetic field. Energy spectra steepened during those storms, suggesting the waves carry energy tied to uneven proton temperatures. Right handed waves were rarer and matched fast magnetosonic waves, appearing when extra proton beams raised the heat flow along the field. A machine learning tool helped pin down the heat flow threshold at which those waves switch on.
arxiv-2512-11482:
Melih Catal, Pooja Rani, and Harald Gall apply differential privacy to code generating language models so they stop memorising their training data. Code models can reproduce training snippets verbatim, risking privacy breaches and intellectual property violations that keep them out of sensitive settings. Differential privacy adds calibrated noise during training to protect individual examples while preserving general patterns.

The authors first investigate what drives memorisation during fine tuning, then measure how privacy training changes it. Memorisation fell substantially across every snippet type tested, and the snippet types most prone to being memorised were also the ones privacy training protected best. Perplexity rose slightly, yet code generation ability was preserved and sometimes even improved. Training time and energy use barely changed. The study, presented as the first comprehensive evaluation of its kind, argues private code models are practical today.
arxiv-2512-11682:
Tim Cofala and co-authors report how TxAgent, an AI agent for drug choice help, fared in the CURE-Bench contest at NeurIPS 2025. Picking drugs is high stakes work shaped by patient traits, disease paths, and drug effects. TxAgent answers by repeated search and reasoning steps.

It uses a tuned Llama model that calls a shared tool set fed by the FDA drug API, OpenTargets, and Monarch. The contest grades not just final answers but the reasoning trace and the tool call order. The team shows that better tool search lifts the whole system. Their entry won the Excellence Award in Open Science, and the study maps where agent drug help still needs care.
arxiv-2512-11782:
Peiqing Yang and co-authors present MatAnyone 2, a system that cuts moving subjects out of video with fine edges. Video matting is held back by small, tame training sets. Adding segmentation data helps meaning but not hair thin borders.

Their Matting Quality Evaluator grades alpha mattes pixel by pixel with no ground truth, flagging good and bad zones. That grader guides training live and also curates new data by merging the strengths of top models. The result is VMReal, a set of 28,000 real clips with 2.4 million frames. A training trick that looks at far apart frames handles long videos. MatAnyone 2 topped prior methods on synthetic and real tests.
arxiv-2512-11982:
Nolan Koblischke and co-authors build a search engine that finds galaxies by meaning across more than 100 million images. Hunting rare objects by hand labeling is hopeless at that scale. Their pipeline lets vision language models write captions for unlabeled galaxy images.

Those captions train a model that aligns an astronomy foundation model with text, producing searchable embeddings. The search beat plain image similarity and set state of the art zero shot marks on rare object hunts, despite training on random images. A caption based re ranking step nearly doubles recall in the top 100 for the hardest targets. The hunt surfaced 36 new candidate stellar streams. The recipe suits any huge unlabeled science image archive.
arxiv-2512-12382:
Yaogan Mensah and Isiaka Aremua study spectral Barron spaces for vector valued functions in a 2025 math paper. Such spaces hold functions on a compact group whose Fourier transforms meet a summability rule. The values lie in a Banach space, so outputs can be vectors or more general objects, not just numbers.

The authors map the basic properties of these spaces and show how they embed into Sobolev spaces and bounded function spaces. Their main theorem gives an approximation rate: in a Hilbert space target, matrix coefficients of unitary representations approximate each function with error shrinking like n to the minus one half. A variant covers targets of Rademacher type 2.
arxiv-2512-12482:
Haipeng Li, Nanzhe Wang, Louis J Durlofsky, and Biondo L Biondi build a Bayesian method to monitor stored carbon dioxide underground in a 2025 paper. Watching buried CO2 plumes matters for storage safety. Full-waveform monitoring reads seismic data at high detail, but standard inversion gives no uncertainty and uses little prior knowledge, and sparse noisy data can make it unreliable.

Their framework mixes reservoir flow physics with a generative prior. Flow simulations on varied geology create sample plumes, and a variational autoencoder compresses them into a simple latent space. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo then infers plume changes from time lapse seismic data with uncertainty bounds. Tests stayed stable and accurate under very sparse, noisy setups.
arxiv-2512-12882:
V. A. Dzuba, V. V. Flambaum, and G. K. Vong compute a tiny effect in atoms called parity nonconservation, where a process that should be mirrored is not quite symmetric. They study rubidium and a strontium ion. Two electron jumps in each system are their focus.

Their results cover parts that depend on nuclear spin and parts that do not. They stress the possible effect of a hypothetical light particle, a Z prime boson. In light atoms, that new effect grows fast compared with the known one as nuclear charge falls. Light atoms may also allow cleaner theory, aiding searches for new physics.
arxiv-2512-13182:
Romana Mikusincova and co-authors report the first X-ray polarimetry of an eclipsing neutron star binary, AX J1745.6-2901. The source sits very close to the Galactic center and was caught by chance during a 150 kilosecond IXPE observation of a neighbor. Separating its signal from nearby glow was the main hurdle.

After careful handling of contamination, they found a polarization degree of 14.7 percent, plus or minus 4.0 percent, at an angle of 122 degrees, plus or minus 8 degrees. During eclipse, the degree rose to 34.2 percent, plus or minus 8.7 percent. That rise suggests the polarization comes from scattering, likely in disk winds.
arxiv-2512-13282:
Endri Taka and co-authors study GEMM performance, the matrix multiply operations at the heart of AI workloads, across generations of AMD Ryzen AI neural processing units. Getting the most from each chip generation takes careful tuning of tiling, data layout, and scheduling. Their paper's title frames the task as striking the right balance.

The work compares how matrix multiplication kernels perform as the hardware evolves from one generation to the next. Such studies guide compiler and kernel writers who must retune core routines for new silicon. Practical speed on these laptop class AI chips decides how fast local models run, making this optimization work directly relevant to on-device AI.
arxiv-2512-13582:
Roman Klopsch and co-authors study turbulent air flow over a Gaussian-shaped bump, in attached and separated forms. They focus on where slow, coherent structures in the flow come from. Their work blends time-resolved lab measures with linear physics models built on mean flow fields from the same data.
