Their title reports a stratification: the field's layers are arranged in an ordered, layered pattern across the outflow's many scales.
arxiv-2601-15682:
Wei Dong and Li Ge set tight bounds for a private statistics task in a 2026 arXiv paper. The task is estimating the mean of a Gaussian distribution. The privacy rule is personalized differential privacy. Under it, each record carries its own privacy budget. Not everyone needs the same level of protection. The authors study two common variants of the setup.

In bounded PDP, budgets are public, and neighboring datasets differ by replacing one record. In unbounded PDP, the rules differ in how records enter or leave. Tight bounds mark the best accuracy any method can reach. They also show that a matching method exists, or that none can do better. For data holders, such bounds tell them the true price of personalized privacy.
arxiv-2601-15782:
An unsigned 2026 arXiv paper surveys mesoscopic fluctuations in statistical systems. A fluctuation counts as mesoscopic when its size sits in a middle range. It is much larger than the spacing between nearest neighbors. It is still much smaller than the whole system. At that scale, fluctuations behave unlike the matter around them. They can be read as patches of one phase forming inside another host phase.

The abstract frames the topic in general terms, without naming authors or a specific system. Readers should expect a broad theoretical treatment. Mesoscopic effects matter in small devices and materials, where the middle scale is the working scale.
arxiv-2601-16082:
Marcos Silva studies where a star would tear apart near a black bounce. His 2026 preprint works with the Simpson and Visser space form. That form bends the black hole view into a bounce. Tidal pull from a black hole can rip a dense star as it nears. The rip point is known as the Roche limit.

Silva works out the tidal pull in this bounce space. He asks how the bounce shifts the rip point from the known case. Shifts would show where this space form parts from the old view. Such maths helps teams test new gravity forms with star acts. The work stays at the level of pure theory and proof.
arxiv-2601-16182:
Arshia Ataee Naeini and three coauthors solve live text search with wild card marks. Their 2026 preprint deals with search where marks can stand for any sign. Up to a set count of wild marks may sit in the search term. Both the text and the term can change live. Changes span add, drop and swap of signs.

The team gives steps that keep search fast through all such changes. Fast live search serves code bases and data sets that shift oft. Wild marks add reach but also add cost to each check. Steps that hold cost down have wide use. The work is in the theory of text code steps.
arxiv-2601-16282:
Peter Jansen and three coauthors build science views from huge text sets at scale. Their 2026 preprint deals with the build of theories, not just tests. Past AI work in science has stressed tools that run tests. Tools that build views from past work are far less built. A theory here joins rules of both kind and count type.

The team frames how to draw such rules from big text hoards. They then test the frame on sets drawn from past work. Drawn rules that hold true would speed new science thought. The work aims at the high level step of theory craft. It treats past texts as the raw ore for views.
arxiv-2601-16482:
A study of the Langmuir film task weighs if its maths is well set. The 2026 preprint deals with thin films on a fluid base. The film is of the Langmuir type, one grain thick on top. It pairs to a Stokes flow in the fluid just past it. Past bulk terms can be cut to leave a film lone flow.

That cut leaves a flow ruled by a Dirichlet to Neumann map. Well set means small data shifts give small act shifts. Proof of that trait lets codes trust the film maths. It also firms the base for wave and flow sums. The work is a maths check of the film model.
arxiv-2601-16582:
Yuqian Zheng and Mariana Georgescu build a composed video search tool in plain form. Their 2026 preprint, named X-Aligner, deals with search by pic plus words. A user gives a clip cue and a word cue as one ask. Past tools fuse the two cues in one step at once. That one step fusion gave just small gains past base tools.

A staged align of cues aims for more large gains. Each stage lines cues up in a more fine way. Plain form with strong scores would ease real use. Search by cues serves clip hoards in film and news work. The work strips spare parts from the tool build.
arxiv-2601-17282:
Nathan Shettell and Alexia Auffèves measure how well Bayesian inference uses each new clue. Inference is how an agent updates belief as data comes in. It sits under science, machine learning, and daily choice. Each measure cuts doubt about a hidden state. The authors define an inferential efficiency as a ratio tied to that cut.

They call the frame entropic efficiency. It asks how much of the gain a protocol could get, it does get. A clear yardstick lets users compare protocols on fair terms. It may also show where data is wasted. For sensor and lab design, waste means cost. A sharp measure helps teams spend measures where they count most.
arxiv-2601-17682:
David M. T. Kuo tests if topological interface states in graphene nanoribbons survive their environment. He studies sandwich structures with armchair graphene heterostructures. Boron nitride ribbons flank the graphene core. One stack keeps the same topology on both sides. The other reverses it. Interface states live at the joins between zones.

Environmental breakdown would limit real devices built on these states. Stability checks must come before device claims. Kuo asks the question in the title with care: is breakdown true? The paired stacks give a controlled comparison. Graphene nanoribbons are a test bed for topological electronics. Results here guide whether that promise holds in air and heat.
arxiv-2601-18282:
Lei Wei, Jinpeng Ou, Xiao Peng, and Bin Wang make language models think inside the act of calling a function. Their 2026 preprint deals with function calling for autonomous agents. Models are good at it, yet they lack clear reasoning while they fill in parameters. That gap bites for complex functions whose parameters depend on each other. Chain-of-thought prompting works at the agent level, above the call itself. It cannot give fine-grained reasoning at the point where a value is chosen.

The authors embed the reasoning inside the call. Think-augmented calling aims for more accurate parameters. Agent tools are only as safe as the values they pass. Small parameter errors can book, buy, or delete the wrong thing.
arxiv-2601-18382:
Kees Wapenaar, Johannes Aichele, and Dirk-Jan van Manen study two sound tricks and how they link. One trick plays a sound field back in time to focus it at its source. The next trick pulls a key response curve out of noise, with no need for a real source at all. For still stuff that does not change with time, the link between the tricks is well known.

Fresh work has pushed both tricks to stuff whose traits shift as time goes by. The team asks how the two tricks link in that new case. They also ask how that link maps to the old case. Sound tools of this kind serve scans of the earth, tests of parts, and care of health. A clear link helps staff pick the right trick for each job.
arxiv-2601-18582:
Yuan Cao and six colleagues recast a trait-guess task as a rank task to get more from language models. The task reads a person's posts and guesses their type on a famed four-scale quiz of traits. Past tools had models pull key text from posts and then train a sorter to pick one type. That pick is coarse: a near miss counts the same as a wild one.

A rank list is finer. It can put the true type high even when the top pick is off. The team train and grade models to rank types, not just to name one. A finer grade should show small gains that a plain pick would hide. It may also give users a range of fits, not a flat tag. Trait tools are used in hires and ads, so fine grades count.
arxiv-2601-19082:
Trung-Kiet Huynh and a large team test how stakes and language steer model agents in cooperation traps. As language models act more on their own among other agents, their strategic choices matter for safety and for shared systems. The team places agents in classic dilemmas where greed and trust pull apart.

They vary two things: how big the payoffs are, and which language the game is played in. Both knobs, it turns out, are worth watching as shapers of agent conduct. Knowing what bends an agent toward or away from cooperation helps design multi agent systems that do not spiral into mutual harm.
arxiv-2601-19182:
Roberto Rubboli and Marco Tomamichel pin down a hard limit on pulling clean randomness from weak sources when a quantum foe watches. Randomness extraction turns messy random data into near perfect random bits. A strong converse exponent grades how fast the chance of failure grows when you push past the limit.

The pair find a tight value for that exponent under a composable error rule. That rule stays safe when the bits are used inside larger protocols. Tight limits tell builders of quantum safe systems exactly how much clean randomness a source can yield.
arxiv-2601-19382:
David Jones and a large team find a carbon rich dwarf star hiding inside a nebula that looks carbon poor. The Necklace nebula is a two lobed planetary nebula left after a shared envelope phase between two stars. Its central star has been shown to be a dwarf carbon star, rich in carbon by type.

Yet the nebula around it reads as poor in carbon, a flat contradiction at first glance. The team appraises how both facts can hold at once. Cases like this test the story of how paired stars trade material and shed their outer layers.
arxiv-2601-20282:
Viet Hung Dinh, Ming Ding, Youyang Qu, and Kanchana Thilakarathna study how transformer models retrieve what they have memorized. Interest in explaining these models is rising, partly due to rules that demand transparency and accountability. Machine unlearning, which removes chosen data from a trained model, also needs this understanding to protect privacy.

The authors use the encoding specificity principle, an idea from memory research, to read how attention layers store and fetch information. That lens may show where a memory sits inside the model. Such insight would help builders delete data on request and prove that it is gone.
arxiv-2601-20782:
Massimo Solinas and three co-authors ask how little numerical precision quantum simulations can get away with. Their 2026 paper studies neural quantum states computed in mixed precision. Scientific computing has long relied on double precision, with sixty-four bits per number. That standard guarantees accuracy in simulations of real phenomena. But it is slow and hungry next to newer hardware.

Graphics processors now make low-precision formats attractive. They run faster, use less memory, and save energy. The question is whether neural quantum states stay accurate when parts of the math use fewer bits. Mixed precision blends formats, using care only where it counts. The paper tests that trade-off for a method that represents quantum wave functions with neural networks. Its lessons guide simulations that need both speed and trust.
arxiv-2601-20882:
Yuheng Tang and a large team test AI agents on the full life of software. Their 2026 paper presents DevOps-Gym, a benchmark for agents in the DevOps cycle. AI agents shine at writing code and fixing issues. Their skill at building, shipping, and running real software is still unknown. DevOps work demands more than code. It needs project-scale analysis and choices made in sequence.

An agent in this cycle has to work through large projects. It must grasp how programs behave as they run. It must use trade tools with care. And it must plan many steps in order. DevOps-Gym measures agents on that whole cycle. The test exposes gaps that pure coding tests hide. It gives labs a harder target for agent research.
arxiv-2601-20982:
Samantha Adams and a large team of co-authors catalog polarized radio sources in a deep sky field. Their 2026 paper studies the Wide Chandra Deep Field South. The field covers ten square degrees. Observations span the S-band, from two to four gigahertz. The image reaches an angular resolution of fifteen arcseconds. Its noise level is about fifty microjanskys per beam in total intensity.

The team measures linear polarization for the sources in this field. Polarization reveals magnetic order in distant galaxies and jets. A wide, uniform catalog lets astronomers compare source classes fairly. It also feeds studies of how cosmic magnetism evolves. The paper is a survey report, rich in measured properties. It gives radio astronomers a reference sample for follow-up work.
arxiv-2601-21182:
Xin Peng and Ang Gao revisit how generative models are refined after sampling. Their 2026 paper rethinks refinement for diffusion and flow-based models. Such models often exhibit systematic biases that degrade sample quality. The problem grows in high-dimensional settings. Refinement methods exist to correct those biases. The standard view ties correction to resampling with fresh noise. The authors show that view is too narrow.

Effective bias correction, they demonstrate, can be a post-hoc procedure. It needs no noise injection and no multi-step resampling of the sampling process. A finished sample can be adjusted directly. That makes refinement cheaper and simpler to bolt onto existing models. Better samples matter in imaging, design, and scientific generation. The paper simplifies a step many pipelines rely on. It reframes refinement as cleanup, not regeneration.
arxiv-2601-21282:
Rishi Upadhyay and nine co-authors build a test for whether AI world models truly grasp physics. These generative models are pitched for hard jobs like robot planning and training self-driving systems. For such work, a model must mimic real dynamics with high fidelity, not just look plausible.

Their benchmark, WorldBench, is designed to separate look-alike cases that obey different physical rules. A model that confuses them will fail when the hidden rule matters. The tests work as a diagnostic, showing which parts of physics a model has learned. That helps builders fix weak spots before trusting a model with real tasks.
arxiv-2601-21382:
Madona Mekhael, Timo Stolt, and five co-authors build a surface that shapes light differently at each color. Patterned surfaces can steer light and change its frequency in compact devices. Older designs based on geometric phase give a fixed response with no color selectivity.

Their thin film of lithium niobate uses tuned resonances to shape doubled-frequency light. Because the response is tied to resonance, it can pick out chosen wavelengths. That selectivity opens finer control for tiny optical devices. The work points to chips that route and convert light with color-level precision.
arxiv-2601-21582:
Jonas Knupp, Jan Hendrik Metzen, Jeremias Bohn, Georg Groh, and Kristian Kersting give latent reasoning in language models the attention it lacks. Depth recurrence lets a model think by looping through shared layers. Past work, though, compared unfair baselines and left much of the depth unused.

A fixed hidden size also chokes long chains of hidden thought. The authors mix attention across depths to loosen that choke point. Their checks match rivals on compute, size, and memory for fairness. Stronger hidden reasoning could let small models punch above their weight on hard problems without writing long visible chains.
arxiv-2601-22082:
Yi Fei Cheng and co-authors give conversational agents a voice that seems to come from somewhere. Embodiment, having a perceptible body, raises how present an agent feels. That presence is usually built visually, through avatars. But visual channels are not always available, as with headphones or glasses without displays.

The team explores auditory embodiment instead: spatialized sound and situated audio cues that place the agent in the listener's space. Their 2026 preprint tests how those cues affect the sense of presence. Voice-only interfaces are everywhere, from earbuds to car assistants, so knowing how sound alone can ground an agent has direct design value.
arxiv-2601-22282:
Huyen Nguyen, Haim Bar, Zhiyi Chi, and Vladimir Pozdnyakov model how stem cells renew a tissue over time. Stem cells can copy themselves or turn into cells with a set job. Their 2026 preprint uses a branching process whose rates shift as time passes.

In such a model, each cell may split, change type, or die. Tracking the counts shows how a tissue grows, holds steady, or heals. It can also show how a fault tips growth toward disease. The math gives labs a frame for real cell counts. It links cell fate rules to whole-tissue trends.
arxiv-2601-22382:
Natalie Maus and a large team let AI agents, with no task training, search for new biological designs. Their 2026 preprint frames drug finds, germ-fighting peptides, and protein design as black-box searches over vast spaces. Past tools lean on raw shape data and skip the rich text of past science.

Their agents read that text and use it to guide the search. The method needs no gradient or model of the space itself. It aims to find good designs in far fewer costly tests. The work suits any lab task where each test is dear. It turns reading into a search skill.
arxiv-2601-22582:
Youngeun Kim strengthens a group-based training method for the case of few tries per prompt. Group-relative methods grade a batch of model replies against their shared mean. Their 2026 preprint, MC-GRPO, notes that with small batches that mean is noisy.

Noise can flip the sign of the learning signal, teaching the wrong lesson. Centering on the median, not the mean, steadies the baseline. Steadier signals matter most where compute is tight. The fix is small but pointed. It aims to keep cheap training honest. Small budgets are where most teams live.
arxiv-2601-22682:
Yaoshuai Ma, Xiao Wang, Wei Yao, and Jin Zhang work on bilevel optimization spread across many machines. In bilevel problems, one task sits inside another, like tuning settings while a model trains. Their framework, SUN-DSBO, handles cases where the inner task is not convex, a shape older methods mostly avoided.

Nonconvex inner tasks are common in deep learning, meta-learning, and tuning work. A shared framework that does not need a central server lets groups train together while keeping data local. The authors aim to close the gap between theory and real, messy models.
arxiv-2601-22782:
Qishuo Yin and Dylan S. Small look at how the design of an observational study shapes its trust. In such studies, a treatment was not assigned by chance, so hidden traits may bias the results. The authors ask how a study should split its sample to test that bias well.

A split sample lets one part build the study plan and the other part test it. How the split is done changes how much hidden bias the study can stand before its findings fall apart. Good splitting rules give health and social research a fairer test of cause and effect.
arxiv-2602-00382: Jennifer G. Winters and team report radial and rotational velocities of a volume complete sample of M dwarfs within 15 parsecs. From five years of spectra of 413 M dwarfs, 10 to 30 percent of the Sun in mass, they report mean systemic radial velocities and rotational broadening. Typical uncertainties stay below 50 m/s for slowly rotating targets, and below 1 km/s for rapidly rotating stars. With astrometric data, radial velocities yield space motions for thin or thick disk membership. Most members, 81 percent, are likely thin disk, and 8 percent are likely thick disk.
arxiv-2602-00782: Jiahao Zhang and colleagues present a first systematic study of repetition in protein language models, which often collapse into harmful repeats when making proteins. In text, repeats only hurt reading, but for proteins it weakens structural trust and functional use. They propose metrics for motif-level and homopolymer repeats and show repeats harm folding quality. The resulting steering vectors target repetition without hurting foldability. Applied at run time, they cut repeats without further training or heuristic rules, beating decoding penalties and baselines while preserving AlphaFold confidence.
arxiv-2602-00882: Anindya Biswas gives a condition sufficient to realize a Pick body on a Carathéodory hyperbolic domain as a Pick body on the disc. He studies how Pick bodies on Carathéodory hyperbolic domains relate to contractions on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The result thus turns a question about Pick bodies on such domains into one about Pick bodies on the open unit disc.
arxiv-2602-00982: Phu-Hoa Pham and colleagues report the work from Team HCMUS_TheFangs in the NeurIPS 2025 Mouse vs. AI contest. For visual robustness, a two-layer CNN with Gated Linear Units and normalization scores 95.4% in the test. For neural alignment, a ResNet-like net with 16 layers and GLU-based gating takes top-1 neural prediction rank. A study of checkpoints finds scores do not rise with training time, with the best mark near 200K steps. The work argues that simple builds win on robustness, deeper builds on neural fit.
arxiv-2602-01182: Zhichao Chen and co-authors probe diffusion nets for time-series fill-ins and build SPIRIT to fix their wobble. Shifting time trends skew fill paths and favor wild outputs, while diffusion training prizes varied samples over true point scores. A proximal-operator read finds a hidden Wasserstein pull that blocks trend fixes and boosts variety at truth's cost. SPIRIT loosens mass-keeping with an entropy Bregman gap, forming a semi-proximal gap proven tough to trend shifts, then drops the wasteful part for a full fill plan.
arxiv-2602-01382: Fu-Yun Wang and co-authors show prompts matter in reinforcement learning for flow picture makers. Current flow RL plans suffer thin sample use, low variety and stark prompt overfit, memorizing train wordings, collapsing on same-sense rewordings. Their PromptRL plan plants language models as trainable prompt polishers inside the flow RL loop, growing sharp rewrite skills and reshaping train dynamics. It tops benchmarks on GenEval, OCR accuracy, and PickScore, and lifts a big edit model's EditReward past a rival flagship with far fewer rollouts than naive flow RL.
arxiv-2602-01582: Haoyu Lei and colleagues probe whether AI error correction decoders earn their edge, testing them against small shifts in channel output. Under clean noise they beat belief propagation decoding, but input dependent and universal adversarial nudges erode that lead sharply. Harmful shifts transfer well between AI decoders yet barely touch belief propagation designs, and universal shifts hurt far more than random shifts of the same size. The findings point to a robustness price behind the reported gains, with AI decoders more sensitive to channel distribution than nominal scores suggest.
arxiv-2602-01882: Maximilian Gorsky and colleagues give explicit polynomial bounds for the Homogeneous Wall Lemma. The lemma first appeared in Robertson and Seymour's 13th Graph Minors entry. A wall with bricks is homogeneous when every brick carries the same color set. The lemma says a wall with bricks colored from q colors contains a k wall. The bound grew like k to a power growing with q, causing non uniform dependencies and blow ups. Their new bound grows like q to the fourth times k to the sixth, answering Sau and coauthors.
arxiv-2602-01982: Yanrui Du and colleagues give chain of thought models a fast thinking mode like human System 1 reasoning, cutting redundancy. Their self sampling framework uses activation steering to induce variable length style aligned traces from target models, without teacher guidance, easing supervision scarcity for SFT methods. Filtered gold answer data trains efficient chain of thought learning through dual cognitive systems and a compression curriculum. A self evolution regime trains SFT solely on prediction consistent data, removing gold answers. Math benchmarks plus medicine tests show stable improvements for general and R1 models.
arxiv-2602-02082: Xin Wang and colleagues study the middle Lie algebra E7+1/2 gauge theory, between E7 and E8. They propose a UV finish via a 6d super theory with a pure E7+1/2 gauge sector. 6d anomaly cancellation and the 5d prepotential from M-theory geometry test the proposal. As a nonperturbative check, they determine the single-string worldsheet elliptic genus using modular bootstrap. The corresponding vertex operator algebra's vacuum character matches the result, completing the elliptic genus correspondence along the Deligne-Cvitanović series.
arxiv-2602-02182: Tjaša Arčon and others evaluate how much large language models know about linguistic structure across the languages of the world. Existing benchmarks cover narrow phenomena and favor high-resource languages, rarely probing metalinguistic thought. The team converts traits from the World Atlas of Language Structures into several-choice questions spanning thousands of languages. Results show limited knowledge: the best model reaches only moderate score and none beats a simple majority-class baseline. Accuracy tracks digital presence, with resource indicators predicting results better than geography, genealogy, or sociolinguistic factors.
arxiv-2602-02382: Ziyan Zhang and others propose ROG, a retrieval-augmented method for first-order logic queries on incomplete knowledge graphs. ROG combines neighborhood retrieval with chain-of-thought thought, decomposing a multi-operator query into sub-queries grounded in query-relevant neighborhood evidence. Answer sets from steps are cached and reused, improving consistency on deep chains.
arxiv-2602-02482:
Yuda Song and 7 co-authors study text feedback as a middle-strength training signal for language models, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning from binary rewards gives one bit of information per attempt, while distillation gives dense supervision but needs costly demonstrations. Written critiques sit between the two: richer than a score, cheaper than a worked solution, and already produced by users and judges everywhere.

Their setup makes feedback available during training but not at test time, so models must internalize it. Two methods do that. Self distillation trains the single-turn policy to match its own feedback-conditioned second attempts. Feedback modeling adds predicting the critique as an auxiliary task. Theory supports both methods. Experiments on reasoning puzzles, competition math, and creative writing beat strong baselines consistently.
arxiv-2602-02582:
Chandan Kumar Sah and 4 co-authors benchmark uncertainty and fairness jointly in language-model recommendation systems, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models can recommend movies and music with no task training, thanks to broad background knowledge. Uncertainty and embedded bias threaten whether those recommendations deserve trust.

The team built a data set annotated for eight attributes tied to user groups across movie and music domains, plus a suite of curated metrics. Case studies measure uncertainty through entropy. They find that one major commercial model shows systematic unfairness for certain sensitive attributes, with clear similarity-based gaps. The gaps persisted under typos and multilingual prompts. Adding personality-aware fairness analysis exposed personality-linked bias and sharp trade-offs between tailoring and group fairness. The authors propose an uncertainty-aware testing methodology as a base for safer, more interpretable recommendation systems.
arxiv-2602-02682:
A steady re-testing of the Hartle-Hawking no-boundary proposal comes from Ahmed I. Abdalla and 5 co-authors, whose 2026 paper insists that probabilities need norms, not just amplitudes. The gravitational path integral computes the no-boundary amplitude for a closed cosmos. Dividing by properly computed norms changes the predictions a great deal.

The probability for any closed cosmos turns out to be either nearly one or exactly one. In the Hilbert space the path integral defines, the states that matter for cosmology are all nearly parallel to the Hartle-Hawking state, up to nonperturbative fixes. A statistical reading of the integral, as an average over amplitude products, makes every amplitude exactly one. That matches recent claims that such averages run over 1D Hilbert spaces. Inflationary cosmology shows the steady testing at work. The proposal survives, but its probability content looks very different.
arxiv-2602-02882:
Sarah Ball and 3 co-authors test a different way to predict human preferences with language models in a 2026 paper. Instead of only reading what a model outputs, they probe its internal representations. Election forecasting serves as their test case for the method, which they call mechanistic forecasting.

The team ran millions of configurations across seven models and six national elections. They varied persona traits and prompt wording. They tracked how demographic and ideological details activate internal components that encode political parties. Using that internal signal sometimes beat surface predictions. Effects differed by attribute type, party, country, and model. The findings suggest model internals hold usable information about human preferences.
arxiv-2602-03082:
Neural networks that must respect geometric constraints are organized by Karthik Elamvazhuthi and 6 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Architectures enforce such constraints through projections, exponential-map updates, constrained output layers, or manifold differential equations. The authors unify them by where and how enforcement happens, either throughout intermediate layers or only at the final output of the network.

That perspective reveals gaps in existing theory. The authors prove approximation theorems for several architecture families on prox-regular constraint sets, including smooth manifolds with boundary. Experiments cover synthetic dynamics on spheres, disks, and rotation groups, plus real protein backbone data. Final augmentation proved simpler and won most tasks. When the constraint set is unknown, projections can be learned from diffusion models.
arxiv-2602-03282:
Global shape of a vector space says little about composition, according to Jiwan Chung, with 1 co-author. Representation learning often assumes well-distributed vectors imply robust, generalizable traits. Global geometry encodes which elements are present in an image. It can be insensitive to how those elements are composed. That is the binding problem: whether a model knows which attribute belongs to which object in a scene.

The authors test whether geometric metrics predict compositional binding across a diverse suite of vision encoders. Standard geometry statistics showed near-zero correlation with binding ability. Functional sensitivity, measured through the input-output Jacobian, tracked the capability reliably instead. An analytic account traces the disparity to training objectives, which constrain vector geometry but leave the local input-output mapping unconstrained. Geometry, they conclude, is only a partial view.
arxiv-2602-03682:
Pierre Aguié and 2 co-authors sharpen the theory of a workhorse algorithm for principal component analysis when matrix products come back noisy. Their 2026 paper analyzes the Accelerated Noisy Power Method, which gains speed from acceleration but whose earlier guarantees demanded unrealistically small perturbations. That restriction limited its use for decentralized PCA across machines.

The new analysis keeps the accelerated rate under much milder noise conditions. The authors also prove the result is worst-case optimal: neither the rate nor the noise conditions can be improved in general. Applying the theory, they derive an accelerated decentralized PCA algorithm whose communication cost matches non-accelerated methods. They describe it as the first decentralized PCA method with provable acceleration.
arxiv-2602-03882:
People differ in how they expect faces to look, and Haijiang Yan and 2 co-authors found a way to measure those expectations. Their 2026 paper introduces PriorProbe, a method that recovers a person's prior beliefs about expressions using a sampling technique adapted from Markov chain Monte Carlo.

Feeding each person's recovered priors into a top neural network sharpened its predictions for that person. The gains beat both the network alone and priors from other sources. Accuracy on clear-cut labels stayed intact. The work points toward AI systems tuned to individual judgment rather than population averages.
arxiv-2602-04082:
High-frequency waves defeat fixed-rule neural solvers, so Yicheng Zou and 2 co-authors go probabilistic. Their 2026 paper builds a diffusion-model framework for the Helmholtz equation, which governs how waves spread. At high frequencies, tiny input changes swing the solution, and plain networks blur the oscillations.

A score-based conditional diffusion operator generates answers with uncertainty attached. Stability analysis of the Helmholtz operator backs the design. Across frequencies, the method posted the lowest errors among tested methods in several norms. Alone, it also captured how uncertainty in the sound-speed map spreads into the solution. Acoustics and medical imaging both need exactly that honesty.
arxiv-2602-04282:
A gas of particles with memory, wandering a tangled random medium, still obeys limit laws. Jiaming Chen studies the Levy-Lorentz model in a 2026 paper. In it, a stochastic gas is driven by a long-range random walk on a correlated, entangled integer lattice.

Chen adds step reinforcement, giving the walk memory of its own history. Central limit theorems are obtained for both the reinforced and unreinforced dynamics. Scaling limits tell physicists what the motion looks like from far away, washing out microscopic detail. Proving them under long-range jumps, disorder, and memory together extends the rigorous theory of anomalous transport.
arxiv-2602-04482:
Proactive assistants try to help before a user asks, but judging them requires realistic data. Yuanbo Tang and 8 co-authors introduce ProAgentBench in a 2026 paper on evaluating such agents in real working situations.

The benchmark splits proactive help into two parts: predicting when to step in and deciding what help to offer. Its dataset holds tens of thousands of events from hundreds of hours of real user sessions, collected with privacy safeguards. The data preserve bursty patterns of human activity that synthetic data miss. Experiments showed that long-term memory and past context improved prediction. Models trained on real data also beat those trained on synthetic data.
arxiv-2602-04682:
Emma G Crenshaw, Yuhua Zhang, and Jukka-Pekka Onnela develop a statistical framework for sparse networks with many node features, in a 2026 paper spanning social science and infectious disease research. Existing methods struggle when networks are thin and each person or node carries high-dimensional information.

Their joint latent space model links network edges and node variables through shared hidden positions. A group lasso step, a selection technique, screens for relevant covariates. A stabilization term corrects bias from using estimated positions. The method uses isolated nodes instead of discarding them. Theory gives prediction error rates, and simulations stayed stable as features grew sparser. An application to village household networks in India showed leaner study designs.
arxiv-2602-05082:
An explanation of a model's choice is only useful if it stays steady when nil key changes. Poushali Sengupta and 4 co-authors built a yardstick for that steadiness in this 2026 machine learning paper. Loved tools such as SHAP and Integrated Gradients rest on sound attribution axioms, yet their outputs can swing under small input shifts, redundant features, or minor model updates.

The Explanation Reliability Index measures steadiness against four axioms: surviving small perturbations, staying consistent when features duplicate information, shifting smoothly as a model evolves. It also holds up under mild shifts in the data. A companion measure covers sequential models over time, and a benchmark called ERI-Bench stress-tests methods on synthetic and real data. The tests found widespread reliability failures in loved explainers, which the authors offer as a base for more trustworthy explainable AI.
arxiv-2602-05182:
Teams of language models outperform single models, but running several at once costs several times more. Shangbin Feng and 3 co-authors propose a loop that keeps the gains while shedding the cost in this 2026 paper. The recipe is distillation: let models collaborate, train a single model on the collaboration's outputs, and at run time deploy only that one model, which has absorbed the team's habits.

The loop then closes. The improved single models collaborate again, distill again, and the system evolves collectively. Across seven collaboration strategies and fifteen tasks spanning question answering, reasoning, and factuality, individual models improved by about eight percent on average after distillation. The second-generation collaboration beat the original system by about fifteen percent. The authors report the loop outperforms other evolutionary AI schemes and works across many model and distillation choices.
arxiv-2602-05282:
Solar flares release energy through magnetic reconnection, and radio waves from the low corona can image that process directly. Yingjie Luo and 7 co-authors present the first detailed imaging spectroscopy of a flare with the MeerKAT radio telescope in this 2026 astronomy paper, accepted by The Astrophysical Journal Letters. MeerKAT is a precursor to the coming SKA-Mid array, and its image quality sets the study apart.

The target was a mid-sized M1.3 flare. The images reached a dynamic range above a thousand, letting the team study bright coherent bursts and faint diffuse emission in the same frame. Several distinct coherent sources appeared, pointing to separate populations of accelerated electrons, and the diffuse emission stretched beyond structures seen in extreme ultraviolet, revealing hot dilute plasma those instruments miss. With hard X-ray images and magnetic field models alongside, the radio sources sit inside distinct magnetic structures.
arxiv-2602-05382:
When a vision-language model fails an IQ-style puzzle, the failure could be in seeing the pattern or in reasoning about it. Tina Khezresmaeilzadeh and 2 co-authors built VRIQ in this 2026 computer vision paper to separate those stages. The benchmark holds 1,391 human-verified visual reasoning puzzles in five psychometric categories, each appearing in both abstract form and as natural images.

A diagnostic subset of 209 items pairs each puzzle with a verified, rule-neutral text description, so reasoning can be tested with perception removed. Across 21 models, the non-frontier systems averaged under 27 percent on abstract puzzles, and even the strongest 2026 frontier models, while much better, stayed uneven and below human performance. Given correct descriptions, top models still missed about a tenth of the items. Adding true descriptions or tools helped, most on spatial categories, without eliminating the errors.
arxiv-2602-05482:
Starlight appears shifted in direction when seen by a moving observer, an effect called aberration, and standard relativity says that shift does not depend on the light's polarization. Bahram Mashhoon reviews the locality assumption behind those standard formulas, then examines a small correction that arises when the observer rotates. The twist of the light, known as its helicity, couples with the observer's spin in this effect.

Because of that coupling, the direction shift for polarized light gains a slight helicity-dependent term that the standard formula omits. Mashhoon traces the physical origin of the correction and estimates how large it should be. The review also covers the related Doppler effect for both light and gravitational radiation. The paper is a single-author survey for readers in relativistic measurement. It clarifies where textbook formulas hold and where rotation forces a small change.
arxiv-2602-05582:
Judging how much one camera measurement should move a pose estimate is central to robot localization, and weak geometry can make that judgment treacherous. Joe-Mei Feng, Hsin-Hsiung Kao, and Sheng-Wei Yu introduce the Geometric Observability Index, a per-feature sensitivity measure for pose estimation on the space of rotations and translations. It gives the size of the pose shift a single measurement induces through the Gauss-Newton curvature, limited to the observable directions.

The authors prove the index equals the norm of the influence function from robust statistics, and that the curvature operator behind it is the Fisher information. Experiments on synthetic data and on TUM RGB-D and KITTI sequences test two gating rules. Raw-influence gating over-rejects valuable measurements when geometry is weakly observable, while residual gating holds up better. Code is released.
arxiv-2602-05882:
Spotting what changed between two satellite images is a workhorse task of earth observation, and most methods pay for it with heavy twin encoders and complex decoders. Mubashir Noman, Mustansar Fiaz, and 5 co-authors propose EoCD, an encoder only change detection method that strips the design down. Temporal images are fused early, before encoding, instead of being processed by a Siamese pair.

A parameter free multiscale fusion module replaces the decoder entirely, cutting model complexity sharply. Across a variety of encoder architectures, the method found an optimal balance between detection quality and prediction speed. It also held its own against late fusion methods, which early fusion designs usually trail. The authors present the simplicity as the contribution: comparable results without the overhead that production change detection pipelines usually carry. The work targets remote sensing teams that process large image archives, where per image cost decides what is feasible.
arxiv-2602-06382:
A humanoid robot that walks by camera alone must survive noisy depth images and wildly different ground. Wandong Sun and 12 co-authors present an end-to-end learning framework for exactly that job. Simulated training usually transfers poorly, because real depth sensors leave artifacts that simulators omit.

Their depth simulator reproduces stereo matching flaws and calibration errors. A distillation step then transfers skill from clean height maps to the noisy depth view, guided by tasks that ignore noise. Separate reward shaping and paired critic and discriminator networks handle each terrain's distinct dynamics. Policies ran on two real humanoid platforms with different cameras, crossing harsh terrain while keeping the distinct motion style each surface demands.
arxiv-2602-06482:
Estimating parameters by matching moments works through a special family of functions, but the classic Stein approach leaves two choices unpinned. Alfred Kume and Stephen G Walker show that one natural choice, the derivative of the density score with respect to the parameter, turns the method into a generalized score matching estimator. A weight function remains to be chosen.

That weight, they show, behaves like a transformation of the data. The best transformation sends the sample toward normality, as a Box-Cox transform does, when paired with a score estimator. They compare this proposal against an alternative that handles the weight through a generalized method of moments estimator. The comparison clarifies when each handling serves best.
arxiv-2602-06782:
Mohamed Khoulane, Aziz El Ghazouani, and M'hamed Elomari examine conformable derivatives, a fractional variant that keeps locality. On smooth functions they reduce to an ordinary derivative times an explicit weight. The paper asks whether time evolution built from them is genuinely new, or just classical evolution seen through a changed clock. The answer, proved in full, is the latter.

Every conformable semigroup is shown to equal a classical semigroup evaluated at a nonlinear time. The two share the same driving rules on a common domain, and their solutions match one to one under the time change. Orbit sets are unchanged, so orbit-based traits such as hypercyclicity and chaos carry over exactly. As an application the authors transport a classical chaos criterion into the conformable setting. They also show the associated function spaces match the usual ones, so estimates and spectral arguments transfer too.
arxiv-2602-06882:
Christopher J. Eagle and two co-authors continue a study of what K-theory can compute, now for AF algebras. Those algebras grow as limits of finite-size algebras, and Elliott's classification sorts them by their K-theory. The open question is whether that sorting can be made effective, in the sense of algorithms.

From a listable presentation of an AF algebra, the team computes its form as a limit of finite-size pieces. A twin result for dimension groups then yields a computable match between AF algebras and dimension groups, an effective form of Elliott's theorem. The tools also pin down how hard the index and isomorphism problems are for several classes of AF algebras.
arxiv-2602-06982:
Pujitha Mamillapalli and three co-authors tame interference in space-air-ground networks for future 6G. High-altitude platforms and satellites extend ground networks for wide, low-lag coverage. Yet rapid growth in ground devices forces spectrum sharing between ground and non-ground parts, causing severe cross-tier interference. Sharing between the platform-to-satellite uplink and the platform-to-ground downlink boosts spectrum use, but the platform antenna's back-lobe leaks in.

Old zero-forcing codebooks falter when channels shift fast. The team instead uses a reconfigurable intelligent surface with a deep deterministic policy gradient algorithm. It tunes beamforming weights to carve spatial nulls toward interference sources while keeping wanted links strong. Simulations show it beats standard zero-forcing across surface setups, gaining up to 11.3 percent in throughput for a four-by-four surface.
arxiv-2602-07082:
Haoming Wang and three co-authors strengthen spatial reasoning for small vision-language models on device. Embodied AI is moving past object detection toward robot manipulation and action planning. Those tasks need visual spatial reasoning from video inputs, to grasp spatial links between objects and steer device acts. Yet current vision-language models reason weakly about space, lacking 3D knowledge, most of all when tasks span complex relations across many video frames.

Their method, MosaicThinker, is an inference-time computing trick for on-device embodied AI. It gathers fragmented spatial clues from many frames into one global semantic map of space. It then guides the small vision-language model's spatial reasoning over that map with a visual prompt. Tests show it lifts accuracy a great deal on cross-frame spatial reasoning, across task types and complexity levels, on resource-constrained embodied devices.
arxiv-2602-07182:
Cost overruns and failed projects often trace back to tangled specs, written long before any code exists. Maximilian Vierlboeck and four co-authors tackle that early tangle by pulling networks out of spec texts and scoring them with spectral metrics, measures that sum up a network's shape.

Using molecular tasks as stand-ins for spec integration, they run a test of whether those scores predict how much work building will take. The approach matters because specs drive all that follows: catching tangled specs early could save far more than fixing tangled code later. Systems builders get a case, backed by data, for scoring what specs usually leave unscored.
arxiv-2602-07582:
Steering a coupled degenerate parabolic system inside a domain that moves over time raises a hierarchy problem: a leader and others with other objectives. Alfredo S. Gamboa and two co-authors study hierarchical null controllability for such systems under a Nash-Stackelberg game structure.

Local null controllability of the semilinear system follows from an inverse function theorem. The main difficulty lies in fitting a Carleman estimate to the linearized optimality system for degenerate, non-autonomous systems in non-cylindrical domains. Control theorists get a control result for moving-domain systems where the leader-follower setup tangles the classic theory.
arxiv-2602-08082:
Autonomous agents fail when they hallucinate tool use, calling tools wrongly or inventing results, and supervised safeguards need labeled failures to train on. Valentin Noël proposes a guardrail that needs no training, built on spectral analysis of attention topology, the shape of how attention flows inside the model.

On Llama 3.1 8B, multi-feature detection reaches 97.7 percent recall, and a balanced setup gives 86.1 percent recall at 81.0 percent precision, with no labeled training data. Remarkably, single-layer spectral features act as near-perfect detectors, catching 213 of 217 hallucinations at one threshold. The author suggests hallucination is not just a wrong token but a change in the model's internal state, with attention collapsing into noise, a finding agent builders should test.
arxiv-2602-08282:
Predicting where plant species occur at large scales matters for conservation, but sighting data are sparse and biased: exact presence-absence records are scarce, while broad presence-only records carry noisy negatives. Haixu Liu and four co-authors propose Tighnari v2, a multimodal method that uses both data types as one.

A pseudo-label aggregation plan based on satellite-image geographic coverage aligns the label space with remote-sensing traits. The architecture pairs a Swin Transformer for satellite imagery with a tabular network and temporal modeling. By exploiting the strengths of each data type while compensating for their weaknesses, the system improves cross-species distribution prediction. Conservation scientists gain a model built for the messy, biased data the real world actually provides.
arxiv-2602-08482:
Ship-tracking data from the Automatic Identification System is rich but messy, and non-experts struggle to make sense of it. Hengyu Liu and seven co-authors present CLEAR, a platform that turns raw vessel tracks into complete, explorable trajectories with language-model help. Their arXiv paper targets maritime analysts who need transparency, not just plots.

A structured knowledge graph derived from the data organizes each trajectory, and users can inspect raw and filled-in segments side by side with their supporting evidence. A demo lets participants configure downloads, watch trajectories complete and annotate themselves, and explore the graph interactively. Readers get a knowledge-centered approach to vessel analytics that keeps its reasoning visible.
arxiv-2602-08682:
Video generation is moving toward clips where sound and picture are born together, not bolted on later. Ying Guo and fifteen co-authors present ALIVE, a model that adapts a text-to-video system to Sora-like joint audio-video creation and animation. Their arXiv paper unlocks both text-driven and reference-driven audio-video creation.

A joint audio-video branch added to a popular transformer design handles timing: one attention mechanism fuses modalities in sync, while a rotary position scheme aligns sound and frames precisely. A careful data pipeline of captioning and quality control supplies million-scale fine-tuning data, plus a new benchmark. ALIVE beats open models and matches or passes commercial systems. Readers get recipes for building unified audio-video generators.
arxiv-2602-08782:
Bayesian deep learning needs priors over network weights, but choosing those priors by hand is notoriously hard. Tommy Rochussen and Vincent Fortuin propose learning the prior itself from a collection of datasets through per-dataset amortized variational inference. Their arXiv paper bridges Bayesian deep learning and probabilistic meta-learning.

The resulting model reads as a neural process in which the latent variable is the weight set of a Bayesian network, with the network itself as decoder. That view enables studying Bayesian networks under well-specified priors, using them as flexible generative models, and achieving previously elusive feats like within-task minibatching and meta-learning under extreme data starvation. Readers get a principled way to learn priors instead of guessing them.
arxiv-2602-09182:
Chance underpins machine learning, from data sampling to weight setup, yet the fake-random makers behind it vary across setups, linked parts, and hardware, with little stats checking. Kotekar Annapoorna Prabhu and two co-authors probe that pipeline like attackers, showing how weak or uneven chance becomes a hidden attack route with a real history of abuse.

Their tool, RNGGuard, scans a library's source code for random-function use, then at run time swaps unsafe calls for builds meeting safety rules. The design aims to let engineers close chance gaps with low effort. Tests suggest the approach is handy, turning a missed supply-chain risk into a checkable trait of the codebase.
arxiv-2602-09282:
Old-style checking of quantum computing has had an awkward catch: plans demand many copies of the quantum witness and destroy each one. That in effect asks the prover to copy a state that cannot be copied. Yael Tauman Kalai and two co-authors build a plan that old-style checks QMA languages using a single copy of the prover's witness. When the first quantum checker would take that witness with near-certain odds, the new plan has tiny fullness and health errors.

Key point: after talks with a truthful checker, the witness comes back barely changed, so the quantum cat survives checking. Health rests on the post-quantum Learning With Errors guess. A middle finding of solo interest gives witness-keeping old-style cases for NP, letting provers holding mixed states over witnesses win over a checker without shaking them.
arxiv-2602-09382:
Estimating the persistence of a time series is delicate when the autoregressive parameter sits near one, the boundary between stable and wandering behavior. Existing confidence intervals assume a stationary or fixed starting point, and their coverage collapses when that assumption fails. Donald W. K. Andrews and two co-authors introduce a new interval in their 2026 paper whose coverage holds regardless of the starting point.

The interval stays valid both in large samples and in finite samples, a stronger guarantee than rivals offer. When the starting point is in fact stationary or fixed, the new interval costs only a little extra length. It also tolerates conditional heteroskedasticity, where error volatility shifts over time. The paper thus trades a small amount of precision for robustness exactly where older methods break down.
arxiv-2602-09482:
Yue Zhang and four co-authors develop a compact gas-kinetic scheme in a moving-mesh formulation for structured grids. Unlike fixed-grid methods, the moving-mesh approach tracks flow breaks such as shocks and contact surfaces, but mesh motion reshapes geometry and raises cost. Two strategies tame that cost: a gas-kinetic flux giving third-order time accuracy with a single reconstruction and flux calculation per step, updating both cell averages and gradients directly.

The second strategy simplifies fourth-order compact reconstruction to a small matrix, avoiding a costly matrix rebuild at every step. Together, high spatial resolution and time-accurate flux evolution keep the scheme both sharp and efficient. Reconstruction runs roughly two and a half to three times faster than before, and a generalized discontinuity method adds robustness. Standard shock, blast, and implosion tests confirm accuracy and toughness.
arxiv-2602-09582:
The soft X-ray excess below two kiloelectronvolts in active galaxies remains debated: relativistic reflection from the inner disk versus warm Comptonization in a thick corona. Deblina Lahiri and two co-authors investigate the Seyfert galaxy Mrk 110 with six XMM-Newton observations in their 2026 paper. A frequency-dependent lag analysis finds a soft X-ray lag of hundreds to thousands of seconds in combined recent data, supported by cross-correlation and simulations.

Spectral modeling confirms a warm corona in all observations, with a weak relativistic reflection component at low reflection fraction. Reading the lag as light travel time gives a small emission radius for the higher literature black hole mass, favoring reflection, while a lower mass leaves both mechanisms plausible. The warm corona grows in high accretion states, and the persistently low reflection fraction suggests an outflowing inner corona, consistent with recent jet activity.
arxiv-2602-09782:
Reward learning with checked rewards is a key method for lifting large language model thought. Kun Chen and six co-authors note that steady training often leads to entropy collapse: rapid entropy decay causing early hubris, reduced output range, and fading gradient norms that inhibit learning. Gradient-preserving clipping mainly drives these moves, yet current fixes are largely static and lack a frame linking clipping gears to exact entropy control. Their 2026 paper remakes entropy control from the gradient-preserving clipping view.

The authors first verify in theory and in tests how single importance sampling ratio regions add to entropy growth and fall. A novel control gear using dynamic clipping thresholds then manages entropy exactly. Dynamic entropy control plans are built and tested, including increase-then-decrease, decrease-increase-decrease, and waving decay patterns. Results show these plans ease entropy collapse well and achieve better scores across multiple benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-09882:
Quantum computation threatens signature schemes built on classical hardness assumptions. Asmaa Cherkaoui and three co-authors introduce Spinel, a post-quantum digital signature scheme, in their 2026 paper. Spinel combines the proven security of SPHINCS+ with a new family of algebraic hash functions rooted in the hardness of navigating expander graphs, a problem believed hard even for quantum adversaries.

The authors first give empirical evidence for the hash function's security, complementing its original theoretical analysis, then show how it fits within the SPHINCS+ framework to yield a secure scheme. They model and analyze how security degrades, which guides their parameter choices, and they provide an implementation with detailed performance results showing Spinel is feasible in practice. The work lays foundations for algebraic hash-based signature design.
arxiv-2602-09982:
Forecasts that update over time, such as election projections or live win odds, are hard to grade before the final outcome arrives. A 2026 paper by Michael Beuoy proposes grading them like a betting contest. Each model plays as a Kelly bettor, staking its stated odds, and its bankroll rises or falls with each update.

The bankroll then serves as a running score, and market consensus can be refreshed as models revise themselves. In simulations the method distinguished right models from wrong ones more accurately than average log-loss or Brier scores. Beuoy shows the bankroll tracks Bayesian credibility, giving the contest a direct analogue in inference theory.
arxiv-2602-10082:
Clouds battered by galactic winds mix, break apart, or survive depending on cooling and grid fineness, yet the grid rules were murky. A 2026 paper led by Hannah Leary, with two co-authors, runs cloud-crushing simulations to test how numerical grid fineness shapes cloud survival and speed. Both adiabatic and radiative cases are modeled, in subsonic and supersonic winds.

Survival and speed do depend on grid fineness, but no single requirement fits all cases. In the radiative subsonic case, mass growth and speed settle at only four cells per cloud radius. In the supersonic regime, breakup and speed stay grid-dependent even at forty-eight cells per radius, so breakup needs finer grids than growth does.
arxiv-2602-10182:
Chance-based foresight matters most where tail events decide results, yet standard metrics often assume freedom across time steps or factors and dull tail feel. A 2026 paper led by Benjamin R. Redhead, with four co-authors, offers two kernel-based metrics built on the signature kernel: signature maximum mean discrepancy and a novel cut variant. Both capture links across factors and time while handling missing data.

The cut variant favors tail-event foresight while strictly keeping properness, the trait that keeps a scoring rule honest. Together, the metrics allow sounder testing of direct multi-step foresight and support building of more robust chance-based methods for finance, disease tracking, climate science, and other high-stakes domains.
arxiv-2602-10282:
Language models show promise for quality-style causal relations, but number-based causal thought in continuous domains remains little explored. A 2026 paper led by Kanta Yamaoka, with seven co-authors, offers Linear-LLM-SCM, a plug-and-play test setup for LLMs on linear Gaussian structural causal model setup when a directed acyclic graph is given. The framework splits a DAG into local parent-child groups and asks an LLM to write a regression-style structural equation per node, then pools and compares them against ground-truth parameters.

Tests with seven real-world DAGs with ground truth expose limits of LLMs as number-based causal parameterizers. Across most models, coefficient guesses vary and prove touchy to structural shifts. The framework is open-sourced to spur further work on LLM causal effect elicitation in safety-critical domains such as healthcare.
arxiv-2602-10382:
Backdoor attacks on large language models are a serious risk, yet how triggers work inside a model has stayed poorly understood. A 2026 paper led by Théo Lasnier, with four co-authors, gives the first mechanistic analysis of language-switching backdoors injected during pre-training. It studies the Gaperon family at one, eight, and twenty-four billion parameters. Using activation patching, they localize trigger formation and find which attention heads handle trigger and natural language information.

They find trigger heads overlap substantially with heads that naturally encode output language, with overlap scores from roughly a fifth to just over two-fifths across the top ten heads. Triggers thus build no new circuits, the authors argue, but co-opt existing language components and representations. That entanglement matters for defense, since detection methods could exploit it. The work is a first step toward a realistic mechanistic account of such backdoors.
arxiv-2602-10682:
Jorge Sanchez Almeida and three co-authors weigh in on a debated cosmic streak in a 2026 paper. A linear structure reported in 2023 was new either as the stellar wake of a runaway supermassive black hole or as a bulgeless edge-on galaxy. New JWST views target the structure's tip, where the two scenarios predict other physics.

A runaway black hole should produce a bow shock at the tip, while a normal galaxy should host a star-forming region there. Standard emission-line diagrams place the tip's line ratios on the locus of low-metallicity, low-extinction star-forming regions. That locus sits far from shock loci typical of merging galaxies. The spectra thus favor the galaxy reading, with the bright knot as one of its star-forming regions.
arxiv-2602-10882:
David Theidel and six co-authors certify non-classic light from high-harmonic making in semiconductors in a 2026 paper. Quantum tools need platforms that generate complex non-classic states, and semiconductor high-harmonic making is a rising hope. The team reads click numbers of three double-digit tone orders and tests witness rules for non-classic traits.

Higher-order tones driven by a steady laser prove squashed and linked, well told by a linked bell-curve state model fitted to multiple readings. Inter-order flagged readings build emission states with other traits, including sub-Poisson photon numbers and proven quantum non-bell traits. The results prove high-harmonic making as a source of truly quantum light.
arxiv-2602-11382:
Extension hardness measures how compactly a polytope can be lifted. M. Szusterman, writing alone, studies it through randomized communication rules, using non-negative factorizations of slack matrices. A geometric profile based on the width of Markovian rules is offered, as a variant of an earlier frame.

That profile yields a new upper bound for the matching polytope, improving on the standard exponential bound from Edmonds' description. The same machinery recovers Goemans' compact form for the permutahedron via a one-round rule based on sorting networks. The paper tightens a classic hardness measure with a rule-width lens.
arxiv-2602-11482:
Recovering sparse vectors from Poisson-noisy straight models suffers bias under standard control. Kazuki Haishima and two co-authors offer an tool built by externally dividing two Bregman proximity tools, promoting sparsity while mitigating bias from classic absolute-value control. The tool plugs into the established NoLips recipe in place of its standard proximity step.

Two complementary reformulations clarify the tool's shape in primal and dual spaces for the Poisson problem. Numerical tests show more stable convergence than usual divergence-based approaches and greatly superior results on built data and an image restoration task. The work offers a principled plug-and-play upgrade for Poisson inverse problems.
arxiv-2602-11882:
Suraj Ranganath and two co-authors ask where bits matter most when a world model plans under a tight precision budget. They test DINO-WM on a Wall planning task, comparing uniform, mixed, asymmetric, and layerwise bit plans across two planner budgets with paired goals. The question is whether results track total bitwidth, or where bits are placed across modules.

A clear three-regime pattern shows up. Settings at 8-bit and 6-bit stay close to full half precision, while 3-bit settings collapse. At 4-bit, placement matters: keeping encoder precision high beats uniform quantization, and near-size asymmetric plans point the same way. A stricter rerun with 22 cells and fewer episodes per cell finds the 4-bit mixed-versus-uniform edge shifts with budget. The lesson is to set bit plans by module and budget, not by total bits alone.
arxiv-2602-11982:
Cyber security guidance only helps if readers can understand it, yet vulnerability descriptions are written for specialists. Varpu Vehomäki and one co-author test whether large language models can simplify Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures descriptions automatically. They build a baseline for cyber security text simplification and a test set of 40 vulnerability descriptions, evaluated by two groups of cyber security experts across two survey rounds.

The verdict is mixed: out-of-the-box models can make text look simpler while struggling to preserve meaning. That gap matters, since a simplification that drops or distorts a security detail misleads exactly the non-experts it aims to help. The study is the first, to the authors' knowledge, to examine simplification in the fast-changing cyber security domain, and its code and data are publicly available.
arxiv-2602-12182:
Most messages ask a receiver to decode a full text, but identification asks a simpler question: is this the one message I mean? Pau Colomer led this work with three co-authors, extending the rate-reliability trade-off for deterministic identification to general linear Gaussian channels. That step matters because Gaussian channels model many real links, yet prior work stayed with discrete outputs.

Because identification can beat ordinary decoding on efficiency, the trade-off sets what future networks might gain from it. The paper finds close parallels between Gaussian and discrete cases, hinting that similar behaviour may hold for wider classes of continuous channels. Readers get both a first continuous-output analysis and a guide for judging identification in real systems.
arxiv-2602-12382:
Wannier functions give a localised picture of electrons in solids, and Pipek-Mezey localisation is a standard route to them. Gengzhi Yang led this work with one co-author, Hong-Zhou Ye. They extend the second-order co-iterative augmented Hessian method to k-points, as k-CIAH.

Efficient Hessian-vector products give scaling of order Nk squared times n cubed in both time and memory. That matches first-order k-space methods and beats the Nk cubed scaling of Gamma-point CIAH. Tests across insulators, semiconductors, metals, and surfaces show fast, robust convergence. Overall efficiency is about two to three times first-order k-space methods, and orders of magnitude above Gamma-point CIAH for 1,000 to 5,000 orbitals. Resulting band structures from Wannier interpolation confirm the quality of the localised functions.
arxiv-2602-12882:
Manganese doping can tune gallium nitride, but how much manganese actually sticks depends on growth conditions. YongJin Cho and three co-authors grew manganese-doped gallium nitride layers at 680 degrees Celsius by molecular beam epitaxy on a gallium-polar template, testing gallium-rich, nitrogen-rich, and no-flux conditions. Incorporation was highest under nitrogen-rich growth, lowest under gallium-rich growth, and in between with no flux.

Relative to the nitrogen-rich case, the sticking coefficients were 0.31 for no-flux growth and just 0.01 for gallium-rich growth. That hundred-fold contrast gives growers a clear lever: nitrogen-rich conditions favour manganese uptake, while gallium-rich conditions nearly shut it out. The brief report offers a practical calibration for anyone doping gallium nitride with manganese.
arxiv-2602-13082:
Urban mobility involves travellers, modes, and infrastructure together, yet most analyses stop at origin-destination counts. Khristina Filonchik and three co-authors apply process mining to mobility event data from call detail records in Oeiras, in the Lisbon area. They build event logs centred on cases and on objects, and discover models summarising flows and typical durations.

Most trips stay within the municipality, while inter-municipal flows link strongly to neighbouring areas, with typical inter-parish travel near 20 minutes. The object-centric view links trips to modes explicitly, revealing mode-specific duration differences, such as bus versus car, that inform multimodal planning. Contributions include a reproducible pipeline, evidence that mobility data have process-like structure, and the added value of object-centric models. Limits include coarse tower-sector locations and heuristic mode labels.
arxiv-2602-13382:
Ultramassive black holes test a neat theoretical pattern. The link between a central black hole's mass and its host spheroid's velocity dispersion follows the same fourth-power form in spirals, ellipticals, and cluster ellipticals, but with different normalizations. Recent observations appear to confirm that pattern, with the differing levels explained by longer accretion episodes needed to expel gas that could otherwise feed holes in the latter two host types.

A mixed sample of host types will therefore fit a power slightly above four, an artifact of mixing normalizations rather than a new law. Observed masses still fall short of the theoretical ceiling for disc accretion, set where orbital stability meets self-gravity, likely because hosts lack enough gas. Andrew King is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13482:
Picking a classifier is easy to get wrong when only one score is reported, since the choice of metric can flip which model looks best. This tutorial paper walks through the PyCM library for deep evaluation of multi-class classifiers, using two case scenarios to show how metric choice reshapes interpretation. A multi-dimensional view surfaces small but important differences that single scores hide.

Standard metrics, the authors warn, may miss subtle trade-offs between models, and a robust, comprehensive evaluation framework is essential for a defensible choice. The tutorial style makes the material accessible to practitioners who need to compare models rather than merely rank them by accuracy. Sadra Sabouri leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13582:
The spectral gap and diameter of Cayley graphs can depend sharply on the chosen generating set. This paper answers a 2013 question of Pyber and Szabo by exhibiting groups where the choice flips the outcome. A sequence of finite groups with growing order admits bounded generating sets of two kinds. One gives an expander graph, while the other gives a graph with super-polylogarithmic diameter, far from expander-like.

The construction uses a semidirect product of a large elementary abelian group with a symmetric group, with the prime exponentially large in n. The analysis reduces to bounding exponential sums of permutational type. The result shows expansion and diameter can diverge wildly for the same group under different generators. Sean Eberhard leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13682:
A software bill of materials lists a product's parts, dependencies, and metadata, but sharing it in full exposes private dependencies, unpatched flaws, and design strategy. Plaintext delivery can thus harm a company's private property, so organizations often refuse full disclosure. VeriSBOM solves this tension as a trustless, partly disclosed framework that proves claims about a bill of materials with zero-knowledge proofs.

Third parties can verify that software contains genuine dependencies from official package managers and that those dependencies meet policy rules, such as freedom from vulnerable dependencies or adherence to specific license models. A scalable vector pledge scheme with folding-based proof pooling yields short proofs, and checking needs no trust in the publisher beyond the soundness of the underlying primitives. Gianpietro Castiglione leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14182:
Peng Cheng and two co-authors study a 2026 arXiv shadow cast by a rotating traversable wormhole. In the Teo family with a broad redshift rule, the shadow rim is the joint outline of two orbit sets: shaky round orbits beyond the throat, and orbits sitting at the throat. Cusps mark where smooth edges turn cuspy.

Cusps only appear when the redshift parameter lambda is allowed to vary, and a universal critical value lambda-c signals their onset. A phase diagram in spin and redshift reveals four shapes: smooth, cuspy, ears touching, and throat drowning. If future high-resolution imaging resolves such shadows, their shape could help tell compact objects apart.
arxiv-2602-14682:
Generative models make striking samples, but do they match the true spread of the data? Farzan Farnia, with Mohammad Jalali and Azim Ospanov as co-authors, compares generated diversity against test data using Vendi and RKE entropy scores. Across benchmarks, test data scores clearly higher than model samples.

The authors trace part of the gap to finite samples: entropy scores rise with sample size, so training sets understate true diversity. Tuning generators to match finite-set diversity can therefore bake the shortfall in. The paper names this diversity error, explains its statistical roots, and points toward corrections. It reframes diversity as a measurable target, not a vague hope.
arxiv-2602-14882:
Anthony M. Flores and colleagues characterise a dynamically relaxed cool core galaxy cluster at redshift 1.5, ACT-CL J0123.5-0428, among the most massive, highest-redshift clusters in Atacama Cosmology Telescope survey fields. Chandra imaging and spectroscopy constrain deprojected temperature in two spatial bins out to r2500, revealing a relaxed system whose core temperature falls to 1.8 keV within about forty kiloparsecs.

Surface brightness and intracluster density peak sharply in that core, cooling time drops to roughly 280 million years, and forward modelling of XMM-Newton data extends the picture further. A massive cluster already settled and cooling when the universe was young challenges simple formation timelines. Early clusters could calm down fast.
arxiv-2602-15182:
Chitra and colleagues formalize autodeleveraging as online learning. It is a last-resort loss socialization mechanism for perpetual futures venues when liquidation and insurance buffers fail. Despite huge futures markets, it has received little formal treatment. The paper models it as online learning on a profit-and-loss haircut domain. Each round, the venue picks a solvency budget and profitable trader accounts.

Winning accounts are liquidated to cover shortfalls up to the budget. Haircuts fall on positive profit-and-loss, or unrealized gains, not on posted collateral. The model yields robustness results and upper bounds on how poorly a venue can restore health. Applied to the October 10, 2025 Hyperliquid episode, the production queue's regret runs about 50 percent of an upper bound calibrated to the event. An optimized algorithm reaches about 3 percent of the same bound. In dollar terms, the live model over-liquidates trader profits by up to 3 million.
arxiv-2602-15382:
Liu and colleagues offer the Vision Wormhole, which reuses the input door of Vision-Language Models for steady talk between fixed bots. Mixed nets join models with varied skills through a door, but swapping inner moods straight needs mapping between model-specific codes and steering math.

A shared Visual Codec packs each source latent trace into a message, maps it through a zone, and unpacks messages into the target image span. Per-model codecs and reference maps form a hub-and-spoke design with O of N parts for N models. Each model learns its codec alone through self-training on anchor texts, and anchor match allows sharing across partners. Across four VLM groups, six setups, and nine thinking tests, Vision Wormhole lifts scores by 6 points on mean over text-led MAS. It hits about one and two thirds times shape boost in batch-scaled end-to-end run.
arxiv-2602-15882:
Liu and colleagues built PACT-WAM, a world-action model for robot control. It makes a 16-step action path and the matching visual forecast at once, through conditional flow sampling. Robot control needs past context to pick acts and foresight to weigh their effects, but dense views of past and future cost too much to process.

The model codes old views coarsely and recent views finely. It keeps 16 views at 256 tokens per view, 75 percent fewer than dense coding of the same frames. A shared flow stage updates act and visual states through two heads, and a TiTok-VAE decoder rebuilds future views. A Proposal Review stage can vet act plans. Without it, success hits 98 point 6 percent on LIBERO, 92 point 3 percent on RoboTwin 2.0, and 78 point 0 percent on real Piper tasks. With it, the rates rise to 99 point 5, 93 point 4, and 86 point 7 percent.
arxiv-2602-15982: McGovern continues earlier work by realizing irreducible finite dimensional representations of the complex group of type G2 through tableaux. Along the way he exhibits explicit generators for the defining ideal of the flag variety of this group. The tableaux give a hands-on way to see how these abstract objects act, and the ideal generators pin down the flag variety in plain algebraic terms.
arxiv-2602-16082:
