Brillouin light scattering showed the films have cylindrical elastic symmetry instead: isotropic within the plane, but about six percent stiffer in compression along the growth direction. Standard detector heat treatment left the anisotropy unchanged, while hotter treatment nearly removed it. Infrared data backed the picture with uneven oxygen structures along the axis. The findings suggest heat treatment that restores isotropy may help cut coating thermal noise.
arxiv-2605-06382:
Claire McNamara shows that a popular uncertainty measure for evidential deep learning quietly breaks when class counts differ. Vacuity, also called uncertainty mass, scores out of distribution detection by dividing the number of classes by the total belief strength of a prediction. Because the class count sits inside the measure, comparing test sets whose in and out of distribution sides use different counts can distort the verdict. It can do so without any change in the model's actual predictions, as McNamara demonstrates empirically and theoretically.

Swapping class cardinality by just one moved detection scores dramatically in her tests on evidential models fine tuned from a large language model. The shift is an evaluation artifact, inflating results through arithmetic rather than insight. McNamara also questions how in and out of distribution are defined for multiple choice question answering with causal language models. The contribution is a caution the subfield needs.
arxiv-2605-06482:
Irene Aldridge and twenty-seven co-authors build a reinforcement learning framework to expand complaint classification capacity in New York City. Municipal 311 systems receive more complaints than staff can triage, and service quality gaps follow income and racial lines. Their agents act as intake routers for the Department of Buildings, not as replacements for human classifiers.

Six domains are covered, from boiler safety to housing triage, each framed as a decision process where fair coverage counts directly in the reward. Agents assign complaints to escalate, batch, defer, or inspect now. Post-hoc analysis finds complaint recurrence and neighborhood statistics predict real violations better than raw complaint volume alone.
arxiv-2605-06582:
Adhiraj Banerjee and Vipul Arora introduce PairAlign, a framework that turns speech into compact symbolic tokens through autoregressive self-alignment. Learning systems reason over continuous vectors, yet comparison, retrieval, and memory work better with symbols. Existing audio tokenizers control sequence length, consistency, and edit behavior only indirectly through local quantization or reconstruction.

An encoder maps speech to a condition, and a decoder emits tokens trained so two content-preserving views predict the same anchor sequence. Starting from vector-quantized targets, training shifts to teacher self-alignment with anti-collapse controls. On short speech the tokens stay compact and ordered, sharply cutting archive size and edit-distance work on TIMIT retrieval tests.
arxiv-2605-06882:
Chun Zheng and four co-authors test language models on the equivalence class problem, possibly the simplest long-chain reasoning task. Given a set of stated equalities between variables, the model must decide whether two variables end up equal, which requires chaining many steps. The team varies variable counts, connection density, and prompts across reasoning and non-reasoning models.

Non-reasoning models fail the task outright. Reasoning models do far better yet still cannot solve it completely. Intriguingly, the hardest instances differ by model type. For plain models they sit at a known phase transition of the random equality graph. For reasoning models they sit at the largest chain diameter. That split separates confusion from genuine reasoning depth.
arxiv-2605-06982:
Ahmed K. Kadhim and four co-authors speed up a logic-based approach to word embeddings. Tsetlin Machines learn with simple logical rules, an alternative to large neural models like BERT, but training an earlier autoencoder version was slow. Their system, FastOmniTMAE, reorganizes training into two parallel stages.

Across tests of classification, similarity, and clustering, the new version trains up to five times faster in classification while keeping embedding quality comparable. The team also built the method into reusable hardware on chip-based FPGA platforms. Even on small, resource-limited hardware, it produced solid similarity scores with a compact footprint.
arxiv-2605-07182:
Ali Taghibakhshi and nineteen co-authors pack a whole family of reasoning models inside one parent model. Training separate models at several sizes wastes enormous computing effort. Star Elastic adds nested smaller submodels to an existing model in a single post-training run, so one job yields many sizes.

A trainable router learns the nested models, and users can switch submodels between thinking and answering phases to trade accuracy against speed. Applied to NVIDIA Nemotron models, the nested versions matched or beat separately trained rivals at far lower cost. Quantized versions shrink deployment size further while keeping the slicing ability.
arxiv-2605-07282:
Yifan Zhou introduces a diagnostic that reveals when a language model checkpoint settles on its next word. Final outputs hide that timing, so Zhou decodes each layer's prediction and measures its distance to the final answer. Across six paired base and instruction-tuned checkpoints, the tuned versions stayed farther from their finals later into the network.

The effect survived several careful control checks. Swapping late layers between paired models moved the gap strongly in both directions, while random perturbations barely changed it. Late feed-forward layers emerged as the main lever on the delay, identifying a robust signature of instruction tuning in how predictions form.
arxiv-2605-07482:
Zizhao Hu and five co-authors erase unwanted memorized content from language models without needing a curated retain set. Most unlearning methods depend on such a set to protect general ability, complicating deployment. SHRED rests on an insight: within text targeted for forgetting, only the most surprising tokens carry the memorized knowledge, while predictable tokens reflect general language skill.

The method selects those high-information positions, then trains with modified targets that demote the memorized token there while preserving the original distribution elsewhere. Across four benchmarks it sets a new trade-off between forgetting and utility, beating retain-set methods, and it resists relearning and membership-inference attacks over repeated runs.
arxiv-2605-07782:
Jing Xiong and seven co-authors build infrastructure to let language model agents design real circuits inside a proof assistant. Hardware is the bottleneck in agent-driven design: agents struggle to express, compile, and refine designs in a tight loop. Their CktLean system embeds a typed hardware language in Lean, with compilation to SystemVerilog and interactive proof feedback.

On top of it, CktFormalizer generates, repairs, and optimizes hardware and proves source-level equivalence. Across four benchmark suites, compilation rates ran from about ninety-one to over ninety-nine percent, and nearly all simulation-passing designs completed synthesis and layout checks. Interactive proof-state feedback raised equivalence proof completion noticeably, and hardware feedback drove area reductions of up to about fifty-nine percent in the optimization loop.
arxiv-2605-07882:
Katrin Casel and five co-authors compute shortest tours that visit a sequence of orthogonal polygons in order, traveling under Manhattan distance. A tour must touch the polygons in the given order, though not at prescribed points. For ordinary convex polygons under Euclidean distance, near-linear algorithms have been known since a seminal 2003 paper; the orthogonal setting needed its own theory.

For disjoint consecutive polygons they give a truly subquadratic algorithm, near-linear ones for ortho-convex polygons and plain linear time for rectangles, and polynomial algorithms without restrictions. The toolkit is broad: additively weighted Voronoi diagrams, rectangle decompositions, persistent data structures, and dynamic distance oracles on weighted planar graphs.
arxiv-2605-08082:
Francesco Anna Mele reviews recent progress in quantum learning theory for continuous-variable systems. These systems describe light and other bosonic modes, and they are central to quantum optics. Learning theory for finite systems is well developed, but the continuous case has only recently taken shape.

The review asks how many copies of a state are needed to learn it, with and without energy limits. It covers learning Gaussian states, how performance depends on non-Gaussian character, and how to test whether a state is Gaussian or far from Gaussian. It also treats the efficient learning of Gaussian processes, giving readers a compact map of a fast-moving field.
arxiv-2605-08382:
Houjun Liu, Lisa Einstein, John Yang, Joachim Baumann, and coauthors audit the security of code written by frontier models. A model can be told to write secure production code. It can even be handed the weaknesses to avoid. Verifiable flaws still appear in about twenty-three percent of outputs. The count comes from two hundred fifty ordinary coding prompts.

Their SecureForge pipeline first finds benign prompts that trigger statically detectable flaws. It grows them into a large synthetic corpus with a Markovian sampler. The sampler preserves both error rates and diversity. Lessons from the audit are folded into secure system prompts. Those prompts cut flaw rates in tests while keeping unit test performance intact.
arxiv-2605-08682:
Zhikai Li and four coauthors build Verkle trees in TypeScript, with a checker for smart contracts in Solidity. Verkle trees mix hash trees with vector proofs. They should shrink chain storage and proof size. But no one had shown them at work in smart contracts. Their pack is made for web3 back ends.

Tests bring a surprise. Plain Verkle builds cost more than plain Merkle trees. The small proofs in theory do not save much in practice without deep tuning. The team writes up build choices and speed traits in full. Chain coders gain working code. They also gain a clear warning that neat theory can mislead.
arxiv-2605-08982:
Yaniv Oren and five co-authors present Particle Monte Carlo Tree Search, a new version of a planning method used widely in reinforcement learning. The classic method explores game and control problems step by step, which makes it hard to speed up with modern graphics hardware.

Their version runs many search particles in parallel, in a form that suits batch processing on GPUs, while keeping the sound logic of the original method. Tests span chess, Go in two board sizes, a snake game, standard control tasks, and a language model solving Sokoban puzzles. Across these domains the method scaled well with extra computing power and matched or beat popular rival methods.
arxiv-2605-09482:
Morrison and a colleague survey symplectic, Poisson, contact, and metriplectic flows. They link a natural metriplectic dynamical system to the general one-jet bundle J1N, which is both a contact manifold and a trivial Poisson manifold. Their system, unlike the standard contact Hamiltonian system, is thermodynamically consistent: energy stays fixed and entropy never decreases under the flow. Here the Hamiltonian is the energy and the entropy function is simply the bundle's real coordinate.

As an example, they derive the Duffing equation, in autonomous and nonautonomous versions, first as a contact Hamiltonian system, then as a metriplectic system. For both systems the Duffing equation sits inside three-dimensional systems with a thermodynamic part, a form that eases checking whether the relevant equilibrium is asymptotically stable.
arxiv-2605-09582:
Hayashi and van der Vlugt study topology and category theory for product spaces built from singular cardinals. Higher Baire and Cantor spaces are well understood when the cardinal is regular and uncountable. Far less is known when the cardinal is singular, and it is not even clear what should count as a higher Baire space in that case. The authors weigh several function spaces and box topologies as candidates for that role, noting the choices each definition forces.

Their ultimate focus is the cardinal characteristics of the ideal of meagre subsets of these spaces, the higher analogue of the classical Cichoń diagram quantities. The paper gives a systematic study of singular product spaces themselves and of those characteristics. It closes a gap between the classical theory of the reals and the higher theory, where singular cardinals had remained largely unexplored.
arxiv-2605-09682:
Du and five colleagues spot a fresh spin flavor entanglement pattern in Lambda b decays to Lambda D. It links the Lambda spin with the D flavor states. The pattern's information lives in decay rates and Lee Yang parameters across the four neutral D modes. The same pattern gives a fresh route to measuring gamma, the Cabibbo Kobayashi Maskawa triangle's key angle. Experimental uncertainty scales inversely with the Wootters concurrence, tying weak phase precision to the amount of spin flavor entanglement.

That link matters because gamma carries extremely small theoretical uncertainty compared with experimental precision. The Lambda b system thus offers a fresh, clean route to gamma, complementing established B decay methods. By probing the spin flavor density matrix through decay rates and Lee Yang parameters, experimenters can convert entanglement measurements into weak phase information.
arxiv-2605-09782:
Choromanski and three colleagues built GenusSink, a class of approximate generalized Sinkhorn algorithms for optimal transport on bounded-genus graphs. These include planar graphs and meshes that approximate 3D objects. Brute-force Sinkhorn with shortest-path costs runs in quadratic time. GenusSink reaches near-linear time for preprocessing, each iteration step, final transport-plan queries, and memory.

The speedup leans on separator-based graph decomposition and computational geometry. It also uses new fast matrix-vector multiplication results for generalized distance matrices, drawing on Fourier analysis and low displacement rank theory. GenusSink proved orders of magnitude more accurate than other efficient Sinkhorn methods, while still beating the baseline on speed. On graphs of treewidth on the order of log log n, such as trees, it matches brute-force geodesic Sinkhorn numerically.
arxiv-2605-09882:
Zhu and five colleagues present RAYTHEIA, a fast reverse ray-tracing algorithm for three-dimensional equations whose behaviour depends on direction, a common headache in astronomy simulations. Rays are traced backwards from each target point. A dual-grid design pairs the simulation mesh with an adaptive refinement grid for walking rays and adding up contributions. A leaf-only octree, a digital differential analyser for stepping, Morton codes for fast cell lookup and a slab method for path lengths keep the cost down.

A hybrid MPI and OpenMP parallel scheme with chunk-to-chunk messaging reaches near-ideal linear speed-up. Linked to the 3d-pdr code, RAYTHEIA modelled photodissociation-region chemistry inside a turbulent star-forming cloud, on a 512-cubed grid. The authors call that resolution unprecedented, and the run produced sharp synthetic emission maps including a self-absorbed oxygen line.
arxiv-2605-10382:
Apala Chakrabarti offers practical help for design researchers drowning in diagrams. Design Research Methodology backs systematic design research through Reference Models and Impact Models. Yet building and keeping those models by hand means repeated redrawing, layout fixes, and scattered handling of assumptions, sources, and evidence. Her 2026 paper presents DREAMS, an early-stage prototype tool for those models.

Users build typed causal models with relevant elements, define signed causal links, and attach assumptions, inputs from experience, and sources straight to those links. Layout aid and search improve readability, revisability, and recall of supporting facts. A first test with four design-research users against manual practice showed cuts in creation time, revision time, repositioning effort, edge crossings, and evidence recall time. The authors read these as early evidence of potential, not full validation.
arxiv-2605-10882:
Bing-Dong Wan and Sheng-Qi Zhang explain why one decay of the psi(4040) particle is strangely muted while sibling decays stay strong. The particle has ample energy to split into a D and anti-D meson pair, yet that channel stays suppressed while D anti-D-star and strange-meson channels thrive.

Using the instantaneous Bethe-Salpeter equation with a relativistic pair-creation model, the pair traces the suppression to node-induced cancellation. Positive and negative parts of the decay overlap nearly cancel for D anti-D, but not for the other channels. The picture also fits the channel's sharp sensitivity to mass and meson mass splitting. Particle physicists get a dynamical reason for a long-standing hierarchy puzzle.
arxiv-2605-11082:
David Suarez explores dark matter as a source of charged-lepton-flavor violation, the forbidden-in-the-Standard-Model processes that upcoming experiments will probe with enormous new sensitivity. Lepton flavor is no symmetry of nature once neutrino masses exist, yet no flavor-violating charged-lepton process has been seen.

Computing dark-matter relic density and dark-matter-nucleon scattering, Suarez maps parameter space where a dark-matter fermion satisfies collider and direct-detection bounds. The same region also produces positive signals in muon-to-electron-gamma, muon-to-three-electrons, and muon-to-electron conversion in nuclei. The overlap region gives experimentalists a target where dark matter and flavor violation could reveal each other together. Particle physicists get a joint search window for two open questions.
arxiv-2605-11582: Dong and eleven colleagues present an efficient targeting framework for LLM-based advertising. Large language models suit ad creative work and targeting, but live ad systems strain under their latency and compute cost. The framework combines group quantization, layer-wise sparsification and prefix-tree checks to speed inference while keeping quality. Tests on two real-world advertising scenarios show major speedups with small quality loss, making it workable in practice.
arxiv-2605-12182: Dongmyoung Lee, Chengxi Li, and Dongheui Lee present DexTwist, twist retargeting for MR control of dexterous hands. Standard retargeting copies joint angles or fingertips, but body mismatches slide fingertips sideways during twists. Cap opening, key turning, and bolt screwing then drift the screw axis and loosen the grasp. DexTwist spots a tripod pinch, guesses the screw axis and twist size, refines joints to track turning while steadying the tripod shape. Simulated and real tests show better turning-angle tracking and screw-axis stability than a vector baseline.
arxiv-2605-12382: Mozafari, Piryani and Jatowt test whether language models favour famous entities because of training exposure rather than real-world fame. Using the open OLMo models and their full Dolma corpus, they tally exposure for two thousand entities across five types over trillions of tokens. Exposure tracks Wikipedia page views closely, supporting it as a stand-in for real salience during training. The authors find model popularity judgments line up with that exposure, suggesting training counts drive much of the apparent popularity bias.
arxiv-2605-12682: Hyk and Saisubramanian make user preferences explicit for human-aligned decisions by language models. Aligned choices need stated goals and latent tastes that shape how ambiguous cases should be resolved. Existing routes either learn tastes through costly per-chat feedback or leave them implicit in logs tied to one model. Their CLIPR setup writes tastes as a compact set of natural-language rules for run time, drawn from chat and refined with user input.
arxiv-2605-12982: Masuda and Nunota give compact analytic formulas for the Jacobian determinants that convert between orbital elements and Cartesian state vectors in the Kepler problem. Such formulas let priors transform between views, aiding Bayesian orbit fits. They also fix a widely used microlensing formula, showing its wrong ascending-node longitude makes a middle Jacobian singular, and show Cartesian sampling beats orbital-element sampling for speed and toughness.
arxiv-2605-13082: Hattori and Hatomura build the non-quantum twin of feedback-based quantum optimisation, using the quantum-classical correspondence of spin systems to probe possible quantum advantage. They pit the FALQON quantum algorithm and its variant against their non-quantum twins. They then test quantum and non-quantum methods on small cases and non-quantum methods on large ones. Quantum methods win on solution quality while non-quantum methods converge faster, and one non-quantum method scales notably for higher-order binary optimisation problems.
arxiv-2605-13282: Reiter, Gebler and Geffner teach a neural network to learn lifted action schemas for classical planning. Planners work with facts, called atoms, over objects and relations, and schemas that add or delete atoms give strong search guidance. The hard part is learning schemas while also guessing action arguments from state changes alone. Their differentiable design recovers true schema structure across planning domains and stays robust to observation noise.
arxiv-2605-13482: Niclas Hollrigl and three colleagues present an all-optical method for picking single atomic layers in dipolar quantum gases. Layer picking is hard for strongly magnetic lanthanide atoms, since standard magnetic-gradient methods apply poorly. Their method heats chosen spots inside a beat-note superlattice, a light pattern made from two frequencies. A microscope objective acts as a shared reflector for both light parts, holding the lattice planes steady. The team isolates one or two layers at the focal plane, enabling single-atom studies of long-range systems.
arxiv-2605-13782: Jonathan A. Diller and three colleagues present LMPath, a pipe making word-led search priors for UAV search missions from meaning. Given a fence and an object prompt, LMPath uses making word models to find regions likely holding the object. A base vision model over orbital photos cuts sub-regions that form the search prior. Real-UAV runs over large-scale areas and sim runs show LMPath paths beat usual path planning for search missions.
arxiv-2605-13982: Menon and Smith ask whether Lyman-alpha radiation pressure shapes star formation in the dense, compact clusters that JWST observations suggest dominated cosmic dawn galaxies. Post-processing radiation-hydrodynamic simulations with the COLT Monte Carlo code, they find only mild effects, around ten percent, on gas-to-star conversion where dust reaches one percent of solar levels. Even dust-free clouds still convert over a quarter of their gas into stars.
arxiv-2605-14082: Sharma, Bartel and Schaller propose goal-oriented time adaptivity for linear port-Hamiltonian differential-algebraic equations of index one. Such systems encode an energy balance linking energy change to supplied and dissipated energy, and keeping that balance in discrete approximations is a core challenge. Their approach reins in energy-balance violation through time adaptivity, using post-hoc grid refinement built on the dual weighted residual method. That structure itself speeds up error gauges through a dissipativity-aware block-Jacobi approximation.
arxiv-2605-14682: Wirdane announces a series of results on the q-Catalan triangle, defined by a two-term recurrence in n and k. Combinatorial readings are given through a universal family of seven parts: four families of pattern-avoiding permutations scored by inversion or co-inversion counts, Dyck paths, binary words and triangulations. A mirror polynomial with a dual recurrence is introduced, along with a q,p version and a multivariate generalisation. This is the first paper of a planned W0-W5 series.
arxiv-2605-14882: Jiang-Chao Wan and Yi Wang study how the largest matching root of a hypergraph shifts when the graph changes. A hypergraph links groups of vertices at once. Its matching root is the top real root of its matching polynomial. The pair identifies the hypergraphs with the biggest such root among cactus-like families with fixed cycle and edge counts. A key step shows that a classic shifting move never lowers the root. This extends an older result for ordinary graphs.
arxiv-2605-14982: Sanjeev Manivannan and Shuban V develop a second-order actor-critic method for discounted reinforcement learning. First-order actor-critic methods converge to stationary points but ignore curvature, while full Hessian estimation is costly. The pair treats the action-value function as locally constant in policy parameters, an approximation justified when the critic moves on a faster timescale. Hessian-vector products then yield a stable, efficient curvature-aware update for the actor.
arxiv-2605-15082: Libin Zhu and three colleagues study multi-index models. They show that the average gradient outer product from a kernel regression fit can recover the central subspace. The target depends on inputs only through an unknown low-dimensional projection, and prediction normally needs far more samples than subspace recovery. When a low-degree component already carries all predictive directions, the top eigenspace of the gradient outer product recovers the subspace. Samples scale like dimension to a low power plus a small exponent, even while prediction error stays large.
arxiv-2605-15182: Yifan Wang and Tong He propose Warp-as-History, a training-free interface for camera-controlled video generation. Existing methods need large camera-annotated post-training or costly test-time optimization. Their interface turns camera-induced warps into warped pseudo-history. It aligns its positional encoding with the target frames and drops tokens lacking valid source observations. Fed through the model's visual-history pathway, it reveals zero-shot camera following in a frozen generator, and light LoRA tuning on a single annotated video improves it further.
arxiv-2605-15282: Sarah Griebel and Ted Underwood examine the tradeoff between fluency and loyalty in literary translation across 130,486 paragraphs from 106 novels in 16 tongues. Fluency is gauged as source-closeness via a translationese sorter, loyalty via the COMET-KIWI metric, holding for passage length. A steady inverse link emerges: more fluent passages tend to be less faithful. The pattern holds for human and Google Translate output but weakens for TranslateGemma, and segment length matters for auto evaluation.
arxiv-2605-15482: Dmitry Stanishevskii and six colleagues assemble FINESSE-Bench, a suite of eight benchmarks with 3,993 questions for testing large language models on finance. It spans exam-style questions modeled on professional certifications, applied trading tasks, and a Russian-language olympiad set, arranged so scores can be tracked from basic knowledge to expert reasoning. A single protocol covers multiple-choice, numerical, and short open answers, with automated judging for free-form responses.
arxiv-2605-16082: De Le Court and five colleagues implement the SLIM ocean model, a discontinuous Galerkin finite-element model on unstructured meshes, for single and multiple GPUs. Such models capture complex coastlines and refine grids locally, but cost far more compute than older methods. One high-end GPU matched about 1,500 CPU cores in benchmarks, and a four-GPU node ran about fifty times faster than a 128-core CPU node. A Great Barrier Reef run reached five times finer resolution than the best prior model.
arxiv-2605-16182: Salehin, Parisis, and Berthouze present Tempest, a GPU engine for streaming temporal random walks over time-stamped interaction graphs. Real graphs arrive as high-volume streams, demanding continuous ingestion, lean memory, and strict temporal order. Tempest pairs a GPU-native dual-index edge store with a hierarchical scheduler that dispatches walks at thread, warp, or block level. It sustains real-time processing of billion-edge streams under sliding windows, beating prior systems on ingestion and walk-generation throughput while preserving causal correctness.
arxiv-2605-16482: Copetti studies monodromy defects, endpoints of topological symmetry operators. They are sourced by localized magnetic flux. He examines them in gapped symmetry-protected phases and, by inflow, gapless anomalous theories. The flux sources the anomaly, forcing the defect to take the form of a domain wall joining the symmetry generator to an anomaly-induced order. That dressing yields protected chiral edge modes. It pumps gapless modes bound to the flux. He verifies this for anomalous chiral symmetries in the continuum and on the lattice.
arxiv-2605-16882: Wang and a team present E-PMQ, a way to shrink merged neural models to low-bit form for weak devices. Quantization of a merged model fails because two errors mix: one from shrinking bits and one inherited from merging experts. Their method uses source expert weights as targets during layer tuning and anchors the merged weights to keep the combined behavior steady. On merged vision and language tests, it lifts low-bit scores above GPTQ, including a jump from about 35 percent to 77 percent on a 20-task vision merge.
arxiv-2605-16982: Kirillov's team analyses shot noise from subpopulations of neural networks, small random neuron subsets feeding another group. Finite groups fluctuate, and subset noise differs from the whole group's in both intensity and spectral shape, with subset size. Generalising their nesting method, they derive an analytic formula for the power spectral density of subset shot noise, matching numerical simulations well. Unlike studies assuming Lorentzian distributions with diverging moments, they use realistic non-Lorentzian distributions, grounding a new class of stochastic mean-field models.
arxiv-2605-17782: Trung Hoa Dinh explains why a refined version of the Bessis-Moussa-Villani conjecture fails. The refined claim capped a trace average over words with set counts of letters A and B by the clustered word. Counterexamples by Cha already break that cap for 3-by-3 positive semidefinite matrices at n equals m equals 5. Dinh traces the break to commutative common parts: the clustered word is only one candidate, not the canonical one. He proposes a corrected refinement after pinching B relative to A, and proves it when B appears twice.
arxiv-2605-17982: Bilge Varol, Tınaz Ekim, and Kübra Tanınmış apply Benders decomposition to k-defensive domination. The problem models network security and disaster response, with joint attacks, but it has been little studied. They propose cut generation plans, including a combinatorial approach and joint addition of cuts, plus feasibility results. Gains follow: a clique-cover heuristic, the first feasible solution method, and an initial cut heuristic that sometimes settles cases without branching. Tests on Erdos-Renyi, chordal, and Barabasi-Albert cases show the variant solves cases formulations cannot.
arxiv-2605-18082: Stefano Riva and three colleagues present pyforce version 1, a Python package for data-driven reduced order modelling of multi-physics problems, mainly in nuclear engineering. It belongs to the ROSE project, which cuts model complexity, searches for best sensor spots, and folds real measurements into physical knowledge. This version was fully rewritten on pyvista for mesh import, integrals, and result display, with functions stored as numpy arrays for easier use. The package works with any solver that exports results in VTK format.
arxiv-2605-18182: Luca Teodori's 2026 paper re-derives strong-lensing time delays from exact light paths in the Schwarzschild-de Sitter metric. The familiar geometric-plus-Shapiro split emerges only as the first term of a small-angle series. The authors pin down the next correction to that split, and show it adds no fresh cosmological dependence: it is a higher-order effect of the Schwarzschild part alone. At this order the cosmological constant enters only via unlensed distance measures and the unlensed lens-redshift prefactor.
arxiv-2605-18382: Amir Subba and Sanmay Ganguly probe effective-field-theory operators in a 2026 study through four-top-quark production at the LHC, using a hyper-graph neural network to separate multilepton signals from backgrounds. The network reaches an area under the ROC curve of 0.951 and a statistical significance of 9.11 at 140 inverse femtobarns, beating Particle Transformer and ATLAS baselines. From the improved extraction they set 95 percent confidence limits on five dimension-six Wilson coefficients.
arxiv-2605-18682: Pusep and five co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, how electric current reshapes the optical response of a viscous electron-hole plasma. Laser light creates an interband current in a mesoscopic n-doped GaAs channel through recombination of photogenerated pairs. Background electrons drifting under the Hall voltage form an effective Hall current. Coulomb drag from that current piles up light holes, producing a double photoluminescence line from excitons and trions. Without a Hall current, the heavy-hole energy shift comes instead from the field of the Hall potential difference.
arxiv-2605-18882: Wei Shi and six colleagues diagnose why language-model agents keep calling tools even when no tool is needed. Six models on the When2Call benchmark get calls right but hold back poorly, leaving overall accuracy between fifty-five and seventy percent. The authors trace this to a built-in call offset in the decision mapping, recovered with sparse autoencoders. A closed-form steering correction that cancels the offset reduces over-calling and lifts overall accuracy with almost no loss in correct calls.
arxiv-2605-19082: Keiya Murashima and Takanori Sasaki test how the choice of equation of state affects smoothed-particle simulations of the impact behind Uranus's tilt and debris disk. With three equations of state, two simulation schemes, and a three-Earth-mass impactor, they reproduce Uranus's spin. For spin-matching impacts, disk mass, size, and rotation period barely change with the model, being set mainly by impact angular momentum. The disk's rock fraction depends strongly on the equation of state, so pinning down disk composition will require equations of state plus evolution studies.
arxiv-2605-19282: Chongyu Fan and four colleagues show where the Muon optimizer breaks down beyond pretraining. Muon whitens gradient spectra, driving all singular values toward one, which helps language pretraining but amplifies noisy directions in robot-action training and destabilizes reward-based tuning. Their Pion replacement keeps dominant directions at one while pushing noisy tails toward zero, with a per-head mode that preserves learned specialization. It tops Muon and AdamW on robot benchmarks and a real robot arm, and where Muon collapses in reward tuning, Pion still improves.
arxiv-2605-19382: Zhang and colleagues build PRISM, a benchmark that tests whether language models can write code producing spatially correct animated videos. It holds 10,372 checked instruction-code pairs across 437 subjects in English and Chinese, far larger than earlier sets. A four-part funnel scores runnable code, layout accuracy over full animations, and two measures of motion richness. Tests of seven leading models expose a wide execution-spatial gap: code often runs yet lands objects wrongly, with pass rates falling about 41 percent.
arxiv-2605-19582: Allen, Hauke-Treuer and Ramírez prove the inhomogeneous Khintchine theorem in dimension two without any monotonicity. It was already known to be not needed for m at least three and needed in dimension one, leaving two as the last open case in metric inhomogeneous Diophantine approximation. The result also settles the final open case of a Khintchine-Groshev-type theorem for systems of linear forms, proving a conjecture of the first and third authors. The field now aligns with its homogeneous twin.
arxiv-2605-19782: Redko, Fazlyev, Sozykin, Ivanova, Burnaev and Shvetsov test whether language-model agents optimise code from feedback or merely lean on prior knowledge. In black-box optimisation the models behave greedily; in zero-shot kernel generation, input-size hints change nothing and unusual sizes degrade performance in any language. With iterative feedback, CUDA kernels improve steadily while TVM intermediate code worsens, showing optimisation collapses in low-density languages. The verdict: priors, not feedback or agent scaffolding, drive most gains.
arxiv-2605-19882: Sánchez-Martín and colleagues study arm morphology in barred galaxies with off centre bars, including the Large Magellanic Cloud. Internal mass imbalances and bar centre offsets reshape equilibrium points and the invariant manifolds that organise arms. Modest lopsidedness keeping the centre of mass inside the bar preserves five equilibrium points but distorts their manifolds, giving two arms of different density and shape. Once the centre of mass exits the bar ellipsoid, a pitchfork bifurcation removes the unstable points, leaving three equilibria and a single arm.
arxiv-2605-20882: Kukarkin and Patsahan study selective adsorption in a 2D binary hard-disk mixture on patterned adhesive surfaces. They use grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations for this study. The two species share equal diameters and equal bulk chemical levels but differ in attraction to sticky domains. That design separates affinity-driven selectivity from size asymmetry and unequal levels. Results show selectivity depends strongly on surface shape, most of all at low and mid levels, with clear trends across the range.
arxiv-2605-20982: Bole Ma and three colleagues present DODOCO, a cross-architecture tool for checking costs in dispatch operations. AlltoAll dispatch dominates the bottleneck of mixture-of-experts expert parallel work, and the interconnect field has offered four mitigation kinds. All four rest on two assumptions: routing imbalance is correctable at the system layer, and mock-token benchmarks faithfully represent production routing. DODOCO tests both by instrumenting five open mixture-of-experts checkpoints spanning today's sequence-mixer designs under a factorial grid of six data settings.
arxiv-2605-21082: Minghao Chen and three colleagues present AutoRPA, efficient GUI automation through language-model-driven code synthesis. Language-model agents have shown proficiency in multi-step work with graphical user interfaces, yet most research focuses on single-task performance. Real cases often involve same GUI tasks for which calling language-model reasoning again and again, the ReAct paradigm, is wasteful. Old robotic tools offer runtime speed but demand large manual effort. AutoRPA distills the decision rules of ReAct-style agents into sturdy RPA functions, a neat bridge.
arxiv-2605-21282: Zeyuan Wang and colleagues introduce Stochastic MeanFlow Policies, a one-step generative policy class for entropy-regularized mirror descent in off-policy reinforcement learning. Gaussian policies struggle with multimodal targets, while generative policies often need iterative sampling or lack tractable entropy estimates. Their MeanFlow noise-to-action mapping captures diverse action modes, and a learnable Gaussian scale gives an analytic entropy lower bound. That bound regulates stochasticity alongside value guidance and advantage-weighted regression. Across seven MuJoCo benchmarks, the one-step policies perform strongly against Gaussian and generative baselines.
arxiv-2605-21682: Dufresne, Chaboyer, and Rampalli date the ancient, metal-rich star cluster NGC 6791 to about eight and a half billion years. They combine Gaia brightness data with eclipsing binary stars and thousands of simulated stellar timelines, weighing each timeline against the cluster's observed color and brightness pattern. The result points to a birthplace deep inside the Milky Way followed by drift outward, and gives vibration-based age checks a firm anchor at high metal content.
arxiv-2605-21882: Thushara and co-authors build Thermo-VL, a vision-language model that can read heat images as well as ordinary photos. Normal models fail in dim light because they learn mostly from visible-light pictures, while thermal infrared still shows scene shape. Their design adds a trainable heat encoder to a frozen Molmo-7B base, fused by text-guided dual attention. Tests show strong gains on heat-only and combined reasoning tasks, and the team also releases a paired instruction dataset and a screened benchmark.
arxiv-2605-21982: Roy Araiza and Timur Oikhberg study matricial order operator spaces, a generalization of operator systems carrying matricial norms plus matricial order. For these objects they develop duality theory, naming two properties for the interplay of order and norm, called normality and generation, and proving the two are dual to each other. Operator systems, including C-star algebras, and Schatten spaces serve as examples. The authors also lay out the minimal and maximal matricial order structures, again in duality, and show that Banach lattices can carry such structures.
arxiv-2605-22082: Wentian Wang and co-authors present CoRMA, contrastive robotic motor adaptation for contact-rich meta-adaptation in force-dominant assembly. It swaps raw simulator-parameter adaptation for a compact 6D simulator-only semantic contact context describing contact onset, lateral engagement, guided shifts, contact direction, and jamming. A causal Transformer adapter infers this context online from force and related signals. Tested in Isaac Lab and Isaac Sim 5.0 and on a real Marvin arm, CoRMA keeps higher verified real success under target-pose noise than FORGE baselines, which degrade substantially on hardware.
arxiv-2605-22982: Feng and Chu formulate Taylor-Aris dispersion of Brownian rods in regular-polygonal ducts of any side number. Pressure-driven shear lines up the rods and makes diffusion tensorial, while duct shape decides how that tensor is sampled across the cross-section. A shear-aligned Jeffery-Brownian closure yields four transport fields feeding a two-dimensional transverse operator. Alignment shifts mean speed only slightly but boosts the Taylor coefficient by cutting transverse mixing. Low-sided polygons keep distinct shear-sampling signatures.
arxiv-2605-23082: Boulitsakis Logothetis, Wood, and Liò offer KAPLAN-HR, a Kolmogorov-Arnold network for gauging the hazard as a joint function of factors and time. Classic Cox and additive models require time-varying effects to be set by hand, now hard on rich clinical data in practice. A single-layer KAPLAN-HR gives that model, while deeper versions capture those effects through depth. Its error rate depends only on form smoothness, not factor count. On six medical benchmarks it matches or beats known survival methods.
arxiv-2605-23182: Li and Cheung study Good Policy Identification in serial reward learning with bandit feedback. For a reward threshold, GPI needs finding a policy with mean reward in an episode at least the threshold if such a policy exists, or saying None otherwise. They define GPI under the fixed-trust setting, needing the output to be correct with chance at least 1 minus delta, and cutting the mean number of runs tried. They propose method BEE-GPI, giving upper bounds on its sample cost for good and bad cases.
arxiv-2605-23282: Duan and four coauthors propose the Discontinuous Galerkin Neural Operator for disease defocus cleaning. Defocus cleaning in diseased imaging remains hard due to place-to-place varying and locally broken optical blur. Neural nets model defocus buildup straight as a whole operator. DGNO builds the whole kernel using a discontinuous Galerkin setup with element-local volume operators. Tests show that DGNO beats state-of-the-arts, giving sharper rebuilds and robust handling of place-to-place varying blur.
arxiv-2605-23382: Zhang and colleagues build a personalized agentic reinforcement learning framework for settings where one query deserves different plans and tool choices for different users. Generic rewards miss varied tastes, observed behavior mixes in conformity, and flat memory cannot fetch skills by preference. Their PARPO method splits generic task quality from personal preference rewards and anchors learning per user, joined by a two-stage preference-aware reward model and a skill graph memory. Tests on ETAPP, ETAPP-Hard, and SJAgent beat strong memory and learning baselines.
arxiv-2605-24082: Lemke and four co-authors replace the Gaussian odds in searches for gravity-wave lumps with mock-data inference. Pulsar timing arrays have built evidence for a nanohertz gravity-wave background, and lumps in its power could reveal its source as gaps from Hellings-Downs links. Standard tools assume Gaussian-spread links, a shaky guess that badly limits finding reach. A sorter trained on fake data captures the non-Gaussian structure instead, raising three-sigma finding chances by about 90 percent for single hotspots and 200 percent for double hotspots.
arxiv-2605-24282: Tawfik and four co-authors construct a stress-energy tensor for tweaked gravity theory. A new Heisenberg algebra imposes tiny-length limits. An extra term with tiny-length steps yields a torsion-free quantum-deformed metric. The authors argue quantum-induced fixes to the stress-energy tensor plus gauge-related current density belong in the matter action. Zero slope change implies gravity fields do work on matter, so non-gravity energy and push are no longer fully conserved. Old Einstein rules return when tiny-length limits vanish.
arxiv-2605-24482: Yavdat Sh. Il'yasov and Elvira I. Turianova study ground states of a perturbed p-Laplacian boundary problem. Competing superlinear terms drive the equation. A Rayleigh quotient method yields two key parameter values, tied to the Nehari manifold and the zero-energy level. Above the first threshold, no nontrivial weak solution exists; below the second, at least two positive weak solutions appear, one a ground state. As the small parameter tends to zero, positive ground states converge to an exact profile.
arxiv-2605-24782: Dingling Yao and co-authors name a gap they call the Perception-Physics Paradox. Vision models can look right on satellite images while reasoning wrongly. High scores may rest on visual correlations rather than true structure, so skill outside the training range weakly signals scientific use. The team proposes scientific alignment as a goal for learning in science and probes it with a hierarchy of checks. On TC-Bench, a set for tropical cyclone study, models lean on shortcuts that fail in intense storms.
arxiv-2605-24982: Victorita Dolean, Pierre Jolivet, Frédéric Nataf, and Pierre-Henri Tournier survey domain decomposition for solving partial differential systems numerically. From Schwarz's back-and-forth method, the field has grown into methods pairing local toughness with faster convergence and side-by-side work. The chapter reviews overlapping splits, partition of unity, and Schwarz forms in algebra. It explains their use as preconditioners for Krylov solvers and why coarse fixes are needed for scaling. Coarse spaces such as GenEO and DtN-based methods get focus, with fast code.
arxiv-2605-25482: Shilong Liao, Ye Ding, Shangyu Wen, Zhaoxiang Qi, and Qiqi Wu constrain binary orbit inclinations from Gaia DR3 astrometric excess noise. Inclinations set binary masses, so this sharpens mass estimates. For a binary with a radial-velocity solution, excess noise becomes a function of inclination alone. The team simulates Gaia epoch observations under the nominal scanning law and centroid uncertainties, sampling inclinations to match reported excess noise. Internal and external validations show robust performance, most reliably for strong astrometric signals, with caution for weak wobbles or poorly sampled orbits.
arxiv-2605-25582: Changyu Chen and colleagues decouple sample efficiency from KL efficiency in language-model reinforcement learning. On-policy training wastes data after one update, while heavy off-policy reuse collapses entropy and stalls early, and tighter KL caps lower the ceiling. Extreme Region Policy Distillation first mines fixed data with weakly constrained off-policy updates, then distills token-level signals into the base policy under trust-region limits. The distilled policy matches or beats the aggressive policy with smaller divergence, and weak teachers supply useful supervision.
arxiv-2605-25682: Qazi, Iosifidis and Zhang study distributed transformer inference across embedded edge devices, where simulations hide the real hardware costs. On Jetson Orin Nano devices over WiFi, the bottleneck is not only network bandwidth but CPU-GPU staging. Because the integrated graphics lack the PCIe and NVLink path NCCL needs, all traffic must route through GLOO and stage in CPU memory. Their Prism strategy combines Segment Means compression with light offline profiling to choose local or distributed execution. It cuts latency by 65 to 77 percent and energy use by 34 to 52 percent.
arxiv-2605-25882: Chen and Ferson offer a conformalised loose inference approach for robust extrapolation under limited data. Work stresses chance-based and knowledge doubt, yet methods lack promises beyond the domain. Their approach is model-neutral, adding imprecision and distance awareness. It yields probability boxes that stay valid under distribution shift, keeping cover while growing doubt when going beyond. Tests on synthetic and benchmark data show improved robustness and cover, above all with limited data.
arxiv-2605-25982: Zhu, Mocatti and Calandra show that light can flip the electric polarisation of a two-layer material without moving its layers. The material is a rhombohedrally stacked bilayer of transition-metal dichalcogenides, thin sheets held by weak forces. Earlier switching relied on layer sliding, which is slow and needs damaging light levels. Here the flip is purely electronic, driven by dipoles rearranging around tungsten sites. It completes in about 200 femtoseconds, roughly fifty times faster than the usual sliding period.
arxiv-2605-26082: The 2026 proof by Ahmed Bou-Rabee and Ruizhe Xu gives a quantitative form of the Einstein relation for reversible diffusions moving in a random environment. The classic relation says a tiny applied force produces a drift speed whose ratio to the force approaches the particle's diffusivity in that direction. Their version adds an exact algebra-based speed of approach that holds for almost every fixed environment. It tightens a 2012 result proved by Gantert, Mathieu, and Piatnitski.
arxiv-2605-26282: Xiaoyuan Cheng and seven colleagues' 2026 paper names a basic block in scaling world-model reinforcement learning: search and value learning pull apart. They propose Model-Based Diffusion Policy Optimization, which joins search with policy optimization via diffusion policy forms. Rather than a planner, policy learning becomes a flow over searched paths in latent world models, held by a hidden energy function. Tests across offline pretraining, online learning, and fine-tuning from offline to online show steady, rising gains with model size.
arxiv-2605-26482: Sophie Zhu counts components of twisted divisor ranges over number fields. Given an extension K of the rationals with a Dirichlet character, the twisted divisor function sums norm powers and character values over divisors. For real exponent above 1, she studies closure components. Finiteness holds for real-valued characters. Over the rationals, every large integer occurs as a count for fixed exponent. Every integer occurs as the character varies for large exponent. Galois extensions yield exponential lower bounds. Counts grow unbounded across degree-s extensions for fixed s above 1.
arxiv-2605-26582: William Yuan, Sungwon Jeong, and Amirali Aghazadeh ask how much randomness helps discrete diffusion sampling. Very fixed steps converge fast but pile up errors, while noisier steps move slowly yet finish cleaner. The trio trace the gain to redundant swaps that trade mass between states and provably shrink sampling error. Their DCRS sampler alternates forward and reverse runs to inject measured noise. On images it cuts steps up to tenfold at matched quality, with mixed gains on text.
arxiv-2605-26682: Melanie Neubauer and five others release SteelDS, a labeled video dataset of shredded steel and copper scrap moving on a belt. Shot in a lab at the post-magnetic sorting stage, it mirrors the point where workers still pick copper by hand. The set holds 24,297 frames in five subsets, with 396 steel and 101 copper pieces sized and masked pixel by pixel. It benchmarks material sorting, detection, and segmentation under varied spacing and density. Its aim is catching copper impurities in messy scrap streams.
arxiv-2605-26782: Garzás-Villar and five colleagues test whether tweaking the feel of virtual objects can train precise force control for post-stroke rehabilitation. Fifty healthy volunteers stretched a virtual spring in a curling-style task to launch a stone with a target force, under linear, Gaussian, or antisymmetric-Gaussian spring laws. The antisymmetric-Gaussian group aimed most accurately during training, yet no spring type improved long-term retention. Players leaned on learned stretch length rather than force, a habit future training must break.
arxiv-2605-26982: Dimitrieva, Tambovtseva, and Grinin study veiling of photosphere lines in spectra of RR Tau, a young irregular variable star of UX Ori type, across brightness states. Using Nordic Optical Telescope spectra taken as the star ranged from magnitude 10.6 into deep minima, they examine how circumstellar emission veils spectral lines at brightness minima and discuss its origin. The comparative analysis tracks how line veiling changes as the star dims and brightens.
arxiv-2605-27682: Debojyoti Dey, Ron Ofir, and Christian Grussler study inversion of the multiplicative matrix compound operator. The number of matrices whose kth compound equals a prescribed matrix depends on rank. At rank at most 1, endless matrices qualify, fully mapped, while above rank 1 exactly one matrix qualifies up to an overall sign. An algorithm finding such a matrix is detailed with its runtime analyzed.
arxiv-2605-28082: Chang Liu, Ruichao Niu, and Yuefeng Yang prove a strong cycle property for split-star networks. They show the network is two-disjoint-cycle-cover vertex pancyclic: any two vertices sit on separate disjoint cycles of complementary lengths, for every length from three up to half the factorial of the order. The result holds for networks of order four and above.
arxiv-2605-28182: Arttu Arjas and Italo Atzeni improve channel estimation for extremely large antenna arrays, where sparsity helps but prior assumptions mislead. Their cross-predictive sparse Bayesian learning tunes sparsity weights by predictive consistency on random data splits, not by likelihood maximization. Across varied signal, pilot, antenna, and path settings it beat standard sparse Bayesian learning at similar cost, with no hand tuning.
arxiv-2605-28482: Daniel Rodriguez-Cardenas and four colleagues bring Pearl's structural causal models into empirical software engineering with their CausalSE framework. Plain association methods can mistake a link for an effect when hidden bias lurks, so it uses causal graphs and propensity matching to isolate treatment effects. A case study on prompt-engineering strategies for GPT-3 code generation shows link-based gains that causal analysis does not confirm. The work adds a guide method and case study to help research teams design tests with fewer false alarms.
arxiv-2605-28682: Élie Casbi builds a homological approach to q-characters for quantum affine algebras. For any acyclic quiver without multiple edges, he constructs a monoidal category whose indecomposable objects are tensor products of modules over the path algebra. He proves chain complexes with good properties exist, unique up to homotopy and preserved under tensor products. When the quiver admits a height function, Euler characteristics of these complexes match truncated q-characters of standard modules. For Dynkin type A quivers he reads cluster values as Euler numbers of chain complexes.
arxiv-2605-28882: Yihang Lin and five colleagues present GrowLoop, a growing conversation evaluation system from human seeds. Human-like quality is tacit knowledge humans perceive by feel. Its rules resist explicit wording as models advance. From minimal human seed notes, LLM agents extract scoring rubrics step by step through rule-of-thumb Learning. They require human-AI accord where raters agree, and only sense where they diverge. The Rubric-Case co-growth loop expands reach with new human seeds. And the rubric-guided AI judge clearly beats older scoring methods.
arxiv-2605-28982: Robin Neumayer proves qualitative stability for a family of trace Sobolev inequalities in a short note. The family was first proven by Carlen and Loss for p equals two, and by Maggi and Neumayer for p between one and n. The result answers an open problem raised by Fan, Li, and Zhang. Combined with their local analysis, it yields sharp quantitative stability for the family when p equals two.
arxiv-2605-29082: Tyler Akidau and colleagues present the Redpanda Agentic Data Plane, carrying security context outside the agent's read and write path. Out-of-band channels move policy signals, audit trails, and classifications across mixed infrastructure, so agents can neither see nor bypass them. Governance applies at every stage: scoping access on entry, constraining actions during execution, and capturing tamper-proof transcripts on exit. Christopher Tiede, David O'Neill, and Daniel D'Orazio ask in 2026 whether pairs of massive black holes can stop feeding for long stretches inside the gas disks that surround them. Earlier simulations assumed a fixed temperature pattern, which left the question open.

Their new grid simulations let the disk heat and cool self-consistently, with blackbody radiation carrying energy away. Gas piled up and warmed at the cavity edge, yet the lanes that launch feeding streams stayed cold, so the feeding rate could stay suppressed as outside supply dropped. The effect was weaker than in the fixed-temperature runs. Even while starved, such binaries should glow and flicker enough for wide-field surveys, though they would look oddly faint in X-rays.
arxiv-2606-04182:
Thanh Nguyen-Tang and Raman Arora frame exact unlearning for reinforcement learning in 2026. After a user asks for their data to be deleted, the learner must act exactly as if that data had never been used.

Most unlearning work covers fixed datasets, not agents that learn by acting. The pair show this demand is stricter than it sounds. The learner's past actions shaped the data it later saw, so deletion must rewind that chain. They give an algorithm that meets the demand without full retraining. Its cost depends on how much the deleted data steered the learner. The analysis also shows a basic tension: stability of learning fights exact forgetting. Their framing sets terms for privacy rules in adaptive systems.
arxiv-2606-04482:
Huang, Myroshnychenko, Tatarko, and Yaskin extend a classic question about centers of shapes into curved space and into the world of functions, in a 2026 arXiv geometry paper. Grünbaum and Loewner asked a subtle question. How often can a flat slice through the centroid have its own centroid at the same point? Earlier work built a body in five or more dimensions with exactly one such slice. Dimensions three and four stayed open.

The authors study analogues in hyperbolic space. That is the negatively curved geometry. They also study s-concave functions. Their main hyperbolic theorem builds a convex body in every dimension from three upward. The body sits inside the hyperbolic ball. Its centroid sits at the origin. Its slice centroids are pushed strictly to one side. The proof uses the Fourier transform of distributions. The paper thus carries the Euclidean phenomenon into hyperbolic space.
arxiv-2606-04682:
Hernández and his coauthors study a family of math operators called Calderón commutators in this 2026 arXiv paper. A commutator here measures how two operations interfere when their order is swapped. The graph is a curve whose slope stays bounded, a shape mathematicians call a Lipschitz graph. The main question asks how fast the size of the nth such operator can grow.

They prove the operator size grows at most in step with its order for general curves. Extra smoothness in the curve improves that growth to a slower rate tied to the square root of the order. They reach the first result by a symmetry trick and a standard test for such operators. The sharper result uses different smoothness conditions, reached through a separate route. Counterexamples show that the two extra smoothness conditions do not imply each other.
arxiv-2606-04782:
Doff computes how the scalar sector of an electroweak theory is constrained by measurements, in a 2026 arXiv particle physics paper. The 331RHN model extends the Standard Model with a larger gauge symmetry and right-handed neutrinos. Extensions like it are tested through the oblique parameters S, T, and U. Building on earlier results in the same framework, Doff analyzes the contributions of the model's scalar particles to these parameters.

He shows that the parameter T provides the constraint on the scalar mass spectrum. Current bounds on T imply a nontrivial upper limit on the model's symmetry-breaking scale, at about ten tera-electronvolts or below. The findings highlight the sensitivity of electroweak precision data to the scalar sector of 3-3-1 models. Even particles too heavy to produce directly leave fingerprints in precision observables, and those fingerprints already fence in the theory's viable parameter space.
arxiv-2606-04882:
Peixoto and Silva review and extend high-order finite difference schemes for seismic wave modeling, asking whether fancy stencil shapes earn their cost, in a 2026 arXiv numerical analysis paper. Finite differences approximate wave equations on grids, and seismic modeling depends on them, but classical Taylor-based schemes suffer numerical dispersion. The authors build a general framework deriving schemes of arbitrary order for different stencil geometries, implemented symbolically in the Devito framework.

Non-cross shapes like rhombus and square stencils do not necessarily provide added accuracy or dispersion reduction despite their increased computational cost. Dispersion-optimized cross stencils deliver adequate accuracy at reduced cost on more compact stencils than classic approaches. The implementation also eases full-scale acoustic seismic inversion. The message is that stencil geometry is not where accuracy hides; optimizing the coefficients of the humble cross does the work.
arxiv-2606-04982:
Luyu Cen and co-authors analyze when parallel domain-splitting methods converge for time-harmonic Maxwell equations in this 2026 arXiv paper. These equations model electromagnetic waves, and splitting a large problem into overlapping subdomains is a standard way to solve it on many processors at once. The methods here use impedance boundary conditions, which mimic how waves pass between neighboring subdomains.

The authors prove the parallel iterative method is well-posed in a suitable function space. They describe error propagation through impedance maps that capture how subdomains interact. For strip-shaped splits they derive explicit convergence rates from the sizes of those maps. They then build the finite-element counterpart with Nédélec elements and show the discrete method inherits the continuous behavior when the maps are well approximated. Numerical experiments cover strip layouts and checkerboard layouts that go beyond the theory.
arxiv-2606-05082:
Premachand Mahapatra, Andrew Miller, and Prasanta Das set the first constraints on dark matter inside neutron stars using continuous gravitational-wave searches in this 2026 arXiv paper. If self-interacting fermionic dark matter accumulates inside a spinning neutron star, its uneven distribution can raise equatorial deformations. These bumps, nicknamed dark mountains, make the star slightly lopsided so it emits steady gravitational waves. The team developed a formalism linking dark matter accumulation to the star's structure, its moment of inertia, and its wave emission.

Applying results from all-sky searches in LIGO's third observing run, they placed the first constraints on dark-matter-induced ellipticities across the full analyzed frequency range. The constraints hold for a range of self-interaction strengths. The same data exclude parts of the dark matter mass and coupling parameter space that would have produced detectable signals. The authors also show next-generation detectors will reach much further.
arxiv-2606-05282:
Aurélien Dersy and Matthew Schwartz give an account of resurgence in the symmetric double-well potential in this 2026 arXiv paper. The double well is a simple quantum system where perturbative and non-perturbative physics are entangled. Energy levels expanded in the inter-well separation have growing coefficients, while the level splitting is exponentially small and invisible to perturbation theory.

The paper builds that trans-series from first principles through two routes in one notation, with series through the four-instanton level and three-loop order. In WKB analysis, Stokes phenomena encoded in the Delabaere-Dillinger-Pham relations govern continuation past turning points, and a quantization condition in Voros symbols fixes the series. In the path integral, saddle points are elliptic functions and a Lefschetz thimble split decides which ones count. The result is a partition function series whose terms at each instanton order are polynomials in temperature.
arxiv-2606-05382:
Ankit Pratap Singh, Xin Su, and Phillip Howard build synthetic contrastive reasoning traces for multi-table question answering in this 2026 arXiv paper. Answering questions over several tables demands retrieving evidence, linking schemas, and reasoning across joins and filters. Existing resources supply only questions and answers, with nothing explaining how an answer is derived. The authors manufacture that missing supervision.

Using heterogeneous language models, they generate validated positive reasoning traces alongside plausible but flawed negative traces for the MMQA dataset, forming preference pairs. Open-weight models are then fine-tuned on those pairs with Contrastive Preference Optimization. Across Qwen3-14B, Mistral-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B, the training delivered average gains over question-answer supervised fine-tuning ranging from 9.7 to 16.3 percent, with gains up to 21 percentage points on MMQA itself. Ablations showed that drawing the traces from heterogeneous generators strengthens the signal.
arxiv-2606-05482:
Kritzer, Nagel, and Pillichshammer study how evenly points can fill a space in a 2026 arXiv paper on pure math. Even spread matters when computers estimate integrals by sampling points. Two measures track the spread: discrepancy, which counts gaps and clumps, and diaphony, its close cousin. The authors ask which endless point sequences spread best. They focus on digital sequences, built digit by digit from simple rules.

The team proves that order-two digital sequences reach the best possible spread rate. The result settles a long-standing guess about these sequences. It also beats the older order-five constructions. A key trick cuts the size of the building blocks from five times the dimension to twice the dimension. The authors then extend the bounds to a broad family of smooth periodic functions. Their sampling rules keep the same low error rates across that whole family.
arxiv-2606-05682:
Fangbo Tu and colleagues look inside low-precision model training and find hidden damage in a 2026 arXiv paper. Shrinking a language model to four-bit numbers saves cost but loses accuracy. Distillation can recover much of it by matching a big teacher's outputs. The team shows matching outputs can hide inner decay: many inner states give the same outputs. A similarity measure called CKA exposes the drift layer by layer.

Output-only training lowered inner similarity to the full-precision teacher. The drift ran worst in models that had prior reinforcement training. It also tracked with weaker reasoning and coding scores. The fix, CKA-QAD, adds a light penalty that keeps inner geometry aligned during distillation. On two current models it sharply improved alignment. Reasoning and coding accuracy rose with it, at modest extra training cost. Output matching alone, the authors argue, is not enough for low-bit recovery.
arxiv-2606-06482:
Two networks can share the same community structure while their links form at very different rates. Brahma, Agterberg, and Chen build a statistical test for that situation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Instead of comparing the networks link by link, they compare the subspaces, the low dimensional patterns that encode shared groups such as communities in a social network.

Their test measures the gap between the leading subspace patterns of the two networks, then centers and scales that gap so it settles into a bell shaped distribution as the network grows. They supply working estimates for the test's average and spread, and they map how much power it has to spot real differences when the networks are dense enough. Computer simulations back the theory, and an application to United States flight data shows the test at work on a real transport network.
arxiv-2606-06882:
When several traders chase the same stock, each one's buying moves the price for all. Safwan Hossain and co-authors model that rivalry in this 2026 arXiv paper. The resource is divisible and costly, like shares or computing capacity. Standard execution plans assume a lone trader. Competition turns the problem into a game.

The analysis spans two information settings. With a common prior, the team proves a tidy result. A Bayesian Nash equilibrium exists, is unique, and can be computed efficiently. They also bound the price of anarchy, the cost of selfish play. The harder setting drops the shared prior entirely. Agents must learn from repeated market feedback alone. The authors give conditions where simultaneous learning settles at that same equilibrium. Simulations on real financial data illustrate the theory. The work speaks to trading desks and shared resource markets alike.
arxiv-2606-06982:
Designing a wireless network means squeezing the most data through a web of links. Wadayama and Siqi offer one engine for that whole job in this 2026 arXiv paper. The networks are linear Gaussian graphs, chains and branches of noisy channels. The goal is mutual information, the total flow the network can carry.

Their K-recursion walks the graph in order, building every pair's covariance. Cross terms between distant nodes matter when paths branch and merge. Those covariances yield an exact formula for the end to end information. Automatic differentiation then computes exact gradients in one backward sweep. No per topology gradient formulas are needed. Gradient ascent climbs to the best design under a power budget. The same code matched the classic water filling optimum where that answer is known. It also improved branched and relay networks. A five layer, eleven node test showed it scales.
arxiv-2606-07082:
On policy distillation trains a student model on its own outputs, scored by a teacher. Zhennan Shen and co-authors map the geometry of that training in this 2026 arXiv paper. They track how the model's weights move through parameter space. Two established methods, supervised fine tuning and reward based reinforcement learning, provide the comparison.

Distillation's updates occupy a relaxed middle regime. They touch fewer weights than fine tuning and shun the main directions more strongly. They are less tightly confined than reinforcement learning updates, though. A second pattern is subspace locking. Updates quickly enter a narrow, low dimensional channel and stay there. Freezing training inside that early channel preserved distillation's performance. The same trick badly hurt fine tuning. Mixing the objectives changed the dynamics, while sparser tokens did not. The authors urge designers to steer the geometry itself.
arxiv-2606-07182:
A generated soundtrack can match a video's actions yet sound wrong: the instrument's tone or the tempo feels off. AudioIM adds style control to video to audio synthesis in this 2026 arXiv paper, led by Jiahui Zhao and co-authors. Reference audio supplies the missing style, but earlier methods swallowed it whole. Timbre and tempo stayed tangled together.

Two separate encoders untangle them. One extracts timbre, the character of the sound source. The other extracts tempo, its rhythmic pace. Both feed the generator as global conditioning signals. A masking based training scheme teaches the model to use latent prompts at inference. On the VGGSound benchmark, style similarity improved measurably. Semantic alignment with the video and synchronization timing were preserved. The result is a Foley style tool where a creator can borrow a reference's feel. Sound design gains knobs that pure text prompts cannot express.
arxiv-2606-07282:
Sun, Johnsson, and Banerjee ask whether radio behavior betrays network attacks that routing data alone might miss, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is the Internet of Things, specifically low-power networks using the RPL routing protocol. An intrusion detection system based on machine learning normally watches routing statistics to spot attacks. The authors add transmit and receive radio counts, which reflect how hard each device's radio is working.

They tested a recurrent neural network detector against three attack types, including flooding and a worst-parent attack that corrupts route choices. Networks ranged from five to twenty nodes in their experiments. Adding the radio features improved detection scores by up to about four percent, with the largest gain on the worst-parent attack. A configuration using only radio features performed best overall, and receive-side activity proved more informative than transmit-side activity in their comparisons.
arxiv-2606-07382:
Chalvidal, Coeurdoux, and Vanden-Eijnden rebuild a classical statistics technique inside a generative modeling framework in this 2026 arXiv paper. Estimating a covariance matrix, which captures how variables vary together, fails in high dimensions because sample estimates are noisy. Shrinkage fixes this by pulling the estimate toward a simple anchor, trading a little bias for much less variance. The authors recast shrinkage as risk minimization over a stochastic interpolant, a random path blending a source and target distribution.

That lens reveals three separate risk-reduction paths: the interpolation schedule, the coupling between distributions, and early stopping of an integrated flow. Known shrinkage estimators appear as special cases in their setup. They then propose a neural estimator of it, bound its error, and validate it on synthetic data. Applied to real neuroimaging data, it showed regularization power, suggesting the interpolation viewpoint yields practical tools beyond retelling old ones.
arxiv-2606-07582:
Joyjit Roy, Singh, and Shaw predict which bank customers will leave by stacking a transformer on top of boosted trees, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Retaining customers costs less than acquiring new ones, but churn data are imbalanced and full of nonlinear interactions that defeat models. Their hybrid first runs an FT-Transformer, which turns each tabular feature into a token and applies attention to capture higher-order interactions. Gradient-boosted trees alongside capture decision boundaries.

Out-of-fold stacking then feeds both models' predictions to a logistic meta-learner that recalibrates overconfident outputs and learns combination weights. On a dataset of 10,000 customers with a fifth churning, the hybrid reached an F1 score near 0.62 and an AUC near 0.86. That beat a multilayer perceptron baseline by over 3 F1 points with statistical significance under cross-validation. Class weighting handled imbalance without synthetic oversampling. Ablations confirmed that both parts contributed to the gain.
arxiv-2606-07782: This 2026 manuscript from arXiv puts forward new research. Its title describes the subject as Non-Archimedean Polydisc Spaces and. This is a science and technology paper — careful study of how the natural and built world works. The paper delivers its results to the wider research world.
arxiv-2606-07882:
Radwan reports that very different vision models secretly organise their internal representations around the same geometric object, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Thirteen modern vision encoders were trained for different jobs: labelling photographs, contrasting image crops, filling masked pixels, and matching images to captions. One would expect their internal spaces to differ accordingly.

They do not. The top sixteen directions of variation inside every encoder converge to the same sixteen-dimensional structure, Radwan's cross-architecture substrate. It survives transport across four visual domains, from photographs to medical scans and satellite images, with median similarity near sixty-eight hundredths. Across eight domains the median stays near sixty hundredths, and every pair scores at least forty hundredths. The effect also survives a strict calibration subtracting the similarity expected from random data, ruling out a known measurement artefact.
arxiv-2606-07982:
Shreesh Bhattarai and Harish Chandra Bhandari of Kathmandu University pit a physics-informed neural network against the classical finite difference method for heat diffusion, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The test is harsh by design: heat spreading in one, two, and three dimensions with noisy boundary conditions.

The classical method collapses under noise. With twenty percent boundary noise in three dimensions, the finite difference solver kept only about thirty-six percent accuracy. The neural solver, which builds the heat equation into its training loss, held about ninety-one percent. On a physical copper system the network cut boundary reconstruction error about threefold. A second crossover appears with dimension: in three dimensions the network needs fewer nodes than the grid method. The authors' conclusion is a selection rule: choose solvers by noise exposure and dimension together, not accuracy alone.
arxiv-2606-08182:
Jiang and co-authors present a 2026 arXiv paper on black hole physics in more than four dimensions. The work extends a quantum-corrected model of collapsing matter, called the Oppenheimer-Snyder model, by adding a cosmological constant, a fixed energy term built into empty space. The setting is anti-de Sitter space, a curved spacetime whose boundary behavior makes heat and pressure easier to define.

For small black holes in this setting, the temperature no longer climbs without limit as the hole shrinks, as in the classical picture.
