Instead it falls toward zero, a sign that quantum effects soften the final stage of evaporation. The heat capacity, which measures how much energy a hole absorbs for a given rise in temperature, also shows an extra change of pattern. The authors read that pattern as a further phase transition, a sudden shift in state, caused purely by the quantum correction.
arxiv-2606-08382:
Bhatnagar and colleagues shrink the memory that language models need while generating text, in this 2026 arXiv paper. During generation, a model stores a key-value cache, the remembered representations of all previous tokens. That cache grows with context length until it dominates memory use. Low-rank projection compresses the cache by exploiting redundancy in the hidden dimensions. Earlier methods choose the rank by fixed rules and struggle to compress hard without hurting accuracy. STAR-KV makes rank selection adaptive.

Three ideas combine. A differentiable thresholding mechanism learns suitable ranks at the level of individual attention heads and blocks. A hybrid decomposition applies different low-rank factorizations to key and value projections according to their sensitivity. A last step then squeezes the cache further. Across several models and benchmarks, STAR-KV achieved up to three quarters compression of the cache on its own in the reported evaluations.
arxiv-2606-08582: Made public on arXiv in 2026, this research paper details a new study. The title's topic is Soft Algebra for. This is a mathematics paper — the study of numbers, shapes, patterns, and logical proof. It records a new contribution to human knowledge.
arxiv-2606-08682:
Qi Cao and colleagues ask whether a popular control technique carries a hidden safety cost, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Activation steering modulates a language model's behavior at inference time. A steering vector built from examples of a target behavior is injected into inner activations, giving flexible control without permanent parameter updates. Separately, emergent misalignment is a safety concern: models fine-tuned on unsafe examples from one narrow task generalize to broadly unsafe behavior. Whether steering can induce the same phenomenon was unexplored.

This paper presents a full evaluation of steering-induced emergent misalignment across behaviors, strengths, and settings. The concern is real in the reported experiments. Steering toward a narrow trait can shift behavior broadly, even though no weights change. Because steering is applied at deployment, the authors argue it deserves the same auditing as training-time methods.
arxiv-2606-08782:
Nakane and Ouchi read chemical fingerprints of gas in eight distant galaxies using the James Webb Space Telescope, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The galaxies sit at redshifts between 7.2 and 10.6, so their light left when the universe was young. Absorption lines, dark notches the gas carves into the spectra, reveal its elements. The team picked eight from three hundred sixty-two galaxies and fitted lines of carbon, oxygen, iron, and other elements.

Five galaxies showed several lines; the other three showed one or none. Compact galaxies blazing with star formation had weaker lines, suggesting their activity suppresses it. Two galaxies near redshift seven were rich in iron, near the Sun's iron-to-silicon ratio. That early iron favors Type Ia supernovae, exploding white dwarfs, as its source. The rival explanation, pair-instability supernovae, would leave a strong odd-even pattern in aluminum that the spectra do not show.
arxiv-2606-08882:
Baldi, Binyamini, and Urbanik prove well-behaved points are dense in families of algebraic varieties, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A family of varieties is a varying collection of shapes defined by polynomial equations. Each member carries a Hodge structure, a decomposition recording its periods. A point is Hodge generic when its periods satisfy no unexpected algebraic relations. Such points, taken among those defined over algebraic numbers, are dense in the base space.

Under a large monodromy assumption, they prove the statement that points whose periods avoid extra relations up to a degree are dense. As a by-product they establish new cases of the Mumford-Tate conjecture, beyond the realm of abelian motives. When the base is a curve, they give quantitative estimates for such points. The engine is a theorem about relations among solutions of G-operators, built on height estimates from Bombieri and André.
arxiv-2606-09182:
Chen and colleagues ask the people actually deploying the Model Context Protocol inside companies what works and what hurts, in this 2026 arXiv paper. MCP, proposed by Anthropic in late 2024, connects large language models with external tools and data. Research so far has mostly examined its technical design. This study ran interviews with 20 practitioners from 8 companies in the internet and financial sectors.

Users valued MCP for cross-system teamwork, task decoupling, and knowledge reuse in model workflows. But uptake is constrained by a fragmented ecosystem, hard coordination, and unresolved problems in distributed state management and fault diagnosis. Participants wanted better standards, lower barriers through low-code or plugin tooling, and more ops support. The contribution is a reality check: users confirm its value, and the gap between a clean specification and a deployable platform.
arxiv-2606-09282:
Ni, Akopian, Kouvelas, and Makridis audit SUMO's fast traffic model and find it understates congestion, in this 2026 arXiv paper. SUMO's mesoscopic model tracks vehicles at macroscopic cost. In its current model, vehicle movement follows dynamic headways between road segments. It does not fully comply with the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards model, traffic flow's foundational theory.

Two defects stand out: queue dynamics are incomplete, and backward-traveling spaces, congestion's upstream spread, are barely implemented. In 2 case studies the flaws produce unreal onset and recovery patterns, congestion generally underestimated: a dangerous bias for planning. Their fix is a proper mesoscopic link transmission model, discrete-time, following the LWR principle, adding backward-traveling spaces for queue spillback. Its link density outputs agree with kinematic wave theory and with SUMO's own microscopic simulation, confirming the fix. The paper is both a bug report on a trusted tool and a drop-in theory for repairing it.
arxiv-2606-09682:
Jaber Jaber and Osama Jaber present a system that fuses a whole language model into one graphics chip kernel in this 2026 arXiv paper. Text decoding is bound by memory flow: each token streams all weights through the chip once. The usual route launches one kernel per operation and parks data in memory between steps. Their AutoMegaKernel instead builds a single persistent kernel for the full forward pass.

No hand-written code is needed per model. A frozen checker vets each plan before it runs, screening for deadlocks and race faults by static graph tests. Across more than seven thousand crafted plans, most of them unsafe, the checker let no bad plan through. It passed all three hundred sixty real plans. One source retargets three chip lines, and ten of ten supported models built cleanly. On a real small model, output matched the reference token for token.
arxiv-2606-09982:
Nee and colleagues test whether grand unified theories built in F-theory can hide axion-like particles with unusually strong photon couplings, in a 2026 arXiv paper on theoretical physics. F-theory is a string theory framework, and its unified theories break symmetry using hypercharge flux, a threading of fields through extra dimensions. That breaking creates axion-like particles coupled to photons but not to the strong force. A known bound limits their coupling relative to mass.

The authors compute the axion potentials and show every such particle's coupling-to-mass ratio lies well below the QCD axion prediction, satisfying the bound. Small threshold corrections to gauge couplings make the particles heavy through unsuppressed instanton effects. They examine loopholes that might push the ratio far above the axion line and argue none works in controlled regions. The bound persists even when large corrections force extra matter at intermediate scales.
arxiv-2606-10182:
Tian and Sterman examine how automating biology labs changes how doing science feels, in a 2026 arXiv paper on human-computer interaction. Biofoundries automate biological testing at huge scale, promising speed, steady results, and access. Through in-depth talks with nine scientists and experts across universities and firms, including biofoundry developers, automation engineers, and end-users, they examine how creative work is enacted under automation. Biofoundries displace sensory cues that researchers once relied on at the bench.

It also shifts duty between humans and machines and transforms fixing faults from an embodied, local practice into a social, interpretive one. Rather than framing biofoundries as mere factories, the authors argue they should be understood as creativity support tools. Their design in turn shapes how researchers notice breakdowns, use judgment, learn from failure, and progress through success.
arxiv-2606-10282:
O’Keeffe extends his swarmalator research by letting the particles propel themselves, in a 2026 arXiv paper on active matter dynamics. Swarmalators combine swarming with synchronization, each unit carrying a position and a phase. In the one-dimensional version, units live on a ring. Adding self-propulsion means each swarmalator swims along the ring at a speed set by the sine of its orientation. That single change unfolds the static states of the ordinary model into traveling, breathing, split-wave, and chaotic states.

Several new states admit analytic reductions. Numerical evidence suggests the transition to chaos under broad random initial conditions arises not from local destabilization of ordered clusters but from basin reorganization among coexisting attractors. The states may serve as qualitative signatures for confined arrays of active oscillators, from synthetic swimmers to coupled biological units.
arxiv-2606-10382: Posted in 2026 to arXiv, this research paper introduces a new investigation. The title promises work on UMI-Bench 1.0: An Open and Reproducible Real-World Benchmark for Tabletop Robotic Manipulation .... Expect artificial intelligence throughout: the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. A common yardstick is proposed here, letting the field measure progress.
arxiv-2606-10682:
Mohammadi, Budman, and Pulsipher make neural network surrogates obey physics exactly in this 2026 arXiv paper on process engineering. Physics-informed networks add equations to the loss, but that only nudges them toward constraints, still violable at prediction time. The proposed PL-KKT-hPINN instead projects outputs onto the feasible set using the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, handling nonlinear equalities via piecewise-linear approximations. The result is a static, non-iterative design with hard guarantees.

The test case is a continuous stirred-tank reactor, a workhorse chemical reactor, with one and two inputs. The hard-constrained model matches a standard network's accuracy while cutting constraint violations substantially. In low-data regimes it also beats the unconstrained network on prediction error, a practical edge when plant data are scarce. The only error source is the piecewise-linear step, bounded in advance, which suits surrogate modelling of nonlinear chemical systems.
arxiv-2606-10982:
Mujaddiq tackles a three-way tension in stake-based consensus in this 2026 arXiv paper. Proof-of-stake chains drift toward centralization: proportional rewards enrich the rich, while fairer weightings invite Sybil attacks, splitting one stake across many fake identities. FairWave, an asynchronous DAG-BFT protocol, splits the difference by decoupling two channels.

Anchor selection weighs stake super-linearly, so splitting never pays, while rewards follow a square-root rule that flattens inequality. Across roughly 550,000 simulated rounds it posts a Gini coefficient of 0.140 against 0.490 for pure proof-of-stake, and validator concentration halves over fifty thousand epochs. Liveness fades smoothly, from about 94 to 74 percent as the faulty share rises, with no cliff.
arxiv-2606-11282: Published as an arXiv preprint in 2026, this manuscript presents new research. The title points to The Statistical Compass as its subject. The field in play is science and technology: careful study of how the natural and built world works. The paper delivers its results to the wider research world.
arxiv-2606-11382:
Nguyen, Hong, Toshniwal, Liu, and Luttens present GLACIER in a 2026 arXiv paper, a foundation model for predicting molecular properties. Deep learning helps discover molecules among billions of candidates, but top models grow ever more expensive, and most are unimodal, ignoring other data types. GLACIER is a student-teacher framework integrating graphs, SMILES strings, and physicochemical descriptors into rich embeddings.

Three student encoders are pretrained on 100,000 drug-like molecules: a message-passing network for graphs, a transformer for SMILES strings, and a multilayer perceptron for descriptors. A Finsler geometry-aware module fuses the three inputs. Knowledge from large teachers, including MiniMol and MolFormer, is distilled into a single lightweight model via contrastive learning. Despite pretraining on only 100,000 compounds, GLACIER performs strongly across eleven benchmarks while keeping high inference speed. The authors argue compact models can rival larger ones for screening and lead optimization.
arxiv-2606-11482:
Yu, Zhao, Lin, and You teach language models to predict how social beliefs move in a 2026 arXiv paper. Understanding how beliefs evolve after events, from policy changes to scientific breakthroughs, is a fundamental challenge in social science. Their Social World Model learns state-transition functions for social beliefs by mining temporal patterns in social data, optimizing a variational bound. It needs no human annotations linking events to belief shifts, and no census data.

To evaluate, they build SWM-Bench from real prediction markets, Kalshi and Polymarket, with over twelve thousand points spanning politics, finance, and cryptocurrency. The model significantly outperforms time-series foundation models, with state-of-the-art results on Kalshi and competitive performance on Polymarket. It also offers interpretable insights into the mechanisms of belief dynamics. The authors frame it as a toolkit for quantitative digital sociology, while noting belief forecasting could be misused for manipulation.
arxiv-2606-11782:
He-Bi Yang leads an eight-author team sharpening 3D scene rendering in this 2026 arXiv paper. 3D Gaussian Splatting renders scenes in real time by scattering millions of soft blobs, but it often blurs fine, high-frequency textures, especially when models are compressed for memory or file size. Pixel-perfect training objectives reward smoothness over plausible detail.

Their plug-and-play wrapper adds a small synthesis network after rendering. Guided by random noise shared between views, it invents texture matching the local statistics of real detail rather than exact pixels, trained under a Wasserstein distortion measure. The wrapper works across plain, memory-constrained and compression-optimised variants of the method. Subjective and objective tests show clearly better perceptual quality at sharply reduced sizes: for one compressed variant the file shrinks sixfold, an eighty-three percent saving. The cost is slower training and rendering, which the authors call a reasonable trade.
arxiv-2606-11882:
Seunghun Lee and Eun-Gook Moon compute quantum quantities that need huge matrices in this 2026 arXiv paper. The trace norm of an operator, the sum of its singular values, underlies measures such as entanglement negativity, fidelity and quantum Fisher information. For many-body systems the matrices grow too fast to solve exactly.

Their tensor-network method avoids exact solving. It approximates the sign function with a rational function, following Zolotarev's classical construction, and solves the resulting problem DMRG-style. Accuracy improves with the approximation parameters and the spectral weight near zero. It computes negativity, fidelity and Fisher information for mixed states beyond exact methods' reach. Its accuracy is far better than polynomial-based Lanczos approaches, whose errors can stagnate or even grow. Trace-norm quantities thus become practical targets for tensor-network studies of mixed quantum states.
arxiv-2606-11982:
Aleksandar Taranovic and eight colleagues fix a mismatch in learning from human preferences in this 2026 arXiv paper. Preference-based reinforcement learning trains robots from comparisons between behaviours rather than hand-designed rewards. Standard methods learn a utility score from whole trajectory segments, but then optimise the policy using per-step utility estimates, a train-test mismatch. That mismatch shifts the data distribution and wrecks temporal credit assignment, deciding which actions in a segment deserved the praise.

Their method, PAWS, removes the mismatch: it learns a segment-level advantage function and updates the policy directly with advantage-weighted segment data. Utility training and policy optimisation then speak the same language. Experiments on simulated robotic tasks show PAWS consistently beating existing preference methods, with preferences from a simulated oracle and real humans. Ablations show the gains come from distribution alignment rather than architecture, and are largest in the low-data regime.
arxiv-2606-12082:
Sh.M.Nagiyev and co-authors solve a relativistic wave equation exactly in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is finite-difference relativistic quantum mechanics, a form of quantum theory built on step-like differences in a curved momentum space. The particle moves in the ring-shaped Quesne oscillator potential, a bowl-like trap with a ring term, used for ring-shaped molecules and deformed nuclei.

The team separates the equation into radial and angular parts and solves each one in closed form. The radial wave functions come out as continuous dual Hahn polynomials, a named family of special functions. The angular parts come out as Jacobi polynomials, another standard family. The energy levels form a discrete spectrum, and both energies and wave functions reduce correctly at low speeds. A symmetry group for the radial part also yields the spectrum by pure algebra.
arxiv-2606-12182:
Ana Larrañaga and co-authors ask how little data can reveal the equations behind a moving system, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their base method, SINDy, fits sparse equations, only a few terms surviving, to measured motion. Data are costly, so the team adds active learning: an ensemble estimates its own uncertainty and requests samples where ignorance is highest. The approach covers ordinary and partial differential equations, the standard forms for change over time and space.

On the chaotic Lorenz system, sampling outside the attractor, the pattern motion settles into, proved critical. The loop found the correct governing equations with fewer than fifty data points across noise levels. Two spatial systems test it further: Burgers' equation, where a sharp shock front splits informative from dull regions, and the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, with messier structure. In every case, guided sampling found the true dynamics with far fewer samples than random sampling.
arxiv-2606-12782:
Li and colleagues push periodic coupled-cluster work for solids to much denser momentum sampling, reaching infinite-size limits, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Coupled-cluster theory with single and double excitations, CCSD, is a precise method for electron correlation. But its cost has limited solid-state calculations to coarse sampling of the Brillouin zone, the momentum space of a crystal. Sparse sampling leaves finite-size errors that are hard to extrapolate away.

The team built a distributed-memory implementation that runs on up to 12 nodes with 96 cores each. It enables sampling with up to 216 k-points, far beyond the previous practical ceiling of 64. For 8 simple semiconductors and insulators, they report cohesive energies and band gaps settled to within 0.1 electronvolts, giving definitive benchmark values at the CCSD level. Against experiment, cohesive energies err by 0.1 to 0.2 electronvolts on average, usually underestimating, while band gaps err by about 0.4 electronvolts, usually overestimating.
arxiv-2606-12882: Added to arXiv in 2026, this scientific paper communicates fresh results. The title frames the subject as HarnessBridge: Learnable Bidirectional Controller for LLM Agent Harness. Its home field is artificial intelligence (the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data). It places a new research result before the scientific community.
arxiv-2606-12982:
Halevi and colleagues characterise when uniform finiteness holds in the imaginary sorts of a weakly o-minimal structure, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A definable set has uniform finiteness if, across any definable family of its subsets, infinitude is always detected by exceeding one finite bound. Weakly o-minimal structures, whose definable sets are unions of convex sets, have uniform finiteness for real sorts by definition. But the property can break down for interpretable sets, as the p-adic value group shows.

For a countably saturated weakly o-minimal expansion of an ordered group, the authors prove a clean criterion. The expansion in imaginary sorts has uniform finiteness if and only if the collection of definable convex subgroups has uniform finiteness. When the structure expands an ordered field, checking the definable convex valuation subrings is sufficient.
arxiv-2606-13582:
To and colleagues design secure beams for a network that senses and communicates in this 2026 arXiv paper. Integrated sensing and communication systems use the same transmissions to talk to users and to scan the environment. Sensing users, whose echoes the system needs, are untrusted: they may eavesdrop on confidential messages meant for communication users. The authors formulate an optimisation that maximises the minimum secrecy rate across users, promoting fairness, under a power budget and sensing quality limits stated as beampattern matching bounds.

The problem is highly non-convex, so they attack it twice. First, a semidefinite relaxation combined with branch-and-bound finds the globally optimal solution within a set accuracy. Second, a low-cost algorithm delivers near-best designs at a fraction of the cost for real use. The work matters as dual-function radar systems move toward real networks where sensing targets cannot be assumed friendly.
arxiv-2606-13982:
Dia tackles a hidden control knob in how language models write long answers. Sampling decides which candidate next words stay in play at each step. Fixed cutoffs, like top-p, cannot adapt as text grows easier or harder. His 2026 arXiv paper introduces Adaptive Nucleus Truncation Sampling, ANTS. It builds on top-n-sigma sampling, which keeps words whose scores sit within a window below the best score, judged before temperature scaling.

ANTS adjusts that window using the model's uncertainty, steered by an entropy-based controller. A Thompson controller tunes strength across rollouts, and a fallback arm restores open sampling whenever cutting looks unsafe. Tests used a sparse mixture-of-experts model with thirty-three billion total parameters. Average gains grew with budget: plus one point nine at eight thousand tokens, rising to plus five point two at thirty-two thousand. Instruction following gained over ten points at the largest budget.
arxiv-2606-14082:
Li, Wang, and Yin follow a family of expanding surfaces in Minkowski space until it settles, reaping inequalities from the journey. Minkowski space has one time dimension; the surfaces are spacelike and cocompact. The flow moves each surface along its normal at speed given by the inverse of a Hessian curvature function, a balanced combination of principal curvatures. Their 2026 arXiv paper proves this inverse flow exists for all time and converges.

The curvature function is the k-th elementary symmetric polynomial of those curvatures, normalized and rooted, for each order k. Settling is tricky: speeds must stay tame, shapes must not collapse. From the flow's steady growth, the authors establish quermassintegral inequalities for these surfaces, relations among mixed volume-like quantities that resist direct proof. The work extends Euclidean inverse flow theory to the full Hessian family in Minkowski space.
arxiv-2606-14282:
Ornig and Carlsson simulate flares over sunspot umbrae and finally reproduce the white-light brightenings quiet-Sun simulations miss. Some flares shine in visible continuum light, but models struggled to match observed enhancements. Their 2026 arXiv paper runs one-dimensional radiation hydrodynamics simulations with the RADYN code, starting from an umbral atmosphere, darker and cooler than the quiet Sun, varying the electron beam's duration and strength.

Simulated white-light increases ranged from forty to three hundred thirty-five percent, matching observed values. For one twenty-second beam, the relative continuum increase at 6684 angstroms was an order of magnitude higher than the matching quiet-Sun run. The main reason is the dim umbral background, making the same emission far brighter in relative terms. Hydrogen recombination in the optically thin chromosphere dominates the excess; the heated photosphere contributes later. Shorter, more intense beams drove larger enhancements; maximum beam flux was the dominant parameter.
arxiv-2606-14382:
Adrian and co-authors present a 2026 arXiv paper in statistics about judging how close two probability distributions are. Their measure, built on the expected misclassification rate, asks how often a classifier would confuse draws from one distribution with draws from another. High confusion means the distributions agree closely.

The authors study how to tune parameters so a model distribution matches a reference one as closely as possible, including a regularized version that avoids overfitting. They connect the measure to the better known Kullback-Leibler divergence and to synthetic Bayesian emulation, a way of standing in for costly models. A leading use is mixture synthesis, blending given distributions into one forecast, illustrated with scenario forecasting for macroeconomic policy, where Monte Carlo simulation makes the tuning practical.
arxiv-2606-14582:
Ray, Noor, and Siddiqui build a planning framework for railways in a 2026 arXiv paper. It is designed to be disruption aware. Heterogeneous networks mix track gauges, train speeds, and stopping patterns. Single-track lines force trains to share track and switch often. Random disruptions push operations off the timetable. Blocked tracks, failed engines, and slowdowns all occur. Most research stops at high-level scheduling. It leaves track-switching choices to human operators.

Their framework poses railway work as a temporal planning problem. It uses the PDDL planning language. It models gauge compatibility and disruption cases explicitly. It outputs conflict-free, timestamped plans. The plans carry both schedules and executable action sequences. The benchmark held two hundred instances. They used up to one thousand track points and one hundred twenty trains. Two top planners and a validator confirmed the plans work. Manual decision-making drops as a result.
arxiv-2606-14682:
Giri and Mertens test how foreground cleaning biases reionization measurements in a 2026 arXiv paper. The twenty-one-centimeter signal from early hydrogen probes the epoch of reionization. Foregrounds overwhelm it by orders of magnitude. Two mitigation strategies exist. One avoids the contaminated Fourier region. The other removes foregrounds by Gaussian process regression, which exploits their spectral smoothness.

Both strategies introduced systematic biases. They reached up to about one standard deviation in key parameters. Those include the minimum star-forming halo mass and the ionizing escape fraction. Avoidance gave broader posteriors because it uses fewer modes. The global reionization history was recovered within the ninety-five percent credible interval. Late-time neutral fractions stayed biased. Excluding poorly mitigated redshift bins cut the biases a lot. But spotting those bins requires independent quality metrics.
arxiv-2606-15182:
Metelkin and Vowinckel simulate how particle permeability changes suspension settling in a 2026 fluid mechanics study. Settling slows as particles crowd together, an effect called hindered settling. Real sediment flocs are porous, so fluid can pass through each particle, not just around it. Such flocs dominate fine sediment in rivers and estuaries. The authors run particle-resolved simulations of porous spheres settling under gravity. They vary how permeable the particles are and how crowded the suspension is.

Settling still follows the classic Richardson-Zaki power law for every permeability. Yet more permeable particles settle faster as crowding grows, because they stir up weaker upward counterflows. At thirty percent volume fraction, the speed gap reaches about one hundred six percent between extremes. Velocity fluctuations and self-diffusion also grow with crowding. Particle clustering, meanwhile, weakens as permeability rises. The results matter for predicting how fine sediments and treatment-plant sludge actually settle.
arxiv-2606-15382:
Dehghan and coauthors demonstrate a way to run a full Bell test in a single camera shot in a 2026 quantum optics paper. Entanglement, the linkage between paired particles, is usually verified by rotating measurement settings one at a time and combining the results. Here a liquid-crystal metasurface, called a CHSH plate, assigns different polarization measurements to different sectors of the light beam. All sixteen settings of the test then happen at once across the beam's profile.

Photon pairs sample the sectors according to their emission direction, and the spatial pattern of coincident detections reveals the Bell violation directly. The same trick works with a programmable light modulator when settings need to change on demand. A related element reads the wavefront curvature of the photon-pair state from the image pattern. Single-shot Bell measurements make checking spatially structured entanglement fast, which suits new photon sources built from engineered materials.
arxiv-2606-15782:
Hariharan and colleagues build a reliability-aware inference framework in 2026 so multimodal models stop answering confidently when visual evidence is weak. Such models hallucinate when images are ambiguous, and most fixes improve matching or retrieval without asking whether a prediction deserves trust. Their framework asks exactly that, per instance, before answering.

It retrieves nearest neighbours from an external database of visual features, then scores the prediction with indicators: similarity strength, class-support agreement, evidence margin, and entropy-based doubt. A gate accepts the answer, answers with caution, or abstains when support runs short, and the response layer phrases output to match. On ImageNet-100, accepted accuracy rises from about eighty-six to eighty-nine percent at roughly eighty-nine percent coverage. The rate of confidently wrong answers falls from about fourteen to about eleven percent. Selective trust, backed by retrieved matches, buys accuracy without retraining the base model.
arxiv-2606-15882:
Nikolaeva and Novikov present torch_vn_algebra in 2026, an open-source PyTorch library for experiments with finite-dimensional type I von Neumann algebras. Such an algebra is a direct sum of matrix algebras, the structure forced on quantum systems by superselection rules or symmetry constraints. NumPy, QuTiP, and Qiskit lack native support for these block-diagonal structures.

Operators sit in a compact batched tensor layout covering samples and direct summands, with lazy evaluation to save memory. It generates random operators with user-supplied eigenvalue distributions and standard unitary ensembles. Functional calculus, absolute values, square roots, inverses, and entropy come from singular value decomposition. Three trace functionals are provided, including the von Neumann tracial state. GPU acceleration handles studies such as twenty thousand samples of hundred-by-hundred operators, validated against Haar moments. Benchmarks on a Tesla P100 map where the GPU wins and where it does not.
arxiv-2606-16682:
Liu studies self-evaluating AI agents in a 2026 paper on evaluator preference collapse. When an agent uses a model to grade its own outputs in a loop, biased preferences can take over. One strategy gets rewarded again and again, while others fade, even when they work better. Liu tests whether adding images and other modalities makes this collapse worse.

Using one commercial model to evaluate another across text and visual tasks, a single step-by-step strategy absorbs nearly half of all weight. That is more than three times the collapse seen in text-only loops, while visual ones share only a small slice. A second effect, cross-modal coupling, shows preferences learned on text corrupting choices on images, and vice versa. Across thousands of rounds and many repeat runs, self-evaluation stays nearly immune while cross-model judging couples strongly. The findings warn agent builders to watch who grades.
arxiv-2606-16782:
Murphy leads a large team studying starspots on a young Sun-like star in a 2026 astronomy paper, the second in the KRONOS series. When a planet crosses its star, it may pass over a dark starspot, and the dip in light reveals the spot's properties. The host star here, V1298 Tau, is only a few tens of millions of years old and heavily spotted.

Using James Webb telescope transit observations of its three planets, the team catalogs fourteen spot crossing events across two visits. Spot contrast spectra across near-infrared wavelengths can only be explained if each spot has both a dark core, the umbra, and a lighter rim, the penumbra, like sunspots. Derived temperatures put umbrae far cooler than the bright surface, penumbrae in between, with umbrae covering about a third of each spot. Ground monitoring adds five more large active regions no planet crossed.
arxiv-2606-16882:
Andrews and colleagues classify pieces of unitary Shimura varieties in a 2026 algebraic geometry paper. Shimura varieties are geometric spaces encoding deep arithmetic data, and in positive characteristic they split into Ekedahl-Oort strata, layers distinguished by the torsion structure of the underlying abelian varieties.

The classification covers indecomposable strata, the building blocks that cannot be split further, for varieties tied to the unitary group over an odd inert prime. Every such stratum is one of four types, whimsically named for cycles: unitary unicycle, unitary bicycle, and Serre unicycle or bicycle, the latter pair honoring a tensor construction of Serre. An algorithm translates between the word-based description of a stratum, over a two-letter alphabet, and its Weyl group coset form. Using a p-adic lift, the team builds a canonical point in each stratum and computes its Newton polygon. Unicycle strata of both kinds always meet the supersingular locus.
arxiv-2606-16982:
Landry rebuilds electromagnetic cosmos models inside a modified gravity theory in a 2026 relativity paper. Teleparallel gravity rewrites gravitation using torsion rather than curvature. Its F(T) variant lets the action be a general function of the torsion scalar. Kantowski-Sachs geometries, which expand at different rates in different directions, provide the stage.

Using a covariant coframe and spin-connection method with an invariant classification, Landry derives the field equations. He then rebuilds the function F(T) directly from the geometry's dynamics. In a Maxwell-compatible branch, the field's balance laws force a specific scaling of its energy density. Power-law and exponential starting guesses produce distinct branches tied to electric, magnetic and transverse field sectors. That branch naturally contains de Sitter-like limits, the accelerating states cosmology prizes. Some branches also mimic black hole interior behavior. Basic sanity checks filter the acceptable branches. The setup stays local throughout.
arxiv-2606-17182:
Khan presents a 2026 arXiv paper on concurrency bugs in multi-agent language model systems. Agents in such systems share memory stores, vector indices, and tool registries. Khan works under deterministic-generation semantics, the regime that durable-execution engines enforce. Four anomalies are formalised, each modelled on a classic database isolation problem.

Each anomaly comes with a machine-found counter-example in a formal specification. The core result is a machine-checked chain of five consistency levels. Detectors are proved sound and complete, and Rust runtimes realise the lower levels. Prevention proved cheaper than often assumed in the reported tests. Snapshot isolation added only a small token overhead on one workload, and locking cost far less than the feared order-of-magnitude penalty.
arxiv-2606-17282:
García-Martínez presents a 2026 arXiv paper settling an algebra question modelled on the classic isomorphism problem for groups: can two different restricted Lie algebras share the same restricted enveloping algebra? For ordinary groups and their algebras the answer has long been known to be yes in some cases. The restricted version, raised as an open problem in a survey, asks whether the enveloping algebra still fixes the Lie algebra.

For every prime and every field of that characteristic, García-Martínez builds pairs of finite-dimensional restricted Lie algebras that are not isomorphic yet have isomorphic enveloping algebras. The pairs are also nilpotent in the restricted sense, so the counterexample survives strong extra assumptions. Such pairs exist in every dimension from a stated bound upward, with the two algebras differing in derived-algebra size by one. The restricted problem thus has a negative answer in full generality.
arxiv-2606-17482:
Do and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on generating adversarial driving scenarios that target a self-driving policy's actual weaknesses, rather than a language model's guesses. Finding rare, dangerous cases matters because real-world collection of them is costly and unsafe at scale. Their framework, SPHINX, follows a simple motto: first explain, then explore. Explainability tools diagnose why the policy fails, before new scenes are invented to stress exactly those failure modes in simulation.

Explainability methods surface the visual concepts driving the policy's choices and the uncertainty around them. A vision-language model then critiques the failure modes in words, and those critiques steer scenario generation toward the diagnosed gaps. The generated cases feed policy retraining, closing the loop between diagnosis and improvement. Across benchmarks and varied driving architectures, SPHINX gave consistent robustness gains over rival scenario generators.
arxiv-2606-17682:
Chen and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper turning the trainee into the trainer: the model being trained redesigns its own next training environment. Reinforcement learning pipelines usually pause between stages while experts read failure logs and hand-tune the setup, a slow and heuristic craft. In the proposed framework, the current policy reviews its failed attempts plus context about the task, then writes the configuration for the next stage. The aim is exactly the weaknesses its own behaviour just exposed in testing.

A controllable testbed based on multi-agent pathfinding in a frozen lake supplies graded environment settings for the experiments. With a mid-size open model as backbone, the self-engineered loop beat larger proprietary models and fixed-environment training overall. Analysis shows good redesigns lean on failure evidence and keep settings that already work untouched. Curiously, a trained checkpoint proved a better engineer than its own base model.
arxiv-2606-17882:
Wałęga and Cuenca Grau ask what graph neural networks can express, judging by the structure they preserve, in a 2026 paper. Earlier answers fixed design choices like aggregation style and matched those narrow classes to logic formulas. The authors instead take a semantic route, sorting network classifiers by whether their verdicts survive embeddings, injective maps, or plain homomorphisms between graphs.

For each preservation property they find an exact match in graded modal logic. Preservation under embeddings corresponds to the existential fragment, under injective homomorphisms to its existential-positive part, and under homomorphisms to existential-positive modal logic. Each class also admits a concrete network design with the same reach. The trade-off is crisp: stronger preservation means simpler logic but weaker expressive power, a map that holds regardless of architectural fashion.
arxiv-2606-18082:
Chaitra and colleagues rerun the same simulated universe four times to see how much the answer wobbles, in a 2026 astronomy paper. Cosmological hydrodynamical simulations model galaxy formation inside a growing cosmic web, but chaotic star formation and feedback make each run a sample, not a certainty. The team evolved four identical zoom-in simulations of a galaxy cluster with the OpenGadget3 code, holding compiler, libraries, and hardware fixed.

Comparing matched galaxies across runs, they find dark matter and stellar masses vary by roughly ten to twenty-five percent between realizations. That scatter sits above the shot-noise floor and traces to stochastic star formation and feedback, growing worse when black hole physics joins in. Feedback also regulates, trimming scatter in stellar and black hole masses. The study gives simulators a benchmark noise level to quote beside any prediction drawn from a single run.
arxiv-2606-18482:
Kokkinis, Betouras, and Chubukov build a microscopic theory explaining a strange change in the superconductor beta-PdBi2, in a 2026 condensed matter paper. Tunneling experiments had shown that a magnetic field switches this multi-band material from a fully gapped superconducting state to one with gapless, nodal excitations.

Their model includes spin-orbit coupling and the Zeeman splitting a field imposes on the electronic bands, and it finds two competing attractive pairing channels: a conventional s-wave channel and a p-wave channel. At zero field the s-wave wins, but the field quickly undermines it by splitting the surfaces, letting the hardier p-wave channel take over. At higher fields the p-wave spectrum goes gapless, with nodes appearing between the split surfaces. The authors argue that this sequence accounts for the observed transition and should apply to other multi-band superconductors tuned by magnetic fields.
arxiv-2606-18782:
Brynjólfsson and the team build a benchmark for the redaction of personal information that respects context, in a 2026 paper on privacy and language models. Redaction is now a mandatory cleaning step before sensitive documents reach language models. But whether a phone number is private depends on who holds it and why. So benchmarks that treat redaction as plain entity spotting miss the task.

RedactionBench contains two hundred marked documents across eleven domains, mostly seeded from real-world sources. Its character-level R-Score metric treats equivalent redactions as equal, and ignores shallow formatting differences. Testing thirty-five models, from named-entity tools to frontier agentic systems, the authors find contextual redaction remains unsolved. A human study with eighty-five participants sharpened the point. Annotators agreed by far with mandatory labels, yet agreed with contextual labels less than half the time. That shows contextual privacy is a matter of taste.
arxiv-2606-18882:
Junqueira and the team train a neural network to estimate unbalance masses in rotating shafts, and correct for changes in operating conditions, in a 2026 health monitoring paper. Diagnosing rotor unbalance from vibration data is an inverse problem. A model trained under one setup can fail when the machine's behavior shifts. That is a domain discrepancy that data-driven monitoring often ignores.

The team took data from a test rig. Its primary shaft carried a flange with unbalanced masses at a fixed radius, and ran at varying speeds. A secondary shaft could be switched on, to add domain discrepancy on purpose. Triaxial accelerometers recorded the response. Their network is trained with a maximum mean discrepancy strategy, which aligns feature representations across the source and target settings. Tackling the shift head-on improved prediction accuracy, especially when the system's physics were not fully known and fell outside the training settings.
arxiv-2606-19282:
Chen and colleagues report the first detection of dense gas in a massive main-sequence galaxy at cosmic noon in 2026. Dense gas is the direct fuel for star formation, but measuring it at high redshift is hard, especially in typical star-forming galaxies rather than extreme starbursts or quasar hosts. The team targeted the galaxy BX610 at redshift just above two, when the universe was a few billion years old and star formation peaked.

Emission from HNC and CN lines is detected, concentrated in the galactic center where intense star formation is ongoing. The line ratio resembles starburst galaxies at like redshifts and sits below quasar host values. The fainter HNC line disfavors a strongly buried active nucleus, matching optical diagnostics. Radiative transfer analysis favors dense gas at high density and moderate temperature. A first dense-gas census in a normal massive galaxy anchors how fuel drives star formation.
arxiv-2606-19382:
Kushwaha and colleagues present DynAMO in 2026, an engine that runs industrial asset workflows with language model agents. Agent systems promise end-to-end automation of asset lifecycles. Real factory deployment is hindered by latency, unstable parallel runs, and safety risks. DynAMO plans first, then executes, and produces workflow graphs. It supports step-by-step workflows and parallel ones that respect task dependencies, so structure stays correct while independent tasks overlap.

Across six controlled experiments, parallel runs cut end-to-end latency a lot against step-by-step runs. The gain grows on workflows with more parallel slack. When tool calls are given realistic delays, timing breakdowns show model reasoning still takes over ninety percent of total time. Pruning context in a structured way cuts inference latency by roughly thirty percent. Behavior stays correct throughout, with graceful degradation under stress. Agent builders should aim effort at inference cost.
arxiv-2606-19482:
Boren Gu and six colleagues introduce a family of quantum error-correcting codes in 2026 that works on a flat square grid. The codes are quantum low-density parity-check codes, which spread each check over few qubits to cut fault-tolerant overhead. Most rival codes need long-range links or qubit shuttling, both hard to build in superconducting hardware.

Neighbouring qubits swap roles through iSWAP walks, and those walks both set the check pattern and carry out its measurement. Measurement depth stays constant as the code grows, and leakage leaves the system as check and data qubits trade places each round. One example code packs 14 logical qubits into 323 physical qubits with distance 15. At about 30 circuit qubits per logical qubit, the best layouts cut logical error rates by up to a factor of 1,000 against surface codes. Planar, local hardware can thus host codes once thought to need exotic wiring.
arxiv-2606-19782:
Aravind Narayanan and Shaina Raza build an auditable financial chart question answering pipeline in 2026. Regulated finance needs more than accuracy: staff must know which answers deserve trust. Many firms also cannot send client data to outside model providers.

AgentFinVQA splits each query across agents for planning, text extraction, legend grounding, visual inspection, and verification. Every step lands in a traceable Model Evaluation Packet per question. On the FinMME benchmark the pipeline beats a matched zero-shot baseline by wide margins. Gains hold with a proprietary backbone and with an open-weights model served on site. The verifier's verdict doubles as a confidence signal for routing human review. Confirmed answers prove far more accurate than revised ones. Error study blames question misunderstanding, legend confusion, and extraction slips for most failures.
arxiv-2606-20082:
Xiaoyu Li, Junwei Yu, Jiaojiao Jiang, Junbin Gao, and Andi Han speed up computation of the John ellipsoid, the largest ellipsoid fitting inside a symmetric polytope. Their 2026 paper revisits leverage-score algorithms, which since 2019 have needed iterations growing with the inverse accuracy target. The authors argue this cost bundles three jobs: certifying accuracy, identifying key constraints, and achieving accuracy itself.

Through the equivalent D-optimal design form, they show the accuracy cost is largely an artifact of certification. The standard certificate, the uniform average of iterates, improves only linearly with iteration count, however cheap each step becomes. Pointing the same oracle at the last iterate instead is fast, with a warm start and acceleration. The result separates what is truly hard here from what was only hard to certify.
arxiv-2606-20182:
Sunil Gangwar and C. S. Yadav trace the anomalous transverse responses of Mn3SnC, an antiperovskite that is both a nodal-line semimetal and a magnet with mixed ordering. Their 2026 paper studies the anomalous Hall effect, where a transverse voltage appears from magnetization rather than an external field, and its thermal twin, the anomalous Nernst effect. Here antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic order coexist, a rich test case for how topology and magnetism interact.

Measurements and analysis show the intrinsic Berry curvature effect dominates both responses. The authors link the Hall and Nernst signals through Mott's relation, giving one unified picture instead of two separate stories. Scattering of electrons from both kinds of magnons shows up in the Nernst signal. The ratio of Nernst to Hall conductivities is a sizable fraction of a natural constant, pointing to Berry curvature as the main driver of the thermal response.
arxiv-2606-20282:
Junhui Li, Jialu Li, and Youshan Zhang build a deeper Mamba network for salient object detection, picking out the most prominent object in an image. Their 2026 paper introduces U2Mamba, a two-level nested U-structure built from multiscale Mamba blocks. Mamba models handle long sequences efficiently, which suits high-resolution images, but earlier versions underexplored context and network depth. The nested U-shape merges receptive fields from shallow and deep layers.

Rich context flows in without the resolution limits constraining older designs. Training also changes: losses are computed hierarchically at each level, not just at the top. Extensive experiments show performance highly competitive with state-of-the-art detectors. The contribution is architectural discipline: depth, context, and supervision arranged so each level of the network learns at its own scale.
arxiv-2606-20482:
Haw-Shiuan Chang and four colleagues harvest mouse movements and eye gaze as preference signals for aligning language models. Their 2026 paper notes two limits of standard alignment: users rarely give explicit feedback, so good annotations are expensive, and implicit feedback is ignored despite powering the moats of internet giants.

The team builds IFllm, a dataset of 1,336 multi-turn questions from 59 Mechanical Turk workers, with their mouse trajectories and gaze points recorded. The data let them quantify how much alignment signal implicit behavior carries beyond the response text. If attention and cursor hesitation reveal preference, alignment data could be gathered passively at scale. The study opens a cheaper, richer channel between users and model trainers.
arxiv-2606-20682:
Jaganadh Gopinadhan addresses automated processing of Indian bank cheques in a solo 2026 paper, starting with the need to locate fields before any reading can occur. The fields are the date, legal amount, IFSC code, account number, signature, and payee name. The only public collection named, the IDRBT Cheque Image Dataset, ships with no field annotations and unclear redistribution terms, which limits shared research.

Gopinadhan releases bounding-box annotations for all 112 cheques, distributed alone and keyed to original filenames so the source terms are respected. A second release holds 295 fully redistributable synthetic cheques made by pasting real field patches onto cleaned bank templates at their source coordinates, so labels carry over unchanged. A ResNet-50 baseline predicts all six fields in one pass. Open data matters because automation cannot improve if teams rebuild private datasets.
arxiv-2606-20882:
Brett Wheeler argues in a solo 2026 paper that AI code generation breaks a core assumption in software team metrics. For decades, teams inferred knowledge from authorship. Metrics such as truck factor and degree of authorship assume writing code implies understanding it. That proxy worked when code entering a repository was usually written by a person. Writing forced at least brief understanding.

AI generation severs that link, Wheeler argues. An agent can generate a module and a human can merge it. Version control still records a human author. That record is now consistent with full, partial, or no understanding. The metric still returns a number. But the number no longer measures knowledge. The claim is stronger than decay: the whole class is invalidated. Teams that rely on such metrics to judge risk, such as who can safely change a system, may be misled badly.
arxiv-2606-20982:
Louis Diaz computes Kodaira dimension in a solo 2026 mathematics paper for moduli spaces of degree two rational maps with prescribed orbit portraits. A moduli space collects all maps of a given type up to change of coordinates. Doyle and Silverman introduced spaces where the pre-periodic structure is fixed. One such space, for a six-cycle, was known to be of general type.

Diaz treats all portraits with up to six pre-periodic points. The Kodaira dimension, a key measure of a space's geometric complexity, is computed in each case. All four possible values appear across the family: negative infinity, zero, one, and two. That spread shows the family ranges from very simple to fully general behavior. Classifying these spaces helps dynamicists know which tools apply to each portrait, since Kodaira dimension governs what kind of geometry and curves a space can contain.
arxiv-2606-21182:
Vedant Mokal and Shantanu Desai probe isotropy in 2026 in the sky spread of gamma-ray bursts from the Swift catalog, testing a core premise of cosmology. That premise holds that the universe looks the same in all directions at large scales. Their probe is independent of galaxy surveys. A harmonic split of the sky gives dipole and quadrupole amplitudes for burst positions. Simulations of an isotropic sky give the null baseline.

Raw data show apparently strong signals. The team then builds an exposure map from the telescope's pointing history and related factors. Judged against that map, both signals fall below one sigma. The burst sky is thus consistent with isotropy. The map is released publicly. The lesson is methodological: apparent cosmic asymmetry can be an artifact of where a telescope happened to look.
arxiv-2606-21282:
Anagha Athavale and five colleagues present a static analysis method in 2026 for proving global robustness of neural networks: that no small input change anywhere can flip a prediction. Local robustness, around one input, is far easier; the global version quantifies over all input pairs, making it a harder two-safety property. Their tool, TwoSafe, tracks pairs of perturbed inputs together through the network using differential halo zonotopes, geometric sets that bound how far the pair can diverge.

A symmetric, confidence-based variant of the property ignores cases where both outputs are low-confidence, widening the class of networks that can be certified. On standard verification benchmarks, TwoSafe beats prior tools in precision and scale, handling networks an order of magnitude larger. Stronger guarantees of this kind matter for networks in security-sensitive roles.
arxiv-2606-21582:
Noah Grodzinski, Robert Jack, and Sarah Loos study a ferromagnet in 2026 whose bonds are partly nonreciprocal, meaning the influence between two spins does not run equally both ways. Such asymmetric couplings drive systems out of equilibrium, but their effect when sprinkled randomly through a material was largely unexplored. The team analyzes a two-dimensional Ising model with nonreciprocal bonds at density p, frozen in place.

A gauge-invariance argument caps the critical density at one half, and mean-field theory sketches a phase diagram that proves qualitatively right. A continuous nonequilibrium transition survives down to absolute zero at finite bond density. Unlike equilibrium disordered magnets, the low-temperature dynamics never freezes: rare regions flip without thermal help, and domains coarsen only logarithmically, an activated creep that keeps the system restless forever.
arxiv-2606-21682:
Isabella Graßl and Benoit Baudry ask in 2026 whether jokes belong in a software testing classroom. Testing strikes many students as monotonous, which dulls engagement with a core quality practice. The authors slipped humorous elements into introductory testing courses at universities in Canada and Germany, then ran a mixed-methods study of the students' experience.

Humor had a strong positive effect: students found testing more engaging and less monotonous, felt more comfortable and accepted in class, and reported thinking more creatively about test tasks. The gains were especially marked for female students, above all in sense of belonging. As interventions go, humor is low-threshold and nearly free, yet it made the learning environment noticeably more welcoming, a result with implications for how required but unglamorous subjects are taught.
arxiv-2606-22082:
Wang and colleagues present CodeTeam in 2026, a multi-agent framework that builds a whole software repository from a requirements document written in natural language. Repository-level generation is far harder than writing functions: plans must stretch over many files, interfaces must stay stable, and cross-file inconsistencies need debugging. CodeTeam separates the work into coordinated planning, decision, and implementation stages staffed by different language model agents.

In planning, several Architect agents draft competing design sketches, sometimes grounded by retrieved references. A chief technical officer agent then picks and normalizes the best sketch into a machine-checkable contract covering file ownership, interfaces, and dependencies. Developer agents write code under a dependency-aware scheduler with Git-based coordination, while a quality agent runs tests and drives repairs. On an execution-based benchmark, CodeTeam reached the highest average test pass rate in both tested settings, 34.6 percent and 42.3 percent for its two variants.
arxiv-2606-22182:
Masclef and colleagues present, in 2026, a dual-stream model that decodes three-dimensional shape perception from EEG brain signals. The brain's vision splits processing into a ventral pathway for object identity and a dorsal pathway for spatial orientation. The authors mirror that split with separate decoding modules, applied while objects rotate.

One module identifies the object, and the other predicts its angle by circular regression, which respects the wrap-around of angles. An EEG-conditioned multiview diffusion model then reconstructs the 3D shape from the neural activity. The system successfully decodes both identity and orientation from EEG. Channel analyses show ventral, dorsal, and motor-related channels contributing over time in a structured way. Object and angle decoding are therefore not supported by a static dominance of the ventral stream.
arxiv-2606-22882:
Mark Lewko advances the finite field restriction problem in this 2026 paper, the second in a series using a bilinear approach. Restriction theory asks when a Fourier transform on a surface extends to a bounded operator between function spaces. Lewko studies paraboloids over finite fields of prime order where negative one is not a square.

For the three-dimensional paraboloid, he proves the extension operator maps square-integrable functions into a higher integrability space, with an exponent of about three and a half. The argument combines his bilinear method with point-line incidence estimates, bounds on how often points and lines can meet. For the six-dimensional paraboloid he proves the sharp estimate, including the endpoint that earlier work had missed. He also shows the endpoint conjecture in three dimensions would imply a number-theoretic statement about lattice points on the Euclidean paraboloid.
arxiv-2606-23282:
Massimo Fornasier and Giacomo Sodini generalize a method for approximating Sobolev functions in a 2026 analysis paper. Sobolev functions are functions whose smoothness is measured through their derivatives in an averaged sense. The authors' earlier work approximated such functions on spaces of probability measures from finite random samples. This paper asks how far that recipe travels. They identify a broad class of metric measure spaces where the needed structure holds. The space must behave like a Hilbert space. It must also carry a computable algebra of well-behaved test functions.

Fornasier and Sodini verify the hypotheses for weighted Riemannian manifolds. They also verify them for spaces of measures under the Hellinger-Kantorovich distance. Inside the abstract framework, the core results from the earlier work carry over. Functions can be recovered from random point values. One method thus serves many infinite-dimensional spaces of current interest.
arxiv-2606-23382:
Jakub Dotlačil and Ece Takmaz test whether energy-based transformers predict reading difficulty in a 2026 psycholinguistics paper. Transformer language models already model human sentence processing. Measures like surprisal, how unexpected a word is, and attention entropy predict reading times well and capture different parts of the load. Energy-based transformers add a principled link to associative memory theory, the Hopfield network tradition. The authors compute an energy measure from such a model and ask whether it predicts how long people spend reading.

Dotlačil and Takmaz evaluate across three reading corpora, covering natural stories, eye tracking, and self-paced reading. The energy measure robustly predicted reading times in all three, adding fit beyond surprisal each time. In a controlled relative clause experiment, energy at one layer captured the known object-subject asymmetry. Evidence suggests energy subsumes effects previously split between two separate measures.
arxiv-2606-23482:
Sergey Belov and colleagues hunt for anomalous solar and stellar flares in a 2026 astrophysics paper. A flare's light curve, its brightness over time, encodes the physics of the eruption. Flares that break the standard profile may reveal new physics. The team trains an unsupervised deep model that learns a compact description of normal flares. Their training data are synthetic light curves built from an existing analytical flare model. Any real flare that fits the learned description poorly is flagged as a time-domain anomaly.

Belov and colleagues built the model on the Deep Support Vector Data Description method, which squeezes normal examples into a tight region of a learned space. Anomalies fall outside that region. The pipeline draws on data from the STIX X-ray instrument aboard the Solar Orbiter spacecraft. The aim is a systematic census of odd flares for follow-up physics.
arxiv-2606-23582:
Kryhin, Lunts, Patel, Sachdev, and Nosov study how a special kind of disorder reshapes superconductivity in quantum critical metals, in a 2026 condensed matter theory paper. A quantum critical metal sits at the edge of a phase change, where fluctuations of a bosonic field make electrons behave unlike an ordinary metal. Those fluctuations can also glue electrons into Cooper pairs. Harris disorder is random variation that locally pushes the system toward or away from criticality.

That randomness creates localized pockets of the bosonic field even while electrons move freely. These pockets produce both a random pairing strength and a random landscape for the pairs. At high temperature, pairing starts as compact puddles on the most localized pockets. At lower temperature a spread out pairing state appears, still scarred by disorder. The spread of local pairing scales follows a power law tail, unlike ordinary disordered superconductors, matching tunneling data on cuprates.
arxiv-2606-23682:
Parihar, Raina, Babu, and Patashnik speed up image generation guided by reference pictures simply by throwing most reference tokens away, in a 2026 paper on generative models. Reference based diffusion models steer generation with elements from input images, enabling editing and subject driven creation. Their cost grows steeply with each added reference, because every image becomes a dense grid of tokens that the model must attend to. Much of that grid carries little useful information.

Dropping a large share of reference tokens at inference barely harms quality. Fine tuning with random token dropping then makes the model robust to any partial reference set. At run time, task aware selection keeps the most informative regions. The result is four times faster generation with multiple references, without visible quality loss.
arxiv-2606-23882:
Merai and Anevski propose a way to estimate time varying risk effects in survival data that respects a natural ordering, in a 2026 paper on statistics. The Aalen additive hazard model writes a patient's event risk as a baseline plus covariate effects that change over time. Estimating those effect curves nonparametrically usually needs kernel smoothing with a hand chosen bandwidth. The authors instead impose monotonicity, projecting the naive least squares estimates onto the space of monotone functions.

The projection acts like a smoother whose bandwidth the data choose themselves. The paper works out the pointwise limit distribution of the estimators under right censored data. Convergence runs at the cube root rate typical of shape constrained problems, with the Chernoff distribution as the limit law. Clinicians gain a principled route to effect curves over time.
arxiv-2606-23982:
Spronk, Stokke, and Thamizhazhagan extend a family of algebras that encode symmetry for locally compact groups. The Fourier-Stieltjes algebra gathers well-behaved functions that arise from group representations. Its spine subalgebra is a smaller, distinguished piece with a tractable spectrum. Their 2026 generalisation starts from any chosen set of topologies on the group, arranged as an upper semilattice. From that set they build a matching generalised spine algebra.

Each such algebra breaks into a graded direct sum of maximal copies of Fourier algebras. Its spectrum is a semilattice of groups. The authors craft examples where the spectrum can be controlled in fine detail. They then define compatible fusions of homomorphisms and affine maps. With those, they characterise all completely positive and completely contractive maps from such an algebra to a Fourier-Stieltjes algebra. The result is new even for the classic spine algebra, and even when both groups are abelian.
arxiv-2606-24382:
Yang constructs a quantum field theory living in de Sitter space, the exponentially expanding geometry of an accelerating universe, built directly out of conformal field theory data. Holography for de Sitter space has long lagged its anti-de Sitter cousin, Writing alone in 2026, Yang mirrors his own anti-de Sitter scale-space construction. De Sitter geometry becomes the moduli space of oriented balls. Operators are lifted from the lower-dimensional theory by conformal-family Casimir completion.

Two parent theories give two representations. A Euclidean parent conformal theory yields a finite wavefunction representation of the de Sitter theory. A Minkowski parent yields a double-time representation, unitary when measured in the parent theory's time polarisation. Yang offers the framework as a cleaner arena for the notorious puzzles of de Sitter quantum theory. Exactness and finiteness are built in from the start, rather than recovered through asymptotic expansions.
arxiv-2606-24582:
Özdem reads pentaquarks' internal structure, exotic particles made of five quarks, through their magnetic fingerprints. Mass measurements alone cannot tell apart a compact pentaquark, a true five quark object with diquark links, from a loose molecule of ordinary hadrons. Magnetic moments can, since they depend on how spin and charge are arranged inside. Multi current QCD light cone sum rules supply the machinery for the hidden charm states examined here.

Two exact signatures emerge, for compact diquark diquark antiquark setups. For every interpolating current considered, the light quark parts of the magnetic moment obey an exact ratio. It is fixed purely by the up and down quark charges, through a shared kernel coupling them only through charge. For one specific current, the charm quark's contribution vanishes exactly, for structural reasons traced in the analysis. Writing alone in 2026, Özdem offers these charge algebra relations as tests future measurements can use.
arxiv-2606-24782:
Amit Acharya develops a variational minimum principle for linear Cauchy elasticity, including materials with no stored energy function. Classical elasticity theory usually leans on such an energy function to frame its equations. Heterogeneous materials, whose properties vary from place to place, may lack one. Acharya's approach changes variables into a new set of dual fields. In those fields a functional can be posed whose equations reproduce the original problem.

The dual dynamic problem takes a surprising form. Its Euler Lagrange system is degenerate elliptic, even though the primal elastodynamics is hyperbolic. Acharya sketches uniqueness claims for both the dual dynamic and the dual static problems. He also draws out what the degenerate ellipticity implies. Further discussion covers mixed materials directly. Materials with indefinite moduli are covered as well. The work extends a dual field technique the author and others built for systems whose primal form resists variational treatment.
arxiv-2606-25182:
Jailbreak prompts coax aligned language models into answers they were trained to refuse. Sofiia Nikolenko and three colleagues look for the fingerprint inside the model. They track how token level predictive entropy, the model's uncertainty, evolves across layers of a frozen model read through the logit lens.

Simple summaries of prompt entropy, its mean or variance, carry almost no signal about an attack. Features that capture how entropy moves across token positions, such as rank based trend scores, separate attacks far better. The signal is not spread evenly through the network. It concentrates in the intermediate layers and fades at the final layer, so mid network representations show jailbreak structure most clearly. The pattern holds across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models and several adversarial benchmarks, with no extra training.
arxiv-2606-25382:
A famous solar active region produced a major flare in February 2011, and researchers still use it to test how flares ignite. Matthias Rempel and Georgios Chintzoglou simulate that region in 2026 by moving model sunspots along the paths the real ones took. Four sunspot groups in a quadrupole arrangement collide and shear, winding stress into the corona above the line where magnetic polarity flips. Stored free energy climbs past the level the real event released.

The simulation erupts with an X class flare followed by smaller ones, and the four strongest launch coronal mass ejections. A twisted magnetic flux rope forms an hour or two before the main flare and starts rising minutes before it. Eruption begins where the rope enters a zone matching the torus instability criterion. Flare energies scale with X-ray brightness much as observed, though durations run short.
arxiv-2606-25782:
Every harmful chatbot answer that slips through is a safety failure. The judges screening answers are usually big language models: accurate, but slow and costly at scale. Han Jeon, Shiv Medler, Joseph Voyles, and Matt Wood ask in 2026 whether small encoder classifiers suffice. They fine tuned models from the ModernBERT family, on labels from judge ensembles under majority voting. The encoders were then scored on a golden holdout set. Rivals included rule based matching, fine tuned decoder classifiers such as LlamaGuard, and prompted judges, one of them Claude based.

Performance is reported through F1, false negative rate, and precision recall curves. Results are also broken down by attack style. The styles are single turn prompts, decomposition, escalation, and context manipulation. That breakdown shows where cheap encoders track expensive judges, and where they part ways. The output is practical guidance for builders choosing guardrails under latency and budget limits.
arxiv-2606-25882:
Francisco Javier Sáez-Maldonado, Juan Maroñas, and Daniel Hernández-Lobato study a failure mode in deep Gaussian processes, layered probabilistic models prized for strong predictions. Fitting such models relies on variational inference, an approximation scheme that can collapse: the fitted posterior falls back to the prior, and the model explains the data as pure noise. Collapse is a known nuisance, but its causes inside these layered models were murky.

Links emerge between collapse, the Double Stochastic training algorithm, and the linear prior mean used in nearly every layer. Sáez-Maldonado and colleagues show the linear mean helps not by dodging a pathology of very deep models, as many believed. It helps by making the optimization better conditioned at the start. A zero-mean model initialized to mimic that start trains just as well, so the prior can be chosen for modelling reasons instead of training convenience.
arxiv-2606-26382:
Mayumi Mohan, Ju-Hung Chen, and Alexis Block test whether small language models can help screen papers for a systematic review of social-physical human-robot interaction, a fast-growing field with messy terminology. The review pipeline they chart covers work from 1992 onward.

No small model matched human reviewers on its own, but the models ran locally and screened far faster than people. An ensemble of them also caught 39 relevant papers the humans had missed, about a tenth of the final dataset. The authors conclude that small models can widen and speed up large reviews without replacing expert judgment.
arxiv-2606-26482:
Songyan Luo and Yunxin Zhang build faster optimal transport methods for mixture models. Optimal transport measures how much work it takes to reshape one distribution into another. Standard discrete methods match individual sample points. Their cost grows at least with the square of the sample size. Location-scale mixtures, blends of shifted and stretched copies of one shape, offer a shortcut.

The authors define distance measures for such mixtures using generalised Minkowski inequalities. They characterise the optimal transport maps between the underlying families. A key result reduces the big matching problem to transport between mixture components only. Components are few, even when samples are many. Computing time then grows only linearly with sample size. Tests on the VisDA-C domain adaptation benchmark followed. Domain adaptation reuses a model trained in one setting in a different one. Accuracy stayed competitive while cost and memory fell substantially.
arxiv-2606-26582:
Shravan Luckraz extends the theory of time structure in extensive games. Extensive games model players moving in sequence, with information sets grouping situations a player cannot tell apart. A time structure assigns clock times consistently to those information sets. Earlier graph-based results covered finite games only. Many real settings, though, involve vast or continuous flows of information.

Luckraz lifts the theory to countable and continuum-sized games built on real trees. He introduces a quotient structure of information sets as the canonical object a clock must order. For that structure he develops a reduction theory and proves existence and uniqueness under a finiteness condition. Further conditions yield real-valued time labels and measurable selection methods. Constructive algorithms accompany the theory. A differential game example shows the ideas at work. The work bridges discrete and continuous models of timing in games.
arxiv-2606-26682:
Marvin Ködding and Bianca Truthe continue a study of contextual grammars and the families that control them. A contextual grammar builds sentences by adding word pairs around a starting core. A a selection set decides which cores may grow at each step. This work examines selection languages that are idefix-free, meaning no word contains another as an inner part, prefix, or suffix.

The authors compare these new families against many known families below the regular level. Subregular means simpler than fully regular languages. The comparisons cover finite, definite, commutative, circular, and other classic types. They then compare the rankings that external contextual grammars generate under each selection type. New families slot into the existing rankings, extending them. The results refine knowledge of how grammar power depends on the selector's simplicity.
arxiv-2606-26982:
Abla Bedoui, Ashley L. Greene, and Mohammed Cherkaoui audit how framing changes language model behaviour in mental health conversations. The same concern, worded with different context, can draw different responses. In sensitive support settings, such wobble undermines trust and complicates safety checks. The authors test matched prompts across several framing conditions and model families.

Framing shifted the models' interpretive tendencies in every family tested. Probing the models layer by layer showed that behaviour-linked information stays readable throughout the network's depth. How strongly it read out varied by architecture. Held-out framing probes tested whether the effect generalises to unseen framings. The findings argue that reliability testing for mental health tools must vary wording, not just content, since stability under reframing is part of safety.
arxiv-2606-27182:
Desmond and colleagues test two classic checks of cosmic expansion inside a simulated universe. The Tolman test watches how galaxy surface brightness fades with redshift, meaning distance in cosmic time.
