Stuart Jackson, Fred Cummins, and Nuala Brady timed flips in a reversible moving figure in 2008. Some images can be seen two ways, and perception swaps between them. A biological motion figure, like a walking person, is one such case. The authors studied how fast those swaps happen.

Their PLOS ONE article compares biological motion with other moving figures. Timing patterns reveal how the brain settles and unsettles a percept. A walking figure may flip at its own characteristic pace. The work adds to models of how perception stays stable, then changes. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004082:
John Paul Eichorst, Shaoying Lu, Jing Xu, and co-authors measured a cell movement switch in 2008. RhoA is a molecular switch that helps cells crawl and change shape. Biosensors using FRET light transfer can watch RhoA in live cells. Large image sets from those sensors need automated analysis.

Their PLOS ONE article compares RhoA dynamics in moving and still cells. Automated image analysis made the comparison consistent across many cells. Migratory cells showed different RhoA patterns from stationary ones. The method lets labs quantify movement signals without hand scoring. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004182:
Lingyun Zhu and colleagues published this vascular study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Atherosclerosis, the hardening and narrowing of arteries, grows partly through the rapid multiplication of vascular smooth muscle cells in vessel walls. Diabetes raises the risk, since high blood sugar drives these muscle cells to grow and move.

The team focused on PGC-1α, a regulator of cell energy use. They report that it is a key controller of the growth and movement that glucose triggers in these cells. The finding ties a metabolic regulator to the vessel damage that makes diabetes so dangerous for the heart.
plos-pone-0004282:
Hoau-Yan Wang and Lindsay Burns published this pain pharmacology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chronic morphine makes the mu opioid receptor switch its coupling from Gi/o to Gs proteins, producing excitatory signalling linked to tolerance and dependence. Ultra-low-dose naloxone prevents that switch and softens tolerance, but how was unclear.

The authors traced naloxone's protective effect to a pentapeptide binding site on filamin A, a scaffolding protein. Binding there blocks the receptor's switch and the CREB activation that follows acute morphine. The site offers a precise target for keeping opioids effective.
plos-pone-0004382:
Rhodopsin is the light-sensing protein in the eye's rod cells. It belongs to the large G protein coupled receptor family. Peter Hildebrand, Patrick Scheerer, Jung Hee Park, and co-authors studied its close relative opsin. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper maps a route through the protein. The route is a channel for the light-sensitive molecule retinal.

Inside rhodopsin, retinal sits in a pocket among seven coiled segments. Light flips retinal from one shape to another, starting vision. The authors describe how a ligand channel could let retinal move through the protein. That path helps explain how the sensor resets after firing. Receptor channels also interest drug designers who target this protein family.
plos-pone-0004482:
A silenced gene that brakes cell growth can be switched back on in a rare childhood tumor, report Elizabeth Algar, Andrea Muscat, Vinod Dagar, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tumor is rhabdoid tumor, an aggressive cancer of the kidney and brain in young children. It is defined by the loss of a gene called SMARCB1, which helps control how DNA is packaged.

The missing gene seems to let other controls be silenced, including CDKN1C, a tumor suppressor imprinted from one parent. Restoring SMARCB1, or using drugs that block histone deacetylases, turned CDKN1C back on in the team's tests. That reawakening suggests a treatment angle for a tumor that now has few. It also shows how one lost gene can mute a whole safety system.
plos-pone-0004582:
Genes inside a famous autism-linked stretch of chromosome 16 are tested one by one by Ravinesh Kumar, Christian Marshall, Judith Badner, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Autism is a complex childhood neurodevelopmental disorder with a strong genetic basis. A deletion or duplication on chromosome 16p11.2, spanning about two dozen genes, is the second most frequent chromosomal disorder associated with autism.

Which of those genes actually drive the risk was unknown. The team ran association and mutation analyses on sixteen candidate genes from the region, on their account. Narrowing a whole region down to specific genes is slow, essential work. It points genetic counseling and brain research at the few genes that matter most.
plos-pone-0004682:
Xian Qi and colleagues described H5N1 bird flu viruses taken from raccoon dogs in China, for PLOS ONE in 2009. The H5N1 virus is a strong bird flu strain that can infect many kinds of animals. It poses a steady threat to farm stock and to human health as well.

Many forms of the virus occur in chickens, but few are linked to infection in mammals. The team read the genes of viruses from raccoon dogs to place them among known forms. Placing mammal cases in the family tree helps track spread. It also helps warn which forms may pose more risk to people.
plos-pone-0004782:
Cinzia Scambi and colleagues reported early evidence that folate, and Vitamin B12 may improve cell membranes in children with cystic fibrosis, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cystic fibrosis is a common fatal inherited disorder in Caucasian populations. It stems from mutations in a gene for a channel that moves salts and water across cell surfaces in the lungs and gut.

New strategies propose dietary supplements to support membrane health. The single arm trial gave 5-MTHF and B12 to affected children. Early signs pointed to membrane improvement. Larger controlled trials would be needed to confirm benefit. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0004882:
Katarzyna Bozek led a team that mapped how the body clock controls genes in mammals for PLOS ONE in 2009. The clock turns thousands of genes on and off in a daily rhythm. Each tissue keeps its own rhythm, and the same gene can peak at a distinct hour in the liver than in the brain. Many control steps must work at once to make that pattern so exact.

The team read the start regions of clock driven genes on a large scale. They looked for shared codes that predict when and where a gene is switched on. Those codes help explain how one clock drives so many rhythms. They may also guide the best hours to give drugs.
plos-pone-0004982:
Klebsiella pneumoniae is a germ that often lives in soil and in the gut without causing harm. It can also cause serious hospital infections of the urine, lungs and blood. Sylvain Brisse and colleagues hunted its most dangerous clones. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They studied the clones' genes and traits together.

The team picked out the deadly clones from the wider group. They then sketched how these killers evolved. The family tree shows which lines turned dangerous. Hospitals gain a way to spot the worst strains early. The work also shows how a quiet gut germ can become a feared cause of disease.
plos-pone-0005082:
Tracking MRSA outbreaks needs fast, sharp strain fingerprinting. Current techniques are either resource-intensive or too blunt. Leo Schouls and colleagues tested a newer method in PLOS ONE in 2009. It is called MLVA. It counts variable repeats at several DNA loci. They compared it with two workhorses: pulsed-field gel electrophoresis and spa-typing.

The comparison shows where MLVA wins on speed and detail. It also shows where the older methods still hold up. Hospitals gain a practical tool for tracing staph spread. Rapid typing can catch transmission routes early. Stopping spread early saves lives and money. The study gives infection-control teams an evidence-based choice.
plos-pone-0005182:
Hedgehog signals guide how embryos build their bodies, and a protein called Smoothened carries those signals onward. In mammals, Smoothened moves to a tiny cell antenna, the primary cilium, when the signal arrives. Wilson and colleagues examined the shapes Smoothened can take in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team found that Smoothened can rest in several active and inactive shapes. All of those shapes can still travel to the cilium. That flexibility helps explain how the signal can be tuned up or down. It also matters for drugs that target Smoothened in cancer, since shape decides drug response.
plos-pone-0005282:
Cell division runs on a strict timetable in which key proteins must appear and then be destroyed. Van Leuken and colleagues traced one such timed destruction in PLOS ONE in 2009. It involves Aurora A, a kinase that helps organize division.

Polo-like kinase-1 is switched on before division by Aurora A itself. The team showed Plk1 is also required for Aurora A's timely destruction, by activating the APC/C-Cdh1 disposal machinery. A protein helping to destroy its own activator is a neat timing loop for orderly division. Cell division fails if these parts linger too long, so the loop that builds and then clears them is one of the checks that keeps each new cell sound.
plos-pone-0005382:
RNA interference uses small RNA pairs to switch off chosen genes, a workhorse research tool. Which strand of the pair guides the silencing was thought to be settled: one guides, the other is discarded. Wei and colleagues challenged that picture in mammalian cells in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Using small RNAs aimed at complementary targets, they showed both strands can guide posttranscriptional gene silencing. Strand selection in the silencing complex is therefore less one-sided than assumed. Designers of RNA interference experiments must account for activity from the strand they meant to ignore.
plos-pone-0005482:
Dong-Young Choi and colleagues studied brain inflammation and Parkinson-like illness in rats, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Parkinson's disease slowly kills nerve cells, and its cause in most cases is unknown. Signs found after death hint that inflammation in the brain may help drive the damage.

The team triggered inflammation in a movement area of the rat brain. The rats went on to show Parkinson-like signs and nerve cell loss. That supports the idea that inflammation is not just a side effect. It is part of how the disease harms the brain, and a possible target for treatment.
plos-pone-0005582:
Allister Crow and co-authors solved the structures of a bacterial weapon protein in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Many harmful bacteria shoot proteins straight into the cells they infect. One such protein family, called Cif, helps the bacteria take over host cells.

The team worked out the shapes of Cif proteins from two different pathogens. Comparing the shapes shows what the family shares and where it differs. A clear shape helps workers guess how the protein acts and how it might be blocked. Shapes from two species side by side also reveal which parts of the protein a drug would need to fit.
plos-pone-0005682:
Stephanie Watts and colleagues reported in 2009 that serotonin can attach itself to proteins in blood vessel walls. Serotonin is best known for mood, but it was first named for its power to tighten blood vessels. Most work has focused on serotonin latching onto receptors on the cell surface.

The team shows a second route: serotonin is bonded onto vessel proteins in a process called serotonylation. Those proteins help drive contraction of the vessel wall. This route may change how scientists think about blood pressure and vessel tone. It also opens a new place to look for drugs that relax vessels.
plos-pone-0005782:
Takao Fukui and co-authors described in 2009 a strange illusion from their lab: a moving phantom limb sensation. Sometimes a well-understood action fails even with full skill and a clear plan. One exception they probed involves a phantom that seems to move on its own.

The odd feeling appears to trigger a subconscious motor program, a set routine the body runs without orders. Studying such slips reveals how much of movement is automatic. The work speaks to rehab after amputation and to the design of prosthetics the brain will accept. Small illusions can expose big control systems.
plos-pone-0005882:
Fiona Pryde and co-authors tied a chemical mark on histones in 2009 to the schedule of DNA copying. Different stretches of DNA copy at different times in S-phase, set by their neighborhood. A protein called Cdc45 must load onto origins to start copying.

Methylation of histone H3 at one spot helped determine when Cdc45 associates with origins, the team found. That links a chromatin mark directly to replication timing. Timing faults can destabilize the genome, a cancer hallmark. The study names one timer among several, giving the replication field a firmer parts list.
plos-pone-0005982:
Dodder is a parasitic plant that steals food from its hosts and barely needs its own green tissue. Joel McNeal, Jennifer Kuehl, Jeffrey Boore and colleagues traced how its chloroplast genome has shrunk in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper follows one intron, a spacer inside a gene, and the helper enzyme, called a maturase, that cuts it out.

The intron and its helper were lost side by side across the dodder genus, a pattern the title calls parallel loss. A parasite that drops photosynthesis can afford to drop the tools that served it. The twin loss makes a clean case of genome streamlining, useful for reading how other parasites trim their genes.
plos-pone-0006082:
Stem cells from a human embryo and from a mouse's early lining look different, yet may obey the same rules. Ludovic Vallier, Thomas Touboul, Zhenzhi Chng and colleagues tested that in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper compares early cell fate decisions in human embryonic stem cells and mouse epiblast stem cells, the choices that start the making of body tissues.

The same signaling pathways control those first choices in both, the title reports. Shared rules mean mouse findings can guide human stem cell work with more confidence. That matters for regenerative medicine, where steering stem cells into the right tissue is the whole craft, and where human cells are costly to test directly.
plos-pone-0006182:
Parts of the genome are packed shut and kept silent in a form called heterochromatin. Elena Gracheva, Monica Dus, and Sarah Elgin studied two related proteins in the fruit fly Drosophila in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The proteins, VIG and Vig2, belong to the RISC complex, which is best known for silencing genes with small RNAs.

Their results support a role for both proteins in building the silent packed regions. That links the RNA silencing machinery to the wider packaging of the genome. Keeping the right regions shut protects gene control and genome stability. The fly work offers clues that may apply to many animals, since these systems are widely shared.
plos-pone-0006282:
Viruses and their hosts shape each other over evolutionary time, leaving matching marks in their genomes. Francisco Lobo and colleagues compared short nucleotide patterns in flaviviruses and their hosts in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The flavivirus family holds fast-changing RNA viruses infecting mammals, birds, ticks, and mosquitoes.

Common patterns of motif usage appear across the viruses and the animals they infect. Shared usage hints at long co-evolution between virus and host. Such fingerprints can reveal which hosts a virus is adapted to. They also help predict how readily a virus might jump species.
plos-pone-0006382:
Cells pull on the jelly around them, and the jelly's answer can carry information. Jessamine Winer, Shaina Oake, and Paul Janmey studied non-linear elasticity of extracellular matrices in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. On soft linear substrates, sparse tissue cells stay small and round; they spread as stiffness rises, up to a limit.

Because matrices stiffen as they are pulled, one cell's tug can be felt at a distance. Contractile cells can thus communicate local position and orientation through the material. That mechanical signalling complements chemical messages. It matters for wound healing and tissue engineering.
plos-pone-0006482:
Matteo Garofalo, Thierry Nieus, Paolo Massobrio, and colleagues compared methods for mapping brain cell networks in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied neuronal networks grown in vitro, recorded with micro-electrode arrays. Different statistical algorithms can estimate functional connectivity, the pattern of which cells influence which. The team first evaluated how these methods perform.

They applied information theory-based methods and cross-correlation to the same array data. Knowing which estimator to trust matters, since wrong maps mislead experiments. Their comparison guides neuroscientists who infer networks from spike recordings. It also shows where each method breaks down.
plos-pone-0006582:
Andrea Serino, Laura Annella, and Alessio Avenanti studied the space right around the body in PLOS ONE in 2009. An object moving toward the body needs fast work by the brain and a quick motor response. In monkeys, networks at the front of the brain merge senses to map this near space. The team asked how this peripersonal space works in humans, with a focus on its motor side.

Near space is the zone where we reach, grab, and defend. Its motor traits show the zone is mapped for action, not just for seeing. Knowing how it works informs robot design and rehab after brain injury. The study brings monkey brain findings into human terms.
plos-pone-0006682:
Zul Premji and co-authors ran a large malaria drug trial in Africa for PLOS ONE in 2009. The trial compared two combination treatments for uncomplicated falciparum malaria. One treatment joined chlorproguanil, dapsone, and artesunate in a fixed dose. It was designed to be affordable and simple for use in Africa. The other was the established pairing of artemether and lumefantrine.

Children and adolescents with malaria took part in the study. The trial was randomized, double-blind, and run as a phase three study. That design is the standard final test before wider use. Comparing a cheaper, simpler option against a proven one matters for clinics with tight budgets. The results inform which combination doctors in Africa can rely on.
plos-pone-0006782:
Eduardo J. M. Nascimento and his team linked one arm of the immune shield to bad dengue in PLOS ONE in 2009. The shield is the complement system. It can fire in three ways: the classic way, the lectin way, and the other way. Dengue can be mild, or it can turn grave. What tips a case toward grave is in part the immune reply itself.

The team checked complement parts in blood from dengue patients. The other pathway ran off track in step with how sick patients were. Off-track readings rose as the illness grew worse. Such checks might flag grave cases early. They also hint that calming this arm could help the sickest patients.
plos-pone-0006882:
Antonio Salas and colleagues read mitochondrial DNA to trace El Salvador's first settlers in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Mesoamerican isthmus channeled movement across the Americas. It shaped variability from Paleo-Indian times to recent history. Genetic information from Central America was scarce. El Salvador's population history was especially thin.

Mitochondrial DNA passes from mothers to children, preserving lineage history. The authors found echoes of first settlement in modern samples. They also found evidence of genetic continuity across time. Continuity means later upheavals did not erase the founding lineages. The results anchor El Salvador in the peopling story of the Americas.
plos-pone-0006982:
Robbert van der Most, Andrew Currie, Amanda Cleaver, and colleagues combined chemotherapy with immune attack in PLOS ONE in 2009. A cancer drug can both drain immune cells and stir them up. Earlier work showed chemotherapy can team well with immunotherapy. The question was how to turn that pairing into tumor control.

Using cyclophosphamide, the team made tumor cells more open to immune killing. The attack depended on a death signal called TRAIL and on CD8 T cells. Tumor growth was then suppressed. The result supports schedules that use chemo first to soften tumors for the immune system.
plos-pone-0007082:
Katiuska Molina-Luna, Ana Pekanovic, Sebastian Röhrich, and others studied dopamine and skill learning in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dopamine by mouth seemed to help people learn motor skills. It also seemed to aid recovery of movement after stroke. How it did so was not known.

The team showed that dopamine in the motor cortex is needed for skill learning. They tied it to the strengthening of links between nerve cells. Rats without that signal did not improve as they should. The work helps explain a drug effect doctors had only seen from outside. It may guide stroke care that pairs practice with dopamine support.
plos-pone-0007182:
Anita A. Kumar, Emmanuel Bhaskar, Ghanshyam Palamaner Subash Shantha, and colleagues reported a 2009 PLOS ONE study of muscle breakdown during severe infection. The condition is rhabdomyolysis, where damaged muscle releases its contents into the blood. It often appears alongside sepsis, a life-threatening response to infection.

The authors review cases of community-acquired bacterial sepsis in a South Indian cohort. They record which bacterial pathogens were involved and what factors were linked to muscle breakdown. Clinicians can use the pattern they describe when they watch sepsis patients closely for this serious complication.
plos-pone-0007282:
Adrien Ducret, Etienne Maisonneuve, Philippe Notareschi, and colleagues built a microscope system for watching bacteria live in 2009. Most time-lapse studies of bacterial growth and movement use thin nutrient agar pads. That setup limits researchers, because conditions cannot be changed dynamically during an experiment without disturbing the cells.

The authors present an automated fluidic system for microscopy. Fluids can be swapped while bacteria are observed in real time. Their PLOS ONE tool opens studies of growth, cell cycle progression, and motility under changing conditions. Microbiologists gain cleaner tests of how bacteria respond to sudden shifts.
plos-pone-0007382:
Sreya Chattopadhyay, Sankar Bhattacharyya, Baisakhi Saha, and colleagues studied how tumors weaken helper T cells in 2009. Many tumors show decreased cellular immunity and high levels of prostaglandin E2. That compound, called PGE2, is a known inhibitor of CD4 T cell activation and biases immune responses in tumors.

Its role in T helper cell survival remained unclear. The authors show tumor-shed PGE2 impairs a receptor signaling pathway needed for CD4 T cell survival. They also study regulation by theaflavins, compounds from tea. Their work links a tumor product to immune cell death.
plos-pone-0007482:
Eugénie Ansseau and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, a common inherited muscle-wasting disease. The condition is linked to a shrinking repeat array in the DNA of chromosome 4. Inside each repeat sits a gene called DUX4, normally silent in adult muscle. The team studied a related variant, DUX4c, and its behavior in patients' cells.

They found DUX4c is switched on in muscle from FSHD patients. Once active, it raises production of MYF5, a protein that guides muscle development. It also pushes muscle precursor cells to multiply. Those effects place DUX4c on the list of concrete players in the disease. A named molecular culprit is easier to target than a silent repeat. The work gives therapy research a specific gene to aim at.
plos-pone-0007582:
Julien Pothlichet and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on RIG-I, a sensor that detects invading viruses inside cells. RIG-I is pivotal: it spots many RNA and DNA viruses and raises the alarm. A defective sensor could strongly impair antiviral immunity. Yet little was known about natural human variants of the gene and their effects. The team scanned its single-letter polymorphisms for functional impact.

Two variants stood out with opposite effects. One strengthened the antiviral immune response, the other weakened it. The same virus can therefore meet different defenses in different people. Knowing which version a person carries may help explain uneven outcomes in infection. It also flags variants worth checking in patients with unusual viral illness. The study turns genetic trivia into working immunology.
plos-pone-0007682:
Bryan Moyer, Peter Hevezi, Na Gao and their co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on taste buds in primates. The team had earlier built a large list of genes active in taste buds, drawn from two tongue sites. That list held more than two thousand genes linked to taste.

Here they narrowed in on genes that make proteins spanning the cell membrane many times. Such proteins often act as receptors, the cell's sensors for the outside world. Mapping which ones sit in which taste cells helps explain flavor detection. It also shows what sets one taste cell apart from another.
plos-pone-0007782:
Shevin Jacob and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It reports how severe sepsis is treated in two Ugandan hospitals, and how patients fare. Sepsis, a runaway response to infection, likely drives much illness and death in low-income countries. Data from sub-Saharan Africa were very limited.

The study followed patients prospectively, watching care as it happened. Most of the patients were also infected with HIV-1. The team recorded treatments given and outcomes achieved. First-hand numbers like these show where simple improvements could save lives. They give hospitals and ministries a baseline to build on.
plos-pone-0007882:
Isabelle Ote and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It maps the jobs of one protein from the chickenpox virus, varicella-zoster virus. The protein, IE4, regulates how viral and cell genes are expressed. Its effects seem to act after genes are copied into RNA.

The exact mechanisms behind IE4 were not fully known. The authors show IE4 interacts with SR proteins, which help process RNA messages. IE4 also exports those messages through the TAP/NXF1 pathway. Tracing that export route explains how the virus gets its proteins made. It may reveal points where antiviral drugs could intervene.
plos-pone-0007982:
Jianhui Guo and colleagues hunted for faults in a growth-signal brake in colon tumors, for PLOS ONE in 2009. The brake gene is NKD1, the human kin of a fly gene found in wing studies. The signal it brakes, called Wnt, runs wild in most colon cancers.

Tumor samples held changed forms of NKD1, and tests showed those changes warp the Wnt signal chain. A faulty brake fits the picture of a signal left on too long. The work adds a new name to the list of gene faults behind a very common cancer.
plos-pone-0008082:
Lisa Meeks and colleagues charted a gene family that finishes plant messages in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzymes, poly(A) polymerases, add the tail that most messenger RNAs need to work. Plants carry small families of these genes rather than one.

Comparing the genes across several plants showed signs of past copying, with the copies taking on split duties. One copy may serve seeds, another leaves, and so on. That division of labor helps explain how plants fine-tune their messages for each tissue and stage of life. More copies mean more chances to tune that tuning.
plos-pone-0008182:
Motoko Mukai and colleagues studied song sparrows in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Male song sparrows defend territory all year long. Yet their hormone response to a fake rival differs by season. In spring, a staged intrusion raises luteinizing hormone. In autumn, the response looks quite different.

The team compared gene activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region that helps control hormones. They sampled birds in breeding and non-breeding seasons. The profiles show which genes shift as aggression changes with the season. That helps explain how the same behavior can run on different brain settings across the year.
plos-pone-0008282:
Andrew B. Nesterovitch and colleagues reported a mutation with striking effects in PLOS ONE in 2009. Angiotensin-converting enzyme, or ACE, breaks down many peptides in the body. It plays a key role in blood pressure control and vessel remodeling. Raised ACE levels may increase risk of heart, vessel, and lung diseases, including asthma. The mutation studied is named Trp1197Stop.

Carriers showed a dramatic increase in blood ACE levels. A single gene change thus has a large effect on this enzyme. Knowing such mutations helps explain why ACE varies between people. It may also refine risk estimates for related diseases.
plos-pone-0008382:
Ken Tsumiyama, Yumi Miyazaki, and Shunichi Shiozawa proposed a theory of autoimmunity in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cause of autoimmune disease remains unknown. The authors investigated it from a different angle, looking at defects in the immune system itself. In mice not prone to autoimmunity, repeated immunization caused systemic autoimmune disease. That paradox is the starting point for their theory.

They frame autoimmunity through self-organized criticality, a concept from physics. A system at criticality can tip into large responses from small triggers. This view could explain why autoimmunity erupts suddenly. It offers a fresh framework for research.
plos-pone-0008482:
James Dillon and co-authors present software called AutoEPG in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their tool analyzes electrical signals from a tiny worm, Caenorhabditis elegans. The worm's throat circuit is a model for studying nerve networks. A method called the electropharyngeogram records its electrical activity. Those records have shown how the feeding circuit works. But reading them by hand is slow and uneven.

AutoEPG processes the records in an automated, consistent way. It finds spikes and patterns that mark circuit states. Faster analysis lets labs run larger drug and gene screens. The tool serves work on feeding behavior and nerve control more broadly.
plos-pone-0008582:
Davida Smyth and co-authors map a resistant staph group in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The group is ST239-MRSA-III, a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus lineage. It is notable for its hybrid origin, mixing two parent strains. It has caused sustained hospital epidemics worldwide since the late nineteen seventies. The team study the population structure of this clonal group. They sample isolates from many places and times.

Their analysis shows how the hybrid lineage is structured and spread. Distinct subpopulations track with geography and hospital outbreaks. Knowing that structure helps track and control MRSA spread. It also shows how hybrid germs can become global hospital threats.
plos-pone-0008682:
Janina Hellmann, Sylvia Münter, Michael Wink, and coworkers tested two plant chemicals against malaria parasites. Their report came out in PLOS ONE in 2010. One chemical, EGCG, comes from green tea. The other, digitonin, comes from foxglove plants. They studied sporozoites, the form of the parasite that a mosquito injects.

Plant medicines often mix many active parts, and parts can help each other. The team measured survival and movement of sporozoites under each chemical alone. They then tried both together and looked for effects beyond simple adding up. Strong combined action would hint that plant mixtures deserve a closer look as drug leads.
plos-pone-0008782:
Marshall Hampton, Wayne Xu, Brian Kram, and colleagues read the gene tags active in flower nectar glands. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nectaries make the nectar that lures pollinators to flowers. Despite their key role, the molecular recipe for nectar stayed murky. Brassica rapa, a mustard relative, offered a workable study plant. Expressed sequence tags give a snapshot of active genes.

Sequencing those tags from nectaries revealed which genes were switched on. Candidates for sugar making and secretion stood out. The list gives pollination biology a molecular starting point. Breeders may someday tune nectar to support bees better.
plos-pone-0008882:
Silvia Cainarca, Simone Fenu, Cinzia Ferri, and colleagues built a glowing calcium meter into mouse stem cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drug screening usually forces test genes into altered cell lines at unnatural doses. Such forcing can distort the results badly. Embryonic stem cells offer a cleaner, more natural platform. A photoprotein that glows when calcium rises serves as the meter.

The sensor reported calcium movements in living cells on demand. It also worked inside living animals, not just dishes. Screening in a natural cell setting should cut false drug leads. The platform suits targets that altered cell lines handle poorly.
plos-pone-0008982:
Jonathan Touboul and Alain Destexhe asked whether a fashionable brain pattern could be a statistical mirage, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Brain researchers often report neuronal avalanches, bursts of activity of many sizes. The sizes follow a power law, which some take as proof the brain sits at a critical point. Criticality is said to keep the brain poised between order and chaos.

The pair showed that plain random dynamics can also produce power-law patterns. A straight line on a log plot, they argue, does not prove true criticality. Random noise, measured the usual way, can wear the same disguise. The paper urges more careful tests before claiming the brain is self-organised critical.
plos-pone-0009082:
Jonas Waldenström and co-authors dosed wild birds with the food-poisoning germ Campylobacter jejuni, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Campylobacter is a common cause of bacterial stomach illness in most of the world. It infects many kinds of animals without making them sick at all. Birds are suspected of spreading it into water and food supplies.

The team built a controlled infection experiment using captive wild birds. They tracked how long the birds shed the bacterium in their droppings. Shedding came in changing patterns rather than one steady stream. Knowing those patterns sharpens estimates of birds' true role in human infections.
plos-pone-0009182:
Junjie Luo and colleagues published this systems biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Its subject is chemotaxis, the way bacteria swim toward food and away from poisons. Bacteria sense chemicals around them and steer by switching between runs and tumbles. If scientists understood that steering circuit fully, they could reprogram it.

The authors reverse engineered the pathway using frequency domain analysis, a math tool borrowed from engineering. They fed the bacteria chemical signals that rose and fell at set rates. Watching how the cells responded at each rate revealed how the circuit is wired. The design rules they extracted could guide efforts to steer bacteria for useful tasks.
plos-pone-0009282:
Chiara Azzari and co-authors published this diagnostics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pneumococcal disease in children is usually typed by the Quellung reaction, the classic gold standard. That test needs living bacteria grown in culture. Many sick children's samples grow nothing, leaving doctors without a type.

The team compared two DNA-based tests on such culture-negative samples. Real-time PCR proved more sensitive than multiplex PCR for finding and typing the bacteria. A more sensitive test means more cases get a firm diagnosis. It also improves tracking of which pneumococcal types vaccines must cover.
plos-pone-0009382:
Takako Shima-Sano and co-authors published this HIV testing study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Testing pregnant women for HIV is essential to stop the virus reaching their babies. Screening tests, though, often return false positives in pregnancy. A frightened mother then waits for a confirmatory result that clears her.

The team designed a screening algorithm meant to cut that false alarm rate in Japan. Their stepwise approach sorts true infections from test noise faster. Fewer false positives mean less needless stress for expectant mothers. The work shows screening programs must be tuned to the population they serve.
plos-pone-0009482:
Song Liu examined how genes start their messages in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many genes have more than one start site, called a promoter. Using a different start can change when and where a gene is active. Unusual start choices have been tied to disease. Liu asked whether genes with more start sites behave in a distinct way.

Across the data, genes with richer sets of start sites varied more in activity between tissues. They were also more often linked to disease risk. That means start site choice is not a minor detail. It helps shape how flexible a gene is, and how prone it is to go wrong.
plos-pone-0009582:
Juan Wang and co-authors pinned down how a malaria drug works in PLOS ONE in 2010. Artemisinin is the most potent drug against malaria. For years, experts argued about how it kills the parasite. The team had built a yeast model that pointed to mitochondria, the cell's power units. Now they tested that claim directly on the malaria parasite.

The drug acted on the parasite's mitochondria and was switched on inside them. That local activation explains its killing power. Knowing the true target matters as drug resistant parasites spread. It helps chemists protect the drug's action and design successors if resistance wins.
plos-pone-0009682:
The left and right halves of the human brain do not split every job evenly. Gjurgjica Badzakova-Trajkov and colleagues studied that uneven split in PLOS ONE in 2010. They asked whether the two sides work as partners on shared tasks or run as separate, independent systems.

The team compared performance on tasks that lean on one side more than the other. Their results pointed to both patterns at once, with some processes backing each other up. Other processes ran on their own without help from the opposite side. The work helps explain how a two-sided brain organizes thought.
plos-pone-0009782:
Stacy M. Holzbauer and co-authors published an outbreak study in PLOS ONE in 2010. In October 2007, a cluster of nerve illness was found at a pork slaughter plant. Workers at the head table, where pig heads were processed, were hit hardest, and the illness was unlike known job-linked diseases.

Fifteen cases were found at the plant, with onsets from May 2004 to November 2007. Cases were far more likely than controls to have removed brains, or worked near that task. Brains were removed with blasts of air that made a fine spray. The three plants that used the method stopped, and no new cases came in 24 months of follow-up.
plos-pone-0009882:
Cooperation is fragile: cheats can wreck it, yet groups somehow keep it alive. Bo-Yu Zhang, Ross Cressman, and Yi Tao modeled one way groups hold cooperation steady. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The puzzle sits at the heart of game theory.

The mechanism is periodic impulses, regular jolts applied at set times. Pulses like these can push a wavering system back toward cooperation. Stability through impulses is a known control idea borrowed from engineering. The model asks whether the same trick works in social and biological groups.
plos-pone-0009982:
Embryonic cells move toward chemical signals as the body takes shape. Thomas Southgate and colleagues studied a protein that tunes that movement in mouse embryonic cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Chemotaxis is movement directed by a chemical trail. CXCR4 is the receptor that reads one such trail. Cell movement sculpts tissues long before birth. The team showed that 5T4, an oncofetal glycoprotein, tunes how CXCR4 drives that movement. Oncofetal means the protein appears in embryos and again in some cancers. Tuning movement matters in development and in cancer spread. The cells came from mouse embryos.
plos-pone-0010082:
Igor Kuznetsov, Marc Herant, and Micah Dembo analyzed moving cell machinery in a 2010 paper. Their subject was actin, the protein that forms a moving scaffold inside cells. They used a rat fibroblast line that moves fast. A method called FLAP let them tag actin and follow it after light bleaching.

Tagged actin traveled from mid-cell to the leading edge surprisingly fast in their recordings. The PLOS ONE study worked through what those transit times mean for the leading lamella, the cell's front sheet. Fast actin flow helps explain how crawling cells push forward.
plos-pone-0010182:
Lucília Miranda, Allen Collins, and Antonio Marques used DNA to untangle a jellyfish relative's life in 2010. Cnidarians, the group that includes jellyfish, have life cycles that vary widely and are hard to document. The newest proposed class, Staurozoa, was especially poorly known. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE that year.

Genetic data tied together two forms once thought to be separate animals. A tiny form called Microhydrula limopsicola proved to be an early life stage of an Antarctic stalked jellyfish. Matching stages by DNA can rewrite life histories that observation alone could not settle.
plos-pone-0010282:
The authors were Noa Madar-Balakirski, Catherine Tempel-Brami, Vyacheslav Kalchenko, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study attacked solid tumors in mice through their blood vessels. Vessel-targeting therapies delay tumor growth, yet none had shown long-term cures. The team used vascular targeted photodynamic therapy with a drug called Tookad, activated by light at the tumor site.

A single treatment, they report, permanently closed both feeding arteries and draining veins of tumors. Starved and unable to drain, such tumors may die outright. The result suggests vessel shutdown can be complete, not just a delay.
plos-pone-0010382:
Chia-Feng Liu, Keith Parker and Humphrey Yao studied how female germ cells survive in the mouse ovary for PLOS ONE in 2010. Egg precursor cells are essential: without them, no follicles form and the ovary fails. Two related signals, Wnt4 and beta-catenin, had been shown to protect these cells. Turning either off in the fetal ovary caused losses. The team traced how the protection works.

The pathway guards the cells by holding down another signal, activin beta B. Too much of that signal appears harmful to young germ cells. Balance between the two signals decides survival. Understanding that balance may inform research on infertility and ovary development. It also shows development often runs on brakes as much as accelerators.
plos-pone-0010482:
Andreas Hinz and colleagues solved the structure of a llama antibody that blocks HIV for PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV enters cells by latching its surface protein, gp120, onto CD4 and then a second receptor. Antibodies covering the CD4 site can stop entry cold. Llamas make unusual small antibodies; one, called D7, neutralizes HIV. The team crystallized D7 and worked out its shape.

They also mapped how D7 grips gp120 at the entry site. A tiny antibody that reaches a guarded spot is valuable for vaccine design. Vaccines try to teach our bodies to make such blockers. Seeing exactly how D7 fits shows what a vaccine should aim for. Small llama antibodies may also become drugs themselves.
plos-pone-0010582:
Cristina Becchio, Morena Mari, and Umberto Castiello studied visual perception in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their volunteers were children with autism spectrum disorders. The task involved judging pictures where shadows fell across a scene.

Shadows can mislead anyone, since a dark patch can be mistaken for a hole in the ground. The children handled shadow information in a way that differed from typical patterns. They seemed less likely to discount a shadow when judging what they saw. Small differences like these can reveal how autistic perception weighs parts of a scene, and they may inform better tests of visual processing.
plos-pone-0010682:
Nidhi Gupta and colleagues tested a drug that silences a cholesterol gene, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene makes PCSK9, a protein that removes cholesterol-clearing receptors from liver cells. With fewer receptors, harmful LDL cholesterol stays in the blood, raising heart risk.

Their drug was a locked nucleic acid, a tough synthetic strand that binds the gene's message. In cells and in mice it cut PCSK9 and raised receptor numbers. Blood cholesterol fell as a result. Work like this paved the way for a whole class of gene-silencing heart drugs that followed in later years.
plos-pone-0010782:
Jeff Shrager simulated scientific publishing under different review rules, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Peer review before publication is science's main quality gate. The internet made looser and tighter gates both possible, and debate about them runs hot. Real journals cannot be experimented on lightly, so a simulation offers a safer test bed.

Virtual scientists in the model made discoveries, wrote them up, and passed review gates of varying strictness. Very loose gates flooded the record with errors. Very strict gates slowed true findings and wasted reviewer effort. Middle settings performed best overall. The model cannot settle the debate, but it gives reformers numbers instead of slogans.
plos-pone-0010882:
Andreas Oberbach, Nadine Schlichting, Matthias Blüher and co-authors published this bladder study in PLOS ONE in 2010. People with type 2 diabetes get urinary tract infections more often, for reasons that are not fully explained. The authors suspected that high levels of free fatty acids, common in obesity, might stir inflammatory signals in the bladder wall itself.

They grew human bladder smooth muscle cells taken from surgical biopsies and exposed them to palmitate, a common fatty acid, or to a bacterial toxin. Both triggers raised production and release of IL-6 and MCP-1, two chemical messengers that draw immune cells and drive inflammation. Oberbach and colleagues thus link a diabetes-related fat signal to an inflamed bladder lining. That connection may help explain why infections take hold so readily in diabetic patients.
plos-pone-0010982:
Pika Miklavc, Manfred Frick, Oliver Wittekindt and co-authors published this lung cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Calcium is essential for the moment a secretory vesicle fuses with the cell surface and releases its cargo. What calcium does after fusion was undescribed, so the team watched single vesicles in rat lung cells that secrete surfactant, the substance that keeps air sacs open.

They combined light-scattering and dye signals that mark pore opening with calcium-sensitive imaging. Most fusion events, they found, trigger local calcium entry right at the fusion site. This happens during the slow release phase. Miklavc and colleagues call this a postfusion active zone of elevated calcium. Discovering a signal after the main event rewrites the timetable of secretion, and may matter for surfactant release in newborn and adult lung disease.
plos-pone-0011082:
Dickson, Wahl, Fernandes and colleagues addressed a methods problem in PLOS ONE in 2010. Scientists line up protein sequences to compare them, but those line ups can contain silent errors. Worse, there was no check that did not depend on the same ideas used to build the line up.

The team used paired changes inside a single protein as an independent test. When two spots in a protein tend to change together, that pattern can reveal where a line up has gone wrong. Their approach offers a fresh quality check for a basic tool in biology. Stronger checks mean more trust in results built on sequence data.
plos-pone-0011182:
Roa, Li, Peled and colleagues examined antibody making cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. To build better antibodies, certain immune cells mutate their own antibody genes on purpose. An enzyme starts that process by damaging DNA, and repair proteins then decide how the damage is handled.

A repair pair studied here did two jobs at once. It fixed some damage cleanly, without error, and it promoted deliberate mutation at other sites. That dual role fine tunes the balance between safety and variety in antibodies. Understanding it deepens basic immunology and may inform work on immune disorders.
plos-pone-0011282:
Brauner, Bashamboo, Rouget and colleagues analyzed eleven young patients in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ovarian cysts before puberty are uncommon and can trigger signs of early puberty. The team carried out clinical, biological and genetic analysis of isolated cysts in eleven girls to understand their cause.

Detailed cases help doctors tell harmless cysts from those needing surgery or hormone care. Families facing a rare diagnosis need clear answers most of all. The genetic side of the study checks whether inherited factors explain why cysts arise so early. The report guides children's hormone care with evidence from careful case work.
plos-pone-0011382:
Jarod Swant and co-authors measured in 2010 how methamphetamine rewires signaling in the mouse hippocampus, a brain region central to memory. The drug is known to harm learning in users, but the exact electrical changes behind that harm needed pinning down. The team worked with thin slices of mouse brain kept alive in the lab.

In the slices, the drug weakened the strengthening of connections that underlies learning, while raising the background level of signaling between cells. Together, those changes leave the circuit noisy yet poor at recording new information. The paired result helps explain the memory problems seen in people who abuse the drug. It also gives addiction researchers defined circuit changes to target when they test whether the damage can be reversed.
plos-pone-0011482:
Rainer Stollhoff and co-authors timed in 2010 how the brain compensates in people born unable to recognize faces. Congenital prosopagnosia leaves face recognition severely impaired from birth, yet affected people manage social life by leaning on voice, hair, and gait. The team measured the earliest moments of face processing to catch the workaround as it starts.

Their measures showed an early time course of compensatory processing that differs from typical face processing from the first fractions of a second. The brain does not simply run the normal system more weakly; it reroutes early. Charting that rerouting in real time shows the brain's capacity to build an alternate path around a missing function. It may also guide training that strengthens the compensatory route on purpose, instead of drilling the broken one.
plos-pone-0011582:
Kaspar Delhey and colleagues studied how bird feather colour shifts with the seasons, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Feather colour helps birds signal quality to mates and rivals. Birds make colour in three main ways: through feather structure, through dark melanin pigments, and through carotenoids that come from food.

The authors tracked all three colour types across seasons to see which ones fade or change most after moulting. Their comparison shows the three systems do not age in the same way. That helps explain why a bird that looks bright in spring may look dull months later, even without growing new feathers.
plos-pone-0011682:
Anna Kuta and co-authors catalogued parts of the mouse cell's freight machinery, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells haul organelles, vesicles and RNA cargoes along inner tracks to keep working. The dynein complex is a key motor for that transport, and its intermediate chains help decide what gets carried and where.

The authors identified new versions of these chains produced by alternative splicing, and charted where each version appears across mouse tissues. The fuller parts list refines the blueprint of the transport system. It also gives researchers precise targets for studying transport failures in disease.
plos-pone-0011782:
Yuji Yoshiko and co-authors watched bone cells switch sides in a rat cell culture, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bone-building cells and fat-storing cells come from kin lines, and grasping how a cell picks one fate over the other matters for growth and for disease. Shifts in that pick change bone mass and body fat alike.

The team found a subset of bone cells with high levels of the fat-driving factor PPAR gamma left their bone fate and became fat cells. The swap marks the point where a cell's path tips from bone toward fat. Moving that balance could one day matter for weak-bone disease.
plos-pone-0011882:
Sandrine Adiba, Clément Nizak, and Minus van Baalen argued in 2010 that many bacterial weapons may be accidents of a different struggle. For many disease bacteria, humans are a dead end they rarely spread from, so it is odd that they carry such harmful traits. The coincidental evolution idea holds that these traits first helped against predators that graze on bacteria.

Under that view, defenses built to survive being eaten by amoeba-like hunters later proved harmful inside human tissue. The study weighs this case for how virulence factors arise. If the weapons were honed elsewhere, then the environments bacteria live in outside the body become part of the story of human disease.
plos-pone-0011982:
Sophie Laget and co-workers reported in 2010 a surprise about two human proteins named for a domain they may not use as expected. MBD5 and MBD6 carry a methyl-binding domain, a part that in related proteins reads methylated DNA and helps silence genes. The pair were otherwise almost uncharacterized.

The team found that both proteins associate with heterochromatin, the tightly packed silent DNA, yet do not bind methylated DNA. That combination breaks the family rule and demands another explanation for what they do there. Proteins sitting on silent regions without reading the usual mark may guard those regions in a different way, an open question for gene regulation research.
plos-pone-0012082:
Dalila Martínez and co-workers built in 2010 a simple rule to sort tuberculosis patients by their risk of drug-resistant disease. Multidrug-resistant TB resists at least isoniazid and rifampin, the two best TB drugs, and confirming it takes time and lab capacity many clinics lack. A clinical prediction rule was developed and internally validated among adult patients with pulmonary TB.

The rule stratifies patients so that those likeliest to carry resistant disease get tested and treated accordingly first. In settings where drug-susceptibility testing cannot cover everyone, ranking risk is not a shortcut but a necessity. Used well, the rule speeds the right treatment to the patients whose wrong treatment would do the most harm.
plos-pone-0012282:
Diana Spitznagel, John O'Rourke, Neal Leddy, and co-authors characterized an odd motor protein in the sleeping sickness parasite, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Myosins are molecular motors that haul cargo and shape cells, and most creatures own dozens. African trypanosomes make do with only two candidate myosins, which turns the parasite into a clean test bed for what each motor does.

Their unusual class I myosin proved to work in the traffic of vesicles, the cell's shipping bubbles. Parasite plumbing that differs from ours is a potential drug target, since blocking it harms the parasite alone. Basic studies of this kind stock the list of targets that drug hunters draw on.
plos-pone-0012382:
Ömer Saraç, Volkan Atalay and Rengul Cetin-Atalay built a tool that predicts what a protein does, described in PLOS ONE in 2010. Assigning jobs to proteins is a core task in biology, and many computer methods exist, each using clues such as shape, sequence, or known motifs. No single method wins on all proteins, so the team combined several classifiers into one system called GOPred.

GOPred votes among its combined methods to assign Gene Ontology terms, the standard labels for protein jobs. Pooling methods beat single ones on their tests. The tool helps labs that sequence new proteins daily and need a fast, reliable first guess at function before bench work begins.
plos-pone-0012482:
Felix Schaller, Antonio Fernandes, Christine Hodler and colleagues compared Y chromosomes in chimpanzees and bonobos, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The male-only Y region differs dramatically even between humans and chimps, and it evolves fast. Chimps mate in multi-male groups with intense sperm competition, while bonobos follow different social rules, so the two species test whether mating systems shape the Y.

The team found Y variation that tracks those mating differences. A fast-changing Y that mirrors mating strategy supports the idea that sexual competition drives its evolution. The comparison also cautions against treating the human Y as a general primate pattern.
plos-pone-0012582:
Lu Lin, Houhui Song, Yuetong Ji and fellow researchers used sound waves to move DNA into tough bacteria, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their targets were heat-loving, thick-walled bacteria that live without air. Such germs shrug off the usual ways of adding new genes, both the chemical baths and the electric shocks labs rely on. Without gene transfer, no one can improve these strains for making fuels or chemicals.

Brief bursts of ultrasound opened the way, and the bacteria took up the new DNA. One workable method can unlock a whole class of microbes for the biofuels field. Heat-loving strains are prized for brewing, since hot tanks resist spoilage and react fast, so the gain is more than a lab trick.
plos-pone-0012682:
Gong, Bourhis, Chiu and co-authors tested how blocking antibodies treat different Wnt signals differently. Wnt signals guide growth through a receptor pair, and a partner called LRP6 is needed to pass the message. Their 2010 study used antibodies against LRP6 to probe the system.

Some antibodies shut signalling down while others made it stronger, and the effect depended on which Wnt form was present. That split behaviour matters for drug design, since Wnt faults drive cancers and bone disease. A blocker for one signal may need to spare the rest.
plos-pone-0012782:
Maan, Maan, Nomikou and co-authors built lab tests that can name all seven types of a livestock virus. Epizootic haemorrhagic disease virus attacks wild deer and can cause a bluetongue-like illness in cattle. Their 2010 RT-PCR assays read the virus's RNA and sort each sample by serotype, the version that immune defences see.

They used the tests on strains from the Mediterranean region and North America. Fast, exact typing lets vets track which versions are moving where during an outbreak. That tracking guides vaccine choice and animal movement rules.
plos-pone-0332982:
Lidane Noronha, Brian P. Lazzaro, and Patrick M. O'Grady study a fruit fly that breeds only in rotting saguaro cactus in the Sonoran Desert. What the fly's food provides may decide how many young survive. Their 2026 study raises the flies on two lab diets, with and without cactus-derived additions, and tracks survival stage by stage.

Cactus additions often hurt survival from egg to the resting stage, yet helped survival from that stage to adult. The net effect flipped with the base diet: additions hurt on banana food but helped on cornmeal food. Feeding amounts did not explain the gaps. The work shows that judging a specialist's diet takes watching each life stage, not just the final count.
plos-pone-0337882:
Annemieke Boendermaker, Gideon Latten, Jelle Prins, Kiki Lombarts, and Paul Brand published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a cross-sectional survey of emergency physicians in the Netherlands. Four things are measured together: how engaged the doctors feel, whether they burn out, whether they plan to leave, and what the workforce guidelines say.

Emergency medicine loses experienced doctors when exhaustion outweighs engagement, the energy and pride in the work. Linking official workforce guidelines to those feelings tests whether staffing rules protect or strain doctors. Hospital leaders and physician associations in the Netherlands and beyond can use this evidence in workforce planning.
plos-pone-0337982:
Hassan M Aljohani and colleagues tackle a statistical estimation problem: pinning down the coefficient of variation, a unit-free measure of spread, for lifetime data that follows a weighted exponential distribution. Their 2026 study works under a flexible censoring scheme that lets life-testing experiments end early or adapt mid-course, saving time and test units.

They build estimators two ways, a classical maximum likelihood route with bootstrap confidence intervals and a Bayesian route using computer sampling with informative prior beliefs. A worked simulated example and a large Monte Carlo study compare the approaches, and the Bayesian estimators with good priors come out more precise. Reliability engineers use such estimates to judge whether a product's lifetime is consistent enough to trust.
plos-pone-0338282:
Helen Hynes and colleagues mapped what is known about how doctors trained abroad experience the clinical skills exams required to practise or specialise in a new country. These international graduates form a large share of many health workforces and often score lower, for reasons mixing personal, social, and institutional forces. The 2026 scoping review gathered forty-four publications covering more than seven thousand doctors from fifty-four countries.

Studies clustered in Britain, Australia, and Canada. Influences on exam experience fell into personal factors, social factors such as bias and belonging, and systemic factors in how assessments are designed. Almost nothing is known about age, time away from practice, or weaker language skills. The authors press for fairer, better-supported assessment routes.
plos-pone-0342982:
Badriyeh Karami and colleagues surveyed older adults during the COVID pandemic. Three hundred and forty one adults took part. All were over sixty years old. Forms measured social support and resilience. Forms also measured life quality tied to health. A structural model placed resilience in the middle. It carried part of the support effect.

More support linked with higher resilience scores. Support also linked with better life quality directly. About half the total gain ran through resilience. Supported elders coped better each day. Coping then lifted daily health and function. Future crisis plans should teach resilience skills. Support networks alone may not be enough.
plos-pone-0343182:
Songsen Su and Yanfang Lin study a rare illness in which blood vessels become inflamed and swollen. People with the illness often have asthma and high levels of a white blood cell type called eosinophils. In their 2026 paper, the authors look for a pattern of small chemicals in blood that could help doctors tell this illness apart from plain asthma.

Blood samples came from ten patients with the illness, ten with asthma, and ten healthy adults. Lab tests found hundreds of chemicals at changed levels, grouped in a few body pathways. A small set of these chemicals separated the illness from health well in tests. The pattern could one day support a blood test, though the group studied was very small.
plos-pone-0343482:
Sarah Griffiths led a team of five authors studying dementia care planning in primary care, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Care plans for people with dementia should be personal, built around the person's own goals. In busy primary care, appointments are short and planning talks can feel rushed. The team captured how those conversations are perceived by those involved.

Griffiths's study names three needs in its findings: time, talk, and teamwork. Planning works when staff have minutes to listen, words that fit the family, and roles that mesh. Those are cheap ingredients, but they are often the first cut under pressure. The study gives practices a concrete picture of what good planning conversations require.
plos-pone-0344082:
Song, Zhou, and Li studied cell cleanup failure in diabetic nerve damage in a 2026 paper. Using cell and animal models, they showed that long-term high blood sugar slows the cleanup system that recycles worn cell parts. Marker patterns confirmed stalled cleanup, tied to one growth signal switching on and one energy signal switching off.

Gene analysis flagged three master switches of the cleanup program as disturbed. Cleanup failure and fat handling also worsened each other in a loop, deepening nerve cell harm. Breaking that loop could offer a new treatment angle for a painful complication that current care only partly controls.
plos-pone-0345782:
Olivia Chivers and colleagues interviewed twenty-five older adults living in the community about the first, subtle signs that getting around is changing. Mobility here means everything from walking to driving and buses, and its early decline quietly shrinks daily life. Through themed analysis of the conversations, four shared threads emerged about how people notice and respond to the shift.

Everyday tasks were described as costing more energy than they used to. People spoke of watching risks more carefully, of a use-it-or-lose-it determination to keep moving, and of measuring themselves against neighbours and friends. The authors say support should arrive at this early stage, tackling expectations about ageing and keeping people engaged in activities they value. All this should happen long before a fall or a surrendered licence forces the issue.
plos-pone-0346682:
Rafayet Rahman Ridoy and co-workers study who gets a skilled attendant at childbirth in Bangladesh and why poorer families miss out. Their 2026 study layers classic statistics, an inequality breakdown, and ten machine learning models over survey data, then explains the winning model's reasoning.

Wealth, schooling, and proper pregnancy checkups from qualified providers predicted skilled attendance most strongly. Dhaka and Khulna regions and cities ran ahead of rural areas. Usage tilted heavily toward richer households, with checkups, wealth, and schooling driving most of that tilt. A neural network predicted attendance best. Closing the gap, the authors say, means funding checkups and schooling where mothers are poorest.
plos-pone-0347282:
Tengyao Niu and co-authors used computer toxicology to ask if sweeteners might harm bones, joints, discs, and muscle. Sweeteners get most study for weight and blood sugar. Their muscle and bone effects were near blank. Their 2026 study wove web analysis, docking, and motion runs across four ills, from worn discs to thin bones.

The screen met on thirty-five core protein targets, bunched in swelling, metabolism, and linked signal paths. Two plant sweeteners showed the strongest grip on the targets. Runs confirmed firm grip with three named proteins. Niu and colleagues stress the work is a computer view that yields targets for lab tests, not proof of harm at food-level doses.
plos-pone-0347582:
Linda Visser, Jan-Henning Ehm, and Janin Brandenburg used a huge study of US youth. It held near twelve thousand kids, aged nine or ten at the start. The team tracked three things over four waves: school marks, inner pain such as fear and low mood, and signs of ADHD. They asked how the three move each other with time.

Marks and inner pain were linked, but each did not drive the next wave of the other. ADHD signs tied to both marks and pain. Low mood, in a twist, came before falls in ADHD signs. The team says ADHD does not explain the marks and pain link. Spot low mood early, they urge.
plos-pone-0347682:
Abeer A. Mabrouk, Sameh H. Ismail, Ahmed G. Soliman, and Mervat M. Omran compared silver, gold, and mixed metal nanoparticles as wound treatments in rats. Metal particles are meant to deliver the healing punch of metal ions with fewer side effects. Thirty-two rats with standard cut wounds received daily treatment for three weeks with one formulation, a standard antibiotic cream, or nothing.

Both silver and gold formulations shrank wounds effectively and sped repair, boosting new blood vessel growth and collagen deposition, the scaffolding of healed skin. Tissue chemistry and microscopy backed the improvement, and computer modelling explored how the particles interact with inflammation enzymes. The authors rate the nanoformulations as genuinely effective wound healers.
plos-pone-0347782:
Inhye Seo and co-workers build a scoring system to guide how cities care for the carbon stored in parks and green spaces. Trees and soils hold carbon, but each city patch differs in how much it holds and how much more it could take up. Their 2026 paper combines fine-scale maps of plant carbon, soil carbon, and yearly uptake into one index.

A case study in Suwon, South Korea, showed sharp differences even inside a single green patch. Edge zones scored far lower than interiors, marking spots where care would help most. The method then points to fixes matched to each weak spot, such as keeping leaf litter, loosening packed soil, or planting in layers. City crews gain a map for spending effort where it counts.
plos-pone-0347882:
Quynh Nga Duong and Nguyen Thuy Khue Tran modelled how the shadow economy, all the work and trade hidden from tax and regulation, shapes growth in emerging economies. Rather than study informality alone, they let it interact with taxes, institutions, foreign investment, trade openness, government size, and population growth inside one Bayesian model that handles uncertain, limited data gracefully.

Across their panel of developing countries, a bigger shadow economy dragged down income per person. Strong institutions, healthy foreign investment, and open trade blunted the damage, while fast population growth and bloated government consumption made it worse. The authors argue that the harm of informality is not fixed: tidy institutions and sensible fiscal policy can shrink both the shadow and its cost.
plos-pone-0348182:
Vi T Le and Jennifer A Bailey led a study of parents in Washington State. Legal shops for cannabis opened there in 2014. The team asked if living near more shops shifts parents' own use and views. They surveyed four hundred seventy-one parents in 2015, 2016, and 2017. They counted shops within a short drive of each home. They also asked parents how many shops they felt were near.

Parents in shop-dense areas used cannabis more. They found parent use more okay and saw it as less habit-forming. Over time, a rise in shops near a home tracked a rise in how okay use felt. The team says shop spread may set new norms for parents.
plos-pone-0348282:
Jianchun Wei and co-workers track falling platelet counts in emergency patients with sepsis and test how well the fall predicts death within a month. Platelets help blood clot and fight infection, and their slide is a known danger sign. Their 2026 study reviews more than three hundred sixty sepsis cases at one Beijing hospital, scoring the lowest count, the size of the drop, and when it happened.

Patients who died bottomed out far lower and dropped much further than survivors. Risk rose step by step with deeper and bigger drops. Timing mattered too: drops landing in the middle or late phase carried heavy risk, while early ones did not. Watching the whole platelet path, not a single reading, sharpens judgment at the bedside.
plos-pone-0348582:
Shangjun Piao and Jiantao Guo modelled how seafood buyers should run purchasing auctions when sellers may lie about where the fish was caught. Origin fraud distorts prices and punishes honest suppliers, and penalties alone deter weakly. The authors derived the outcomes of two auction designs, one judged on price only and one scoring quality and origin claims alongside price. Then they varied how much fraud and how much buyers care about true origin.

Counter to intuition, the plain price auction often served the buyer better, and its edge grew when buyers prized origin most and when detection technology existed alongside heavy fraud. Under some conditions, knowingly buying from cheap, low-value origins even suited the buyer. The authors argue auction design itself is a fraud-fighting tool, and that scoring systems can backfire by rewarding polished lies.
plos-pone-0348682:
Bayley Levy and co-workers set out a plan to review how research teams use implementation science frameworks in children's rehabilitation. Such frameworks help proven therapies actually reach clinics, yet their use in this field has never been mapped. Their 2026 protocol describes a scoping review across nine databases, covering English studies since two thousand six.

Two reviewers will screen and extract data independently, settling clashes by discussion or a third vote. Counts will summarize where and how frameworks were used, and text analysis will sort the purposes they served. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet. The finished map should show which frameworks suit the teamwork-heavy world of pediatric rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0348782:
Tika B Adhikari, Frank J Louws, and co-authors sequenced the genomes of fifty strains of a fungus that has lately hammered strawberry crops with leaf spots and rots. Little genomic information existed for this emerging pathogen group. Their 2026 study, sampling major strawberry regions in North Carolina, mapped the strains' family relationships, their arsenals of plant-attacking proteins, and mutations tied to fungicide resistance.

Strains split into two lineages of one species plus a third distinct group. Each genome carried hundreds of enzymes for digesting plant walls and around ninety predicted effector proteins used to manipulate hosts. Resistance mutations were widespread for two fungicide classes, including one that defeats a common spray, while two other classes showed none. The authors say the catalogue can guide resistance-aware disease control.
plos-pone-0348882:
Raymond Vera, Anamaria Berea, and William G Kennedy built a computer simulation of a crewed lunar base to explore how astronaut teamwork and psychology might decide the fate of long Moon missions. NASA's Artemis program aims at a permanent lunar presence, where social friction cannot be escaped by coming home. Their 2026 model gives each simulated astronaut cognitive skills, emotional states, and personality traits, drawing on research from Antarctic stations and past spaceflight.

Running tens of thousands of simulated missions, the model varies outside shocks and inside group dynamics to find which factors tip a base toward sustainability or catastrophe. Settings cover a lunar gateway station and a south pole surface base. The authors offer the model as a benchmark planning tool for mission designers who must plan for people, not just hardware.
plos-pone-0349282:
Fatemeh Shakeri and four colleagues tested a new way to kill staph germs on living tissue, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Staphylococcus aureus infects wounds and resists many antibiotics. Cold atmospheric plasma, a stream of energized gas that stays near room temperature, can kill germs without heat.

Shakeri's team applied the plasma to staph colonies growing on living animal tissue and measured the effect. The test asks whether plasma can clear germs while sparing the tissue beneath. If it holds up, wound care could gain a tool that works where antibiotics fail. Plasma devices are already used in some clinics, so evidence on living tissue is a key step toward wider use.
plos-pone-0349582:
Jarosław Herbert and co-authors strapped motion sensors to more than five hundred Polish children aged five and six to compare how active they are at kindergarten and at home. Parents also reported family details such as education and income. Objective measurement matters here, since adults often guess wrong about how much young children actually move through the day.

Children gathered more gentle movement at kindergarten, but their harder, health-building activity ran higher at home, and daily step counts were higher at home too. Boys out-moved girls in both settings. Surprisingly, children from less advantaged families often moved more, not less. The authors say the home environment deserves as much attention as the classroom when adults try to keep young children active.
plos-pone-0349682:
Georgios Nalbantis and co-authors asked whether star employees help an organization more as deep specialists or as versatile generalists, and what happens when a star switches roles. They built a game-theory model to generate predictions, then tested them on professional basketball data, where stars and roles are easy to track. Their 2026 study also allowed stars to move between roles over time rather than fixing them in place.

Teams with generalist stars outperformed teams with specialist stars, matching the model. Moving a generalist into a specialist role always hurt performance, while moving a specialist toward a generalist role could help. The pattern held most clearly for teams built around a single star rather than several. The authors suggest managers should think twice before narrowing a star's remit.
plos-pone-0349782:
Napat Jantaraprasit and colleagues built a forecasting chain for oil palm harvests in Surat Thani, Thailand. Good forecasts guide farm work and long term climate planning, yet coarse weather grids and crop model bias blur accuracy. Their chain sharpens weather data to fine local scale, feeds a crop simulator, then lets a learning model mop up leftover errors.

The hybrid cut forecast error by more than half versus the simulator alone. Seasonal outlooks made with sharpened data matched those made with past observed weather, giving useful forecasts up to eight months ahead. Century scale outlooks hint at steady yields early on, a modest mid century dip, and later change. Growers gain lead time to plan labour, milling, and planting.
plos-pone-0349882:
Eranga Pawani Witharana and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies the plastome, the DNA of the chloroplast, in the plant subfamily Aurantioideae. From plastome evidence the authors also build a classification of Citrus, the genus of oranges, lemons, and their kin.

Plastome evolution tracks how this DNA changed as the group diversified, giving a family history written in genes. Citrus classification has long been tangled by hybridization, so a DNA-based scheme offers firmer ground. Botanists and citrus breeders both use such classifications, breeders because knowing true parentage guides new variety development.
plos-pone-0350182:
Jiangxue Tian, Handong Li, and Shuran Lv built a fire risk forecasting system for Beijing's urban villages in 2026. These dense settlements mix homes and workshops with weak infrastructure, making fire both likely and deadly.

Their model pairs a long memory neural network with an improved swarm search that tunes it, plus step by step updating so it learns from fresh incidents without full retraining. Fed with real fire records from fifty-five villages, it cut forecast error sharply against a plain network. City teams could use such forecasts to aim inspections and crews at the blocks most likely to burn next.
plos-pone-0350282:
Samuel Anyaso-Samuel and Mark Ramos asked American adults how well they think they understand statistics, using a nationally representative survey. Numbers steer choices about health, money, and public policy, yet many people meet terms like p-value with a blank stare. The authors used the survey to measure confidence and to ask whether people would use statistics more if the ideas were clearer.

About six in ten adults admitted they had little or no idea what statistics means. Even so, nine in ten said they would base decisions on reported statistics at least sometimes if they understood them better. Schooling raised confidence, while older generations rated themselves lower. People who felt more literate were also more willing to act on numbers. The gap points to a teaching problem, not a lack of interest.
plos-pone-0350382:
