Chengfu Zhang and co-authors studied how rocks that generate oil and gas behave under different salt conditions in China's Dongpu Depression in 2026 work. Salt levels in the ancient lakes where the rocks formed vary sharply across the basin.

Twenty rock samples were analysed chemically, and three went through sealed tube heating experiments to extract generation rates. Basin modelling then combined those rates with the area's heat history. Salty environment rocks yielded the most hydrocarbons, fresh water rocks the least. Zones passing a set generation threshold were flagged as prime exploration targets. Salt, it turns out, is a friend to oil formation here.
plos-pone-0350782:
Jutamas Shaughnessy and colleagues built a compound that turns the gonorrhea germ's own camouflage against it. Their 2026 study starts from the germ's trick. It grabs human proteins that block the immune system, and hides behind them. The team fused the grabbing part of one blocker to an antibody tail. The tail was reshaped so six copies bunch up, boosting its grip.

The bunched compound killed gonorrhea germs in the dish. It was hundreds of times stronger than its single-copy earlier version. It also helped immune cells engulf the germs. Given into the vagina daily, it cut infections short in specially bred mice. Gonorrhea now resists nearly every drug, and no vaccine exists. A smear-on immune weapon is a truly new path, still at proof-of-concept stage.
plos-pone-0350882:
Tadanao Hiroki led a team of eight authors on this 2026 treatment study for chronic neck pain from tight, tender muscle tissue. Thirteen adults received an ultrasound-guided injection of salt water into the fascia around a neck artery, meant to loosen the tissue. Pain at rest and in motion, disability, and blood flow were checked before and after.

Movement pain dropped within fifteen minutes and stayed lower a week later. The procedure proved quick and safe in this small group. With no comparison group, Hiroki labels the results an early signal that larger controlled trials should test.
plos-pone-0350982:
Yvette Neema Ufoy Mungu and colleagues screened women in Kisangani, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for viruses linked to cervical cancer. The area also carries high rates of the sickle cell trait. More than seven hundred women gave cervical samples and answered health and life history questions, with lab tests for virus types and cell change.

Just over one quarter carried a high risk virus type. Three types led the list, and gene reading turned up two new variants. Major cell changes linked with factors the team modelled from survey and lab data together. In a region where cervical cancer leads gynaecology cancers, local virus maps help target vaccines and screening where they will count most.
plos-pone-0351082:
Van Thuy Tran and Huu Loc Nguyen ran lab tests on what makes bolt tightening fall short or overshoot. When a nut is tightened, only part of the turning force becomes clamping force. That share shifts with friction, surface roughness, and how hard the metal is. Getting it wrong can loosen joints or damage parts.

A curved model captured how the three factors interact. The team then searched for settings that keep the clamping share inside a safe band with very high certainty, using random trials plus an evolution style search. Their reliability based search beat plain best fit methods. Touchy factor checks showed which inputs matter most, giving builders a firmer way to set torque.
plos-pone-0351782:
Mark G Anderson led a team of five authors designing a freshwater refuge network, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. As the climate shifts, fish and other freshwater species must move to cooler or wetter refuges, but dams and dry reaches block them. The team mapped a network of waters that could stay livable and stay connected.

Anderson's blueprint shows conservation staff which streams and lakes to link and protect so species can shift as conditions change. Planning connections now is cheaper than rescue later. Freshwater life is declining faster than life on land or in the sea, yet it gets less attention. A ready map of resilient, connected waters gives funders and agencies a place to start.
plos-pone-0351882:
Emily Jakob and colleagues present a protocol for a scoping review on getting people with multiple sclerosis to move more. Exercise programs do help this group on average, but their effects swing widely from study to study. The reviewers suspect the missing piece is moderation: a program feature may help one subgroup and do little for another, depending on symptoms, setting, or support.

The planned review will search eight databases plus reference lists and citing papers, screening studies that report physical activity in people with the disease. Charts will lay out which populations and methods dominate, and a tree display will gather every reported moderation finding. As a protocol it contains no results. Its aim is practical: future programs should be matched to the people they actually help.
plos-pone-0352182:
Nicole Cranston and four colleagues present a research protocol, published in 2026, for a planned review of how young horses are weaned. Separating a foal from its mother is among the most stressful events in a young horse's life. Yet breeders still lack clear guidance on which methods cause the least harm.

The team plans to search six databases plus grey literature, screen studies with two independent reviewers, and compare weaning methods through pairwise and network analysis. Outcomes will cover body changes and behaviour, graded for bias and confidence. Because no results exist yet, the value lies in the careful plan itself, which aims to give horse owners evidence-based advice for gentler weaning.
plos-pone-0352282:
Shenzhen Ding and six colleagues coach platoons of connected vehicles through traffic lights. Their 2026 simulation study addresses jammed urban intersections. It assumes vehicles that talk to each other and to the lights. Groups of them, platoons, are recognised first. Six passage scenarios follow from whether a platoon will be blocked at the signal. Three guidance styles answer them: speed up, slow down, or split the platoon. A commercial traffic simulator staged the test junction.

Against unguided traffic, guidance cut everything that wastes time and fuel. Fuel consumption fell sharply. Delays shrank from over nine seconds to under four. Stops nearly vanished. Benefits grew clearer as the share of connected vehicles approached seventy percent. Below that share, mixed traffic dilutes the choreography. City engineers weighing smart-intersection investment gain a concrete threshold story: platoon guidance pays, but only once enough communicating cars fill the road.
plos-pone-0352382:
Kyoung Ae Kong studied where South Korean adults actually get their physical activity. National survey data covered thirty-two thousand adults. Activity was split into three domains: leisure, transport, and work. Each person's main domain was then tied to how healthy they rated themselves. South Korea reports some of the lowest activity levels in the world, so the pattern matters.

Under half the adults met the activity guidelines. About a third were nearly inactive. Among the active, transport was the main source for most people. Walking and cycling to get places carried the load. That pattern was strongest in women, older adults, and the barely active. Leisure exercise was a minority pursuit. Protecting everyday walking may matter more than preaching workouts.
plos-pone-0352582:
Zhu and colleagues tested walking with tight leg cuffs in inactive college students in a 2026 trial. Cuffs partly limit blood flow during easy exercise, a method meant to bring bigger training gains from gentle work. Sixty students each tried five-minute walks at four cuff pressure levels, in random order.

Only the middle-high pressure raised heart rate clearly more than no cuff, and the change stayed modest and safe for healthy young adults. Higher pressure felt harder and more uncomfortable, and students took fewer steps. The authors favor low to middle pressure as the sensible range, while noting that lasting health effects still need study.
plos-pone-0352682:
Adi Shuchami leads a team of six asking whether emergency departments repeat blood tests that community doctors just ran, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Children often arrive at the pediatric emergency department hours after a clinic blood draw, and the tests are frequently ordered again. Using records from a nationwide Israeli health organization, the team judged each repeat against preset criteria for whether it could change care, covering blood counts, electrolytes, and an inflammation marker.

Useful repeats were rare: roughly thirteen, sixteen, and nineteen percent for the three test families respectively. The rest consumed money, time, and children's comfort without guiding decisions. A standard gradient boosting model then learned to predict, from the community results and the child's background, whether a repeat was actually necessary. The authors propose decision support at the ordering screen, sparing most children a second needle while flagging the minority whose numbers genuinely need rechecking.
plos-pone-0352782:
Gao and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, improve how fleets of warehouse robots share work and plan routes. In warehouses with movable storage pods, robots often drive empty, respond slowly to new tasks, and crowd onto the same paths. Their approach joins task scheduling with live map planning instead of treating them apart.

Long trips are split into two stages: a haul across the warehouse, then a precise placement step, with different robot types suited to each stage. A pre-allocation trick lets a robot claim its next job before finishing the current one, cutting empty driving. Routes update on the fly, with a traffic control step for busy spots and a fast method for patching local paths. In a simulated multi-zone warehouse, the combined approach lowered empty running, eased congestion, and improved overall performance against standard practice. The authors present it as a template for busier automated warehouses.
plos-pone-0352882:
Osama Abdelrahman and five colleagues classify mental workload from brainwaves in this 2026 study. Knowing when an operator is overloaded matters in cockpits and operating theatres. Brainwave systems promise that knowledge, but noise and individual differences defeat many models. Their hybrid framework attacks all three weaknesses at once. An autoencoder cleans and compresses the signals. An attention module then spotlights the most informative channels and places. A memory network reads how the patterns unfold over time.

Tested with each person held out in turn, the system averaged about eighty-four percent accuracy. It sorted four workload levels and beat the baseline models overall. Removing any single component hurt performance, confirming each part earns its place. Tuning settled on ten-second windows as the sweet spot. Because the attention module can show what it focused on, the system explains itself better than most black boxes, a real virtue in safety-critical monitoring.
plos-pone-0352982:
Nila Kusumawati and five colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One survey of what rural Indonesian teenagers know, believe, and do about type 2 diabetes. The disease is rising among young people as lifestyles change, but rural adolescents have rarely been studied. The team questioned more than fifteen hundred high school seniors in Riau Province's Kampar Regency, during late 2024 and early 2025.

Students knew little about diabetes risk factors, symptoms, and complications, and their daily habits, especially physical activity, lagged behind their generally positive attitudes. Girls, students near towns, and those previously exposed to diabetes information scored higher. Knowledge alone was only weakly tied to healthy practice, so the authors favor school programs that pair information with peer support and routines that build habits.
plos-pone-0353182:
Zhong and colleagues tested frog-skin peptides against a deadly brain tumor in a 2026 study. In dish tests, the two peptides slowed tumor cell growth, raised a growth-control protein, and quieted a pathway that drives spread and blood vessel growth. Cell death came mainly through a programmed route.

In mice without working immune systems, the peptides changed immune cells inside tumors but did not shrink them. In mice given human immune cells, tumors shrank clearly, with more killer immune cells entering and a key immune brake lowered. The peptides thus seem to fight both directly and by rallying immunity, a dual action worth developing.
plos-pone-0353282:
Mohammad Alyetama and five colleagues published this 2026 data paper enriching a giant citizen science collection. Volunteers on iNaturalist post millions of mammal observations, shown as photos of living animals, carcasses, tracks, or droppings, but most posts never say which. The team trained machine learning to label the evidence type for well over a million North American mammal records.

Each record now carries a category and a confidence score. Knowing the evidence type helps scientists model how observations arise, for instance whether dead animals cluster near roads. The dataset is released for ecological reuse.
plos-pone-0353382:
Michael Rubinigg and colleagues introduce the Pollinator Ontology, a formal word list for describing pollinators and their links with plants, people, and the environment. It was built for the European Union's Pollinator Hub platform. Their 2026 paper defines the classes, properties, and links involved. These let databases across countries record bees, hoverflies, and their interactions in exactly the same terms.

The word list ships inside open-source software. It is designed to keep growing under community control. Its purposes are practical. Standardize pollinator data across borders, make datasets findable and reusable under FAIR principles, and end the chaos of every project inventing its own labels. Better shared data is a precondition for tracking pollinator decline and judging which rescue policies work.
plos-pone-0353482:
Fien Hermans and colleagues studied thirty-six patients with chronic lung disease. They asked whether moving more changes the nervous system's grip on the heart. That grip is a control system that often malfunctions in this illness. Their 2026 study measured heart rate patterns during sleep and recovery after a walking test. It tracked daily steps with accelerometers. Everything was re-measured after a six-month activity coaching program.

At baseline, faster heart recovery traveled with brisker walking and longer distance. Over the program, patients who added steps showed falling resting heart rates. They also showed healthier variability patterns. The clearest links sat in those not on beta-blocker drugs. The associations are modest, not dramatic. But they suggest everyday activity, not just formal training, may retune the heart's control system.
plos-pone-0353782:
Kalafat and colleagues tested three AI chat tools on children's elbow X-rays in a 2026 study. The injury studied, a break just above the elbow, is common in children and can harm nerves and blood flow if missed. Records covered three hundred children seen at a city hospital in Turkey, half with the break and half without.

Each tool saw the same images three times on different days. Answers were fairly steady for two tools and less steady for the third. Sorting breaks by severity grade worked best for one tool, yet overall skill stayed limited. The authors warn these tools are not ready to judge such breaks alone and need training built for children's bones.
plos-pone-0353882:
Man-Fung Yuen and five colleagues model a cheaper way to watch for liver cancer in Hong Kong, in this 2026 PLOS ONE health-economics study. People with chronic hepatitis B or cirrhosis need regular checks, usually ultrasound plus a blood marker, but ultrasound slots are scarce. The alternative pairs that same marker with a second blood protein that rises when vitamin K is absent — a combination needing no scan appointment.

In their simulation the blood-only strategy caught more cancers at an early, treatable stage and produced fewer false alarms. It also gained a sliver of healthy life per person while saving money. The benefit was clearest for hepatitis B patients without cirrhosis, who often wait longest for scans.
plos-pone-0354082:
Tang and colleagues set out a pilot plan in 2026 to add hearing checks to a meal delivery service in Australia. Many older adults live with hearing loss that no one has found or treated. Under the plan, trained meal volunteers and hearing students will visit clients at home with a small ear scope and a tablet hearing test.

Visitors will also teach basic ear care and refer people who need fuller testing. The pilot will judge how well the visits work in practice, how clients respond, and what the service costs to run. Using a trusted home service could reach older people who rarely visit clinics, making hearing care fairer for those with few options nearby.
plos-pone-0354382:
AK Kakkar led a team of eight authors on this 2026 global study of heart rhythm patients who go without blood thinners despite stroke risk. The GARDENIA registry enrolled just over seven hundred high-risk atrial fibrillation patients with bleeding concerns across many centers, and recorded why anticoagulants were withheld and what happened over follow-up.

Past major bleeding, doctors' fear of bleeding, and patient refusal topped the reasons. Modeling suggested treatment would have cut strokes and deaths by more than it raised bleeding. Enrollment lagged, ending the study early. Kakkar urges rethinking blanket caution.
plos-pone-0354482:
Qin Qin and co-authors investigated a nucleus-anchor protein, Nesprin-1, in drug-induced heart failure in mice. The protein ties the cell nucleus to the skeleton, and its role in failing hearts was unsettled. Their 2026 study induced failure with daily injections of a stimulating drug for over three weeks and confirmed the model with scans and tissue markers.

The team measured heart chamber sizes and pumping fractions by ultrasound. Staining and protein checks tracked the anchor protein, a gap-junction partner, DNA damage signs, and gene-silencing marks. Oxidative stress gauges and a growth signalling pathway completed the panel. Qin and colleagues frame Nesprin-1 as a candidate link between nuclear strain and the failing heart's electrical and structural decay.
plos-pone-0354682:
Firdaus Aziz led a team of seven authors on this 2026 study predicting which Malaysian patients skip their prescribed medicines. Patients with diabetes, high blood pressure, or high cholesterol answered questions about their background, treatment, and beliefs in complementary and alternative medicine. The team trained a dozen standard algorithms plus blended ensembles on the survey answers.

A stacked model that combined several algorithms performed best, and a chosen cutoff sorted patients into lower and higher risk of skipping doses. Aziz argues that adding cultural beliefs to the data sharpens prediction and helps clinics target support instead of wasting medicine.
plos-pone-0354882:
Yuxi Xie and five colleagues published this 2026 computer study of a medicinal plant, Centella asiatica, and diseases that destroy the brain. The plant is eaten and used as medicine, with hints it calms brain inflammation. The team combined network analysis, gene data, machine learning, and molecule docking to shortlist its active ingredients.

Sixteen plant compounds passed filters for drug-like behavior and reaching the brain, pointing at hundreds of possible targets. Shared targets across Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's diseases were checked against patient data. Xie is clear these are candidates for lab testing, not proven treatments.
plos-pone-0354982:
Eshetu Mekonnen and four colleagues published this 2026 study of a traditional Ethiopian medicinal plant, Ehretia cymosa. Healers use its leaves for wound infections, fever, stomach ulcers, and toothache, but proof was scarce. The team made a leaf extract with methanol, tested it on bacteria in dishes, and treated infected burns in mice.

The extract slowed common infection bacteria in the lab and helped infected burns close faster in mice, especially against staph germs. Chemical screening found flavonoids, tannins, and similar plant compounds. Mekonnen says the results back traditional use and justify isolating the active ingredients.
plos-pone-0355282:
XiaCheng Song and co-authors survey humanities undergraduates in China about working with generative AI on creative and study tasks. The question is not just whether students hand work to the tool, but what kind of handing-over helps. Borrowing a trigger-response model, the team asked several hundred students how the tools feel to use, how much control they keep, and how confident they feel about future tasks.

Features students liked were tied to healthy offloading, the kind that frees effort, and to a stronger sense of control and self-belief. Those states, in turn, tracked with richer joint creation and more confidence ahead. Reliance that felt dependent showed no such gains once the other states were counted. Song and colleagues advise teaching productive use, not mere use.
plos-pone-0355382:
Shan Yan and colleagues assessed in 2026 the quality of colored rice varieties, pairing practical grain measures with a profile of their pigments. Colored rice, with red, black, or purple grains, draws interest for its looks and for the pigments linked to nutritional value. Judging such varieties fairly means measuring eating and milling quality alongside the chemistry that gives them their color.

The team combines an integrated quality assessment with pigment profiling across the varieties studied. That pairing lets breeders and buyers see whether the most colorful grains are also the best to grow and eat. As demand for specialty rice grows, grounded comparisons like this help farmers choose varieties that command a premium without sacrificing yield or taste.
plos-pone-0355482:
Benjamin Asare and co-authors build in 2026 local formulas for estimating wood volume and above ground weight of a fast growing tree planted in Ghana's Kwahu Highlands. Crews measured trunk width, height, and crown shape on dozens of trees, then cut and weighed a smaller sample. Several formula shapes were tried against the real values.

Formulas that used trunk width, total height, and wood density together fit best for both volume and weight. Simpler formulas using only width and height were fair for volume but off for weight. Better local formulas, the authors argue, make carbon counts for such plantations more trustworthy for climate reporting.
plos-pone-0355682:
Azeze Wubie Kassa and seven colleagues evaluate black cumin varieties for Ethiopia's Amhara Region in this 2026 field study. Black cumin seed is a valued spice and medicine, yet regional yields trail the national average because improved varieties are scarce. The team grew eighteen promising genotypes plus two standard varieties at three sites over two seasons, measuring yield, quality, and how consistently each line performed when conditions changed.

Environment drove more than half of the yield differences, which is exactly why stability matters. Two genotypes stood out for combining top yields with steadiness across sites and years, beating the standard varieties by a clear margin. One of them also carried good levels of the seed's prized oil extract. That line was released for commercial production in 2024 under the name Tena, and the authors recommend it for similar growing zones.
plos-pone-0356182:
Wei Xu and coauthors published a 2026 materials study in PLOS ONE on coating aviation titanium alloy with a titanium-aluminum layer using selective laser melting. A laser fuses powder into a hard protective skin. Surface quality of titanium parts decides safety in service, yet no clear guidance existed on the best laser power for this coating. The team varied power across a narrow band and examined the coatings' structure, phases, chemistry, and hardness.

Power proved decisive. At the two lower settings, long cracks ran through the coating and bonding to the base metal was poor, risking peeling. At the middle setting the coating bonded cleanly with no obvious defects, formed new strengthening phases, and reached the highest hardness measured. One step higher, cracks returned and performance fell. The authors offer the middle setting, and the reasoning behind it, as a reference point for coating titanium parts in aerospace manufacturing.
plos-pone-0356382:
Timothy Mulvany and seven colleagues test how the way a tumor is outlined on a scan affects computerized measurements used to diagnose children's brain tumors, in this 2026 study. Radiomics extracts numbers from MRI scans that machine learning can turn into diagnoses, but humans draw tumor boundaries differently. Using scans from just over one hundred young patients, the team shrank and expanded expert-drawn outlines to imitate cautious and generous drawing, then watched what happened to the measurements.

Expanding outlines disturbed nearly all measurements, and far more than shrinking them did. Diagnosis models trained on expert outlines lost accuracy under either change, but less when training included the altered outlines and only the steadiest measurements. The authors advise that when boundaries are ambiguous, leaving doubtful tissue out beats including it, and that model builders should plan for drawing variation from the start.
plos-pone-0356482:
Lisha Zou and three colleagues build a decision aid for the earliest stage of drug discovery in this 2026 paper. Virtual screening ranks thousands of molecules against a disease target, but labs can only afford to test a shortlist, and raw ranking scores say little about how much to trust them. Their package, TASC-VS, adds test-time adaptation, statistical calibration, and uncertainty-aware ranking to turn ranked lists into fixed-budget choices.

On a curated fifteen-target benchmark, the full package beat a strong comparator on enrichment and on the quality of its top twenty picks, though some gains lost significance after strict statistical correction. A separate stress test on another benchmark favored the simpler rival. The authors are frank about the limits: the method offers calibrated shortlist support on the tested subset, and broader use needs fresh validation.
plos-pone-0356782:
Maria Hjorth and Anna Forsberg report a qualitative study, published in 2026, on setting up nurse-led follow-up care for people with liver cirrhosis. Six clinics tried the new arrangement, and the researchers interviewed nurses, doctors, and managers repeatedly over several years of rollout. Their analysis looked for what helped the change take hold and what got in its way.

They found just over twenty influencing factors, split almost evenly between barriers and supports. Staff shortages, unclear roles, and weak leadership support hindered the work. Some staff also felt a moral strain when patients who needed the extra care could not all receive it under the trial's random assignment. On the positive side, the follow-up was seen as safe and worthwhile, and managers who backed the nurses strengthened their standing in the team. Simple tasks nurses could own outright worked best.
plos-pone-0356882: Iqra and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in pure mathematics. They prove new Newton-type inequalities, bounds named for a classic rule for estimating integrals. The work covers a class of curved functions shaped by a hyperbolic form, using fractional integrals of the Riemann-Liouville type. Number checks back up the proofs. Such bounds help scientists estimate quantities that cannot be computed exactly.
plos-pone-0357382:
Xuan Wang and coauthors published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE on shrinking three-dimensional animation files so they stream and render smoothly on modest devices. Animation data is bulky and repeats heavily between frames, but older compressors cut it into blocks with sloppy boundaries and leave redundancy behind. Their scheme tidies scattered vertex data with an improved clustering method, carves the animation into blocks adapting to how the scene moves, and polishes the result with boundary editing and matrix reorganization.

Across four datasets, the optimized algorithm compressed files to roughly a seventh of original size, beating a leading comparison method widely while cutting reconstruction error substantially and keeping structural similarity high. On mobile devices, loading times fell by over two thirds and rendering frame rates rose by nearly half. The method is presented as practical support for virtual reality, games, and digital twins on limited hardware.
plos-pone-0357482:
Sangrak Son and colleagues trial a smart watering system that feeds liquid organic fertilizer to greenhouse lettuce only when plants seem to need it. Organic fertilizer costs a lot, so feeding on a fixed calendar wastes money. Cameras measured leaf canopy size every few days and shared data online. In the smart beds, a sensor switch ran the pump only when canopy growth lagged behind hand-fed beds by a set margin.

Lettuce weight and leaf area ended up nearly equal in both setups. The fixed schedule, however, used about four times as many feeding events and left far more unused nutrients in the growing mix. Son and colleagues say growth-guided feeding can cut fertilizer bills sharply while keeping yields, a useful result for small greenhouse growers.
plos-pone-0357782:
Elena García-López and Fabrice B. R. Parmentier published a 2026 experiment in PLOS ONE on how an unexpected sound distracts people in the middle of a task. In their setup, volunteers identified where a visual target appeared while tones played in the background, most of them standard and a few rare and deviant. The key question was whether a deviant sound affects a person differently when the correct next action repeats the previous one versus when it changes.

Deviant sounds slowed people when the response repeated, in both the two-choice and four-choice versions. That braking effect did not depend on how many choices were available. The same sounds sped up response changes, though, and that benefit shrank when the choice set grew. The split suggests distraction works through two mechanisms: one inhibiting action repetition, one helping switching, with only the second sensitive to context.
plos-pone-0358182: Feng and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on diabetic retinopathy, an eye disease that can blind people with diabetes. They hunted for new marker genes tied to two cell stresses: low oxygen and a copper-driven cell death called cuproptosis. They then probed how those markers might drive the disease. Fresh markers could lead to earlier tests for a condition often found late.
plos-pone-0358482: Mutuyimana and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how suffering is voiced in Eastern Africa. They built a new survey, a Cultural Scripts of Trauma Inventory, tuned to local ways of expressing pain after trauma. Imported surveys can miss local idioms of distress. A tool built from local scripts can help counselors hear what patients truly mean.
plos-pone-0358882:
Matthew Wassall and colleagues worked in 2026 on telling apart the activities of people who use lower limb prostheses, using motion sensors worn in everyday life. Knowing whether a prosthesis user is walking, climbing stairs, sitting, or standing matters for judging how well the device serves them. Laboratory tests capture only a slice of that life, so the team used inertial sensing, the motion tracking built into small wearable devices, under real world conditions.

The study builds classification methods that read those sensor streams and sort them into activities. Reliable real world measurement would let clinicians see how a prosthesis performs across weeks, not minutes. It could also guide better fitting and fairer comparisons between devices.
plos-pone-0359282: Özel and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE trial on easing pain after open-heart surgery. A cut through the breastbone, called a median sternotomy, leaves strong pain as it heals. The trial tested elastic therapeutic taping, sticky bands meant to support tissue and ease pain. Patients were assigned at random to taping or standard care. A cheap, drug-free aid would be welcome after such major surgery.
plos-pone-0359782:
Peter Oloche David published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It proposes the Genomic Equity Accessibility Framework, shortened to GEAF. The framework models what such therapies cost people and how fairly they are shared: genomic and regenerative treatments, built on genes and lab-grown tissues, that often carry very high prices.

The author stresses that the framework's measures are built to fit together in a disciplined way. Such a model gives policymakers a structured way to ask who can actually get these therapies and who is priced out. Health economists and access advocates are the readers for a tool built on fairness.
pmc-11223882:
Madeira, Madhusoodanan, Lee, and co-authors describe the 2024 state of the Job Dispatcher tools at EMBL-EBI. Their framework gives scientists free access to popular programs for analysing DNA, RNA, and protein sequences. Users reach the tools through a shared web service rather than installing each program alone.

Along with the tools, the service supplies the sequence datasets those programs need. That pairing lets a researcher run a standard analysis even without local computing power. Keeping such shared services current matters more each year, as sequence data grows faster than most single labs can handle.
pmc-13121982:
Ahammed Mekkodathil leads a 2026 narrative review of electrolyte-based indices in traumatic brain injury. Electrolytes are charged minerals in blood, and their imbalance can worsen swelling and cell harm after a head injury. Simple ratios built from routine lab tests could help doctors judge risk quickly and cheaply.

The review covers the glucose-to-potassium ratio, osmolality, a measure of fluid concentration, an ion shift index, anion gap, and combined disturbance scores. The glucose ratio and osmolality showed the strongest power to predict death and poor recovery. Others look promising but need more testing. Correcting sodium and calcium values for glucose and protein levels prevents misreading. Standard thresholds and larger studies are the next steps.
pmc-13188982:
Ingrid de Souza e Sousa is first author on a 2026 review of new drug targets for chromoblastomycosis, a chronic fungal skin infection classed as a neglected tropical disease. The fungi resist standard antifungal drugs, burrow under the skin, and form protective biofilms, slimy cell layers, making treatment long and often unsuccessful.

The authors' group found the fungi use surface enzymes, protein-cutting secretions, and a signaling protein called calcineurin to grow, change form, and grip host cells. Blocking those systems with known inhibitors, including some HIV drugs and immune drugs, impaired the fungi. Metal compounds built around a chemical scaffold called phenanthroline also killed them potently. New treatment strategies follow from these targets.
pmc-13195182:
Sifan Cao is first author on a 2026 preclinical study of a robot and augmented reality system for jaw tumor surgery. Removing facial tumors and rebuilding the jaw demands exact bone cuts and plate placement. Freehand template methods risk tissue injury and inconsistent alignment, especially when fitting a straight leg bone into the jaw's curve.

The proposed system pairs robot-assisted bone cutting, aligned by optical registration to the preoperative plan, with augmented reality guidance that projects the virtual jaw model into the surgeon's view. A calibration method reduces marker errors. Tests on cadaveric and animal specimens showed favorable cutting and alignment accuracy and low overlay error. The workflow is feasible in preclinical settings, the authors conclude.
pmc-13202082:
Farm work in rural India strains backs, shoulders, and joints, and a 2026 plan headed by Gurjeet Kaur plans a scoping review of that burden. The plan focuses on agriculture-related musculoskeletal disorders among vulnerable rural groups, including tribal groups, marginal farmers, and agricultural laborers.

Following established scoping review guides, the team will search several major databases plus grey literature for English studies issued from 2010 onward. Extracted data will cover farming techniques, disorder patterns, risk factors, programs, and access to healthcare in each study. A narrative and thematic synthesis will then map knowledge gaps and regional gaps to inform occupational health plans.
pmc-13202182:
Care for fluid and air problems around the lung varies between hospitals, and a 2026 quality standard by Mark E Roberts sets minimum expectations for the United Kingdom. The British Thoracic Society document defines markers of high-quality, cost-effective care for adults with pleural disease in primary and secondary care settings.

Roberts and co-authors derived each statement from the society's evidence-based pleural disease guideline, following the national quality standard process as their model. The standards are meant for clinicians and services delivering pleural care, and also for commissioners, planners, and patients judging what care should look like. Together they translate guideline recommendations into concise, auditable statements for everyday practice.
pmc-13202682:
Two mushrooms new to science are described from southwestern Guizhou in a 2026 taxonomy study from Heng-Ting Chen. The research article names Collybiopsis guizhouensis and Collybiopsis anlongensis, two small agaric fungi in the family Omphalotaceae, based on specimens collected in China.

The team combined microscopic morphology with a three-gene phylogenetic analysis using ribosomal and protein-coding markers. Each species landed in its own distinct, well-supported branch of the family tree in both maximum likelihood and Bayesian analyses. Clear structural gaps from known relatives backed the molecular split, and the descriptions add to a genus whose small, plain fruiting bodies long hid its true diversity.
pmc-13212382:
Maarten V. de Hoop and co-authors tackle a pure mathematics problem in 2026: can a hidden obstacle be pinned down from measurements taken only at a body's surface? The setting involves elastic material pressed against a rigid support, where each boundary point follows one of two possible contact rules.

The authors prove that a single paired measurement of movement and surface stress can determine the obstacle uniquely, apart from one natural obstruction they identify. Their argument moves from a simpler scalar version to the full elasticity system. Methods developed along the way may also serve other inverse problems stated as differential inequalities, widening the paper's reach beyond contact mechanics.
pmc-13213582:
Akram Fallah and colleagues review in 2026 plastic-based materials that block electromagnetic interference, the stray signals that disrupt dense modern electronics. Metals shield well but are heavy, stiff, and corrode, so engineers want lighter, flexible alternatives.

Blending conductive fillers such as carbon nanotubes, graphene, or metal particles into polymers creates networks that reflect and absorb stray waves. Treating filler surfaces helps them spread evenly and strengthens absorption over simple reflection. The review covers materials, shielding mechanisms, and uses from aircraft to health devices. Scalability and weather resistance make these composites attractive, and the authors frame them as central to next-generation shielding design.
pmc-13214082:
Junfa Yang and colleagues test in 2026 a ginger-derived compound, 6-shogaol, against liver scarring that can end in cancer. No effective anti-fibrosis drug for humans exists yet, so natural products with anti-inflammatory records are tempting candidates.

Two mouse models of liver scarring both improved on the compound, with better liver function, quieter scar-driving cells, and less deposited matrix. In cultured human stellate cells, the compound likewise blocked activation. Tracing the mechanism, the team found it throttles sugar-burning metabolism in those cells by suppressing key enzymes, and it binds a stress-sensing protein flagged by network analysis. Multiple binding tests confirmed the pairing.
pmc-13214282:
Amanda Gezelius, Anton Westman, and Johan Hylander interview in 2026 Swedish mountain rescuers about the frustrations built into their work along the long Scandes range. Twenty-one rescuers from four counties described operations where weather, distance, and rules collide.

One complaint gives the study its title: even licensed medical staff among them are not allowed to give pain relief in the field. Bureaucracy inside their own organisations slows response, and helicopter access for moving staff and casualties faces legal hurdles. Injury assessment in harsh terrain is hard, and welfare on long missions suffers. Fixing the drug and helicopter rules, the authors argue, would shorten time to real treatment.
pmc-13215182:
Rong Li, Jun-Qi Fan, and Bin Lin identify in 2026 a structural protein as the hub of a self-feeding inflammation cycle that destroys the retina in retinitis pigmentosa. The inherited disease kills light-sensing cells progressively, and immune cells in the retina fan the damage.

Profiling a mouse model of the disease, they found the protein, tropomyosin 1, coordinating skeleton, metabolism, and immune signals at once. Deleting it calmed retinal immune cells and preserved vision. Boosting it set off a four-part loop. The loop mixed cell ageing signals, weak debris clearance, fat droplet build-up, and an inflammatory relay between cells through a galectin pathway. Blocking that relay offers a precise therapeutic idea.
pmc-13215482:
Ya-En Catherine Lin and co-authors report a 2026 experiment on how sponsorship labels on social media posts affect teenagers in Taiwan. The study compared posts with full disclosure, partial disclosure, or no disclosure of paid promotion.

In all, 3,149 high school students from 36 schools took part in a 2022 survey experiment, each shown one of the three post types at random. Teenagers who saw full disclosure spotted the advertising more often and scored higher on advertising knowledge. Spotting an ad also made students warier, which in turn linked to weaker buying plans. The authors argue that clear labels are a practical protection for young users.
pmc-13215682:
Luke B. Harrison and co-authors present a 2026 narrative review of rapid laboratory tests for sepsis, written as a primer for critical care clinicians. Finding the causative microbe quickly matters because early, well-matched antibiotics save lives.

The review sorts tools into three families. Some speed up work on positive blood cultures, still the standard test. Others detect microbial DNA directly in patient samples, and a third group detects antigens instead. Direct methods can return answers within hours but trade off sensitivity, specificity, and ease of interpretation in different ways. The authors stress that availability and performance vary widely, so choosing tools is a joint decision with the microbiology laboratory.
pmc-13216282:
Mohamed Ali Hassan and co-authors present a 2026 materials study on loading titanium dioxide into metakaolin-based geopolymer, a cement alternative with a smaller carbon footprint. The goal was a denser material that resists wear and heat for demanding structural uses.

Mixes carrying 0 to 50 percent titanium dioxide by weight were cast and tested. Density climbed steadily while porosity and water absorption fell, and microscopy showed the particles filling pores without breaking the geopolymer network. Heat tests showed better thermal stability. At 40 percent loading, the wear rate dropped to about a third of the plain material's value and friction eased as well. The authors describe titanium dioxide as both filler and reinforcement.
pmc-13216582:
Johanna I. Hütner-Reisch and co-authors present a 2026 surface science study challenging a textbook picture of alumina, a workhorse material for catalysis and thin films. Its common crystal face was long modelled as a flat, uniformly aluminium-topped surface.

Combining atomic force microscopy with density functional calculations, the team shows that this unreconstructed surface is metastable and, in practice, rough and disordered, with only nanometre-scale patches of the neat ordered structure. Calculations explain the instability: the surface aluminium atoms sit badly undercoordinated, and even after relaxing inward they leave the surface energetically unfavourable except where a large reconstruction forms at high temperature. The authors warn that models assuming a perfect flat termination may mislead.
pmc-13217982:
Ruijie Xie, Christian Herder, and Ben Schöttker ask in a 2026 study whether layering several kinds of molecular data improves prediction of type 2 diabetes. Doctors already estimate risk with a clinical score that includes blood sugar history and body measures. The team tested what genetic, metabolite, and protein measurements add on top of that score.

Working with 42,840 UK Biobank participants who had no diabetes at baseline, the researchers built models in one half of the cohort and validated them in the other. Over ten years, 1,090 participants developed diabetes. Protein measurements gave the largest single gain over the clinical score, and adding metabolite data plus a genetic risk score improved accuracy a little further. Because the full model needs many more measurements for a small extra gain, the authors suggest the protein-only version may translate into routine care more easily, pending outside validation and cost analysis.
pmc-13220182:
Olivia H. Wilkins tells of her route into physical chemistry in a 2026 interview from the Seasons of a Career series, published across the American Chemical Society's journals. The series invites researchers at every stage to narrate how they arrived where they are, on the theory that career paths inspire the community. Wilkins is an assistant professor of chemistry at Dickinson College.

Her early influences were domestic: parents, a mother who tolerated a child dismantling the vacuum cleaner to see how it worked, and digging for rocks and fossils that never materialized. Library books on phenomena, the Mount St. Helens eruption, and family trips to sites and railroads fed the interest. High school chemistry won her over by being the science, a way to avoid choosing one kind of scientist, and a love of math pointed her toward its mathematical branch. The interview frames a career in its early season.
pmc-13220482:
Flavio Palmieri and colleagues search children's DNA methylation for a forecast of who will succeed at losing weight in a 2026 study. Lifestyle programs help many children with obesity, before puberty, but response varies for reasons doctors cannot see. A signature that predicted response could let clinicians personalize treatment from the start.

Twenty-six prepubertal children completed a six-month lifestyle intervention centered on diet. Comparing children who responded strongly with those who responded weakly yielded 214 methylated sites, which the team narrowed to eight markers. A model built on eight classified children with eighty-four percent precision against their change in age-adjusted body mass index. The marked genes included GSDMD, GFRA1, and NRP2, all connected to inflammation, metabolic regulation, or fat handling. The authors stress the cohort is small and homogeneous, so larger and more diverse studies must confirm the markers before a clinic could use them to triage children.
pmc-13220582:
Camila Heredia and co-authors cross-check Japan's essential medicines list against the country's medicine supply problems in a 2026 study. Essential medicines lists are meant to guarantee the drugs a population most needs, and Japan pairs universal coverage with promotion of cheap generics, a policy now blamed for shortages. Whether listing protects a medicine from supply trouble was the open question.

The analysis worked from the April 2024 pharmaceutical supply survey, deduplicated to 1,107 unique medicines by ingredient and route. Of these, 401, thirty-six percent, had shipping or supply issues, generating 847 problem entries. Being on the 2024 essential list was no shield: eighty of its 167 medicines, half, had supply issues. Causes ranged from pricing decisions and quality failures to manufacturing trouble, demand spikes, and raw material shortages, with antibiotics the hardest-hit group. The authors call for continuous list updates and a national supply strategy so priority status means availability.
pmc-13221282:
Rakan Mal and co-authors report an unusual abdominal injury in a healthy 32-year-old football player, in a 2026 case report. A direct knee blow during a match tore the tissue anchoring his bowel, creating a bucket-handle defect. Such injuries usually follow high-impact deceleration, so the low-energy cause misled the first assessment.

The man was sent home, then returned three days later with signs of bowel obstruction. Imaging suggested internal herniation, and surgery confirmed a trapped, oxygen-starved bowel segment inside the defect. Surgeons removed the damaged section and repaired the tear, and recovery was uneventful. The case warns clinicians to suspect serious internal injury even after modest trauma.
pmc-13221582:
Chen Meng writes a 2026 letter to the editor responding to a study of magnetic resonance neurography for posterior interosseous nerve damage. The original work identified nerve enlargement and bright T2 signals as possible markers. Meng praises its value for early diagnosis, especially in athletes and active people prone to peripheral nerve injuries.

Concerns follow in the letter. No standardized imaging thresholds exist, so readings can vary between clinicians, and Meng urges multicenter work to set shared criteria. The letter also asks for patient grouping by age, sex, and activity level, plus fuller comparison of the separate MRI sequences. Such steps, Meng argues, would sharpen personal care and return-to-play decisions.
pmc-13222582:
Tina Wullum Gundersen and co-authors link social and mental health hardship to pregnancy outcomes in type 1 diabetes, in a 2026 Danish nationwide register study. Singleton pregnancies from 1997 to 2021 numbered 5,478. Hardship measures covered family poverty, low schooling, jobless benefits, and a psychiatric diagnosis before pregnancy for either parent.

About forty percent of the women faced at least one hardship. Preterm birth risk ran higher across every hardship measure, with risks clearly above one after controls. Very large babies showed no such increase, with a slight downward trend instead. Splitting by blood sugar control before pregnancy barely moved the results. Focused support for families facing hardship is the authors' call.
pmc-13224782:
Martin Lindström and colleagues follow a 2026 Swedish cohort linking how recently people used dental care with their risk of death. A 2008 postal health survey reached adults in Scania, southern Sweden, and answers from 26,115 respondents were tied to death records over about eight years. Roughly two thirds had seen dental care within the past year.

Groups whose last visit lay further back faced higher death rates from all causes than the recent-visit group, even after statistical adjustment. A nested case-control analysis sharpened that gradient, and some links also appeared for cardiovascular and cancer deaths. The authors treat dental attendance as a marker entangled with broader health and social patterns, not proof that visits themselves extend life.
pmc-13227382:
Ji-Eun An and colleagues indirectly compare a 2026 pair of escalation drugs for pulmonary arterial hypertension, a disease of stiffening lung arteries. Patients already on two standard drug classes often respond inadequately, and two next-step options exist: switching to riociguat, or adding selexipag. No trial has tested them head to head, so the team compared them through their separate trials against the shared background therapy.

Three randomised trials fed the analysis. On clinical worsening, walking distance, and a heart-strain blood marker, the two strategies showed no significant differences. Overall side-effect risk also looked similar. Wide confidence intervals reflect the indirect method's limits, but the results give clinicians a first comparative foothold where direct evidence is absent.
pmc-13231682:
Franck Katembo Sikakulya and colleagues review in 2026 how pork tapeworm larvae in the brain can set the stage for epilepsy. The infection, called neurocysticercosis, is a leading cause of acquired seizures in regions where the parasite circulates. Older views blamed seizures mainly on the host immune attack against dying cysts.

Newer evidence shows larvae actively shape their surroundings by adjusting immune signals and leaking chemical products. As cysts break down, those products fire up support cells, boost excitatory signaling, and weaken calming signals, which lowers the seizure threshold. Scarred tissue around old lesions then keeps brain networks jumpy for years. Stopping transmission through pig and sanitation work remains vital beside seizure care.
pmc-13232782:
Xu Zhang and colleagues build in 2026 a stacked machine learning model that flags malnutrition risk within a day of intensive care arrival. Standard scores rely on slow or judgment-based inputs, which delays feeding support for the sickest patients. Records from a large public intensive care database covered more than fifty thousand stays with first-day vitals and labs.

Four learning methods fed their outputs into a final combining model, a design called stacking. The stack sorted future malnutrition cases far better than the standard score and slightly better than its best single member. About one patient in twelve in the cohort carried the risk label. Explanation tools showed which inputs drove each call, keeping the model open to clinical judgment.
pmc-13234082:
Nidhal Khazaal Maraie and Ali N. Wannas published a 2026 pharmaceutical study designing a cheek film that delivers doxazosin, a blood pressure drug, through the mouth lining. Swallowed doxazosin dissolves poorly and the liver destroys much of it before it can work. A mucoadhesive buccal film, stuck inside the cheek, bypasses the liver and promises faster onset.

The team cast films by solvent evaporation, first screening which ingredients governed stickiness, then optimizing the two main ones, a cellulose polymer and glycerin plasticizer. Their best formula held about two-thirds polymer and a fifth glycerin. It released all its drug within fifteen minutes, and tissue permeation tests passed ninety-one percent in the same span. Microscopy showed a fairly uniform surface. The authors conclude the film could raise doxazosin's availability substantially.
pmc-13234482:
Zhuocheng Bao, Yakun Liu, and Yuxiang Liu studied in 2026 early safety reports for a new schizophrenia treatment combining xanomeline with trospium chloride. The pairing is the first approved oral cholinergic therapy for schizophrenia in decades, marking a shift from dopamine-based drugs. Reports came from the United States adverse event reporting system after marketing began. More than fourteen hundred reports named the combination as the main suspected drug.

Stomach and bowel problems dominated the reports by a wide margin. Unexpected signals included tremor, suicidal thoughts, and sedation, all rated low to moderate in clinical priority. Most events began within the first month, with a median onset near eight days. Onset came earlier in women than in men in the data. The authors advise close monitoring early in treatment, especially for gut and urinary problems.
pmc-13235182:
Thomas Ramo and co-authors studied in 2026 a teaching internship track for junior doctors at a hospital in western Sweden. The voluntary program began in 2018 amid a shortage of clinical supervisors for medical students. Junior doctors with an interest in education supervised students and peers as part of their internship. Ten former participants from the first six years were interviewed about their experience.

Three themes organized what participants said they gained from the program. They built a practical toolbox covering simulation, feedback, and running teaching sessions. Participation also gave them legitimacy as teachers and a platform to shape hospital teaching culture. Many described growing into an identity as a clinical teacher with new confidence. The authors suggest embedding such tracks in internship training can sustain teaching capacity while developing young doctors.
pmc-13235882:
Lin and colleagues offer a new way to estimate how much charge an electric vehicle battery holds. That figure, the state of charge, is a core reading in any battery management system. Guessing it wrong shortens range estimates and can harm the battery, so carmakers need methods that stay accurate as conditions change.

The team pairs a temporal convolutional network, a neural model built for time series, with an Unscented Kalman Filter. The network learns patterns in the battery's recent history; the filter then steadies the output and cuts its wobble. Tested on lithium-ion batteries, the combined method aims at accuracy with smooth, trustworthy readings a driver can rely on.
pmc-13236782:
K Suga and colleagues analyzed a nationwide 2018 survey of cancer patients in Japan for a 2026 study of financial toxicity, the strain that treatment costs place on daily life and care. Nearly 6,800 patients answered the National Cancer Center questionnaire. The team sorted money problems into effects on daily life, effects on treatment behavior, and changes or stops in treatment.

About 30 percent of patients reported financial toxicity despite Japan's universal health coverage. Younger patients and people with no one to talk to faced roughly double the risk in several comparisons. Unstable work also marked higher-risk groups. The authors call for stronger social support so that patients can keep up treatment without sacrificing daily living needs.
pmc-13236882:
Elia Magwaja and colleagues mapped in 2026 how people across mainland Tanzania use health services for diabetes and high blood pressure. Facility records from 2024 covered all 184 districts. Bayesian spatial models, which borrow strength from neighboring districts, linked service use to social and demographic traits.

Use was highest in city districts such as Kinondoni, Ilala, and Arusha Urban, and lowest in remote rural districts. High blood pressure services clustered in space more strongly than diabetes services. Literacy and mobile phone ownership each came with slightly higher use, while larger households came with lower use for hypertension. The maps give planners a way to spot underserved areas and target outreach.
pmc-13236982:
Abdelaziz Rabea and co-authors exposed Nile tilapia to chitosan nanoparticles for 96 hours in 2026 to find where a popular aquaculture additive turns harmful. Fish farmers use nano-chitosan against microbes and to boost immunity, but safety data in fish were thin. Eighty fish swam in water carrying four dose levels, and tissues from gills to brain were examined afterward.

No fish died at the lowest dose, while the highest dose killed half the group within four days. Every organ checked showed oxidative stress, meaning damage from reactive molecules outpaced defenses, and severe tissue injury appeared at mid and high doses. The authors set the safe level below the lowest tested dose and urge strict limits on farm use.
pmc-13237282:
Maoqi Zhu and a large team of engineers built a tiny electrochemical angular accelerometer in 2026 for drone attitude control. Drones usually get angular acceleration by differentiating gyroscope signals, a step that adds lag and noise. Their device, about 2 cm across, senses angular acceleration directly, through fluid flow past plate electrodes.

The sensor proved highly responsive while drawing only a few milliwatts of power, and a compensation circuit widened its working range. Turntable tests and real flights with an advanced nonlinear controller showed faster responses and smaller tracking errors than gyroscope-derived readings. The authors present direct sensing as a new base for steadier small drones. Low latency is the core selling point.
pmc-13238782:
Talha Shamshad and colleagues reported in 2026 a young woman whose dizziness and nausea traced to left ventricular noncompaction, a heart muscle disorder where the wall stays spongy and heavily trabeculated. Her slow heart rhythm looked at first like a dangerous conduction block. Careful tracing reading showed instead a dissociation pattern, where an escape rhythm from the ventricles runs independently of the upper chambers.

That distinction changes everything, because a true block and an escape rhythm call for different next steps, from heart MRI and genetic testing to possible device therapy. The authors argue the condition belongs in the differential diagnosis when young patients show unexplained symptomatic slow rhythms, even if the first ultrasound is equivocal. Precise electrocardiogram interpretation, they stress, directs the whole work-up.
pmc-13239182:
Martina Mussi and team reviewed in 2026 the reported cases of cutaneous lymphomas and related lymphoproliferative disorders arising after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination. Fifteen papers covering thirty-five cases met their rules. Just over half were confirmed lymphomas, led by lymphomatoid papulosis, while the rest were non-neoplastic lymphoid growths that mimic lymphoma.

Most patients had received the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine, and among new-onset lymphomas the first signs appeared between three and forty-two days, grouping within two weeks. The authors are careful: a causal link cannot be established from case reports. They suggest vaccination may have unmasked hidden disease or simply drawn attention to it. Continued close watching, especially in patients with prior lymphoid conditions, is their advice.
pmc-13239382:
Morteza Gholipour and co-authors present a 2026 surgical technique for severe ankle instability affecting both sides of the joint. Their patient, a 25-year-old man, had suffered twenty episodes of the ankle giving way in six months after a sprain.

Surgeons rebuilt four damaged ligaments, two on the outer side and two on the inner side, using a donated Achilles tendon graft. Two ligaments were fully torn and two partly torn, so an open operation was chosen over keyhole repair. At final follow-up his foot and ankle score reached 89, pain was low, and movement stayed near normal. The report details the graft routing for similar cases.
pmc-13239882:
Maryam Karami and colleagues test a nurse-led transitional care model for family caregivers in a 2026 Iranian trial. People caring for relatives with several chronic conditions often suffer falling quality of life and rising burden when hospital care ends abruptly, and structured support across the move home may help.

Sixty-eight caregivers were randomised during 2024 to routine care alone or routine care plus the model, which continued for two months after discharge. The supported group reported better overall quality of life and lower burden scores by the end. The routine group moved the opposite way on both measures. The authors recommend larger trials to confirm the benefit.
pmc-13240582:
Amirhesam Moosazadeh and colleagues present a 2026 computer modeling study of the rotavirus vaccine rollout for young children in Iran. The country added the oral Rotasiil vaccine to its national program in 2024. The authors wanted an early estimate of what that decision could achieve.

Their agent-based model simulated individual children in city and countryside settings, with spread through contact on defined grids. Each scenario ran many times over one simulated year. Vaccination cut yearly cases per child by roughly one third in urban areas and by a smaller share in rural ones. Illness days fell by similar amounts, and outbreak peaks looked lower. The authors still call for real-world monitoring after rollout.
pmc-13240982:
Lebrecht's team at Imperial College London gauged what sets winning human-like virtual influencers apart on Instagram. The dataset covered 157 female virtual profiles, all large accounts. Coders scored realism, identity steadiness, and whether real humans appeared alongside. Reach and like rates were weighed across images and videos.

Bigger accounts led the top content, mainly on video. Among the top clips, openly computer-made personas outnumbered realistic ones. Nearly four in five top accounts kept a stable look and consistent story. The authors conclude tidy, legibly virtual personas engage fans better than realism alone.
pmc-13241382:
Lenga and colleagues at Heidelberg asked whether one quick status question can track recovery after lumbar spine surgery. Two hundred fifty-seven patients answered mobile surveys every two to three days. Six weeks produced one thousand six hundred twenty-seven postoperative check-ins. The single Global Postoperative Status score was tested against pain and medication diaries.

Worse status scores lined up consistently with heavier pain burden. Patients reporting frequent pain peaks scored far lower than pain-free peers. Scores also dropped stepwise as painkillers escalated to combined opioid regimens. The authors stress this is exploratory validity only, pending prospective confirmation.
pmc-13241582:
Lahiri's team at the University of Florida tested whether camera trap orientation changes which animals get recorded at carrion sites. Carrion feeds both vertebrate scavengers and invertebrates, yet most designs target one group. The team deployed horizontal and vertical cameras across 17 carrion placements. The site was Panther Swamp National Wildlife Refuge in Mississippi.

Both designs tallied similar total richness, but the species lists differed sharply. Vertical cameras caught more flesh-eating invertebrates, including blow flies and carrion beetles. Horizontal cameras, with their wider view, recorded more white-tailed deer wandering past. The authors advise pairing both orientations to capture the whole carrion food web.
pmc-13241982:
Jiahui Liu and co-authors publish a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on exercise effects on the gut microbes of older adults. Aging often brings a less diverse, less stable gut community tied to chronic low-grade inflammation. Exercise is a cheap, safe candidate for restoring balance, unlike supplements that add microbes from outside.

Earlier studies disagree: some aerobic programs shifted the microbial community clearly, while mind-body or short programs changed little. Small samples and widely differing routines make single studies hard to trust. The review pools that scattered evidence to judge which exercise forms move gut diversity and helpful species. The authors frame the gut-muscle connection as the mechanism linking activity to microbial and immune health in later life.
pmc-13242282:
Janelle Bellot and co-authors explore cell biology in this 2026 study of YAP, a protein that helps cells grow and survive. Under stress from very salty conditions, YAP gathers into droplets called condensates, but what those droplets do was not clear.

The team used a tagging method to list proteins that touch YAP in its spread-out and droplet states. The partner list changed a lot once droplets formed, shifting from grouping genetic material to switching genes on. Three partners, named JUNB, TCF12, and IFI16, sat inside the droplets. Removing JUNB or TCF12 stopped droplets from forming at all and blocked the genes YAP normally turns on.
pmc-13242382:
Söylemez's team at Mersin profiled circular RNAs in the blood of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy patients. Forty-one patients faced 41 matched healthy controls. Five candidate circRNAs were measured by PCR after RNase treatment. The study is the first to test these rings in this epilepsy syndrome.

Two circRNAs ran sharply high in patient blood; a third ran low. Two others showed no difference between groups. The high and low markers both tracked drug resistance. Sex-split patterns emerged too, hinting at marker promise worth follow-up testing. All were blood-based tests, with blood drawn from both groups.
pmc-13242482:
Yusuf Sülek and co-authors asked whether longer spinal fusions speed up wear in the hip and knee. Their cohort study appeared in the Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery in 2026. They reviewed patients aged forty to sixty-five who had lumbar surgery between 2010 and 2021 at one center. Groups ranged from decompression without fusion to fusions spanning four or more vertebrae, and joint space was tracked on imaging.

Hip joint space narrowed fastest in the long-fusion group, then the short-fusion group, then the no-fusion group. Each added fused level raised the odds of severe hip narrowing, while knee wear showed no clear difference between groups. Back and hip function scores were recorded alongside the imaging. The authors advise closer hip monitoring for patients who receive extensive fusions, so degeneration is caught early. The pattern fits the idea that a stiffer spine shifts load onto the hips.
pmc-13243882:
An Huang, Haopeng Hong, and Yonghui Sun profiled colon cancers by the side of the bowel they grow on, layering genes, proteins, and protein switches. Their study appeared in MedComm in 2026. Left-sided and right-sided tumors arise from different embryonic tissue and already behave differently in the clinic. The team ran exome, protein, and phosphoprotein sequencing on eighty tumor-and-normal tissue pairs to find out why.

Left-sided cancers were driven mainly by chromosomal instability and grew dense in blood vessels. Right-sided cancers leaned on microsatellite instability instead, a scrambling caused by failed DNA repair. Their immune neighborhoods also split: right-sided tumors showed stronger antigen display by M1 macrophages. The share of repair-deficient tumors reaching instability differed by side too. The authors argue these differences explain why targeted and immune therapies land unevenly, and they offer the atlas for tailoring treatment by tumor side.
pmc-13244382:
Molly Milano, Alec Giakas, and Eric Tecce describe a spinal abscess that crushed the cord and then starved it of blood. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Surgery in 2026. A man in his sixties came to the emergency department with sudden paralysis of both legs and intense lower back pain. Imaging placed the damage at the fourth thoracic level, where an epidural abscess was compressing the cord and a secondary cord infarction had followed.

Spinal cord infarction is uncommon and its outlook for recovery is generally poor, with causes that often stay murky. The authors walk through the hospital course to show how the two injuries compounded each other. Published guidance for such cases is thin, and their report adds one fully told case to a sparse literature. For emergency teams the lesson is speed: back pain with sudden leg paralysis is a surgical clock.
pmc-13244482:
Genying Gu and colleagues build a learning model that flags drug-resistant infections as patients enter intensive care in 2026. Resistant germs pose a grave threat in such units, and early warning can guide isolation and drug choice. Their model mixes patient factors with facts about the patient's surroundings.

The team studied 420 intensive care patients, split evenly between resistant cases and matched controls. Five factors stood out, including prior stay in long-term care and a resistant germ in the prior bed user. The best model, a boosting method, sorted patients with strong accuracy. Charts that explain each prediction were added, plus a web tool for bedside use.
pmc-13245082:
Li and co-authors published this short correction notice in Molecular Medicine in 2026. It amends their 2025 paper on how alpha-synuclein clumps abnormally in the brain during repeated low-oxygen episodes, and how a compound called Danshensu methyl ester may protect nerve cells from that damage.

The notice fixes the author credit on the original paper. Juan Li, Na Zhang, Ziyin Zhang, and Jinsai Fu are now marked as equal contributors and co-first authors, which the first version had failed to state. No data, results, or conclusions change; the correction simply puts the shared credit on the record for anyone citing the study.
pmc-13246982:
Coniglio and co-authors mined sawmill waste for antifungal chemistry in this 2026 Bioresources and Bioprocessing study. In Uruguay, Pinus taeda plantations feed a large timber industry whose knot-rich offcuts are usually discarded, yet knots concentrate the tree's defensive compounds. The team extracted those compounds with ethanol, tuning temperature, alcohol strength, and solvent ratio to find the best recipe.

Optimized extractions recovered about a fifth of the knotwood's weight, rich in phenolic antioxidants, mainly stilbenes and terpenoids. In laboratory assays the extracts strongly slowed two wood-rotting fungi, nearly stopping one of them within a week. The authors present knotwood residue as a realistic feedstock for natural wood preservatives, turning a disposal problem into a product within a circular bioeconomy.
pmc-13247182:
Seas wrote this 2026 editorial in Open Forum Infectious Diseases. It introduces a journal supplement on managing infectious diseases where resources are scarce. Infections still claim a huge share of global disability and death, concentrated in low- and middle-income countries. The supplement gathers studies on practical responses, from antibiotic stewardship to HIV and tuberculosis care.

The previews include a stewardship program in a Botswana children's surgical unit. They also cover telehealth supporting stewardship in the rural United States, long-acting HIV prevention and shorter tuberculosis regimens in Peru, artificial intelligence reading chest X-rays for tuberculosis, and mobile clinics preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission in Mozambique. The editorial's message is that progress combines simple clinical tools, digital innovation, and community education.
pmc-13247582:
Ali Sadman Mashrafi and co-authors release a road surface image dataset from Bangladesh in a 2026 data paper. Automated road checks need many labeled photos of damage and street furniture. The team gathered theirs across Sylhet District with four phone cameras.

Photos sort into five classes: normal road, manhole, speed breaker, and minor or major damage. Field collection from late 2025 into early 2026 yielded more than six thousand raw images. Careful screening and controlled augmentation raised the set to 9,107 images at a uniform size. The set supports benchmarking of image classifiers for road monitoring and transport research.
pmc-13248482:
Paudyal and co-authors tested machine learning for spotting hidden udder infection in dairy cows, published in 2026. Subclinical mastitis shows no obvious signs yet lowers milk quality, and cell counts in milk are the usual clue. The team combined heat camera images of udders with milk measurements from one hundred ninety-four Holstein cows.

Sampling each quarter of the udder gave nearly eight hundred data points. A random forest model using both image and milk features reached strong accuracy, with milk lactose among the strongest signals. Heat images alone performed noticeably worse. The authors say combined data looks promising, but larger studies must confirm the approach before farm use.
pmc-13249582:
Wen and co-authors sequenced the full mitochondrial genome of a rare Chinese shrew, in a 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Sorex cansulus lives only in China and is classed as near threatened. The team described the animal's form and its mitochondrial DNA, then compared forty-three shrew species across the five tribes of the red-toothed shrew subfamily.

Selection, not chance, had shaped most of the genome's protein-coding genes, and all ran under strong pressure to stay unchanged. Family trees backed several name changes, including splitting this shrew from a close relative as its own species. Three other species shared an odd extra transfer RNA gene, forming their own branch and raising questions about its function.
pmc-13249682:
B. Penninx and co-authors examine how advice on using biological medicines changed after approval, in this 2026 study covering 2006 to 2025. Biologicals are drugs made by living cells, and doubt often remains about their real-world benefit and safety once they reach patients.

The team compared first and current official product summaries for drugs approved in Europe between 2006 and 2010, and checked them against clinical guidelines. Official changes appeared in 47 percent of cases, mostly widening use and mostly backed by maker-funded studies. Guidelines disagreed with the official text in 75 percent of cases, usually urging narrower use. The authors link funding source to the direction of advice.
pmc-13250182:
Khachidze and co-authors chart falling birth rates in the country of Georgia and project where they lead. Their 2026 BMJ Open study uses national statistics and the national birth registry, covering well over half a million births from 2014 to 2024. The team modeled past trends and forecast the decade ahead.

Fertility fell from a little over two children per woman to well under two across the study years. The steepest drops came among teenagers and women in their early twenties, while mothers grew older on average. If recent trends hold, the models project fertility near one child per woman by 2034. The authors warn that this shift could strain Georgia's economy and its social systems in coming years.
pmc-13250382:
Amito and colleagues survey malaria parasites in northern Uganda for gene changes tied to drug resistance. Their 2026 Journal of Parasitology Research study enrolled fever patients at Gulu Regional Referral Hospital between April 2022 and January 2024. Parasite DNA was sequenced for resistance genes in the multidrug and kelch families.

Among three hundred fifty-three recruits, about three in five carried falciparum malaria, confirmed by rapid tests, microscopy, and genetic checks. Fever, chills, and headache dominated the reported symptoms. Resistance-linked variants were widespread, including changes in the kelch gene associated with artemisinin resistance in about one sixth of isolates. The authors urge ongoing monitoring of these markers to protect malaria control in the region and beyond.
pmc-13250882:
Sun and co-authors examine a long non-coding RNA that seems to protect kidneys in diabetes. Their 2026 Renal Failure study compares samples from about one hundred diabetes patients and a similar number with diabetic kidney disease. The RNA, called LINC00472, also gets tested in kidney cells stressed by high sugar.

Levels of the RNA ran low in kidney disease patients and in sugar-stressed cells, and they tracked closely with kidney function measures.
