Adding extra copies calmed the cells, cutting scarring genes and inflammatory signals. A small partner RNA reversed those gains when boosted, and a signaling gene downstream completed the chain. The authors propose the RNA as both a diagnostic marker and a possible treatment lever for the disease.
pmc-13253782:
Agnieszka Kałmykow-Piwińska and Katarzyna Witkowska study flood pollution in a 2026 paper from Poland. They asked how the September 2024 flood changed trace element levels in floodplain mud where the Nysa Kłodzka River meets the Odra Valley. The team mapped the site and took 112 samples from 56 places.

Lab tests on 44 samples showed surface mud held more trace elements than deeper, pre-flood layers. Lead and cadmium rose clearly, and several scoring tools confirmed higher pollution and higher risk to living things. The authors say floods move and spread pollutants across floodplains, not just wash them away.
pmc-13253982:
Shaghayegh Moradi Alamdarloo and co-authors study urinary injuries during major birth surgery in a 2026 paper from Shiraz, Iran. They reviewed patients with placenta accreta spectrum, where the placenta grows too deeply into the womb, who had cesarean hysterectomy at Namazi Hospital from 2015 to 2024.

In all, 115 patients, or 23.09 percent, had a urologic injury during surgery. Heavy blood loss of 3,000 milliliters or more was strongly tied to injury, with adjusted odds of 7.10. The deepest form, placenta percreta, carried higher risk than accreta. The authors urge expert team care and careful planning before surgery.
pmc-13254482:
Abdoulaye Kone and colleagues describe malaria patterns in Bamako, Mali, in a 2026 study. They enrolled fever patients at two community health centers, one urban and one suburban. All ages joined at the urban site, while the suburban site enrolled children under five years.

Malaria from Plasmodium falciparum was found in sixty-eight percent of fever patients at the urban site and about sixty-one percent at the suburban site. Severe cases appeared at the suburban site, including cerebral malaria in about fifteen percent of its cases. Treated mosquito net use was lower in the suburb, far lower in the suburb than in the city. The authors urge keeping control efforts up even in the dry season.
pmc-13254982:
Jessica Nelson and co-authors present a 2026 case of knee damage caused by long-standing muscle imbalance after spinal tumor surgery. Their patient was a 72-year-old woman who had a spinal ependymoma removed in 2007. Weakness afterward slowly bent both knees far out of line over 18 years, and she eventually lost the ability to walk.

Because she kept normal sensation, her condition differs from Charcot joint disease, where feeling is lost. Surgeons replaced each knee in stages using hinged implants, the most constrained type of knee replacement. The operations restored alignment and stability, eased her pain, and got her moving again. The authors propose hinged replacement as a workable option for carefully chosen patients with this rare problem.
pmc-13255082:
Mardiah Rahmadani and co-authors present a 2026 meta-analysis on feeding oil palm fronds to ruminant livestock. The fronds are an abundant farm by-product, yet their low protein and high lignin make them poor feed on their own. Farms have tried biological, chemical, and physical processing to upgrade them.

Pooling 25 studies found through Scopus, the analysis showed processing raised crude protein and cut lignin in the fronds. Fermentation in the rumen and nutrient breakdown improved in both laboratory and animal tests, with no harm to animal performance. Chemical treatment reduced lignin the most, though all three routes helped. The authors conclude that sensible processing can turn a waste stream into a useful, sustainable feed resource.
pmc-13255582:
Qian Huang and co-authors describe a 2026 computer vision system for finding animals in drone photographs of grassland. Herd monitoring by foot patrol is slow and patchy, while drones cover ground quickly, except that animals shrink to tiny specks in aerial views. Their model, DMN-YOLO, adapts a popular detection network for these small targets.

The system was designed to spot several species at once, including cattle, sheep, and wild animals, against confusing grass and shadow backgrounds. In tests it identified most animal targets and beat the original model it was based on, while also being smaller in size. A compact model matters because field equipment has limited computing power. The authors offer the tool for grazing management, wildlife protection patrols, and grassland conservation work.
pmc-13255782:
Yiting Liu and co-authors report a 2026 study of scent communication in captive forest musk deer, an endangered solitary species from China. For a territorial animal that rarely meets others, chemical messages in urine and feces carry social information. The team observed how deer reacted to each and analyzed the urine's chemistry.

Deer responded much more strongly to urine than to feces, marking urine as the main message channel. Instruments identified 83 volatile compounds in the urine. Those chemical profiles reliably separated males from females and even distinguished individual deer, with different compound sets carrying each kind of information. The authors describe a layered coding system and say the findings can improve captive breeding management and reproductive monitoring for conservation.
pmc-13255882:
Xue Mao and colleagues report a 2026 pot study on growing Cymbidium faberi, a prized traditional Chinese orchid, with help from microbial inoculants. Heavy chemical fertilizer use in orchid growing compacts soil and upsets its microbes, so the team tested combinations of fertilizer with beneficial microorganisms instead. Different blends were compared for plant growth and soil bacterial community effects.

The winning treatment combined fertilizer with two kinds of microorganisms. Plants under that blend grew significantly better, and the soil's bacterial community shifted into a healthier state. Other combinations helped less or changed the soil without the same growth payoff. The authors conclude that well-matched microbial agents create soil conditions this orchid prefers. They pitch the approach as a greener path for the ornamental flower industry.
pmc-13255982:
Jonas E. Gallão and co-authors describe two new cave-dwelling harvestman species from Bahia in northeastern Brazil in a 2026 paper. Both belong to Giupponia, a genus that held a single known species from its naming in 2002 until now. The animals came from the Serra do Ramalho karst, a cave-rich landscape.

These species are troglobites, meaning they live only underground, in humid darkness. Formal species descriptions record their anatomy and how they differ from their one known relative. The authors note that Brazilian cave harvestmen have drawn renewed research interest recently, helped by environmental protection laws. Naming new species, they argue, is not stamp collecting: records like these underpin conservation decisions for cave systems that shelter many still-undescribed animals.
pmc-13256482:
Siqing Chen and co-authors describe a 2026 Delphi study, a method that builds expert agreement through repeated survey rounds. Their goal was a mobile health program to cut sitting time in older adults, who may sit for up to thirteen hours a day. Long sitting is linked to heart disease, diabetes-type disorders, memory decline, and early death, yet few tested phone programs target it in this age group.

The team first built a draft program from past studies, clinical guidelines, interviews, and a survey. Sixteen experts in old-age care, behavior science, and health promotion then refined it over two rounds, with every expert responding both times. They settled on 27 items in three parts: building capability, creating opportunity, and raising motivation, using tools such as goal-setting, feedback, and social support.
pmc-13257482:
Carmela Protano and co-authors develop a sweat-based test for metals that can leach from tattoo inks in a 2026 methods study. Regulators need exposure-relevant measures, yet no standard extraction exists for inks under skin-contact conditions. Seventy-eight commercial inks in many colors were soaked in artificial sweat and measured by mass spectrometry.

Soluble barium, copper, and zinc stayed below European limits in the tested inks. Full digestion still gives total content, while the sweat method estimates what skin might actually meet. Safety assessors gain a transferable tool. Wider adoption could finally make ink studies comparable across laboratories and brands.
pmc-13257682:
Galya Duncheva leads a 2026 study of finishing steps for 3D-printed stainless steel cylinders. Laser-printed 17-4PH parts received two heat treatment routes and diamond burnishing at two forces in a staged design. Printing settings were first optimized, then every finishing combination was tested for strength and surface state.

The richer heat route, ending with deep cooling and aging, delivered the highest yield and tensile strength plus strong hardness. Adding firm burnishing pushed surface hardness higher still and locked in deep compressive stresses in both directions. A small share of retained austenite remained in the best samples. Aerospace and tooling engineers gain a combined recipe that stacks transformation, precipitation, and strain hardening. Printed parts can approach wrought quality when finishing is treated as design, not cleanup.
pmc-13257782:
Melissa L deJonge and colleagues report a 2026 study comparing virtual and in-person exercise programs for college and university students. Physically inactive students with signs of mental ill health joined a six-week structured program led by supervisors. The team measured anxiety and depression symptoms, social connectedness and relationship quality, and overall well-being before and after the program, across three phases of the project.

The in-person group had 87 students and the virtual group 62. Both forms cut symptoms and improved social inclusion and well-being, with moderate-to-large effects, and outcomes did not differ significantly by delivery mode. Gains in social inclusion helped explain better well-being in both groups. The authors say online exercise programs can widen access to mental health prevention for students.
pmc-13258882:
Zhichao Lin, Xiuling Wang, and Yuyang Guo combine visible and heat images to find solar panel faults in a 2026 study. Faults such as hotspots and shorted diodes cut power output and raise safety risk. Single camera methods struggle under changing light and weak heat signals.

Gradient aware fusion aligned features from both image types before detection. Accuracy rose while model size, parameter count, and computing cost all fell. Recall improved notably once a shape aware training loss was added. Separate tests on a public thermal dataset showed consistent gains. Plant operators gain a lighter inspection model that still catches more real faults.
pmc-13258982:
Matylda Kosiorz and coauthors map lifestyle changes after a fibromyalgia diagnosis in a 2026 survey study. Eighty eight patients answered a custom questionnaire on diet and activity changes made since diagnosis. Network and grouping methods searched for patterns in those changes.

Patients most often raised vegetable and water intake. Meat, alcohol, and sweet drinks were the items most often cut. Three groups emerged, from minimal changers to broad changers covering about half, a third, and a sixth of patients. Change pattern showed no link to symptom severity in their tests. Care teams learn that patient self management follows structured habits worth supporting directly.
pmc-13259082:
Alla I. Perfileva and coauthors test a selenium seed soak on sick soybean seeds in a 2026 study. A germ that rots many crops was put on seeds, with or without a selenium based prime step. Young plant fats were checked five days after seeds sprouted.

Seed fat centered on five main fatty acids. The prime step alone left seed fat as it was. Young plants showed a richer mix, with fats that span twelve to twenty carbons. The germ raised the share of soft fats in young plants. Primed sick seeds showed softer harm shifts while growth gains held. Seed firms gain a guard choice backed by fat level proof.
pmc-13261482:
Taiwo Bakare-Abidola and colleagues developed in 2026 reusable beads that pull methylene blue dye out of wastewater. The beads blend alginate and chitosan, two natural polymers, with a menthol-thymol solvent drawn from plant oils. A statistical design method then searched for the best working conditions.

At the tuned settings, the beads removed just over ninety-five percent of the dye, close to the model's own forecast. Uptake followed second-order kinetics, the pattern of a chemically driven grab, and layered coverage on varied surface sites. The process absorbed heat and ran spontaneously under the tested conditions. Most striking, the beads kept removing over ninety-five percent after six rounds of use and regeneration. The authors pitch them as a green option for dye-heavy factory wastewater.
pmc-13261582:
Xuan Liu and colleagues built in 2026 soft fiber mats that break down a common antibiotic drug in water using shaking and light. The drug, ofloxacin, lingers in water and can breed drug resistance. Their mats mix a charge-forming plastic with bismuth ferrite grains doped with two added metals.

The grains seeded the plastic's active crystal form and boosted its charge response. Under shaking alone, the best mat broke down the drug about a fifth faster than the plain plastic. Adding light created a joint effect that cleared most of the drug within three hours. Tests pinned the attack mainly on superoxide radicals and positive holes in the mat. After five reuse rounds the mat kept nearly all its power and its form. The authors present the mats as reusable cleaners for drug-laced wastewater.
pmc-13262582:
Alimujiang Yusufu and colleagues show that where bone cement lands inside a crushed vertebra decides how well the repair works. Vertebroplasty injects cement through a needle to stabilize osteoporotic fractures. Their 2026 review of one hundred forty-five first-time patients sorts X-rays by cement coverage into three groups.

Scanty coverage lagged on every measure. Pushing beyond two-thirds coverage added nothing further, giving surgeons a clear target: cross the middle, then stop.
pmc-13262882:
Ali Sultan Khazaal Nazal and colleagues use computer methods to search for a new HIV blocker in a 2026 journal article. HIV-1 protease is an enzyme the virus needs to mature, and drugs against it are a mainstay of treatment, though resistance grows. The team built a shape-based model from a known blocker complex and screened a drug library for matches.

One candidate, shortened to BAN, emerged from the screen. Docking tests predicted it binds slightly more strongly than the reference blocker. Simulations over 100 nanoseconds showed many tight hydrogen bonds and strong total binding energy. Yet the candidate also made the enzyme more flexible and broke stable salt bridges. The authors propose it as a new scaffold needing lab validation.
pmc-13262982:
Ludmila Anjos de Jesus and colleagues describe nursing technician training in Brazil's federal education network in a 2026 journal article. These mid-level courses prepare the largest share of the nursing workforce for direct patient care. The team analyzed the official teaching plans of 26 courses, using a structured outline and content analysis, to map how the courses are organized and taught.

Shared aims included quality training rooted in social needs and active teaching methods that engage students. Weaknesses included gaps in how plans were assembled and mismatches between stated goals and practical placements. Internship arrangements varied inconsistently between courses. Focus on the Brazilian public health system was still weak, the authors found, and they urge updates to strengthen training.
pmc-13263282:
William Alves de Melo Júnior and co-authors study mouth sores and quality of life in children with leukemia in a 2026 journal article. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common childhood cancer, and its drug methotrexate often causes painful mouth inflammation. All patients in this Brazilian university hospital study also received light therapy for the mouth as routine care.

The cross-sectional study covered 113 patients aged 5 to 18 treated from 2020 to 2024. Most, 85 percent, reported a high impact on quality of life. Worse sores, older age, higher drug doses, and slower healing all tracked with worse quality of life. In adjusted analysis, sore severity and healing time stayed significant. The authors note the design cannot prove the light therapy's own effect.
pmc-13263882:

Their dataset held 105,554 patients diagnosed between 2000 and 2021. The question matters because the label oligometastatic, meaning limited spread, decides who gets extra local therapy.

The authors argue the metastatic site belongs inside any future definition of limited spread. Lumping all sites together, their data suggest, misleads treatment planning.
pmc-13263982:

Outcomes vary widely after an operation, and standard staging alone gives limited personal guidance. The team studied sixty-one patients treated at a Beijing hospital between 2008 and 2022, combining health status before surgery, ultrasound features and pathology results after surgery.

From these factors the authors built a nomogram, a visual scoring chart, to estimate survival at one, three and five years. Internal checks tested how well the scores separated patients and matched observed outcomes. The tool is presented as an aid for risk grouping and follow-up planning.
pmc-13264082:
Changyuan Chen and a large team report a 2026 pan-cancer analysis linking extra copies of chromosome region 8q24 to poor response to immunotherapy. Drugs that release immune brakes help only a minority of patients, and dependable predictors are scarce. Profiling more than ten thousand tumors showed this amplification in about one in ten cancers, with validation in several treatment cohorts.

Tumors with the change held fewer T cells and showed weaker antigen presentation, the process that flags cancer cells for attack. A combined score using this change plus mutation burden and PD-L1 levels identified likely non-responders more effectively. Drug screens in cell lines also revealed weaknesses specific to this group, suggesting combination strategies worth testing in defined patients.
pmc-13264582:
Maria A Papanikolaou and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on the Hippo signaling pathway, a chain of signals that controls cell growth, in brain tumors of children. These tumors are the second most common cancer in children, and standard care can harm the growing brain. Targeted drugs aimed at this pathway offer a possible new route.

The review explains how the pathway links with many other signal chains that drive growth. In high-grade tumors, switching on two partner proteins, YAP and TAZ, helps tumors grow, and blocking YAP slowed tumor growth in lab animals. YAP activity can also help tell severe tumors from milder ones. The authors map which tumor subsets might suit drugs against this pathway.
pmc-13264782:
Esmat Najjar and colleagues report robotic thyroid surgery through the armpit in children in a 2026 institutional study. Fifteen patients aged eighteen or younger had the operation between 2012 and 2022, most of them adolescents and most female. Reasons included uncertain needle results, confirmed papillary cancer and benign goiter. The approach avoids a neck scar, a benefit with lifelong cosmetic and psychological weight for young patients facing thyroid disease.

About half had one lobe removed and half the whole gland, with central neck node clearance in a third. Operating times averaged around three and a half hours and shortened with experience in later cases. No comparison group existed, so results are descriptive. Feasibility and safety in selected children are the main claims.
pmc-13264882:
Meresa Berwo Mengesha and colleagues synthesize evidence on group antenatal care in sub-Saharan Africa in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Group care blends medical checks with education and peer support in shared sessions. Individual African studies looked promising for keeping mothers in care and improving birth outcomes, but pooled evidence on feasibility and acceptability was missing. Searches across major databases followed standard review guidance to gather trials and evaluations from resource-limited settings.

The synthesis weighs whether women and providers accept the model, whether clinics can run it and whether outcomes improve versus individual visits. Gaps for future research are mapped alongside effects. Policy makers weighing maternal mortality strategies gain a regional evidence base rather than scattered pilot reports from single countries.
pmc-13264982:
Xiayun Zhou and colleagues present a 2026 study of brain excitability in generalized anxiety disorder, a long-term condition of excessive worry. Its brain basis is unclear, so the team used magnetic brain stimulation to probe the motor cortex on both sides, and measured two key brain chemicals in blood.

They compared 30 unmedicated patients with 30 matched healthy controls. Patients showed an uneven pattern: the left motor area was harder to excite and gave weaker responses, while the right gave stronger responses than in controls. The left-to-right balance was clearly reduced. Two other measures did not differ after strict correction. Blood levels of glutamate and GABA, the main go and stop chemicals, were also off balance. The authors suggest the paired measures as objective markers to support clinical judgment.
pmc-13266882:
Xue Lv, Fei Du, and Jie Fang compare in 2026 two imaging routes used to diagnose blood clots in the lungs at a hospital in Shandong, China. One route scans ventilation and blood flow together, while the other uses CT angiography, the usual first-line test. Their study reviewed 726 confirmed clot patients treated between 2017 and 2022.

Patients sent for the ventilation-flow scan more often had large central clots, lower oxygen, and a strained right heart, with higher blood markers of strain and injury. The CT group generally looked milder at presentation. A combined model using several measures separated the groups well. The authors argue that each test serves a distinct patient profile in real practice.
pmc-13267682:
Rachael C Crew and co-authors present in 2026 a sheep model of obesity during pregnancy, built to track a mother's circulation in real time. Obese ewes were fed freely on rich feed before and during pregnancy, while controls ate a standard diet. Implanted flow probes and wireless recording let the team measure blood flow in freely moving animals near term.

Obese mothers entered pregnancy about thirty percent heavier and showed high blood sugar, insulin, and fats, plus raised blood pressure near term. Effects on the womb artery depended on the lamb's sex. Mothers carrying females had higher resistance and weaker vessel relaxation, while those carrying males shifted toward a different relaxation pathway. Fetal sex shapes how maternal obesity strains the womb's blood supply.
pmc-13267982:
Nobuyuki Okamoto and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a groin abscess with a hidden cause. Their patient was an 84-year-old woman with advanced breast cancer and a known groin hernia. Four days after breast surgery, a mass in her right groin began to grow. Scans showed a fluid pocket, and a needle draw confirmed pus.

Simple care calmed the abscess for a time, but it returned near the start of the large bowel about a month later. Surgery then revealed a partly burst appendix. Inflammation had spread behind the belly lining to the groin, outside the hernia sac, an unusual route. Removing the appendix solved the problem, with no return at three months. The authors urge early imaging for groin swelling in hernia patients.
pmc-13269782:
Robert S Wong and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on Cx36, a protein that forms direct channels between nerve cells, often called electrical synapses. New detailed structures showed charged spots where two half-channels dock together. The team altered those spots and measured whether working channels still formed.

Computer calculations and electrical recordings in paired engineered cells were combined. At least three charge-matched pairs at each docking face were needed for a working channel. These charge patterns also seemed to keep Cx36 pairing with itself rather than with other brain channel proteins. The authors say the findings explain how these junctions form and choose partners, guiding future treatments for channel faults.
pmc-13269982:
Gabriela Plasencia and co-authors published a policy review in 2026 on language access in United States health care. Over 68 million Americans speak another language at home, and Spanish speakers form 62 percent of that group. The review covered studies, federal rules, and professional guidelines from 2004 to 2025.

Professional interpreters and language-matched care are recommended, yet barriers persist in practice. The authors call for payments that reward better language support and stronger penalties for poor performers. Health systems should test and use bilingual staff skills in an organized way. Language support must also be built into technology standards. The goal is safer care and better experience for patients who prefer other languages.
pmc-13270482:
Yifan Yang and co-authors report in 2026 a hard-won catheter valve replacement in a 59-year-old man whose aorta had been rebuilt before, leaving it exceptionally stiff. Severe narrowing of his aortic valve caused symptoms, but the path from the leg artery crossed an artificial arch, a stent, and a plugged leak. The team weighed five tricks for stiff, twisted anatomy, from buddy wires to snare assistance.

A balloon-assisted tracking technique combined with a long protective sheath finally carried the device through, and the valve anchored successfully in the narrowed zone above the valve ring. The case summary distills a strategy ladder for what the authors call super-stiff anatomy. They also note that in two-leaflet valves, that narrowed zone can serve as a dependable anchor.
pmc-13270882:
Xinhe Wang is lead author of a 2026 journal article re-analysing single-cell gene data from a mouse model of oxygen-induced retinopathy, an eye disease like the one that can blind premature babies. In this disease, low oxygen in the retina drives abnormal new blood vessels that may pull the retina loose.

Using a public data set of mouse retinal tissue, the team sorted cells into ten types and compared gene activity between normal and diseased eyes. Several genes were turned up, including Hnrnpu and Vamp2, and others, including Xist, were turned down. Network analysis flagged hub genes such as Srsf1 and Sf3b1, and the authors discuss how changes in these genes may shape the disease.
pmc-13271282:
Mohamed A. Mabrok wrote a 2026 benchmark study on how breast X-ray classification results are reported. Deep learning papers on mammography often report scores per breast side or per patient, and that choice, he argues, makes results across studies hard to compare fairly.

Using 706 patients with four-view mammograms from a Chinese database, Mabrok tested six model designs crossed with three ways of combining views, under patient-level cross-checking. Side-level scores beat patient-level scores by an average of 17.5 percentage points, far more than the gaps between model designs, which were under three points. A large transformer model trailed every simpler network despite having many more parameters. The lesson is that reporting level drives headline performance.
pmc-13271382:
Donald S. Herzog is lead author of a 2026 cattle feeding study on adding rumen-protected lysine, an essential protein building block shielded from stomach digestion, to lower-protein grain diets for beef cattle. Lower protein diets could cut costs and nitrogen waste, but only if growth does not suffer.

Two experiments tested a standard 14.4 percent protein diet against reduced diets at 12.4 and 11.6 percent protein with lysine added. Ninety steers showed no diet effect on weight gain, feed intake, efficiency, or most carcass traits, though the lowest-protein group had a lower dressing percentage. Six heifers in a rotation design were used to measure nitrogen balance, tracking urine and manure output.
pmc-13271582:
Naoki Iso is lead author of a 2026 development and validation study of VRactice, a virtual reality system for upper-limb rehabilitation training that adds feedback on body position. Virtual reality can aid motor learning, but few studies have checked its tracking accuracy against gold-standard motion capture, especially for arm reaching with shop-bought setups.

Sixteen healthy adults, average age 25.3, performed reaching tasks while tracked at once by VRactice and by a professional Vicon system, with sensors on hand and elbow. The study compared the three-dimensional paths from both systems over the half second before peak reach. The design tests whether the cheaper virtual system measures movement closely enough for rehabilitation use.
pmc-13272082:
Bolun Xu and coauthors tell in 2026 of a large tree branch hidden inside a man's eye socket that was first mistaken for infection. A 60-year-old man arrived with a swollen, painful right eye two days after a branch cut, and antibiotics did not help. Hidden plant material in the orbit is easy to miss and dangerous to leave.

MRI revealed a linear abnormal signal inside an eye muscle, pointing to a retained branch with infected pockets around it. Emergency surgery removed a two-centimeter piece, followed by cleaning and standard medicines. Vision recovered steadily, and double vision had fully cleared by the two-month check.
pmc-13272182:
Yiquan Ji and Bao Chen wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about a study of C-reactive protein patterns after spine surgery and the effect of vancomycin powder placed in the wound. That study, a secondary analysis of a randomised trial in lumbar fusion patients, supported the protein's level on day seven as a rule-out marker for surgical site infection.

The letter praises the work, then argues the analysis missed pathogen type. Aggressive bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus provoke strong inflammation, while low-grade organisms may raise the protein only slightly despite real infection, so one threshold could miss slow infections. It also notes monitoring stopped at seven days, too early for delayed, biofilm-linked infections, and urges combined microbe and marker models.
pmc-13272282:
Martin Seiser leads a 2026 study that builds a low-cost frame to hold broken long bones still from outside the body. Such frames are vital where commercial systems are too costly or hard to obtain. The team made the frame from threaded rods, washers, and nuts sold for building work.

Five designs were tested on young cow bones with a set fracture gap, under repeated up-and-down loading. The commercial frame was stiffest, but the Steinmann pin and two-sided smooth wire designs were close, and no clear gap separated them from it. The authors call the result a first proof of concept, needing more tests before patient use.
pmc-13272382:
Zhaojie Wang and Jing Pang evaluate in 2026 a family collaboration care model for older patients with drug-resistant tuberculosis of the lungs. Treatment is long and demanding, and how patients understand their illness shapes whether they persist. Bringing family into nursing care may strengthen that understanding and daily self-management.

Records from a Henan chest hospital covered 57 elderly patients treated between 2022 and 2024, split between standard and family-collaboration care. The family group reported healthier illness perceptions, clearly higher self-management scores, and better quality of life in every domain. Effect sizes were large, supporting family involvement in resistant tuberculosis care.
pmc-13272482:
Qilan Li, Jinwei Tu, and Biao Zeng examined school leadership and teacher skill in a 2026 survey study. They asked whether transformational leadership, a style that inspires and supports staff, links to teachers' social and emotional competence. They also tested three paths that might carry that link.

The team surveyed 760 primary and secondary school teachers and fitted a multiple mediation model. Leadership showed a clear positive link with teacher competence. Teaching efficacy, meaning teachers' confidence in their own teaching, carried the strongest indirect path. The teacher and student relationship path was real but small, while school climate showed no clear path. Results also shifted somewhat across separate leadership dimensions.
pmc-13272682:
Tao Yang leads a 2026 study linking a protein called AKAP1 to glycogen build-up and liver cancer in mice. Glycogen is a stored form of sugar, and its handling is rewired in many cancers for reasons that are not clear. The team raised or lowered AKAP1 in mouse livers.

Lower AKAP1 cut liver glycogen and slowed both chemical-induced and gene-driven liver cancers, while higher AKAP1 did the reverse. AKAP1 helps a partner protein break down the message for an enzyme that frees sugar, raising glycogen. A peptide that blocks AKAP1 from reaching its site lowered glycogen and curbed cancer in mice, with no clear toxicity seen.
pmc-13272882:
Azar Darvishpour leads a 2026 study of wisdom, sense of coherence, and quality of life in older hospital patients in northern Iran. Sense of coherence means feeling that life is understandable and manageable. The team surveyed 200 patients in hospitals in eastern Guilan in 2024, using standard scales for all three measures.

Most participants were men aged 60 to 74. Both wisdom and sense of coherence linked positively to quality of life, and together the model explained 41.5 percent of its variation. Sense of coherence had a slightly stronger link than wisdom. The authors suggest that programs building these inner resources could help older patients feel better and cope with illness.
pmc-13273482:
Yu Guo and colleagues reviewed research advances and management strategies for frailty in older adults in a 2026 article. Frailty means shrinking physical reserve and greater risk from small stresses, and it predicts disability and death. Care needs better ways to spot and counter it early.

The review ties frailty mainly to whole body dysregulation, with clashes between metabolism and immunity plus faults in the muscle and mitochondria axis standing out. Classic bedside scales still anchor diagnosis, while gene and protein profiling and wearable sensor markers promise earlier, finer risk sorting. For care, combined programs of resistance exercise, better nutrition, and medication review form the core. The authors push for mechanism based precision care and digital tools that build resilience.
pmc-13273682:
Prajwal Ghimire and a large group of co-authors made the case in a 2026 article for two way exchange in global neurosurgery. Operable brain conditions go untreated in rich and poor countries alike, though the mix differs. Traditional missions send skills one way, from wealthy centers outward.

The authors describe a partnership between Nepal and the United Kingdom built to run in both directions. British faculty taught a hands-on cadaver course and oncology workshop in Nepal, while a Nepalese trainee spent six weeks observing advanced practice in Britain. Feedback from ten faculty on both sides rated the learning as genuinely mutual and well matched to local needs. Most planned changes to their practice. The group proposes this reciprocal model for wider international use.
pmc-13273882:
Guilherme Dall'Agnol Deconto and co-authors released a multimodal dataset for detecting room occupancy in a 2026 data article. Smart buildings save energy when they know how many people are present, and many sensor types might carry that signal. Their data come from a real university workspace in Brazil.

Sensors logged carbon dioxide, temperature, humidity, light, and sound every few seconds, alongside power, voltage, and current from smart sockets and switches. A custom built node and commercial devices fed one shared timeline. The key label, the true number of occupants, began as camera based counts from a detection model and was then checked by hand against every image. The public set includes raw readings, device logs, and full setup documents for energy and anomaly research.
pmc-13273982:
Ebraheem Albazee and co-authors pooled trials of dexmedetomidine during thyroid surgery in a 2026 meta-analysis. The drug calms patients and steadies circulation, and its use around surgery is growing. Whether the overall balance of benefit and harm is favorable for thyroid operations was unsettled.

Ten randomized trials with 863 patients were combined. Blood pressure and heart rate ran lower with the drug around tube removal, and pain scores fell at several points in the first day, with less rescue pain medicine needed. Coughing on waking and sickness after surgery also dropped. Waking and tube removal took longer, and low blood pressure was more common, while slow heart rate was not clearly increased. Stay length did not change.
pmc-13274082:
Chinyang Henry Tseng and co-authors tested data balancing for predicting death in emergency department patients in a 2026 study. Deaths are rare next to survivals, so machine learning models trained on raw records often miss the patients most at risk. Balancing the training data might fix that skew.

They used more than two million non-trauma adult visit records from five Taiwan medical centers, covering deaths within one, three, and seven days and overall. Three balancing methods were paired with several learning algorithms. The best model passed earlier work on the same data, and its hits and correct clearances were far more even than a prior lopsided model. Simple random oversampling of deaths worked best overall, and age plus triage level gained importance in the balanced data.
pmc-13274482:
Weimo Li and colleagues wrote a 2026 review article on the electron buffer effect, an idea for keeping catalysts in their best working state. During electricity-driven reactions, a catalyst's electronic structure can shift irreversibly, draining activity and stability. A buffer support can lend or take electrons reversibly, much as a chemical buffer steadies acidity.

The review explains how this steadying keeps active sites at the right oxidation state and tunes how reaction intermediates stick and release. It sorts buffer materials into metal-based and non-metal-based families and surveys their roles in key reactions such as splitting water and reducing carbon dioxide. The authors close with the measurement challenges of proving and precisely controlling the effect.
pmc-13274682:
Tao Meng and colleagues wrote a 2026 review article on turning genetic findings about osteoarthritis into useful clinical tests. Osteoarthritis, the wear-and-pain joint disease, varies hugely between patients, yet doctors lack early risk tools. Gene studies have found many risk spots, but most are small, noncoding, and active only in certain joint tissues.

The review maps a route from gene signal to biomarker. First, pin down the likely effector gene, then place it in the right cells using single-cell and spatial maps of cartilage and bone. Promising outputs include polygenic risk scores, compact molecular test panels, and imaging-plus-omics models. Pitfalls include ancestry limits and tissue access, and the authors set out standards for safe deployment.
pmc-13275082:
Emma L Hutton and co-authors present a 2026 quality improvement report on empowering nurses to lead change in a specialist acute stroke unit. Happy, engaged nurses are linked to safer care, so the project aimed to lift both staff experience and patient outcomes. The team used the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle, a test-and-learn method, inside a daily team framework.

They tracked nurse and patient satisfaction surveys plus safety indicators: falls, pressure injuries from hospital care, catheter infections, and hand hygiene. The report describes significant improvements in falls, pressure injuries, and hand hygiene adherence, while patient satisfaction scores rose. Nurse satisfaction results also improved. The authors stress the changes were relatively easy to implement yet highly impactful.
pmc-13275982:
Sedef Akçaalan and co-authors present a 2026 laboratory study on pairing a plant compound with gene silencing against breast cancer. The compound is quercetin, found in many foods. The gene, XBP1, helps cancer cells survive stress and has been tied to breast cancer growth.

Working with two breast cancer cell lines, the team applied quercetin, switched off XBP1, or did both. Each step alone slowed cell growth and colony formation. Together they worked better than either one. The combined treatment raised signals that drive programmed cell death. It also shifted markers tied to how cancer cells spread, in a direction linked to less spreading. The authors suggest pairing gene-based tools with plant compounds deserves further study as a treatment strategy.
pmc-13276282:
Kagisho Madikadike Molabe and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on genes behind eggshell quality in a South African chicken breed. Cracked eggs waste food and money and let germs in. The Potchefstroom Koekoek is a local breed valued for hardiness, and shell thickness is a key trait for its eggs.

The team kept one hundred hens and collected three hundred fifty eggs over nine weeks of laying. They measured shell traits and read DNA from blood and egg-making tissues. Two single-letter DNA changes in a gene called SCNN1G tracked with shell thickness. Birds with one letter form laid thicker shells than birds with the other. The gene was most active in the magnum, the tube section where egg white forms. The authors say such markers could guide breeding for stronger shells.
pmc-13276582:
Kunjie Wu and co-authors report a 2026 aquaponics trial pairing largemouth bass with hairy basil. Bass farming in China faces heavy losses from bacterial disease, and antibiotic use brings resistance and residue worries. Growing plants in the fish water may clean the water and support fish health at once.

The team built a working aquaponic system with the basil variety and tracked water and fish outcomes. Levels of ammonia and nitrite nitrogen in the water fell under the plant system. Fish showed stronger immune and antioxidant responses than comparison fish. Deaths after bacterial challenge dropped, and gut damage was reduced, which supports plant-based water care as a drug-sparing option.
pmc-13276782:
William Aboucaya and Dastan Jasim present a 2026 linked dataset of doctoral theses defended in France over forty years. Records cover defences from 1985 to 2025 and draw on several national academic sources. Linking them supports research on supervision, examination juries, and how academic communities evolve.

The national thesis platform supplied the core records, enriched with authority and library databases. The pipeline fixed faulty identifiers and added details on people, institutions, and careers. Extra identifiers from major repositories make outside linkage easier for future users. The authors document data quality problems and limits openly, and the dataset is freely posted on Zenodo for reuse.
pmc-13277082:
Bea Klos leads a 2026 study of smell in children and teens with obesity during a stay-in weight loss program. Smell shapes eating behavior, yet little work has tested it in young patients. Sixty young people, about thirteen years old on average, joined a program mixing food therapy, activity, stress care, and behavior work for about thirty-eight days.

Smell tests covered detection, telling odors apart, and naming odors, before and after the program. At the start, scores were mostly in the normal range for their age. After weight loss, only odor naming improved a little; other scores held steady and did not track weight change. Self-ratings of smell also matched test results poorly, the team found.
pmc-13277782:
Clayton C McIntyre leads a 2026 study asking whether a single moment of brain activity can identify a person. Brain network fingerprinting uses patterns of linked activity, like a fingerprint, to tell people apart. Most work averages over whole scans. This team instead estimated links from single scan frames, split-second snapshots, using a phase-based method.

Given enough reference data, single frames could be matched to the right person. Finer maps of brain regions made matching easier. Tasks were also easier to spot within a person than across people, meaning task patterns are more personal than shared. Individual variation may drive much of what single-frame studies see, the authors conclude, so designs must account for it.
pmc-13278382:
Meghan E Carey leads a 2026 study of depression treatment for autistic young people on Medicaid, the United States safety-net health program. Getting treatment after a depression diagnosis can lower suicide risk, yet access is uneven. The team tracked 44,074 autistic enrollees aged eight to twenty-nine for five months after a new depression claim, grouping similar treatment paths.

Four paths emerged. About thirty-nine percent got little or no treatment, while only about twenty-five percent were treated continuously. Others declined gradually or started late. Continuous treatment was less likely for Black and Hispanic enrollees and for those with intellectual disability, and most likely for the youngest group and for females. Many autistic enrollees get no depression care at all.
pmc-13278982:
Jing Guo and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis comparing two pacing strategies for heart failure patients who need cardiac resynchronization therapy. Conduction system pacing stimulates the heart's own wiring, while biventricular pacing stimulates both lower chambers at once. The team pooled 35 studies with 7,019 patients whose hearts pumped weakly.

Across the pooled trials and observational studies, conduction system pacing improved pumping function and narrowed the electrical signal more than biventricular pacing. It also lowered heart failure hospitalizations and shortened X-ray guidance time during implantation, while complication rates stayed similar and overall mortality did not differ clearly. Benefits looked strongest in patients with the classic indications for resynchronization. The authors caution that the certainty of the evidence rates low to very low, so stronger trials are still needed.
pmc-13279282:
Parisa Mazdarani and James Edward Miles report a 2026 lab study of a knee surgery for cats. Cat knee joints, called stifles, can lose steadiness when a key ligament tears. Past bone cut methods failed to restore steadiness in cat limbs. The team test a method called CBLO, which levels the shin bone top by a cut set from a rotation point.

Ten cat hind limbs were pressed in a rig that kept hip motion free. Tests ran with the joint whole, after ligament cut and after surgery. Surgery cut the shin slope from near twenty four degrees to near nine degrees. Yet joint shift stayed like the cut ligament state, not the whole state. In this model, the cut did not restore steadiness.
pmc-13279482:
Alexander Darup and colleagues report a 2026 study of antibiotic powder placed in joints at hip and knee replacement. Joint infection after replacement is a grave side effect that can need more surgery. From January 2023, their centre added one gram of vancomycin powder in the joint before closure as a shield. The study asks if the powder cuts infection rates and if it harms wound healing.

Charts held one thousand four hundred ninety nine first hip and knee replacements from 2022 to 2023. Of those, eight hundred eighteen got the powder and six hundred eighty one did not. The title gives the core result: the powder acts as just a partial shield. Infections were pushed later in time, not stopped for good. Time to infection, wound issues and infection rates were all compared across the two groups.
pmc-13279682:
Raphael Fougeray and colleagues report a 2026 study of moth outbreaks on the coast of French Guiana. The ashen moth Hylesia metabus has females with stinging scales that cause severe skin reactions. Outbreaks hit coasts of Venezuela and French Guiana, yet stay local and hard to forecast. The team ask what habitat and climate traits mark outbreak prone sites.

Field work at thirteen sites read forest shape, tree species mix, canopy cover and bird attack rates on prey. Climate models added rain and heat patterns for each site. Outbreak prone sites held low tree density overall. They also showed small daily heat swings and sharp seasonal shifts between dry and wet seasons. Bird predation rates were weighed as a further check. Such trait maps could warn health teams where skin outbreak risk runs high.
pmc-13280082:
Samantha K Kurosky and colleagues published a 2026 database analysis of ritlecitinib for severe alopecia areata in the United States. The oral drug blocks JAK3 and TEC-family enzymes and is approved for patients twelve and older with this autoimmune hair loss condition. Hair regrowth became more common the longer patients stayed on treatment, rising from 49 percent under three months to 82 percent beyond six months. Recent starters felt embarrassment, frustration, and anxiety from their hair loss before treatment. Physicians chose the drug for its ability to cut scalp hair loss. The authors conclude that sustained treatment matters for reaching goals, a point for setting patient expectations.
pmc-13280382:

Early mortality stays significant, with about six to eleven percent dead in the first one hundred days. Static pre transplant scores cannot track risk as care unfolds. Their framework updates risk in real time from routine clinical data.

An explainability method shows which inputs drive each forecast over time. The approach was evaluated on eight hundred ninety one patients in Dusseldorf from 2004 to 2019. An independent cohort from the MIMIC-IV database gave a second test. Live, explained risk could help teams act before decline sets in.
pmc-13280582:
Antonija Poplas Susic and team give a 2026 Delphi study that sets Community Health Centres as a care model for Europe. Such centres have existed in Europe for more than five decades. They gain praise as models for comprehensive, equitable and integrated primary care. Yet a shared European definition was lacking. From an international federation definition, a refined set of thirty five key statements was built through expert consultations.

A two round Delphi study engaged thirty one experts from sixteen countries. Five point Likert questionnaires rated acceptability and feasibility of each statement. All thirty five statements were rated acceptable and feasible, with mean scores above three. Top rated elements held respect for human rights and access irrespective of socioeconomic status. Interprofessional teamwork also ranked high. A common framework can guide centre setup across diverse European systems.
pmc-13280682:
Margarita Ilinich and colleagues published a 2026 materials study of how four alloys withstand supercritical carbon dioxide, the working fluid in a power cycle that could replace steam turbines. The alloys, two Inconel superalloys, a Haynes alloy, and a stainless steel, sat for over 4,800 hours at 700 degrees and 200 bar, conditions near a turbine inlet. Weight change tracked corrosion, and electron microscopy plus diffraction methods inspected the oxide skins that protect the metal.

The two Inconels gained weight slowly and predictably for the first 2,000 hours. The Haynes alloy slipped into breakaway oxidation partway through, and the stainless steel shed its oxide in flakes. Inconel 625 gained the least mass, yet heavy elements in its oxide raised doubts about long-term stability. Inconel 740H built the soundest skin, a uniform chromium oxide layer over scattered aluminum oxide. The authors judge it the best long-term candidate of the four for this service.
pmc-13280982:
Philani Ezekiel Mkhize and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a pregnant woman who passed far too much urine. She was thirty-six and twenty-eight weeks pregnant. Her blood salt was high, her potassium was low, and her urine was very weak. The cause seemed to be an enzyme from the placenta that breaks down the hormone that holds water in the body. A lab-made form of the hormone, which the enzyme cannot break, helped her fast.

After birth, though, her symptoms came back. Scans pointed to swelling in the stalk of the pituitary gland, the small gland that releases the hormone. That is a second, separate cause in the brain itself. She went back on the lab-made hormone. The authors warn that two causes can hide in one patient, even when the first seems clear.
pmc-13281282:
Ish Sethi and colleagues compared trainee and senior doctors on a hard choice in a 2026 study. The choice is which sick children should get a heart and lung support machine. Such calls vary a lot from doctor to doctor. The study ran at one large children's referral hospital. Trainees in child critical care filled in surveys soon after a child's breathing support began or rose. Senior doctors rated the same children.

Trainees ruled out about one in five children for the machine. Children who arrived with poor daily function were far less likely to be picked. Trainee and senior calls agreed only to a fair degree. The authors say how a child functioned before illness sways these calls. Clearer shared rules could help trainees and seniors land in the same place.
pmc-13281582:

But tumors in time learn to resist them. The team screened close to two thousand approved drugs on resistant cancer cells. Cholesterol pills called statins stood out. They killed resistant cells by choice and shrank tumors in lab and animal tests.

The path feeds a growth switch that keeps resistant cells alive, and statins cut it off. Paired with the gene pills, one statin delayed resistance and hit tumors harder in animals, with fair tolerance. The authors propose trials of the cheap pairing.
pmc-13281882:
Al-Safi Noman and colleagues studied digital tools and birth and death records in Yemen in a 2026 paper. Sound records of births and deaths guide health planning. In war-torn settings, weak systems blur those counts. The team surveyed one hundred nineteen staff across thirty-two public health sites in Sana'a. The survey scored tech gear, software, staff skill, and networks. It also scored how well sites register, cover, and publish their statistics.

Stronger tech went hand in hand with stronger statistics work. The link was large in their model, explaining much of the gap between sites. Tech use itself sat at a middling level across sites. The authors read the pattern as a case for investing in systems and training. They caution that a one-time survey shows links, not proof that tech alone caused the gains. In a fragile state, they argue, even linked gains are worth chasing.
pmc-13282382:
Tim David and co-authors present a 2026 chemistry study on using sound and milling to take apart self-assembled molecular cages. The cages form from palladium metal centres and linking molecules, a family with uses in catalysis, sensing, and drug delivery. Building them is well understood, but controlled disassembly was scarce. The team attached polymer chains to the cage parts so outside forces could pull on them.

Ultrasound sent shear forces through the chains, stressing the metal centres until links broke. In one cage type, that released the anticancer drug cisplatin on demand. Ball milling, grinding in the solid state, achieved full and reversible activation too. The method also dismantled a giant twelve-centre sphere, among the heaviest discrete assemblies reported. Computer simulations mapped the force needed to break the metal links and the step-by-step pathway. The authors offer force as a general tool for responsive materials.
pmc-13282482:

Orbitals are the quantum shapes that describe where electrons live in molecules. A method called photoemission orbital tomography rebuilds them from electrons knocked out by light. Extending it to three dimensions at femtosecond speed, a millionth of a billionth of a second, had been out of reach.

The team paired a new spectroscopy method, ultrafast momentum microscopy, with a tunable extreme ultraviolet source built in the lab. A tailored algorithm rebuilt the full three-dimensional picture from sparse, undersampled data. That pairing sped up collection and cut how much data is needed. They proved it by imaging the frontier orbitals of an organic semiconductor on a silver surface.
pmc-13282682:

The disease comes from the larval stage of a tapeworm, Echinococcus granulosus, forming cysts in organs. The team recorded two hundred ninety-five surgical patients in Urmia treated between 2010 and 2021, and tested seventy-four preserved cyst samples with gene methods.

Cases were more often female, and the liver and lung were the commonest cyst sites. Villagers and people with little schooling featured heavily among patients. DNA was extracted from all tested samples, though only about a third could be sequenced for each of two genes. Every sequenced sample belonged to the same genotype, G1, the sheep strain, with no variation in the stretches read.
pmc-13282982:
Italian health records show what first-line leukemia care really looks like in Valentina Perrone's 2026 population study. New targeted drugs have changed first care for this common adult leukemia. Routine data can show what trials cannot, such as cost and real drug use.

Standard chemotherapy stayed the most common first choice, above all in older patients. Ibrutinib users had lower death risk and longer time to next treatment. Yearly cost per patient was high and driven mainly by drug costs.
pmc-13283182:
Half the hedgehogs reaching a Lombardy rescue center carried drug-resistant gut bacteria, S Raineri and associates found in 2026. Hedgehogs can signal the health of local environments. The team checked dead hedgehogs from a wildlife rescue center in Lombardy.

Most strains resisted many drugs, including key penicillin-type drugs in all cases. Gene tests found TEM most often, then SHV and CTX-M types. Seven strains carried two resistance genes at once. All strains stayed sensitive to colistin and florfenicol in lab tests.
pmc-13283382:
Jun Zhang and Jingru Ma present a 2026 review of nature-inspired polymer particles for liver cancer immune therapy. Liver cancer is often found late and responds poorly to standard care. Immune drugs help some patients but fail many others with this cancer.

Animal studies show better immune cell entry into tumors with these designs. Cancer vaccines and cell reprogramming are covered as partner strategies. Checkpoint drugs worked in synergy with particles in some animal work. Safety and scale remain open hurdles.
pmc-13283582:
Rachel Meyers and co-authors asked in 2026 what drives high school girls to play organised sport. Girls join sport less often than boys and quit at twice the rate, so knowing their motives matters for keeping them in. Before the fall season, 143 female adolescents picked their main reason for playing. The team classed each reason as intrinsic, meaning for the fun of it. Reasons could also be extrinsic, meaning for outside rewards such as scholarships or praise.

Two thirds named an intrinsic motive, against the team's guess that outside rewards would lead. The study then compared the two groups on anxiety, low mood, grit, and body appreciation. It also weighed background and health factors, with adjustments for age and other traits. Early results showed no clear group gaps in background or medical history.
pmc-13283682:
Ryan Turlip and co-authors compared strength recovery in 2026 between two teen knee operations. Kneecap instability and ligament tears are both common in adolescents, yet strength milestones for kneecap surgery are borrowed from ligament surgery research. The team matched 64 kneecap ligament rebuild patients with 64 ligament rebuild patients by age, sex, and body size, all treated at one children's hospital from 2011 to 2023.

Machine strength tests at three, six, and twelve months tracked thigh and hamstring power against the uninjured leg. By one year, ligament rebuild patients reached clearly higher front-thigh strength on peak force, body-weight-scaled force, and total work measures. Hamstring results did not differ between groups. The authors argue kneecap surgery needs its own recovery marks rather than borrowed ones.
pmc-13283882:
Qinling Zhu and a large team asked in 2026 whether a past womb lining overgrowth still hurts fertility after it clears. Endometrial hyperplasia is abnormal thickening of the womb lining, sometimes treated with hormones until it regresses. The team studied 95 patients whose overgrowth had fully regressed before a frozen embryo transfer, matching each to four similar infertile patients with normal linings.

Cases with atypia, meaning abnormal cell features, fared marginally worse still. Longer hormone treatment and slower remission further cut the odds of a live birth. The authors urge tailored counselling for this group.
pmc-13284482:
Marta Ballester Martinez, Giuseppe Filomeni, and Salvatore Rizza present a 2026 laboratory protocol for growing three mouse liver cell types together. Work on metabolic liver disease needs models that keep how liver cells interact in the body. The protocol covers hepatocytes, hepatic stellate cells, and Kupffer cells taken from the same mouse liver.

Keeping conditions close to the body should help labs study normal liver work and disease change with all three cell types present, rather than one type alone.
pmc-13284682:
Fábio Viveiros and colleagues described in 2026 an unusual spread pattern of a rare bile duct cancer. Ampullary carcinoma grows where the bile and pancreatic ducts meet the gut, and it usually spreads to nearby nodes, liver, lungs, or the abdominal lining. Their patient was a 67-year-old man with obstructive jaundice and abnormal liver blood tests.

Scans showed both ducts widened, the classic double-duct sign, without a clear blocking lump. They also showed odd thickening of the right psoas, a deep hip muscle. A scope biopsy confirmed poorly differentiated ampullary cancer, and a needle biopsy of the muscle proved the same cancer had spread there, an extremely rare site. The main tumour was also too advanced locally to remove, so he was referred for palliative chemotherapy.
pmc-13284782:
Nadiya Johal, Badrinathan Chandrasekaran, and Paul Foley described in 2026 a sensing quirk in an advanced pacemaker therapy. The therapy is called left bundle branch optimised cardiac resynchronisation therapy. It combines a standard heart vein lead with a lead placed deep in the heart wall. Together they pace the natural conduction system. That improves pumping more than standard therapy in matched comparisons. Five recipients developed T wave oversensing, where the device mistakes the heart's recovery wave for a new beat.

The problem appeared between two months and two years after implant. Oversensing can trigger wrong shocks or pause needed therapy in other settings, yet none of these patients had symptoms or wrong treatment from it. The report walks through likely mechanisms and fixes, aiming to help implant teams troubleshoot a young technique.
pmc-13284882:
Mohamad Adam Bujang set out practical guidance in 2026 for choosing cut-off scores on diagnostic and screening tests. A test's area under the curve, the AUC, summarises its overall accuracy, yet it does not name the threshold where a result flips from negative to positive. Chasing a single perfect threshold, Bujang argues, is often unrealistic in practice.

The guideline, called AUC-GUIDE, ties threshold choice to the AUC range, to sensitivity and specificity, and to the study's purpose. It shows when to favour catching every case, when to favour avoiding false alarms, and when to balance the two through measures such as Youden's index. The aim is transparent, context-aware threshold decisions for researchers and clinicians rather than mechanical defaults.
pmc-13285582:
Quan Zhou and co-authors revisit data from the BAST stroke trial to ask whether inflammation levels shape how well a drug called butylphthalide works. Their 2026 analysis covers 837 patients whose blocked brain arteries were reopened. Some patients still recover poorly, and lingering inflammation may be one reason why outcomes differ.

Those with favorable or improving patterns had better function at 90 days and fewer repeat events. The best results appeared in patients whose inflammation stayed favorable while taking the drug. Computer analysis of drug targets pointed to pathways involving inflammation, cell stress, and blood vessels.
pmc-13285682:
A cell-cycle brake drug supercharges antibody-guided cancer bombs, Xiao Guo and co-authors show in a 2026 study. The WEE1 blocker azenosertib stalls cells at damage checks, a natural partner for both poison types.

The authors pitch azenosertib as a near-universal booster for this drug class.
pmc-13286182:
Takuma Shimoyama and colleagues probe how people judge minds in edible robots in a 2026 psychology experiment. Eating a thing that seems to have feelings can stir the same moral pinch as eating an animal, a puzzle known as the meat paradox. Their food-like agents could move and make sounds, letting the team vary the show while the food itself stayed the same.

More than a thousand viewers watched two video clips of the agents and rated what kind of mind each seemed to hold. Ratings split into two strands: a sense of doing, and a sense of feeling, and each strand favored a unlike clip. Hesitation about eating the agent also shifted between the clips, while guilt stayed level across both. Oddly, neither mind strand tracked hesitation or guilt in the end, a loose end the authors flag for the study of food and feeling.
pmc-13286282:
Pravesh Parekh and a large team present FEMA-Long, a faster statistics engine for repeat-measure studies, in a 2026 methods article. Studies that weigh the same people again and again bog down when the math insists on tidy, unchanging correlation patterns. Real growth and aging bend those patterns, but flexible fits were too slow for genome-scale data. Their extension lets correlation flex freely, curves bend smoothly, and gene effects change with time.

Applied to a Norwegian birth cohort, it tracked length, weight, and body mass in 68,273 babies across their first year. Heritability and gene correlations shifted month by month rather than holding still. Several gene variants acted only at certain ages, exactly the kind of fleeting signal the tool was built to catch.
pmc-13286782:
Ana Muriel Assunção and colleagues investigate which habits travel with an unhealthy diet among adults in Portugal. Their 2026 study uses a 2019 population survey of 891 adults. Diet was judged by regular meals, enough fruit and vegetables, and moderate alcohol use, following public health guidance. Many Portuguese adults overrate how well they eat, the authors note.

The model's ability to separate cases was modest, a reminder that eating habits have many drivers. Even so, the authors argue that programs tackling smoking, screen time, and food together fit how risks actually cluster.
pmc-13286982:
Ruolin Wu and a nine-author team redate the birth of flowering plants using the whole fossil record in a 2026 evolutionary study. Those data-driven age densities then constrained 110 nodes on a tree of 644 flowering species built from 83 genes. The combined analysis rejected any origin after the Jurassic closed. It settled on a short, late Jurassic history for the crown group, narrowing the long quarrel between rocks and molecules. The authors offer the two-step method as a more objective way to marry fossil and genetic clocks.
pmc-13287082:
Zohreh Hajibarat and Abbas Saidi mine public gene data for soybean stress defenses in a 2026 computational study. Drought, salt, and heavy metals together erase huge shares of the world's soybean harvest. Rather than rerun experiments, the team integrated expression data from 112 samples across stress types. They layered differential expression, correlation shifts, and two machine learning rankers to find genes that respond again and again.

Three genes on chromosome 16 drew the strongest multi-layer support. Cousin genes in wild soybean and two related beans suggest part of the response is ancient and shared. The authors offer the shortlist as hypotheses for lab validation and for breeding hardier varieties.
pmc-13287582:

The version richest in acid groups took up the most chemical, at 389.2 milligrams per gram of material. The plainest version managed 162.5 milligrams per gram. Uptake over time and across strengths fitted standard surface models well. The authors present acid-rich crystals from waste metal as a cheap route to cleaning pesticide-laced water before release.
pmc-13288582:
Rehab M Abdelhamid and colleagues test soaking legume seeds in liquid from a soil bacterium in a 2026 plant study. A 25 percent mix suited common bean best, lifting germination and shoot length, while a weaker 10 percent mix suited faba bean, which reached full germination sooner. pmc-13288682:
Annemieke Wargers and colleagues listen to teenagers themselves through focus groups in a 2026 study tied to the European SEEDS project. Eight discussion groups brought together 35 adolescents aged 13 to 15 from lower-income areas of Spain, the Netherlands, Greece, and the UK, framed by the Theory of Planned Behaviour.

Friends and peers mostly discouraged activity outside physical education lessons, good ties with teachers helped, and families shaped eating more than movement. Cramped schools, little free time, canteens short on healthy choices, and the COVID-19 pandemic all got in the way, while required PE lessons and school clubs pushed activity upward.
pmc-13288882:
David R Strong and colleagues build a yardstick for anti-smoking social pressure in a 2026 analysis of thirty years of United States surveys. Tobacco supplements to a national population survey ran nine times from 1992 to 2022 and reached 1,462,050 respondents, who were asked how willing they were to restrict smoking across ten everyday settings.

pmc-13288982:

The team built a tool called PolyProf to count about two hundred such effector and immunity genes. They applied it to roughly fifteen thousand public human gut metagenomes. Patterns were tested against disease states and early life development.

pmc-13289082:

pmc-13289382:

pmc-13289782:

pmc-13290082:

pmc-13290782:

pmc-13290982:

pmc-13291382:

pmc-13291782:

Twenty-four male Wistar rats were split into four groups: sham, emodin alone, injury alone, and injury plus emodin. pmc-13291882:

pmc-13292582:

pmc-13292682:

The mutation rate matched the 70 to 80 percent range typical of dysplastic nevi generally, far above the 5 to 10 percent seen in early melanomas. pmc-13293482:

pmc-13293682:

Adding a phosphate-removing enzyme pulled the machine off rebuilt chromosomes and undid packing. Frog egg extracts showed the two tags rise and fall on unlike schedules in real division.
pmc-13293982:

pmc-13294182:

pmc-13294482:

pmc-13294682:

pmc-13294882:
