Their series, they note, covers 303 operations through the back of the head, among the largest reported anywhere. They argue that a surgeon's direct view during surgery is valid evidence on its own and offer reasons the vein may escape scans, including its size and drainage pattern.
pmc-13396182:
Avdeeva and co-authors present, in 2026, ArchVelo, a program for charting how cells change over time from single-cell measures of gene activity and chromatin access. Snapshots cannot show motion directly, so trajectory methods infer it. ArchVelo treats chromatin access as archetypes, shared regulatory programs whose shifting weight drives transcription. That lets it split each cell's path into readable parts and name the transcription factors involved.

In benchmarks on mouse brain and blood-formation datasets, ArchVelo beat existing methods on trajectory accuracy and on aligning latent time gene by gene. Applied to CD8 T cells during viral infection, it separated paths of differentiation and growth among the immune cells. Within progenitor exhausted T cells, the cells that sustain immunity, it traced the path from Ccr6-negative to Ccr6-positive ones, a route shared between acute and chronic infections. The authors offer ArchVelo for multi-omic studies across biology.
pmc-13396382:
Yixiao Yuan and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 to their study of a circular RNA called Circ0515 in lung adenocarcinoma. The study, first published in Cell Death and Disease in July 2025, argued that the RNA helps tumors grow. The original work argued that the RNA rewires how mitochondria handle succinate, through the protein SDHB, and thereby feeds tumor growth.

A post-publication review found that two Western blot images, for the proteins mTOR and AKT, had been placed wrongly in Figure 4K during final assembly. The authors state that the underlying data were kept and rechecked, and that the replacement images are the authentic ones. Results, interpretation, and conclusions stand unchanged.
pmc-13397382:
Justine Sunshine and co-authors asked whether the strength of a standard tuberculosis test signal can predict who will actually fall ill. Their 2026 analysis covers 5,246 people aged 15 to 34 in high-burden regions, followed for a median of 525 days.

The QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus blood test reports two interferon-gamma values, TB1 and TB2, which clinics usually read as a simple positive or negative. The authors instead kept the numbers and compared them across people who stayed well, those with suspected but unconfirmed disease, and confirmed cases. A graded signal that forecasts illness would let prevention programs aim treatment at the few most likely to progress.
pmc-13397682:
Meng Liang and others show a Sigma-1R and CD36 axis in myeloid cells easing depression-like behaviors in a 2026 study. Major depression ranks as a leading disability cause, with immune dysregulation ever more blamed, yet key cell subsets and hub molecules were half mapped.

Meta-analysis of five blood gene-read cohorts plus single-cell data charted myeloid expression. Chronic restraint stress mouse tests and cell assays then probed Sigma-1R control of CD36 through the E3 ligase TRIM28, using agonists and antagonists. The axis offers a peripheral inflammation aim for depression treatment. The paper bridges immune biology and mood disorders.
pmc-13397782:
Erman Öğümsöğütlü and Seçkin Özcan studied match videos to find which body positions raise the risk of a broken upper arm bone during arm wrestling. Their 2026 analysis compares injured competitors with their uninjured opponents at the exact moment of fracture. Arm wrestling is popular worldwide, yet the postures that turn a match into a serious bone injury had not been clearly mapped.

Two orthopedic specialists reviewed 74 public videos, recording trunk, elbow, and wrist positions plus match side and setting. Fractures clustered in the defense zone, and trunk rotation toward the attack direction was strongly linked to injury. Misalignment of the wrist, elbow, and shoulder appeared in about four of five injured competitors and was also strongly linked to fracture. The paper gives coaches, players, and clinicians concrete postures to avoid, though video review cannot prove cause on its own.
pmc-13398482:
Shunran Li and colleagues catch light flipping a lead-free crystal into a hidden, long-lived state. Their 2026 study works on the double perovskite Cs2AgInCl6 family, materials that glow white under stimulation and could replace lead-based versions in lights and solar cells. What light does to their inner structure over time was largely unknown.

Fast optical probes, time-resolved X-ray diffraction and absorption, and inelastic X-ray scattering together tracked the change. Disorder among the metal cations (silver and indium swapping places) marks the metastable phase, which lingers far beyond the light pulse. Understanding that hidden state matters because it can trap energy, colour emission and shape how such crystals behave in real devices.
pmc-13398582:
Mahshad Razaghi and co-authors present an older man whose aortic valve choked blood flow almost without any calcium. Their 2026 case report concerns a 79-year-old with a normal three-leaflet valve and severe stenosis, the narrowing that usually grows from chalky deposits. His calcium score read just 76.5 Agatston units, far below what such tight narrowing normally shows.

Multiple imaging methods confirmed the obstruction was truly severe despite the clean-looking valve. Surgeons replaced it with a tissue valve, and he recovered well after the operation. The case warns that calcium scoring can underrate disease when scarring, not calcification, does the narrowing, a rare pattern doctors should keep in mind.
pmc-13399282:
Jiyeon Kim, Myongsun Cho, and Fucai Lin examined how satisfaction with sleep relates to problem smartphone use among Korean adolescents, in a 2026 study. Problematic use means more than long hours on a phone; it involves loss of control plus harm to schoolwork, daily life, or relationships. The authors wanted to know whether anxiety and loneliness carry part of the link between poor sleep satisfaction and heavier phone problems.

Their dataset covered 48,829 adolescents: general users at 72.1 percent, potential-risk users at 24.8 percent, and high-risk users at 3.1 percent. High-risk users averaged about seven hours of phone use and scored higher on anxiety and loneliness. Mediation analysis estimated that anxiety accounted for 30.0 percent of the link between sleep dissatisfaction and problem use, while loneliness accounted for 15.2 percent of it in the same models. The authors suggest improving sleep and easing emotional strain could lower phone problems in teenagers.
pmc-13399382:
Hitomi Soumiya and colleagues examined how salty stress reshapes RNA processing in human kidney cells. Their 2026 study tracks the cleavage factor Im complex, a protein group that helps choose where messenger RNA ends are cut, a step called alternative polyadenylation. How this complex moves and acts during stress had remained poorly understood.

Under moderate hyperosmotic stress, two complex parts, CFIm25 and CFIm68, shifted from nucleus to cytoplasm while total protein levels stayed stable. Target genes NUDT21 and DICER1 shifted toward nearer cutting sites, with different recovery patterns tied to serum conditions, while non-target genes showed no such shift. The authors propose a nuclear shortage model for the effect. The work links cell location, RNA endings, and stress response in a testable framework.
pmc-13399582:
Zhaoyuan Zhang and co-authors tested a new boron drug and accelerator pairing for boron neutron capture therapy in head and neck cancer models, reporting in 2026. The treatment works in two steps: a boron-carrying compound concentrates in tumor cells, then a neutron beam triggers tiny, cell-sized destructive reactions inside them. The team paired a novel boronophenylalanine compound with a radio-frequency quadrupole accelerator neutron source and ran a full preclinical workup.

The compound reached tumors quickly and selectively, settling at a tumor-to-blood ratio of about 3.5 in the reported imaging. Tumor shrinkage grew with dose. Inside treated cells, the therapy provoked a hypoxia-like stress response. Reactive oxygen species piled up and DNA suffered double-strand breaks. Two signaling axes, HIF-1 alpha and NF-kappa-B, switched on along the road to cell death. The authors say the system's safety and mechanism suit translation toward human trials.
pmc-13400182:
Ziqiao Zhong and colleagues built a light-activated gel that floods surgical cavities after tumor removal and turns the wound's fatty environment against leftover cancer cells, in a 2026 study. Their hydrogel responds to light by melting and resolidifying, so it can penetrate deep cavities and stay put.

Inside the gel sits a pairing of lipoxygenase with rapamycin. Freed in the cavity, it runs a coordinated lipid intervention: the enzyme converts tumor-derived fatty acids into lipid peroxides that trigger ferroptosis, an iron-driven death, in residual cancer cells. Rapamycin accelerates lipid droplet metabolism in macrophages and flips them back to the tumor-fighting M1 state, restoring immune watch. The authors present the strategy as precision prevention aimed at the margin, where recurrence is born.
pmc-13401282:
Natalia Chechko, Stefanie Weisenfeld, and Susanne Nehls present a 2026 case report on the blurry boundary between obsessive-compulsive disorder and psychotic illness. Their patient, a 44-year-old man whose symptoms began in his late teens, was first hospitalized in 2009 and diagnosed with psychosis.

His intrusive, almost delusional fears and compulsions came with a sense of being watched and abstract ideas about the self, all with limited insight, which kept the diagnosis uncertain. Antipsychotic drugs did not help him. Starting paroxetine in 2011 brought substantial improvement, pointing toward OCD instead. His diagnosis was revised toward the OCD spectrum after more than a decade. Yet he still held to his old diagnosis and grew obsessive fears of sliding into psychosis, shaped by the earlier label.
pmc-13401582:
Xin Ding and co-authors are named in a 2026 correction in Discover Oncology for their 2025 paper on silencing the moesin gene to make glioblastoma brain tumours more sensitive to radiation. The correction replaces Figure 3, which had been published incorrectly in the original article.

The corrected figure gathers the evidence behind the paper's central claim. It shows moesin protein levels in radioresistant and parental U87 tumour cells, and confirms the gene knockout by western blot. It also charts how knocking out moesin over 24 to 72 hours slows cell growth. It also raises programmed cell death measured by flow cytometry, and weakens survival after radiation in colony assays. Survival curves are fitted with two standard models, and significance markers run from P below 0.05 down to below 0.001. The original article has been corrected.
pmc-13401882:
Yao Liu and co-authors built a survival prediction chart for liver cancer patients whose blood score profile suggests poorer reserves, in a 2026 study from Beijing Ditan Hospital. The HALP score combines haemoglobin, albumin, lymphocytes, and platelets into one index of nutrition and immunity.

The retrospective analysis covered 1,281 patients with early-to-intermediate stage disease by the Barcelona system, treated between 2015 and 2021. A cutoff split them into 457 low-score and 824 high-score patients, and higher scores clearly went with longer survival. For the low group, the team screened predictors with random survival forests, LASSO. Cox modelling, then built a nomogram on 305 patients and validated it on a further 152, plus a later set of 251 patients treated from 2022 to 2025. Time-dependent ROC curves, calibration, and decision analysis checked the chart's worth.
pmc-13402682:
Hagan and co-authors project, in 2026, how the coupling between soil moisture and air temperature, a feedback that intensifies droughts and heatwaves, will shift under future emissions. They use Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 climate model output for boreal summer. Hotspots were regions where at least 70 percent of models agreed the coupling strength exceeded the threshold, and the answer depended on the emissions path chosen.

Under the low-emissions SSP1-2.6 scenario, coupling expanded across all historical hotspots, broadly preserving today's pattern. Under the high-emissions SSP5-8.5 scenario, a latitudinal contrast appeared: coupling weakened and contracted at low-to-mid northern latitudes but strengthened at higher latitudes, with emerging hotspots across mid-to-high-latitude North America and northern Europe. Coupling also strengthened in the humid southern tropics, where evaporation outpaced precipitation gains. Poleward expansion of the Hadley circulation under strong warming pushed soil moisture's control on surface energy further north.
pmc-13402882:
Osman Farah Dahir and colleagues report a successful vaginal delivery in a 20-year-old woman carrying two dangerous heart conditions at once: Eisenmenger syndrome and double outlet right ventricle. In Eisenmenger physiology, a long-standing heart shunt has reversed under fixed lung hypertension, leaving the blood short of oxygen and the body unable to absorb the strain of pregnancy. Her second defect sends both great arteries out of the right ventricle, scrambling oxygen delivery further.

She arrived at 34 weeks, first pregnancy, with worsening breathlessness and whole-body swelling over several days, visibly cyanotic, after only one antenatal visit and no heart assessment. Pregnancy in this setting carries extremely high risk for mother and baby alike. The authors credit a specialist team, individualized monitoring, and tailored delivery planning for the favorable outcome for both, and offer the case as guidance where guidelines run thin.
pmc-13403382:
Bálint Gergely Szabó and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how stool transfer and related gut treatments may aid blood stem cell transplant patients. Gut germs help guard the bowel wall and tune the immune system. Harsh drugs and strong antibiotics often strip that mix down during transplant care.

The review drew on three large databases for work up to October 2025. Stool transfer looked workable in picked patients and may help with stubborn gut infection and graft attacks. Most side effects were mild, yet rare spread of germs shows why donor checks matter. The authors call for set doses, clear timing rules, and stronger product standards.
pmc-13404582:
Lorena Duarte-Peña and team review exosome-like nanocarriers for cancer diagnosis and drug delivery. Their 2026 review covers built vesicles that mimic natural exosomes, tiny cell-made packets, while giving synthetic making flexibility and scale. Cancer drug delivery must beat tumor defenses and off-target harm, yet natural exosome use has been curbed by output and consistency snags.

The review weighs carrier make-up, design, and build, plus diagnostic and theranostic platforms that join therapy and imaging. Built mimics promise better scale, repeatability, and versatility than natural vesicles, with recent studies showing promise to beat natural vesicle limits. The authors present mimics as strong candidates for medical use and sale, while stressing that safety, standards, and human trial proof stay ahead.
pmc-13406882:
Yuanxin Yao and colleagues, writing in 2026, examine a gene called L3MBTL4 that is often switched off in pancreatic cancer by chemical tagging of its promoter region. They measured how often that silencing occurs across early pancreatic growths and full cancers, then probed what the gene does inside cells.

Silencing appeared in about 28 percent of pancreatic cancers and tracked with larger, less differentiated tumours. Restoring the gene slowed cell growth, triggered cell death, and held cells at a cycle checkpoint. The gene also interacts with a repair protein and shifts how broken DNA gets fixed. Cancer cells lacking it proved much more sensitive to a DNA-PK blocking drug, in dishes and in mice, suggesting a treatment marker.
pmc-13407482:
Subhash K. Todi leads an Indian critical care society panel that issued, in 2026, treatment guidance for the toughest drug-resistant gut and lung bacteria in intensive care. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, Acinetobacter, and Pseudomonas kill 40 to 70 percent of critically ill patients they infect in Indian units, yet no standard national guidance existed.

Following the GRADE method, the panel reviewed 52 studies comparing older polymyxin drugs with newer options and sulbactam-based therapy for Acinetobacter. Newer beta-lactam pairings cured more patients with fewer side effects for the first group, and sulbactam pairings clearly beat polymyxins for Acinetobacter, including far less kidney damage. For Pseudomonas, newer options matched efficacy with much lower toxicity. All recommendations rest on very low certainty evidence, so the panel urges proper randomised trials urgently.
pmc-13407682:
Michael Paalani and co-authors examine, in 2026, whether vigorous exercise relates to sleep trouble in a North American church-based cohort. The Adventist Health Study 2 enrolled about 97,000 churchgoers. A psychosocial substudy captured sleep patterns. After removing people with chronic disease, 3,960 participants remained. They were analysed for falling-asleep difficulty and night waking.

More frequent vigorous activity was modestly protective against trouble falling asleep, with each step in frequency trimming the odds slightly. Women, older participants, weekday nappers, and people sleeping nine hours or more faced higher odds of slow sleep onset. Activity showed no relationship with waking in the night. The authors, quoting their own summary line, suggest frequent vigorous activity may ease sleep onset across a multiracial population, while leaving mid-night waking unexplained.
pmc-13408082:
Liang Feng and co-authors build, in 2026, a membrane that fishes lithium from brine without a furnace. Crystalline lithium conductors shuttle lithium ions selectively but must be sintered above a thousand degrees, wasting energy and evaporating lithium. The team therefore embedded conductor nanoparticles in a glassy metal-organic framework, ZIF-62. The composite was cast while cool into a dense, defect-free film.

Transport channels stayed choked until the conductor content crossed a threshold, after which an interconnected network formed and performance jumped. The optimised membrane separated lithium from magnesium with a selectivity near 59,000 in Red Sea water under electrical operation. That is a headline figure for electrodialytic extraction. Performance held stable across diverse natural brines. Scalable, processable membranes for lithium and other ion separations are the wider claim.
pmc-13408182:
Sang-Nee Tan authored a 2026 review proposing that some cancer chromosome rearrangements begin with a cell-death programme that stops halfway. When stressed cells activate a DNA-cutting enzyme from the apoptosis pathway, the cuts land preferentially where chromatin loops anchor to the nuclear scaffold. Cells that recover instead of dying must repair those breaks.

Repair through error-prone joining routes can stitch distant pieces together, creating the rearrangements that mark many cancers. Tan draws on leukaemia studies and experimental work in nasopharyngeal carcinoma, noting that inflammation and virus-linked oxidative stress could drive similar events elsewhere. Readers get a testable framework, plus suggested weak points, such as repair enzymes that surviving cells may depend on, which future treatments might exploit.
pmc-13408682:
Hailey Proud and co-authors explain in 2026 why some HER2-positive breast cancers also carry the estrogen receptor, a combination that changes treatment and fuels resistance. The culprit they identify is a shortened variant of the HER2 growth receptor that skips one building block, known as HER2∆16. Mouse models carrying it developed aggressive tumours of the luminal type.

The variant switches on a gene programme run by the estrogen receptor, and those tumours stayed sensitive to hormone-blocking therapy. Human tumours and cell lines show the same pairing, with more of the variant tracking higher receptor levels. Cells that survived HER2-targeted treatment raised their variant levels and, in doing so, became newly vulnerable to tamoxifen. The work gives researchers a faithful model of the double-positive disease and a possible sequencing hint for therapy.
pmc-13408782:
Kurosaki and Hosaka report, in 2026, the rediscovery of Resupinatus merulioides at its type locality in Nikko, Tochigi Prefecture, Japan. It comes four decades after its 1987 description by Redhead and Nagasawa, with no records from that locality since. The species is odd for its wrinkled, maze-like spore surface rather than gills. The authors collected specimens at Nikko and elsewhere, compared anatomy, and sequenced DNA.

The collections matched the description, though some bodies varied in coloration, and phylogenetic analysis grouped them into one clade distinct from other genus members. Specimens filed under the same name from New Zealand formed a sister clade, distinct and probably a different species wearing the wrong label. Because the new material adds characters and DNA the holotype lacked, the authors designate one Nikko collection as an epitype, a specimen anchoring the name. It was grown and extracted using standard media such as 2 percent extract broth.
pmc-13408982:
Julian Sandbrink and Michael Young warn in 2026 that the law has not caught up with devices that read the brain from inside the skull. Implantable brain-computer interfaces are moving from laboratory demonstrations toward clinical use, streaming neural signals detailed enough to reveal far more than ordinary health records. Existing privacy frameworks, including American and European health data laws, leave that material oddly exposed.

Five gaps structure the review: shaky faith in de-identification, thin individual control over the data, consent bundled into treatment decisions, few guardrails against misuse, and undefined ownership. For each, the authors examine remedies, from protecting even de-identified streams to separate data consent and limits on harmful second uses and on selling the data. They urge clinicians, developers, and regulators to build these protections with users, before the technology outruns the conversation.
pmc-13409082:
Sumana Bajracharya and co-authors interview emergency triage nurses in Nepal in 2026 about what helps and what hinders sorting forty thousand patients a year at Patan Academy of Health Sciences. Triage decides who is seen first, and in crowded low-resource departments its quality rides on nurses' judgement. Nine in-depth interviews, analysed phenomenologically until no new themes emerged, captured their lived experience.

Nurses understood the severity-based system thoroughly. Training, clear protocols, teamwork, and experience made it work. Against them stood resource limits, overcrowding, staff shortages, patchy training, communication friction, and social hierarchy pressing on decisions. Because the study gives nurses' own framing of these forces, hospital managers get a grounded agenda. Protect the facilitators. Relieve the named barriers. Treat triage as skilled work rather than a doorway chore.
pmc-13409182:
Crous and a large team of coauthors published a 2026 survey that names and sorts newly found fungi from sites around the world. Their work adds eight new genera and 28 new species, along with fresh type specimens and new host and place records for fungi already known.

The paper notes where each new find was found. Finds ranged from dead wood and leaves in Germany to fruit in China and bark in Australia. Readers get a clear record of what is new, what was retyped, and where each fungus lives, which helps later work on naming, plant health, and human disease.
pmc-13409282:
Maëliss Jallais and colleagues put two fashionable brain-imaging models under a Bayesian microscope in 2026 and ask an uncomfortable question: which of their numbers can be trusted? Diffusion MRI models promise measurements of grey matter microstructure, including how fast water swaps between compartments, yet their estimates are rarely audited for reliability. A deep-learning Bayesian tool was used to attach uncertainty to every parameter, on simulated and real data.

Some quantities, such as water movement outside cells and the share of signal from neurites, came out robust. Others, notably exchange time and cell body size, carried heavy uncertainty and bias, especially at realistic noise levels and shortened scans. Standard curve fitting gave no warning of this, while the Bayesian approach flagged the unreliable fits for exclusion. The authors argue uncertainty reporting should become routine before such numbers feed biology or clinics.
pmc-13410382: A 2026 journal notice corrects the record for a paper by Silveira and co-workers on electrospun membranes with zinc oxide particles for wound care. The notice is a correction only, and it changes no results or claims. It fixes one author's workplace listing: Edgar Andrés Chavarriaga had been placed with a basic studies unit in Medellín, Colombia. The corrected listing puts him with an environmental and construction sciences unit at ITM in the same city. The journal closes by apologizing for the error.
pmc-13410582:
Anna Oertel and co-workers check in 2026 whether dental training rooms carry waterborne germs that can infect patients and staff. Water lines in dental units favor non-tuberculous mycobacteria, a group of hardy bacteria from soil and water. Training units mirror real ones, yet their water had barely been studied.

Water and biofilm samples came from 24 simulation units in two rooms across two buildings. Samples grew in culture for eight weeks, and species were named with a probe test. The bacteria turned up in 43 of 44 samples, with three species found and one, M. gordonae, most common. Building features did not explain the spread, so attention turns to standing water and cleaning routines.
pmc-13411282:
Khanyisa Mananga, Mandla Bhuda, and Joyce Shirinde survey in 2026 eczema among teenagers in Soshanguve, a township in Gauteng Province, South Africa. Nearly three thousand pupils aged 13 to 14 at thirteen high schools answered a standard allergy questionnaire. Home conditions and air pollution sources formed the focus.

About 27 percent reported current eczema symptoms, and girls reported them far more often than boys. Monthly use of paracetamol tied strongly to symptoms, an association seen in other countries too. Frequent truck traffic past the home, keeping a cat or dog, and tobacco smoke in the house all raised the odds. The pattern points to household and street-level exposures worth tackling.
pmc-13411682:
César Alas-Pineda and co-workers test in 2026 whether the tilt of a nasal spray nozzle decides how much medicine reaches the back of the nose. Sprays promise needle-free delivery, yet aim may matter as much as dose. Their feasibility study paired bench tests in a printed nose model with checks on how lay people handle the spray.

A shallow angle, around 12 to 15 degrees, pushed notably more liquid through to the nasopharynx than a steep conventional angle in both nostrils of the single cast model. Then 191 lay users followed a nine-step routine in simulated and real use. Every essential step cleared the preset success bar in both groups. Broader nose shapes must confirm the bench result.
pmc-13415282:
Atifullah Shinwari and colleagues project how a warming climate shifts when Afghan almond trees bloom, in a 2026 modeling study. Afghanistan grows more than fifty almond varieties, and exports earned about forty million dollars in 2024. The team modeled fifty-one cultivars using temperature records from 1980 to 2023 and bloom observations from 2011 onward.

Their PhenoFlex model reproduced observed bloom within four days for every cultivar. Bloom had already advanced by roughly two weeks between 1980 and 2020. Most cultivars may flower up to sixteen days earlier still by 2085 under stronger warming paths. A few cultivars instead bloomed later, showing variety choice matters for adaptation.
pmc-13415382:
Ali Semati and colleagues merge two optical methods to watch a water surface and the flow beneath it at once, in a 2026 methods study. Fringe projection needs an opaque surface to read its shape, while particle imaging needs clear water to see motion below. A dye solves the clash: fluorescein makes water opaque to blue surface light yet nearly clear to the green laser below.

Three filters kept fluorescence glare and reflections out of each camera view. Surface height error averaged eighteen micrometers at a moderate dye level, checked against a laser reference method. Particle tracking stayed strong up to higher dye levels. Demonstrations covered flow past a cylinder and droplets striking still water.
pmc-13415482:
Gause and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how researchers should estimate heat exposure in health studies. Extreme heat is a growing public health threat, but studies measure it in many incompatible ways. The authors compare weather data sets and heat metrics, from plain air temperature to indices adding humidity, sun, and wind. They also discuss how heat waves are defined for research and for government alerts.

Data choices differ in spatial detail, time frequency, historical reach, and population coverage. Other choices, such as extreme-heat thresholds, population weighting, and urban adjustments, also shape findings. The authors stress there is no single best heat metric. They advise matching the metric to the research question, the population, and the data at hand. Their guidance targets newcomers designing environmental epidemiology studies, meaning studies of environment and disease patterns.
pmc-13415682:
Patrick Cordier, James Van Orman, and Philippe Carrez offer an alternative review of how Earth's lower mantle flows, in 2026. The lower mantle stretches from 660 to 2,890 kilometers deep under crushing pressure and heat, so direct experiments can only go so far. Their approach builds from mineral physics and computer modeling across scales.

Defects, dislocations, diffusion, and grain boundaries each govern flow under different conditions, and the review traces how models grew from atom level calculations to whole crystal simulations. Two minerals, bridgmanite and ferropericlase, serve as worked examples. Scarce diffusion data at high pressure remains a key gap for the field.
pmc-13415782:
Lei Ju and a multicenter team test a fixed dose antibody drug as part of first treatment for B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, in a 2026 study set out as a letter. Inotuzumab ozogamicin targets CD22 on leukemia cells and was approved for relapsed disease in 2017. Their plan pairs it with vincristine and prednisone for new adult cases.

Those aged 17 and up can join, with or without the Philadelphia gene swap, in two linked trials split by that mark. The antibody is given as one milligram on three days, capped by body size. Clear scans for trace sick cells early on mean long calm, which drives this early use.
pmc-13415882:
Travis D. Griffin leads a large team measuring how fast electrons and ions share heat in superheated gold, in 2026. Ultrafast lasers drive gold's electrons to multi electron volt temperatures while its ions stay cold, a warm dense matter state. Direct ion temperature readings have long eluded experimenters.

Fine resolution X-ray scattering finally resolved the ion response as hot electrons dumped energy into the lattice. Energy transfer ran much faster than in gently excited gold. Coupling strength stayed nearly constant across the elevated electron temperatures reached. The results benchmark models of nonequilibrium matter found in planets, stars, and fusion targets.
pmc-13415982:
Fateme Bokaee and Tayebeh Roghani test a hands-on therapy for a stiff, painful elbow in juvenile idiopathic arthritis, in a 2026 case report. The disease is the commonest chronic inflammatory condition of childhood, bringing morning stiffness, swelling, and weakness. Mobilization with movement pairs a sustained joint glide by the therapist with the patient's own active motion.

The single patient case tracks pain scores and elbow extension range before and after treatment. Both measures improved under the technique, according to the authors. Similar methods helped tennis elbow in earlier work, yet this appears to be the first application reported in juvenile arthritis. Caution fits a one patient result.
pmc-13416082:
Aye Nyein Thu and Munir Babar report a life threatening adrenal crisis caused by immunotherapy damage to the pituitary gland, in a 2026 case. A man aged seventy-three with recurrent melanoma on pembrolizumab developed pituitary dysfunction. The drug frees T cells against cancer yet can inflame the pituitary, cutting hormone output.

Loss of the pituitary's adrenal signal leaves the body unable to mount a stress hormone response, a secondary adrenal crisis. Deep fatigue brought the patient to emergency care. New vague symptoms in patients on checkpoint inhibitors deserve prompt hormone checks, the authors warn, because missed endocrine damage can kill.
pmc-13417482: Moghaddam and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their 2012 article on Sprouty proteins in ovarian cancer cell lines. One panel of Figure 1a had Western blot bands for the control protein GAPDH placed in the wrong orientation during figure assembly. The corrected figure is supplied here. The authors also explain how the blot was made: one membrane was probed, stripped, and probed again. The proteins differ enough in size to tell apart on the gels used.
pmc-13418482:
Hui-Hui Zhang and a large team find that a natural compound from a traditional herb rescues the last resort antibiotic colistin, in a 2026 study. Bacteria in the body adapt their surfaces to blunt colistin, a problem distinct from resistance genes. The compound baicalein shifts bacterial iron balance, raising the reactive ferrous form at the expense of other pools.

That iron shift switches off a control system that normally thickens the bacterial surface against colistin, letting the drug bind and rupture the membrane. Extra ferrous iron also fuels damaging reactions inside cells. The pairing killed resistant Gram negative bacteria better in lab and animal tests.
pmc-13419082:
Meiya Suo and colleagues report lip repositioning surgery for a gummy smile caused by an overactive upper lip, not by jaw shape. The patient was a 28-year-old woman whose gums showed by 4 millimeters when she smiled at full stretch. Her face was even on both sides, with balanced proportions in the lower third.

The surgery limits how far the upper lip can lift, covering more of the gum line at rest and in motion. Her smile improved markedly after the procedure, with the excess display brought under control. Careful case choice is the key limit the authors stress, since bone-based cases need other care. For the right patient, the report presents the operation as safe, gentle, and fairly predictable over the short to medium term.
pmc-13419282:
Tim Van Wesemael and colleagues study how feelings about COVID-19 rules spread through the Belgian community on Reddit. Watching online talk can feed disease models and policy choices during a health crisis. The team tracked topic starts and tone across the community over time, testing whether one user's post sparked similar posts from others.

The set held 655,642 posts from 28,559 users, a large base for tracing spread patterns. Posting volume rose and fell with outside events like policy announcements and news reports. A formal model of hidden states fit the spread better than simpler rivals in the tests. Results like these help public health teams tell true social spread from mere shared reaction to the news.
pmc-13420282:
Atassi and co-authors describe in 2026 a suicide attempt in which a 57-year-old woman swallowed two poisons at once: ethylene glycol, the toxic ingredient in antifreeze, and rat poison. The combination made her hospital course unusually complex.

She arrived unresponsive with severe acid buildup in the blood and was placed on a breathing machine, a bicarbonate drip, and emergency dialysis to clean her blood. Doctors suspected ethylene glycol from a mismatch in her lactate readings and started fomepizole, its antidote, before her family found a note beside bottles of both substances. Brain scans showed several small strokes. She stabilized, her thinking steadily improved, and she was discharged to a partial hospitalization program for psychiatric care.
pmc-13420382:
Harriet E. Nuttall surveys early career palaeontologists worldwide on the state of fieldwork skills in their training. The field fears an extinction of experience, where junior researchers never gain the field craft to keep fossil science connected to real ground. An online survey gathered both counts and written views on training and on the ethics of field sites.

Most field skills training arrived before the doctorate, the results show. Ethics and other soft skills were taught far less often than technical skills like fossil naming. Respondents also weighed duties toward sites and toward the communities who steward them. Programs that front-load digging but skip ethics leave new researchers half trained, the paper suggests, and the survey gives trainers a baseline to fix that.
pmc-13420482:
Vaishali N and colleagues present a case of irritable bowel syndrome handled through Grahani care, the Ayurvedic framework for disorders of digestion and absorption. Modern life patterns, late nights, poor diet, and stress are blamed widely for the rise in gut complaints. Population surveys place this syndrome between 10 and 15 percent of people in Western countries, with Asian medians of 6.5 to 10.1 percent in the ranges cited.

The framework reads the condition as a web of altered bowel habits and faulty nutrient uptake rather than a single fault. Treatment under that reading aims to restore digestive fire and rhythm together. The case tracks the patient's course under the protocol in detail. Reports like this one build the case record that formal trials of traditional systems are often accused of lacking.
pmc-13421282:
Jessica Santiago and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, that protein changes in the retina mirror the brain pathology of Alzheimer's disease. Vision problems are a recognised feature of the disease, and the retina offers a potentially accessible window onto changes otherwise hidden in the brain.

Working with paired retina and hippocampus tissue from the same donors — eight with Alzheimer's and eight controls — the team used mass spectrometry to catalogue proteins. They found 372 proteins differing in the retina, including known regulators of amyloid processing and synaptic proteins, and 64 differing proteins were shared with the hippocampus. Enrichment analysis pointed to disturbed synapses, cell scaffolding, mitochondria and adhesion. Several retinal proteins tracked disease stage, raising the prospect of eye-based markers.
pmc-13422082:
Elham Shirdel, Sakine Nazari and Soheila Mohamadirizi lay out, in a 2026 protocol, a study to pin down what fear of childbirth actually means to the women who feel it. Clear concepts guide good care, and Iranian midwives and nurses lack a definition of this fear built from Iranian women's own experience.

Their hybrid concept analysis runs in three stages. A literature review gathers existing definitions, triggers and consequences; fieldwork interviews pregnant women about their experiences; and a final analysis compares the lived picture with the published one, reporting where they diverge. The authors expect the clarified concept to help professionals recognise and respond to the fear more precisely. No results are reported at this stage.
pmc-13422282:
Lei Zhang, Minghe Liu, Xiaojing Li and Chanyuan Zhao compare drug-free treatments for jaw muscle pain, in a 2026 network meta-analysis of randomised trials. Myogenic temporomandibular disorders — aching jaw muscles with restricted opening — attract many non-drug therapies, from light treatment and splints to acupuncture and shock waves, with little head-to-head evidence.

Their network method lets every option be ranked through the web of trials that compare some directly and others only indirectly. Eligible trials enrolled adults and tested ten predefined therapies against sham, usual care or each other, with pain and maximum mouth opening read at the end of treatment. Five databases were searched to October 2025 without language limits. The authors present the ranking as guidance for clinicians choosing among crowded options.
pmc-13422582:
Defresne and co-authors introduce a protein design system that marries deep learning with logical proof, in this 2026 study. The aim is to fix a known weakness of AI protein designers. They generate sequences residue by residue. They cannot think ahead about long-range interactions. Their framework, EffieDes, converts a neural network's sense of a target fold into a probabilistic model that a reasoning engine can search rigorously.

Validation came in two demanding tests. The system designed pairs of sequences that adopt the same fold. The pairs assemble only with their intended partner, a selectivity puzzle. It also produced a brand-new nanobody, a miniature antibody. The nanobody bound an immune-evasive SARS-CoV-2 variant with nanomolar affinity. The reasoning layer can enforce explicit constraints while optimizing the learned fitness score. So the authors argue the hybrid approach suits sophisticated functional objectives. Pure sampling fumbles those.
pmc-13423982:
Einsiedler and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a look-alike illness in an MS patient. Their patient, a 63-year-old man, had multiple sclerosis plus liver cirrhosis. He declined in thinking and walking, which first looked like MS progression. A blood marker of nerve damage also ran high, deepening the suspicion.

A bout of liver-driven confusion forced the team to think again. Brain scans showed manganese building up in deep brain areas over time. That pattern points to acquired hepatocerebral degeneration, a liver-linked brain injury. Another marker, tied to MS activity, had stayed in the normal range. The case warns against blaming MS for every decline in older patients. Careful comorbidity checks should join routine reviews for older MS patients.
pmc-13424782:
Ying Yang and five colleagues profile two opposing T-cell signals, the brake PD-1 and the accelerator CD28, in the blood of patients with non-small cell lung cancer and benign lung nodules. Their retrospective study covered 526 cancer patients, split between early and advanced stages, fifty-five people with benign nodules, and thirty-three healthy participants, combining flow cytometry with tumour markers and immune messengers.

Database checks first showed high PD-1 predicting poorer survival in one lung cancer type, while high CD28 predicted better survival in two types. Blood measurements then found PD-1-carrying T cells expanded in both nodule and cancer patients over controls, while CD28-carrying helper cells thinned out. The shifting balance, the authors suggest, mirrors immune exhaustion as disease advances.
pmc-13425982:
Rasmus Bjerén and colleagues audited prehospital pain care for acute abdominal pain by clinician type in a 2026 retrospective observational study. Ambulance records from an earlier cohort were reviewed in full, including numeric rating scores and free-text pain descriptions. The comparison separated prehospital emergency nurses from other clinicians and also examined patient sex, age, and time spent before hospital arrival.

Outcomes covered whether pain was assessed, whether analgesia was given, whether pain was reassessed, and whether an end-of-encounter score was recorded. Uneven documentation or treatment by competence level would point training toward specific gaps in abdominal pain care. Pain that is not checked, not eased, and not checked once more is pain that rides to the ward door with the sick man or woman.
pmc-13426382:
Eric Emmanuel T. Aragon and colleagues charted kidney problems in Filipino children with COVID-19 in a 2026 retrospective cohort study at Philippine General Hospital. Children with PCR-confirmed infection admitted from March 2020 to April 2023 were analyzed for how often kidney dysfunction occurred, which forms it took, and which factors raised risk. Kidney injury is well documented in infected adults but pediatric data from resource-limited settings were scarce.

Outcomes included need for dialysis-type replacement therapy and death rates across the spectrum of kidney involvement. Local evidence of this kind guides monitoring intensity for infected children whose kidney problems might otherwise surface late. Young kids can not say where it hurts or what feels wrong, so blood and wee tests must do much of the talk in their care.
pmc-13427082:
Barros and colleagues analyze in 2026 how Brazil should deploy its newly approved chikungunya vaccine. The live-attenuated shot was authorized in 2025 against a mosquito-borne virus that causes fever and severe joint pain. They combined national case notifications with social development data to map where transmission and vulnerability overlap.

Transmission moved in cycles and expanded toward the Southeast and South, Brazil's most crowded regions, where population immunity is low. The heaviest burden, though, sits in poorer municipalities in the Northeast, where weak health services also hide cases. The authors recommend a hybrid rollout: start with high-incidence towns in the Northeast, then reach the big southeastern cities before outbreaks grow. They add that vaccine limits in high-risk groups and live surveillance must guide the campaign.
pmc-13427182:
Maike Däther and colleagues show a modified nucleoside drug can raise TET enzyme activity and hydroxymethylcytosine in cells in a 2026 epigenetics study. TET enzymes oxidize methylated cytosine in DNA to the hydroxymethyl form, reactivating genes silenced by promoter methylation. Aggressive cancers such as acute myeloid leukemia and glioblastoma often lose TET function, lowering hydroxymethyl marks and helping tumors develop.

Their carbocyclic 5-aza-2'-deoxycytidine antimetabolite increased TET expression and formation of the hydroxymethyl mark in the systems tested. Restoring an epigenetic eraser pharmacologically could reopen silenced tumor suppressor programs, a strategy distinct from blocking methylation outright. Lost marks of this kind are a hall mark of fast, hard to treat growths. The drug is a tweaked form of a known pill, so its path to test in man may be more swift than a brand new drug would face. The work was done in cells grown in the lab.
pmc-13427482:
Xinting Liu and coauthors report gene therapy after stopping enzyme treatment in children with infantile Pompe disease in a 2026 single-arm trial. Six children aged about 12 to 51 months got one intravenous infusion of AAV9 virus. The virus carried the GAA gene their bodies lack, and the children had previously received between 10 and 98 cycles of enzyme replacement therapy. Earlier work showed infants with minimal prior enzyme therapy stayed free of ventilators and enzyme infusions for at least a year after one dose.

Whether older children with long, high-dose enzyme exposure keep the same benefit after stopping treatment was unknown, so twelve months of follow-up tracked motor, breathing, and safety outcomes. Sustained benefit would reshape lifelong treatment for this muscle disease.
pmc-13427582:
Xuehua Yang and co-authors present, in 2026, a computer-guided way to rebuild mouse antibodies so the human body will accept them. Their targets are orthopoxviruses, the family that includes mpox. Mouse antibodies can trigger unwanted immune reactions in people, yet older rebuilding methods often weaken how well an antibody grips its target. The new method matches three-dimensional shapes instead of only matching letter sequences.

Two rebuilt antibodies kept their grip on the virus, and one neutralized it better than the mouse original. Given together, they protected every mouse in a lethal vaccinia challenge, even when dosing began two days after infection. In a second mouse model they also cut mpox spread through the body. The approach could speed work on antibody drugs for related viruses.
pmc-13427982:
Ebe and colleagues described in 2026 the care of a 57-year-old man whose heart failed badly after he had a mechanical aortic valve fitted. Pumps that pass through that valve, such as the Impella device, cannot be used with a mechanical valve in place. The man's heart failure worsened to shock, a state where blood flow cannot meet the body's needs, and he came to need dialysis for kidney failure.

Ebe's team chose a staged plan: first they replaced the mechanical valve with a tissue valve, which then allowed Impella pump support. The pump steadied his blood flow and his organs recovered, which lowered his risk for the next step. Surgeons then implanted a durable HeartMate 3 pump as long-term therapy, and the patient recovered well enough to leave hospital. The case shows valve conversion can open the way to advanced heart support.
pmc-13428382:
Shahla Vilcassim and colleagues test silencing a gene called Tmprss6 in mice with myelodysplastic syndromes, blood disorders where marrow makes faulty cells and leukaemia risk rises. Iron overload worsens the disease by fuelling oxidative stress and inflammation, yet how chronic excess drives decline was poorly mapped.

A liver hormone, hepcidin, governs body iron, and Tmprss6 normally holds hepcidin down. Silencing Tmprss6 should lift hepcidin and choke off excess iron and its inflammatory fallout. The paper's title reports less iron-driven inflammation and longer survival in the mice, giving a gene-silencing route that disease-modifying care currently lacks.
pmc-13428482:
Juan P Sanabria-Mazo and colleagues ask whether acceptance- and mindfulness-based therapies build psychological flexibility in people living with chronic pain. Psychological flexibility means adapting thoughts and behaviour to personal values despite pain. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis pools randomised controlled trials on this question.

The team searched five databases to May 2025 and included 60 trials with 6,692 participants. The therapies improved overall psychological flexibility after treatment and at short- and long-term follow-up, and improved acceptance at every time point. Effects on committed action and personal values were not significant. Most trials carried a high risk of bias. The evidence certainty was low to very low. Effects were larger against inactive controls and when psychologists delivered stand-alone programmes.
pmc-13429282:
Kanoun and colleagues check the pregnancy safety of modafinil, a wakefulness drug used for narcolepsy, after registry reports raised alarm about birth defects. Their 2026 study uses France's national health database, covering nearly eleven million singleton births from 2009 to 2024. It compares 865 children exposed before birth with children exposed to methylphenidate, a related stimulant, and with matched unexposed children, tracking major congenital anomalies and later development.

First trimester exposure carried a raised anomaly risk next to methylphenidate, though the estimate was imprecise, with a wide range that nearly touched no effect. Against matched unexposed children the raise shrank and its range crossed no effect, so a modest risk can neither be confirmed nor ruled out. Development disorders and specialist visits matched the unexposed group. The authors advise caution in pregnancy while noting the drug showed no sign of harming later brain development in this dataset.
pmc-13431882:
Terry and colleagues used a weakened fruit fly gene in 2026 to study how germ cell development and meiosis, the division that halves chromosome number for eggs and sperm, stay in step. Full loss of the gene mei-P26 causes tumor-like ovaries, but the weakened version left flies fertile enough to inspect chromosome behavior.

In mutants, about 60 percent of cell clusters carried markers of two stages at once, a sign that the switch out of ordinary division ran late. The protein scaffold that aligns chromosomes in meiosis rarely formed full tracks, appearing broken or in dots. Crossovers, the swaps that shuffle genes, still formed but landed in the wrong places, near chromosome centers rather than arms, and their spacing control weakened while their guarantee held. The authors propose that late exit from division lets dividing signals leak into meiosis and scramble its patterning.
pmc-13432882:
Wang and colleagues review bovine endometritis, inflammation of the womb lining after calving, a drag on dairy cow fertility worldwide, in 2026 veterinary research combining a systematic review with meta-analysis. The review centers on Escherichia coli, an early arrival in the post-calving uterus and a key driver of inflammation. Reported disease rates vary widely by region, farm practices, setting, and test method, and the authors set out to map that spread plus the bacterium's weapons.

E. coli causes damage through adhesins that grip tissue, toxins, surface lipopolysaccharides, shielding capsules, iron-grabbing siderophores, and biofilms that resist clearance. Together these factors promote settling, immune activation, and tissue injury. The review then weighs current and new treatments for practicality on farms. Wang notes two limits plainly: disease estimates vary enormously between studies, and promising therapies still lack strong herd-level validation.
pmc-13433382:
Anne Großkopf, Lars Saemann, and Andreas Simm reviewed in 2026 how cell-to-cell talk goes astray in aging and long-run swelling, with aged cells cast as the chief wreckers. Sound talk lets many-celled life hold shape and fight germs. With age, the crisp signal web frays into noise, driven by cells that have quit splitting yet pour out a loud mix of signals.

That loud mix fans swelling body-wide and drags sound cells toward the same aged state. Two drug plans grow from the picture: kill the aged cells, or mute their loud mix while they live. Both plans have won in animal tests. The authors frame the move to human trials as the next gate for the young science of aging.
pmc-13433582:
D Pinilla-Beltrán, Leonardo Duarte-Santos, and Mariana F Nery compared genes across six river whale and dolphin kinds in 2026, hunting shared marks of the shift from sea to fresh water. That shift ranks among the boldest in mammal tales, yet its gene base stayed dim. Three lenses met: picked genes, family size swings, and pace shifts.

Five of six kinds bore pick marks on two genes, one tied to swelling replies and one to digestion. Rich sets lit paths for blood growth, salt balance, bone build, and immune work, which mirror fresh water's strains. Family swings churned immune, control, and grip genes. Pace work found ninety-five genes with matched shifts. Picked gene overlap stayed thin and broke clan lines, which paints fresh water gains as many small roads to like ends.
pmc-13434282:
Anna Maria Goździejewska and colleagues chart who eats whom in carp ponds in 2026. Pond food webs decide how stable the pond stays and how well carp grow. Network maps weighed how much mass each small water species moves and how species help or block each other.

Small water fleas and wheel shaped animals that feed in distinct ways held the web together. Kinds that cope well with blue green algae blooms mattered most. Harmful links from hunting and rivalry played a smaller role. Pond managers learn which tiny species to protect if they want steady carp growth with less feed waste.
pmc-13434382:
Kang and Yu reported in 2026 an 18-year-old man whose sinus mass looked like a cancer. It proved to be a benign tangle of blood vessels inside bone, in the right maxillary sinus. Such hemangiomas make up under one percent of bone tumors and are very rare in the sinuses. Their scans can mimic malignant growths, a trap for overtreatment.

The young man came in with a blocked nose and nosebleeds on the right side. Imaging showed a destructive mass that raised fear of osteosarcoma, a bone cancer. A small biopsy, though, showed only bland bone features that did not match the alarming scans. Surgeons removed the inner sinus wall through the nose, and tissue tests confirmed a venous hemangioma. The authors urge keeping this benign option in mind whenever scans and biopsy disagree.
pmc-13434482:
Jessabell Cabada writes to the editor on lifting maternal nutrition counselling in the Philippines, learning from a recent Ethiopian trial. In Ethiopia, structured clinic-based nutrition teaching greatly improved diet variety and iron-folic acid use among pregnant women.

Repeat standard counselling with picture aids, given by trained health workers, shifted what mothers ate in low- and middle-income settings. Cabada argues the model fits the Philippines too, where poor maternal nutrition and vitamin and mineral shortfalls still persist. Health planners get a tested counselling template, plus a call to adapt its aids and training to Filipino clinics rather than importing it wholesale.
pmc-13434782:
Tianqing Yan and a large team steady a ruthenium water splitter for acid duty in 2026. High charge ruthenium splits water fast in acid, yet that same state dissolves and dies. Single ruthenium atoms pinned at the edges of a manganese oxide host solve the clash here.

Surface hydroxyl groups buffer extra charge and tune how parts bind. The host soaks up strain that would wreck the guest atoms. Activity jumped 223 fold over plain ruthenium oxide, while life grew a thousand fold by one key count. A full cell ran past 1,000 hours at plant level current. Precious metal use fell by four fifths.
pmc-13435382:
Rui Zhang's team studied breathing trials in 2026 to predict who will need a breathing tube again soon after it is removed. A spontaneous breathing trial is the standard readiness test before freeing a patient from a ventilator, but some who pass still fail within two days. Effort during the trial reflects the balance of lung load and muscle strength, yet it is often hard to measure without extra airway steps.

In 150 adults on ventilators for at least two days, the team read a flow index breath by breath from chest impedance imaging during a 30-minute trial. The index was tied to trial outcome and to reintubation within 48 hours, giving staff a continuous, non-invasive warning sign. Intensive care teams get a candidate bedside aid for safer weaning decisions.
pmc-13435682:
Shrestha Barai's team characterized lignin-eating Bacillus strains in 2026 to improve jute fiber processing. Jute carries far more lignin than flax or ramie, and chemical removal harms the environment and costs too much, limiting textile use. The team studied three strains, one each of Bacillus subtilis, amyloliquefaciens, and licheniformis, tuning growth, profiling lignin enzymes, and sequencing whole genomes for key genes.

Paired with proven pectin-eating strains, the trio could form a microbial retting mix that cuts both lignin and retting time, lifting fiber quality for higher-end cloth. Textile teams get a foundation for a greener, cheaper retting recipe. Factory-scale proof will decide whether the lab promise holds in mills.
pmc-13435982:
Aach and colleagues published in 2026 the protocol for a German multicenter trial testing whether exoskeleton-based feedback therapy beats conventional therapy for walking after chronic spinal cord injury. The trial enrolls patients who keep some leg movement despite a long-standing injury. Robotic assistance may retrain walking in ways standard physiotherapy cannot, but proof against an active control has been missing.

One hundred eighty patients across eight injury centers and fifteen rehabilitation centers will be assigned at random, half to Hybrid Assistive Limb therapy and half to usual care. Both arms train sixty minutes, five times a week, for twelve weeks. Success means a clear gain on at least one of three walking measures, scored by assessors who do not know the assignments. Quality of life, pain, and bladder function are also tracked to six months.
pmc-13436682:
Quy Quoc Tran and coauthors report a 60 year old woman whose heart attack masked a body wide clot storm in 2026. Severe rheumatic mitral narrowing plus atrial fibrillation and patchy blood thinning set the stage. She arrived in shock with ST elevation on her heart trace.

Heart imaging showed clot blocks in several small branches with clean artery walls. Suction cleared flow, yet shock, kidney failure, and leg ischemia deepened. Body scans then found clots in gut, spleen, kidney, and leg arteries. She died of multiorgan failure despite care. Heart attacks from clots warrant whole body checks when decline persists.
pmc-13437182:
Behrad Yadolahi, Mehdi Taghian, and Leyli Sadri reviewed new fiber-based systems that deliver drugs straight to diseased gums and mouth lining. Their 2026 systematic review searched five databases for English studies from 2015 to 2025 and kept eight papers, half original studies and half reviews. The carriers were mostly electrospun fibers, thin strands spun from polymers, or sticky patches that cling to wet tissue.

Spinning reliably produced even, porous mats with fibers about 250 to 500 nanometers wide, the review reports. Loads such as doxycycline, curcumin, and neem extract leaked out slowly, over hours or up to a week. The mats stuck firmly, lowered several inflammation markers, and killed up to 98 percent of target bacteria, with no sign of irritation. Yet methods varied widely between studies, and bias risk was rated moderate. The authors ask for shared making rules and long-term stability tests before clinic use.
pmc-13437282:
Mark Windheim and Khadija Aichane-Simon review a viral protein that human adenoviruses use to quiet the immune system. Species D, the largest group, alone carries a protein called E3/49K. Their 2026 review explains how this protein targets CD45, a switch on white blood cells that helps control their activation.

The protein sits in the cell surface and also sheds a soluble piece, the only secreted protein known from these viruses. Both forms grip CD45 tightly, force it to pair up, and block its normal enzyme action. That grip dampens T cells, B cells, and natural killer cells at once. The authors link this trick to how these viruses adapt and persist in people. They also raise a hopeful flip side: a tool this precise at calming immunity might one day serve medicine against unwanted immune attack or in cancer care.
pmc-13437482:
Zhi-Lie Cao and co-authors rework the story of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, a rare inherited condition bringing skin bumps, lung cysts, and kidney tumors. Faults in the FLCN gene cause it, and textbooks long classed it among disorders of runaway mTORC1 signaling. New structural and gene-wide studies, reviewed in 2026, show the gene's product instead steers that switch selectively, choosing which targets it may reach.

Losing both copies in kidney cells locks growth factors in the cell core and rewires fuel use, driving tumors. Losing one copy is enough to weaken lung and skin structure, without the full tumor program. This lens settles an old paradox about signals seeming both too high and too low. The authors point to fresh therapy targets, aimed at the trapped growth factors and rewired enzymes. Their pitch is organ-specific precision care.
pmc-13438882:
Chaves and colleagues evaluate a hypertension control program in a large South Florida health system in this 2026 longitudinal study. Leon Medical Centers serves Medicare beneficiaries who are overwhelmingly of Hispanic origin, a population in which program effects were little studied. The system launched a multicomponent program in 2011 with team-based care, standardized measurement, pharmacy and transport support, and culturally tailored engagement, and the team tracked control rates through 2018.

The patient sample grew as the program matured. It rose from 4,710 to 21,540 people in total. Average age rose too, from about 73 to about 77 years. After full implementation, the adjusted odds of controlled blood pressure were about five to six times higher than before. Crude control rates reached roughly ninety percent using time-averaged readings, while single-visit readings consistently underestimated control and agreed only fairly with the averaged measure.
pmc-13439182:
Maélie Caussé and co-authors report a hydrogen-rich compound that survives the trip back to normal pressure, in 2026 work on hydride chemistry. Squeezing hydrogen with metals past 100 gigapascals can form odd materials with rich hydrogen lattices, some prized as possible superconductors. Most fall apart once pressure drops. The team heated a hydrogen-loaded yttrium and iron mix in a diamond anvil cell, starting near 60 gigapascals.

Crystallography and computer searches mapped the new compound, Y3Fe4H20, built from iron and hydrogen units sharing edge atoms around yttrium centres. Brought back to room pressure, the material held its form for tens of hours before changing. Keeping such phases stable without pressure is a key step toward studying and using them in ordinary labs.
pmc-13439982:
Luisa Klotz's team updated multiple sclerosis research in 2026, summarizing eighteen months of advances in the most common disease where immune attack strips nerve insulation in the brain and spine. Relapse control has improved with immune therapies, yet disease initiation, progression drivers, and prediction remain partly mysterious. The review covers aging effects on glia and immune cells, tissue-resident memory cells, imaging and biomarkers, AI prediction, and trials targeting immune cells inside the nervous system.

Readers get a current synthesis that separates settled gains from open questions, especially around progression biology that current drugs only partly address. Clinicians and researchers can use the update to place new trials and biomarkers in context. It is a review, so its claims rest on the cited primary studies.
pmc-13440682:
Silva and colleagues report a 2026 study of voice and swallowing after total thyroid removal, surveyed in the late recovery period. Seventeen women, at least six months past surgery without node dissection or radiotherapy, completed two questionnaires. One covered thyroidectomy-related voice and throat symptoms, and one covered thyroid-related quality of life.

The median symptom score sat in a range showing persistent complaints for many women, and the team analyzed how voice and swallowing self-ratings relate to overall quality of life scores. Even without nerve injury or added treatments, patients report lasting changes in how the voice feels and how swallowing works, complaints clinics can dismiss as minor. Documenting them with validated instruments makes the case for routine late follow-up and speech therapy referral pathways after thyroid surgery, not only early wound checks.
pmc-13440782:
Naito and colleagues reported a 2026 MRI study on severe facial pain. Trigeminal neuralgia brings short, stabbing pain attacks on one side of the face. A blood vessel pressing the nerve explains many cases, but not all. The team asked whether skull shape itself raises the risk of pain.

They measured scans from 20 patients, 20 people with facial spasm, and 16 controls. Both pain and spasm groups had a shallower back skull space than controls. The gap between key nerves ran smaller in both patient groups as well. On the painful side, nerve spacing shrank further still in the pain group. A cramped skull space may set the stage for nerve trouble. Such measures may one day flag at-risk patients before pain begins.
pmc-13441982:
Jiangwei Yang and colleagues pool trials of acupoint stimulation added to standard care for obsessive-compulsive disorder, publishing a 2026 meta-analysis. Acupoint methods span needle acupuncture, electroacupuncture, and skin-surface electrical stimulation. Twenty-three randomised trials with 1,713 participants were gathered from seven databases to February 2026, with bias graded by standard Cochrane tools.

Adding it improved symptom scores clearly beyond control care on the standard Yale-Brown scale. Anxiety and global impression scores also moved favourably. The largest gains appeared where the method joined both medication and cognitive behavioural therapy together. Reported adverse events ran far fewer in treated groups than in medication controls. Subgroup hints pointed to point sets including PC6, a wrist point, and to twenty to forty sessions as favourable ranges, though those readings rest on few studies. The authors call the adjunct promising and comparatively gentle.
pmc-13442382:
Tania Sharmin and Colleen McDowell review two eye receptors, alpha4 and alpha9, in a 2026 paper on fluid pressure inside the eye. Each receptor pairs with a beta1 partner to form alpha4beta1 or alpha9beta1. Both sit in the meshwork and canal that drain fluid from the front of the eye.

The review sets out how these receptors link cells to the mesh around them and sense stretch and pull. It traces their contact with a fibronectin piece called FN+EDA, a contact that can raise drain blockage. Links with the TLR4 and TGF-beta paths also get close attention, since those links may drive scar-like change in the meshwork of eyes with glaucoma. The authors frame both receptors as fresh drug targets.
pmc-13442982:
Shen Ju Liang and colleagues report a 68-year-old woman with vessel inflammation plus two rare turns in a 2026 case paper. Her illness, microscopic polyangiitis, most often wounds kidneys and lungs. She came in short of breath at rest, with huge thirst and urine flow that pointed to a gland fault in her brain.

Blood tests showed a p-ANCA mark at a titer of 1 to 10 strength, plus myeloperoxidase antibodies. Brain scans confirmed gland injury, and steroid plus immune globulin care helped at first. One week in, a kidney artery balloon burst, and her blood count fell from 95 grams per liter to a low of 47 grams per liter. A dye-guided plug sealed the bleed, and she rallied well on strong drug pulses.
pmc-13443182:
Jalil Jafari Dashkasan and colleagues demonstrate a 2026 optics method for hardening laser beams against air turbulence, a key need for free-space communication and precision light tools. The team generated single and paired partially coherent Bessel-Vortex beams with a spatial light modulator, sending them through a lab turbulence chamber matched to a 1 kilometer sky path.

Pairing beams with same-sign topological charges grew steadily tougher as the charge gap widened, while opposite-sign pairs behaved unevenly, weakest at a gap of 8. Equal-and-opposite pairs degraded steadily up to order 14, a pattern absent in single beams. Encoding beam shape and turbulence on one hologram kept the setup simple. Charge pairing thus emerges as a fresh design lever for resilient optical links.
pmc-13444182:
Sou-Hyun Lee and Kyung-Hwa Kwak review how birth anesthesia shapes later mind health in mothers in a 2026 paper. Postpartum depression and trauma stress can dent mother-child bonds and life quality for years. Their review sweeps risk marks before birth, mode of birth, drug care, and long outcomes.

Full sleep anesthesia for cesarean birth tied to higher severe depression and self-harm risk in the pooled work. Epidural pain care, judged as a yes-no mark, showed no shield against either state. Relief quality, pain during surgery, failed spinal care, and forced switches to full sleep looked like the true levers. Ketamine drugs near birth may cut early depression risk, with long gains unproven. The authors urge trauma-aware talk as core care.
pmc-13444282:
Masayuki Endo and colleagues report two cases of coronary subclavian steal treated through vessel tools in a 2026 paper. The state starves the heart when a narrowed shoulder artery robs flow from a bypass graft. A 75-year-old man held a hard, chalky narrow spot in his left subclavian artery near its start.

Stepwise balloon widening, then a covered stent, fixed his flow. The twin case, an 83-year-old man, had a tight spot with slim room between two branch mouths, plus disease in both spine arteries. Balloons guarded both branches while the stent went in, which kept heart and brain flow safe. The authors tailor each plan to lump shape and branch maps, a rule they urge for this rare steal state.
pmc-13445382:
Wenyan Lu and colleagues design a new compound that hits two targets at once for Alzheimer's disease, in a 2026 drug study. The starting drug blocked a family of enzymes that loosen gene control, and it also propped up a growth signal that fades in the Alzheimer brain. The team reshaped that drug to do both jobs more strongly.

Their lead compound, W2A-28, blocked only the first three enzymes of the family and spared the rest. In cells it raised the growth signal, and in lab tests it held up well in liver samples and crossed barriers with ease. In brain organoids grown from Alzheimer patients, it cut tau tangles and amyloid levels, which marks it as a candidate worth animal testing.
pmc-13445482:
Fatemeh Fereidooni and colleagues pool past studies on tranexamic acid, a drug that slows bleeding, given during bladder removal surgery, in a 2026 review. The surgery saves lives in bladder cancer yet often brings heavy blood loss and transfusions. Whether the drug helps here, and at what risk, stayed unsettled.

Four studies, one trial and three cohort studies, met the search rules, with sizes from sixty-four to nine hundred thirty-six patients. Those given the drug lost less blood and needed fewer transfusions, above all after surgery. No rise in vein clots appeared, and pooled results linked the drug to lower death rates after surgery. The small study count tempers the claim, so the authors frame the drug as promising.
pmc-13445682:
Turki Aldrees and coauthors describe a 2026 look back at germ growths and drug fight-back in long-term sinus illness patients who had sinus surgery. The team went over 444 patients treated at a Saudi university hospital from 2014 to 2018, studying 803 grown samples from sinus scope exams.

Germs grew in 76 percent of samples, led by Staphylococcus aureus at 32 percent, followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Gram-positive germs fared best with vancomycin and ofloxacin, yet many germs fought off drugs in common use. Surgeons gain a local fight-back map for choosing therapy, though single-center data limit how far the results stretch.
pmc-13446182:
Caterina Benedetto and colleagues report a seventy-year-old man with a rare cancer of the tear gland, treated with limited surgery and carbon ion radiation, published in 2026. Tumors of this gland are very rare, and the standard path is wide removal that can cost the eye, followed by radiation. His tumor caused no symptoms and was found as a primary ductal adenocarcinoma.

Surgeons removed the growth with a careful, tissue-sparing operation, yet some disease stayed behind. Carbon ion treatment then cleared the tumor in full, with only mild side effects, since the heavy particles drop their dose with sharp precision. The case shows an eye-saving route for a cancer whose rarity leaves long-term odds murky, and it adds weight to particle therapy for orbital tumors.
pmc-13446482:
Barry L. Westcott reports the crystal structure of a cobalt salt built from a paired-ring ketone ligand, in a 2026 study. Two ligand molecules grip the cobalt ion through a ring nitrogen and the ketone oxygen, while two water molecules cap the top and bottom spots. The shape lands near a stretched octahedron, with the metal on a center of symmetry.

The salt matches copper and nickel cousins reported before, yet its water bonds run far shorter than the copper form, a gap chalked up to the copper ion's known distortion. Tetrafluoroborate anions take hydrogen bonds from the bound waters and stitch the units into layers, with weak extra contacts from the sulfur ring. The report completes a trio of like structures across three metals.
pmc-13447082:
Qi Li and colleagues review how a mother's high-fat diet in pregnancy may raise her child's later risk of Parkinson's disease, in a 2026 paper. The diet stokes low-grade inflammation and oxidative stress in the mother, which reshapes the womb through the placenta. The fetal midbrain cells that make dopamine, the very cells lost in Parkinson's, take selective harm.

Two paths reinforce each other in the account: a stuck-on insulin resistance and inflammation axis, and a choked clean-up system for worn cell power plants. Together they leave dopamine cells with thin reserves for adult life. The authors gather early warning marks across inflammation, clean-up molecules, gene tags, and diet records, and they weigh food, anti-inflammatory, and clean-up boosting plans for prevention.
pmc-13447182:
Dae Young Cheon writes in 2026 about what blood pressure patterns at hospital discharge may reveal after a heart failure flare. The two to three months after discharge carry high risks of death and return to hospital, yet few tools flag who is most at risk at that moment. A study discussed here measured pressure over a full day just before patients went home.

In three hundred patients, unusual night-time patterns, where pressure rose or fell too far, linked to worse short-term outcomes. Higher swing in pressure across the day seemed to reflect illness severity rather than add risk on its own. Cheon frames discharge monitoring as a snapshot of nerve and hormone strain at a fragile handover point. That reading may help teams target closer follow-up where it matters most.
pmc-13447282:
Lulu Xie and co-authors test how shade and soil pathogens together shape Korean pine seedlings in a 2026 controlled experiment. Young pines struggle to establish under dense forest canopy in northeast China. Low light and rising soil disease pressure both threaten survival, yet their combined effect on root choices was unclear.

Seedlings grew under three light levels and four pathogen doses, with survival, growth and leaf and root traits measured. Shade alone cut survival, growth, photosynthesis and plant mass, while high pathogen doses deepened the harm and sharply raised deaths. Leaves responded to light only, growing thinner and richer in nitrogen under shade. Roots shifted strategy under pathogen pressure, moving from thin, gathering roots toward thicker roots richer in defensive chemicals, a trade-off the authors link to forest renewal.
pmc-13448082:
Hao-Ran Yue and coauthors report a 2026 account of how MND1 cuts breast cancer drug response through RAD51-aided DNA repair. The team took MND1 in cell lines, tested growth, fight-back curves, DNA damage, and cell death in cells and animals, and traced protein and gene control.

MND1 ran high in breast cancer and tracked worsening and cisplatin fight-back, calling in USP5 to steady RAD51 and boost matching reshuffle repair. E2F1 drove MND1 through switch unmasking and switch-on. The feedback loop marks MND1 as a healing target for bringing back drug response.
