pmc-13448282:
Chung and colleagues are tracing how T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, a fast-growing blood cancer, enters the central nervous system. Their 2026 laboratory report focuses on the meninges, the membranes around the brain and spinal cord, where this leukemia often settles. Current prevention uses chemotherapy injected into the spinal fluid, which can harm children's developing brains, so a targeted alternative matters.

Chung used a mouse leukemia driven by the NOTCH1 gene and found leukemia cells clustering early under the back of the skull. That spot is rich in bone marrow and tiny channels linking marrow to the meninges. With advanced microscopy, the team is testing whether cells travel through those channels. They are also testing whether a signal chemical called CXCL12, made by meningeal support cells, guides them via its receptor CXCR4. Blocking that route could one day limit brain spread without blanket chemotherapy.
pmc-13448782:
Hamed Al Ahbabi and colleagues report in 2026 a survey from the United Arab Emirates that ranks which childhood illnesses medical students must see during their pediatrics rotation. Students who had finished the rotation and doctors who teach it rated 81 illnesses grouped under common presenting complaints. Each illness was scored on a five-point scale, from must see to must not see.

Forty-nine usable replies came back, 39 from students and 10 from faculty or physicians. Asthma, pneumonia, bronchiolitis, gastroenteritis, iron deficiency anemia, febrile seizure, and heart murmur topped the shared list. Student and teacher rankings agreed closely, with a correlation of 0.863 across illnesses. A reliability analysis found that just ten student raters would suffice to keep such curriculum monitoring dependable over time.
pmc-13449782:
Hong-Yu Wu and colleagues test in 2026 whether the well-known Alzheimer gene APOE changes how strongly high blood pressure predicts the disease. Their data come from 318,923 UK Biobank participants free of dementia at entry, followed a median of thirteen years, with blood protein profiles for 34,141 of them across 2,790 proteins. Models accounted for the competing risk of death.

Hypertension interacted significantly with the APOE ε4 variant, yet the surprise lay in the ordering. The blood pressure association ran strongest in carriers of the normally protective ε2 form, at a hazard ratio of 1.570, then ε33 carriers at 1.213, then ε4 carriers at 1.129. In the ε2 group, two proteins, prosaposin and a ganglioside activator, statistically carried about ten and three percent of the link, both tied to fat metabolism in lysosomes. The authors call the protein clues exploratory.
pmc-13450482:
Batenkova and colleagues showed in 2026 how to coat surfaces with copper oxide nanoparticles, tiny grains used in sensors and catalysts, without any soap-like stabilizers. Electrophoretic deposition, which uses an electric field to pull charged particles onto a surface, is cheap and fast, but dirty particle surfaces make coatings uneven. The team cleaned the grains with mild washing and heating in oxygen or ozone gas.

Two lab methods, one using X-rays and one using antimatter particles that reveal missing atoms, confirmed the cleaning cut surface defects such as single missing atoms and small clusters of them. Cleaner grains carried a far stronger electric charge in ethanol, past the level that keeps suspensions stable, so they moved fast and packed evenly even at high loading. The result was uniform porous coatings free of organic residue, a greener route that works whatever the powder's past handling.
pmc-13450582:
Sakshi Chopra and co-authors tell in 2026 of a cancer drug side effect that looked like a severe drug allergy. The drug, blinatumomab, links immune killer cells to leukemia cells and is used for a blood cancer of B cells. That strong immune wake-up can flood the body with signals that cause fever, rash, and organ strain.

Their patient, a woman aged 65 with the leukemia, grew a syndrome of swelling, rash, and high counts of a white cell type tied to allergy. Those signs match a named allergy pattern called DRESS, yet here the cause was the immune flood itself. Oral steroids settled the episode fast, and the case urges care teams to sort look-alike reactions before changing cancer care.
pmc-13451082:
Katarzyna Nowak, Ashley Elliott, and Michelle McHenry report in 2026 on a plan to steady ultrasound training for joint-care trainees in Northern Ireland. Joint ultrasound is now a daily tool, yet no shared national training path exists in the United Kingdom. Their team first surveyed local trainees on practice, oversight, record keeping, and paths to formal proof of skill.

Most trainees scanned a few times a week, yet oversight varied and only one kept a planned logbook. The team built a logbook tied to European skill levels and launched it at a teaching day, with a bingo game to spur interest. The pack aims to give each trainee a clear road to formal qualification.
pmc-13451282:
Kardelen Akar and co-authors find in 2026 that a no-cost balance test spots early nerve decline in multiple sclerosis better than a timed walk. Strong new drugs leave many patients with low disability scores, so clinics need sharper tools for faint loss. The team ran ten balance tasks with motion sensors on 71 patients and 45 matched healthy peers.

Standing on one leg with eyes shut split early-stage patients from healthy peers, while the timed walk did not. Only a fifth of early patients held the pose for thirty seconds, versus over two thirds of healthy peers. A combined score with two standard hand and walk tests did even better, and a fresh group confirmed the result.
pmc-13451382:
Elbashir and Nour surveyed 261 children aged 5 to 16 in a canal-watered village of Gezira State, Sudan. They checked for urogenital schistosomiasis, the worm infection spread through contact with worm-bearing canal water. Urine was spun down and checked under the microscope for Schistosoma haematobium eggs in this one-time survey.

The overall share reached 44 percent, with 115 of 261 children infected at the time of the survey in the village. Most infections, 102 of the 115, were light by egg-count class used. The sex split was extreme. Boys made up 96.5 percent of infections and girls only 3.5 percent among positive cases found. Frequent canal contact for swimming, bathing, washing, and watering animals was strongly linked with infection. Tap water supplied drinking needs. The authors call for ongoing treatment rounds, health teaching, and sanitation upgrades.
pmc-13451582:
Michelangelo Sartori and co-authors pilot in 2026 a home pump for a blood-flow drug in patients with limbs at risk and no path to vessel repair. The drug, iloprost, ran slowly through a small squeeze pump at home for a year, and its record was set against a hospital group that got faster drips. Side effects were the main score, with death and major limb loss tracked over three years.

Side effects hit about a seventh of the home group, versus near a third of the hospital group. Deaths and major limb losses also ran lower at home, though the groups differed in age and were not a clean match. The authors call the home route better tolerated and ask for firmer trials.
pmc-13451782:
Lu and Chong pilot a mind and behavior program for the persistent tiredness that follows colorectal cancer treatment, known as cancer related fatigue. Their 2026 trial assigned 50 patients who had finished treatment to six weeks of the program or to usual care. The team tracked whether a full trial could run well, checking sign up, attendance, and drop out rates, plus patient satisfaction through surveys and interviews.

The pilot hit its targets: most patients stayed, attendance was solid, and satisfaction ran high. Against usual care, the program group showed a clear drop in fatigue by the week after the program ended. Patients also moved more, ate better, and slept with fewer problems. Mood outcomes were weaker: anxiety and low mood trended down but did not reach clear gains. The authors call for a larger, longer trial to confirm the effects.
pmc-13451882:
Vitor Nascimento Vidal and co-authors review in 2026 how a family of cell gates and body fats team up to drive swelling. The gates, P2X receptors, open when ATP spills from stressed cells, a spill that swelling itself triggers. Fats freed early in swelling can wake cells to spill more ATP, which keeps the loop turning.

One gate sparks pain paths, while another fires a danger assembly that frees a key swelling signal. Other fats, the resolving kind, cool the loop by cutting ATP spill and gate counts. Still others, such as cholesterol, sit in the gate's frame and shape its work. The review maps these ties as leads for pain and swelling drugs.
pmc-13452182:
Evan Kransdorf and Luke Masha reflect in 2026 on gene testing for heart muscle disease, under a title borrowed from a rock song. A firm share of cases in both kinds of heart muscle disease carry a gene cause. Yields run near a fifth to a third in one kind and near half in the other, in clinic cohorts. Sicker patients, those bound for pumps or transplants, test positive more often.

Finding a variant in one patient opens cascade testing for the whole family and can start guard care early. The piece argues that set subgroups also clear the path for gene-tied drugs that change the disease, not just its symptoms. Its core claim: the song of testing stays worth singing.
pmc-13452282:
Sugihara and colleagues reported in 2026 how a steerable microcatheter sealed a giant false aneurysm at the fork of the thigh artery. A false aneurysm is a leaking pocket of blood outside a vessel wall, here left by a long access sheath. The patient had septic shock and poor clotting, ruling out easy surgery.

The leak sat where the thigh artery splits into two branches, and its entry tract was narrow and crooked. Two operators working together bent the steerable tip through the tract under live X-ray guidance. They then injected a small amount of medical glue mixed with contrast oil into the inflow, sealing the pocket. Leg blood flow stayed intact, and the authors present the method as a safe option for fragile patients.
pmc-13453482:
Wu and colleagues pooled randomized trials in 2026 to ask whether immune checkpoint inhibitors, cancer drugs that release the immune system, raise infection risk in patients with solid tumors. Their systematic review and meta-analysis covered 141 trials with 87,484 participants, counting both all infections and severe ones.

When all reported infections during treatment were counted, checkpoint drugs raised any-grade infection risk by about a quarter and severe infection risk by about a third. The increase was clearest in fair head-to-head comparisons against placebo or against chemotherapy alone. When only infections judged treatment-related were counted, no overall increase appeared, though the same fair comparisons still showed one. The authors urge weighing this modest risk against survival benefit for each patient.
pmc-13454282:
Xi Chen and seven co-authors report a 2026 test of a soil cleaner made by loading humic acid onto tiny iron particles. The material targets soils polluted with both chromium and cadmium, two toxic metals that can move into food and water. The team ran soil incubation tests to see how much metal the material could lock in place.

After treatment, the share of chromium that plants could take up fell by about 58 percent, and the cadmium share fell by about 36 percent. By day 50, more metal sat in stable soil forms that move less. Soil microbes grew more diverse, and soil fertility improved. The authors credit chemical reduction, surface binding, ion exchange, and microbe help for the cleanup.
pmc-13455282:
Shui-xiu Huang and colleagues report a 2026 interview study of mothers feeding preterm babies in China. Early birth often lands a baby in intensive care behind strict visiting rules, so mothers pump and store milk apart from their child, and many stop feeding early. Twenty mothers spoke by video at three stages, during intensive care, near discharge and after going home, at a maternal and child health centre in Fuzhou.

Three kinds of help kept coming up in their accounts. Family helped with pumping and storage. Experts helped with diet, starting lactation and feeding technique. Peers and workplaces helped through mothers who had done it before. Mothers wanted steady expert contact across all stages and clear training for family helpers, rather than one-off advice. The study points services toward joined-up, personal support that follows each mother from ward to home.
pmc-13455482:
Susanne Friis Søndergaard, Marie Dahl, and Annette Høgh evaluate, in a 2026 study, a telemedicine link used across hospitals and home care for diabetic foot ulcers. Photo sharing suits wound care well, yet tools often stall at organizational borders. The team observed professionals for 68 hours across Danish hospital and primary care settings during 2023 and 2024.

Three themes organize what they saw. Time came first: tight schedules squeezed the person-centered care the tool promised. Technology hurdles followed, as staff wrestled with devices and differing habits. Relationships proved decisive: where trust between sectors ran strong, the shared platform sped timely action and kept use alive. The authors' refined theory says the tool works when managers fix time and tech friction and when teams know each other well enough to collaborate across the boundary.
pmc-13456882:
Ramos Silva and colleagues review efforts to help primary care patients with long term non cancer pain cut back on opioids, pain drugs that carry real risks with long use. Their 2026 systematic review searched three databases for psychosocial programs, meaning support that targets habits and behavior, tested against a control group in primary care. The team also mapped which behavior change techniques each program used, to see what the working ones shared.

Thirteen studies with 3,130 patients qualified, but most were rated weak in quality, with only one rated strong. Eight programs succeeded in tapering opioid doses in primary care. One technique appeared in every effective program: behavior substitution, which means swapping the drug routine for a safer action or habit. The authors offer that map as a design guide, while warning that mixed study designs and patchy reporting limit firm claims.
pmc-13458082:
Prithbey Raj Dey and David Enke build a spatial map for non-Gaussian surface roughness in precision turning in a 2026 study. Turned surfaces rarely follow a bell curve, and their skewness and kurtosis shape friction and wear, yet roughness models often ignore those traits and average away repeat variation. The authors propose Spatial Non-Gaussian Roughness Metamodeling, pairing geospatial analysis with kriging interpolation to map mean roughness under explicitly non-Gaussian conditions.

Ordinary kriging captured spatial variation from the skewness-kurtosis domain, while universal kriging added machining parameters as drift and won group-wise cross-validation. The framework keeps repeat-measurement variability and reports uncertainty through kriging variance. Machinists gain a digital roughness map that respects real surface shapes and machining settings, rather than a single averaged roughness number.
pmc-13458582:
Yosef Golovachev and colleagues hide coded notes in public images without exchanging keys in a 2026 paper. Standard hidden writing needs shared keys, trained models or prior teamwork, limiting open use, while coding alone advertises secrecy. The authors propose a two-key hybrid inspired by one-time pad rules, hiding data with no key exchange or prior shared knowledge, claiming high secrecy and no trace.

Tests on 100 natural images showed strong defence to advanced hidden-data tests, with shape likeness above 0.97 and peak signal-to-noise ratio above 40 decibels, indicating no visible warping. The method is lightweight and needs no training or guesses tied to one image. Senders gain an open image-based channel for private notes, though outside security review must still probe the keyless design against dogged foes.
pmc-13458682:
Hai-En Tsai and colleagues squeeze more gamma rays from a tabletop-scale source by splitting the laser's job in two. Inverse Thomson scattering bounces laser light off relativistic electrons to make tunable MeV photons, prized for isotope identification and low-dose radiography, but ordinary setups waste the interaction. Their 2026 system drives a laser-plasma accelerator with a 100-terawatt laser giving a second laser the scattering role.

Electron beams tunable from 122 to 204 MeV, tightly collimated, steady in aim, produced gamma rays peaking from 276 keV to 1.2 MeV. Sliding the interaction point and stretching the scatter pulse separately, the team matched the pulse to the walk-off-limited overlap zone. Extending it to 200 femtoseconds raised photon output by 15 percent, beam narrow-band and well-behaved. Test radiographs showed MeV penetration at a tenth-millimeter resolution, and the source ran for hours across days, a milestone for compact gamma sources.
pmc-13459282:
Hongfei Lu and co-authors tested how a critically endangered Chinese fir tree copes with the warmer, drier conditions climate change is bringing to its mountain home. Abies beshanzuensis survives only in cool, high-elevation forests, so the team grew seedlings along an elevation gradient from 500 to 1,200 meters, using lower altitude as a stand-in for future warming. In their 2026 study, they measured growth, photosynthesis, protective chemicals, and gene activity across the gradient to find where the tree thrives and where it fails.

Seedlings grew best at 1,000 to 1,200 meters, while those at 500 meters showed clear stress. Down low, photosynthetic efficiency and protective heat-dissipation collapsed, chlorophyll and biomass fell sharply from their 1,000-meter peaks, and cell-damage markers rose despite strong chemical adjustments by the leaves. Gene activity shifted too, with heat-shock and defense pathways switched on and photosynthesis genes suppressed. Warming clearly overwhelms this relic species.
pmc-13459682:
Sae H. Han and Nicholas D. Soulakis tested in 2026 whether Google search interest could help Chicago's health department predict COVID-19 vaccination demand. Using the search company's vaccination search insights alongside the city's own dose records, they modeled weekly doses across 2021 for neighborhoods grouped by social need. Time-series models with and without the search data were compared on prediction error.

Adding search frequencies, lagged by roughly a week and a half, sharpened in-sample accuracy most clearly in highly vulnerable neighborhoods, where forecast error fell dramatically. Outside those areas, forecasts with search data sometimes did worse. Prediction intervals narrowed everywhere, suggesting greater model confidence. The authors frame search data as an extra planning tool, strongest where need is greatest.
pmc-13463582:
Quehui Tang and eight co-authors present the full mitochondrial genome of Acartiella sinensis, a small estuary copepod. Copepods are tiny crustaceans that anchor food webs where rivers meet the sea. Their genome is the first of its kind for the whole family Acartiidae.

The genome runs 14,368 bases long, with adenine and thymine making up nearly four fifths of its letters. All of its genes sit on one strand, and two genes have swapped places compared with kin species. Family trees built from the data place this species next to Labidocera rotunda and Eurytemora affinis. Readers gain a firm gene record for tracing how estuary copepods split and spread.
pmc-13464082:
Yi Peng and ten co-authors review hypoxia-inducible factors, the protein switches that help tumors thrive in low oxygen. Solid tumors often outgrow their blood supply, and these switches reroute growth, fuel use, and vessel sprouting to fit the shortage. Three main forms exist, each with its own control path.

Genes that never code for protein, cell fuel byproducts, and chemical tags all bend switch activity in tumors. The switched-on program feeds spread and drug resistance across many cancer types. Proof for the third form still runs thin and needs animal checks, the authors note. Blocker drugs against the switches close the review as a hopeful route to cut tumor survival.
pmc-13464282:
Aekapat Phoksiri and colleagues report a 2026 valve replacement in a 62-year-old man with a two-leaflet aortic valve and an anomalous left coronary artery. Severe symptomatic narrowing demanded a catheter valve, yet the artery's odd origin from the right cusp threatened future coronary access and redo valve options. Careful CT planning and patient-specific X-ray angles were used to align the new valve with the coronary openings.

The implant went ahead without complications and preserved coronary alignment, keeping future stenting and repeat valve work feasible. Younger valve patients live long enough to need such second procedures, so alignment matters beyond the first implant. The case shows anomalous anatomy need not block catheter valve care when CT planning is meticulous.
pmc-13464782:
Bahar Uslu Bayhan and four co-authors check whether day-one blood tests after weight-loss surgery flag patients headed for trouble. The team reviewed 260 adults who had elective bariatric surgery at one center. A combined bad-outcome count covered intensive care stays, infections, leaks, and readmission within a month.

About one in five patients met the combined outcome. Longer operations, higher AST liver enzyme levels, and a higher lactate-to-albumin ratio each tied to trouble on their own strength. AST sorted patients best, though only moderately well. The lactate ratio alone sorted poorly despite its link. Since many intensive care moves came before the blood draw, the authors frame the links as warning signs, not forecasts.
pmc-13464982:
Juan Carlos Solomando and six co-authors test a pocket near-infrared scanner for judging berry quality without cutting fruit. One hundred forty-five lots of aronia, haskap, and goji berries, across harvest years and ripeness stages, were scanned and lab-tested. Models tied light patterns to sugar, moisture, acidity, and health compounds.

Cross-checks scored the models strongly, and fresh-lot validation held up well for most traits. Sugar content forecast best of all, while total phenolics proved hardest to pin down. Error ratios supported rough quantity grading fit for field sorting. Growers and buyers gain a fast, fruit-sparing check that can run at harvest, in storage, or at the packing line.
pmc-13465482:
Trude and colleagues present a 2026 participatory design study of AgriShare NYC, a digital platform documenting urban food production across New York City. Top-down farm apps often fail with underserved growers through low digital literacy, mistrust, or poor fit. The team instead ran four design phases with growers: seventeen in-depth interviews and three workshops with twenty-one participants.

Growers' limits shaped the product: labor, time, digital skills, and organizational capacity constrained how much data anyone could monitor or enter. Simplicity became the platform's guiding principle, and design criteria came from growers' stated priorities rather than developer assumptions. The shift shows in what the platform asks of users and what it gives back.
pmc-13465782:
Kübler and co-authors studied a 2026 mouse model asking whether B cells, the antibody making immune cells, are needed for collateral artery growth. pmc-13466282:

pmc-13466382:
Shang Wu and colleagues study how crystal regrowth inside notched aluminum burst vents changes the pressure at which they blow open, in a 2026 study. These vents protect equipment by rupturing at a set pressure, so drift in that setting matters. Samples of the AA8014 alloy were heated across a wide range for times from seconds to two hours.

A standard kinetic model produced numbers describing how fast new crystals form and grow, driven by stored energy from earlier working. A key window between three hundred and three hundred fifty degrees emerged; above it, regrowth and burst pressure stopped caring much about process variation. pmc-13466482:

pmc-13466682:

pmc-13466882:

Forty-five participants from twenty-six institutions in fourteen countries each sewed an eight-stitch join between vessel ends on a chicken leg model. Swapping one for another would quietly change what a training program rewards.
pmc-13467082:
Rosario Mare and colleagues test whether blueberry compounds can shield gut lining cells from a heat-born contaminant found in baked foods, in a 2026 study. The pairing models a dietary counterweight to a processing byproduct.
pmc-13467482:

Of 1,232 women screened, 234 with elevated anxiety joined the PRISM prenatal education program, and 226 completed the follow-up check after delivery. pmc-13468582:

Marks for swelling, food state, and life grade swung both ways. No mix showed a firm lift in tumor kill or life span. Proof strength was graded low to very low.
pmc-13468782:

pmc-13469082:

pmc-13469882:

The team names the protein a possible treatment target.
pmc-13471182:
Luying Qi weighed machine learning in 2026 for spotting fatty liver disease in people who drink little or no alcohol, a liver ill that hits about 32% of adults. Inside checks gave catch rate 82%, true-negative rate 81%, and curve score 88%, while outside checks gave 80%, 72%, and 83%. pmc-13471382:

Overall, untreated hypertension showed no clear survival link, but treated hypertension came with a hazard ratio of 0.81 against no hypertension, hinting at lower breast cancer death risk. pmc-13471482:

pmc-13471582:

pmc-13471982:

pmc-13472182:
Tadanori Koga and colleagues survey in 2026 how scattering methods reveal motion inside polymer nanocomposites at many scales at once. pmc-13472682:
Shibei Ni and Xiaorui Cheng examine in 2026 how money sources and family structure shape the care choices of older adults in China's southwest. Older adults who depended on children for money were more likely to prefer child provided care, and the pull ran stronger among women than men. The gender mix of a persons children, long assumed decisive, showed no significant link. Having four or more children shifted preferences toward mixed family care shared at home. The authors urge stronger pensions so preference can follow choice rather than need.
pmc-13472782:
Zhao and colleagues studied in 2026 how heritage tourism links to well-being in indigenous communities of Southwest China. They surveyed 180 people from the Miao, Dong, and Naxi groups with standard psychological scales. The mixed-methods design let numbers and lived experience check each other.

The study offers local evidence for tourism planners weighing culture against commerce.
pmc-13473682:

pmc-13474382:

Other groups can reuse it to name cell types, hunt defense markers, or merge with later studies. Open data of this kind speeds the search for hardier crops.
pmc-13474782:

Most core energy genes showed signs of purifying selection across history. Links to the wild diploid oat relative were close, and gene flow from the green solar genome was frequent.
pmc-13474882:

pmc-13474982:

pmc-13475182:

pmc-13476582:

pmc-13477282:

pmc-13477382:

pmc-13478582:

pmc-13479382:

pmc-13479582:

The authors report whether staged difficulty, matched to experience level, produces measurable skill gains alongside happy trainees.
pmc-13480182:

pmc-13480282:

pmc-13480482:

pmc-13480782:

pmc-13481382:

pmc-13482582:

pmc-13483582:

pmc-13483682:

pmc-13485082:

pmc-13486882:

pmc-13486982:

pmc-13487182:
