The authors conclude the Epac2 pathway helps carry metformin's central benefit, with more work needed on the balance between brain and body effects.
pmc-13592482:
Toro-Perez and colleagues dissect a seizure pattern in children whose epilepsy is classed as generalized, meaning seizures start across the whole brain at once. Some children begin with an absence, a blank stare spell, that then turns one sided before erupting into a full convulsion. Their 2026 review of a monitoring unit cohort uses EEG, computer analysis of brain wave recordings, to trace that path in children with brain scans.

Seven of 66 children with generalized epilepsy, all girls, showed the pattern, across eight recorded seizures. Wave analysis showed the slow spike wave rhythm of absence first. A focal buildup followed over the side frontal and back regions, stronger on the right, before the convulsion spread to both sides. The syndromes behind the cases were absence and myoclonic epilepsies of youth. The team proposes a relay through the thalamus, the brain's switchboard, and calls for cohorts to confirm the route.
pmc-13592682:
Adi Shuchami and six colleagues ask how often children's emergency departments repeat blood tests that community clinics just ran. Repeats within hours rarely change care, yet they cost money, time, and sore arms. Their dataset covered a nationwide health plan's records for children aged three months to eighteen years. Repeat rates for blood counts, electrolytes, and an inflammation marker were judged against preset need criteria, then a learning model tried to predict which repeats were truly needed.

Only about thirteen to nineteen percent of repeats proved justified, depending on the test. A standard boosted tree model predicted need with up to ninety two percent accuracy, and stayed useful when tuned to miss no needed repeat for two of the three tests. Shuchami and the team say live practice studies come next.
pmc-13593682:
Musab Işık and colleagues tested whether fluoxetine, a widely used antidepressant, can shield the liver from the damage that follows when blood flow is cut off and then restored. In their 2026 rat study, the injury was created by clamping the main abdominal artery for an hour and then releasing it, with one group pretreated with fluoxetine for three days.

Untreated animals showed heavy oxidative stress, inflammation, cell death signals, and visible tissue damage, along with weakened antioxidant defenses. Fluoxetine pretreatment largely reversed that pattern, restoring antioxidant capacity and improving the tissue picture under the microscope. The authors read the protection as working through three routes at once: fighting oxidation, calming inflammation, and limiting programmed cell death. They propose the drug as a possible candidate for liver surgery and transplant settings where this injury is common.
pmc-13594482:
Thai Duy Vo and colleagues describe a rare atypical atrial flutter tied to the right lower lung vein in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Thickened heart muscle scars the atria and slows conduction, setting the stage for odd rhythms, yet flutter from this vein is uncommon. Their 2026 case follows a 44-year-old woman with thickened heart muscle and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation admitted with palpitations and breathlessness.

Tracing the flutter wave shape, heart MRI, and high-density electrical mapping pinned the circuit to the right inferior pulmonary vein, with several coexisting re-entry loops. The team used the combined maps to guide a thorough ablation plan rather than a single-circuit fix. Vo and colleagues argue the case supports mapping the full atrial substrate in such patients.
pmc-13596782:
The PLOS One editors retracted a multilevel study of early marriage among women in Bangladesh. Concerns had been raised that its design could not support its stated aims. The notice sets out the dispute in detail. The central problem was definition: the article measured early marriage as the share of ever-married women aged eighteen to forty-nine who wed before eighteen, which departs from the international standard.

That standard counts all women aged twenty to twenty-four, married or not. Excluding unmarried women skewed the pool and made the reported figures incomparable with official survey and development goal indicators. The author defended the broader age range as support for the modeling method. Two editorial board members advised that determinants analysis may fairly use married women. Prevalence language, they warned, misleads under this design. The editors concluded the reporting could not stand, and the article was withdrawn.
pmc-13599882:
Elīza Ance Beņislavska and three colleagues use Swedish health registers to ask whether being active before a mini-stroke protects against a later stroke. A transient ischaemic attack briefly blocks blood flow to the brain and warns of higher stroke risk ahead. The study covered 1,610 adults treated at stroke units in Gothenburg between late 2014 and the end of 2019, most of them reporting only light activity before their attack.

In simple comparisons, people with moderate or vigorous activity beforehand had much lower rates of later stroke. Once age and sex were taken into account, those gaps shrank and no longer reached statistical significance. Adding clinical, social, and treatment factors changed little. The authors suggest earlier activity may mostly reflect general health, not protection on its own. They note the numbers still leave room for a real benefit that larger studies could settle.
pmc-13599982:
Andreza Parreiras-Gonçalves and colleagues review forecasts of how yellow fever may spread as the climate warms and habits change. Yellow fever is a serious viral disease carried by mosquitoes, now centered in Africa and Latin America but capable of large epidemics. The scoping review screened 1,243 studies and kept 42 using original data to project future trends in the disease or its carriers.

Most were computer models projecting that warming would expand the range and numbers of the main carrier, Aedes aegypti, with temperature and rainfall the top drivers. City and population growth also raised human exposure in many models. Far fewer studies tied the projections directly to future yellow fever transmission, and results there varied. Gaps included other mosquito types, future trends inside Africa, and forest transmission cycles. Shifting climate and land use, they conclude, will likely widen the zone where yellow fever can take hold.
pmc-13601582:
Sizhe Ma and three colleagues release Rail-VIVID in 2026, a paired dataset meant to push railway track monitoring forward. Trains can inspect track as they run, using vibration sensors that feel hidden defects but cannot locate them, or cameras that show surface damage but miss what lies beneath. The two approaches grew up apart, partly because no public dataset paired both signals for direct comparison.

Rail-VIVID records synchronized vibration and video from repeated runs over one track segment with documented faults. Researchers can use it to study how each kind of fault signs itself in each signal, and to benchmark detection algorithms on the same material. It also supports building fusion methods that combine both streams for sturdier detection. The authors frame the dataset as groundwork for predictive maintenance, where catching faults early from ordinary train runs could replace some manual inspection.
pmc-13602082:
Danielle L. Orrell and five colleagues follow one flapper skate through two catches in 2026, using tag data to watch its behavior after each release. Flapper skates are critically endangered, and catch-and-release anglers may hook the same resident fish repeatedly. Off Ireland's southwest coast, a tagged skate was caught, released, and recaptured six days later. Its tag popped off on schedule a day after the second capture, while acoustic receivers tracked it for 212 more days.

After each release, the skate moved far more than usual, with rapid vertical excursions. Models confirmed depth and mobility changes, with settling at 9 hours after the first release and 10 hours after the second. Vertical movement before settling ran 441 percent above the normal hourly rate. Even so, the skate stayed near the capture area both times. The authors offer rare two-event evidence for judging catch-and-release welfare in a threatened species.
pmc-13602582:
Sevilay Aydın Çelik and three colleagues run a 2026 randomized trial in Istanbul asking what a single climate lesson does to pregnant women's minds. Pregnant women are especially exposed to climate harms, and learning about them could raise worry or, handled well, hope. The trial enrolled 154 women at a public hospital, assigning 77 to a 60-minute face-to-face session on climate change and pregnancy and 77 to no training. Scales measured worry, awareness, and hope before and four weeks after.

The trained group rose significantly on all three measures, with large effect sizes. The control group drifted the other way on anxiety and hope, gaining only slightly in awareness. Statistical tests confirmed the groups changed differently over time. Structured climate education, the authors conclude, can raise awareness while feeding hope rather than despair. They suggest antenatal programs use such teaching for awareness and psychological support alike.
pmc-13606082:
Yunxiu Wu leads a seven-author team testing a simple artery measure as a kidney warning sign across two countries. Estimated pulse wave velocity, from age and blood pressure, reflects arterial stiffness without special equipment. The team linked it to chronic kidney disease in US NHANES surveys, representing about 100.9 million adults, and in China's CHARLS cohort of 21,853 people. Machine learning models were trained in one population and checked in the other.

Higher estimated velocity meant higher kidney disease odds in both cohorts, with odds ratios near 1.5 per extra meter per second. The association ran stronger in men and in obese and diabetic subgroups. Machine learning discrimination was moderate, the best model scoring about 0.80, and velocity ranked as the top feature, ahead of uric acid and diabetes history. Cutoffs sat near 10.2 and 10.6 meters per second. No calculated number replaces direct kidney tests, the authors caution.
pmc-13612182:
Mincheng Zou and six colleagues build a decision model for one of children's spine surgery's judgment calls. Children born with a hemivertebra, half a vertebra, develop scoliosis, and removing the malformed bone plus fusing segments is the standard fix. How many segments to fuse trades correction against preserving motion and growth, and choices have rested on surgeon feel. The team studied 36 patients who had posterior resection and fusion, mining imaging for predictors separating short from long fusions.

Screening by effect size surfaced three measurements: lumbar lordosis, thoracolumbar kyphosis, and pelvic tilt. A decision tree built on pre-surgery imaging, stratified by hemivertebra position, classified the needed strategy with 93.5 percent accuracy and an area under the curve of 0.982. The core predictors held across subgroups. The authors offer the tree as a neutral aid for balancing correction against function, noting the modest cohort behind it.
pmc-13616282:
Dong Cheng and colleagues present DUET-seq, an open-source droplet platform that reads both open chromatin and active genes from the same single cell nucleus. Linking the two views shows which control switches drive which genes, yet current tools miss many paired reads, cost a lot, or stay locked behind company systems. Their rig uses dissolving gel beads with two-part tags and a one-step reaction inside each droplet to label both kinds of molecule together.

Library building finishes within twelve hours. Careful tuning, including shutting off a leftover enzyme, yielded about 3,200 genes per test cell while keeping the chromatin picture sharp. Full plans for parts and reagents are published, so any lab can build it. Cheaper, open paired profiling could spread a powerful method beyond wealthy centres.
pmc-13616382:
Yan Zhang and colleagues find, by screening a library of compounds, that an antibiotic called danofloxacin helps mouse embryonic stem cells keep their all-purpose state. Growing such stem cells from many animal species in the lab stays stubbornly hard, and richer culture recipes are needed. Cells treated with the drug formed more undifferentiated colonies and contributed better to chimeric mice, the standard test of true stemness.

The drug lowers the amount and action of HDAC1, an enzyme that strips chemical tags from DNA packaging. With stripping reduced, activating tags rose at two key genes, Tert and Prdm10, which then switched on more strongly. Mimicking the drug by boosting either gene worked, and silencing either broke the effect. A farm antibiotic, oddly, may help labs found stem cell lines for species that have resisted for decades.
pmc-13616582:
J. Tyler Bruce, Tobias Z. Donlon, John L. Bass, and Juan C. Samayoa report a 2026 case series on narrowing at the mouth of the left atrial appendage. The appendage is a small pouch of the heart. The condition is so rare that only 28 adult and two child cases appear in past reports. Most were found by chance, and what the narrowing does over time is unknown. The series adds three patients of their own.

Two were infants born with a membrane narrowing the pouch entrance, one a four-month-old found during a work-up for a heart murmur that proved innocent. The third case appeared after a mechanical mitral valve was placed above its usual ring. With follow-up this scarce, each carefully described case helps cardiologists judge whether a silent narrowing needs watching, treatment, or neither.
pmc-13617682:
Karen Vinall-Collier and eight colleagues report a 2026 qualitative study of oral care in British care homes, where older residents often depend on staff for daily mouth care. The team ran focus groups in 2022 with fifty people: residents, relatives, frontline care workers, managers, and outside dental professionals. Views were mapped onto the COM-B model, which sorts behavior into capability, opportunity, and motivation.

Opportunity dominated the findings, especially the physical environment, context, and resources available to staff. Capability issues centered on skills and self-regulation, while motivation turned on beliefs about consequences and drive. Access to outside dental professionals, training fitted to specific conditions, and strong backing were all judged pivotal. Staff warned that small fixes fail against structural barriers such as scarce dental access and heavy workloads, and relatives asked for clearer guidance to help their loved ones.
pmc-13617882:
Justin Aunger and ten colleagues argue that research governance in England can accidentally break the privacy promises that sensitive health workforce research depends on. Studies of bullying, speaking up, or patient safety need staff and hospitals to trust that taking part will stay hidden, since identifying a site can expose the individuals inside it. Standard steps such as site forms, local investigator rules, research passports, and portfolio reporting can leak that participation before recruitment even begins.

Reforms from the Health Research Authority starting March 2026 streamline set-up for staff-only studies, hide sites, and relax local investigator and passport demands for remote work. The authors say more is needed: special pathways for sensitive team research, restricted-access portfolio reporting, and more centralized governance forms. They recommend co-designing the next changes with researchers and hospital research departments so accountability survives while privacy becomes credible.
pmc-13618382:
Getachew Tadesse Siyoum, writing alone, reports surgical repair of an umbilical hernia in a ram at a veterinary teaching hospital in Ethiopia. The one-year-old ram arrived at Addis Ababa University's hospital with a progressively enlarging swelling at the navel. Examination confirmed a large umbilical hernia, where abdominal contents push through an unclosed ring in the wall, and the animal was admitted for herniorrhaphy.

Under locally infiltrated lidocaine, the surgeon opened the hernia sac, returned the protruding omentum and intestine to the abdomen. The ring was closed with a cruciate, cross-stitch, suture pattern using size two silk. Antibiotics and an anti-inflammatory followed for three days. Healing was uneventful and complete, and at sixty days the ram was healthy and gaining weight. Siyoum concludes the cruciate silk technique is a practical option for hernias of similar size when paired with timely surgery and careful aftercare.
pmc-13621582:
Jesse Johnson, Lynn Griffin, Kathryn Vickery, and Elissa Randall asked whether PET scan numbers can reveal lymphoma hiding in a dog's spleen without a needle. Staging canine lymphoma normally leans on sampling organs directly, yet spleen sampling carries risk and effort. The team followed dogs through chemotherapy with repeated FDG PET/CT scans, outlining the spleen each time and comparing three metabolic measures against the organ's actual cell samples.

Seven dogs contributed seventeen spleen samples. Spleens harboring lymphoma showed clearly higher uptake and tumor-volume measures than spleens with benign findings. Two thresholds separated the groups reliably: the peak uptake value above a modest cutoff, and metabolic tumor volume above a set level. Total lesion glycolysis also ran higher in involved spleens. The authors suggest these scan cutoffs could support noninvasive staging, treatment monitoring, and relapse checks, while cautioning that the group was small and needs confirmation.
pmc-13621882:
Morgan James Morgan and three co-authors test a big idea in the genetics of childhood brain conditions: that one shared genetic factor sits under all of them. Conditions such as autism and ADHD often overlap and share genetic links, so a single factor, nicknamed n, seemed plausible. The team worked from summary results of large genome-wide studies, which scan the whole genome for linked variants.

Using a modelling method that fits shared factors to genetic data, the team found that a single common factor fit the data poorly. A two-factor model fit best instead, which points to more than one genetic route into these conditions. One telling result involved age at first walking, whose genetic links pulled in opposite directions for ADHD and autism. The authors conclude that lumping all neurodevelopmental conditions into one genetic bucket would mislead research and diagnosis.
pmc-13622882:
Tuğba Şahin and Nazurah binti Nik-Eezammuddeen compare gum health in smokers and non-smokers attending a periodontology clinic at a Turkish university. Smoking is a known driver of periodontal disease, the infection and breakdown of tissues that hold teeth in place. Their cross-sectional study, run from 2024 to 2026, enrolled adults with no major systemic illness.

The study included 484 people, split evenly between current smokers and non-smokers. Overall diagnosis patterns looked similar, yet smokers far more often showed the fastest-progressing form of gum disease. Smokers also carried more plaque, though their gums bled less when probed, a masking effect tobacco is known for. Longer smoking histories and higher lifetime cigarette totals tracked with worse disease. The authors say the results strengthen the case for helping dental patients quit, since quitting protects the tissues that anchor teeth.
pmc-13623882:
Qiming Dai and Jin Xiang published a 2026 analysis of the global asthma burden tied to four risk factors. They used Global Burden of Disease data from 1990 to 2021 and forecast to 2050. Asthma burden was measured in disability-adjusted life years, a count combining years lost to illness and early death. The four factors were smoking, high body mass, workplace exposures, and nitrogen dioxide pollution.

Burden from most factors fell worldwide across the three decades, and test runs confirmed the forecasting model was reliable. Smoking showed the steepest drop, and pollution and workplace burdens fell by roughly half. High body mass resisted the trend, shrinking least and even rising in lower-middle development regions. By 2050 it is projected to be the only factor still climbing, with its rate up by more than a third over 2021. Development level changed the picture sharply, the authors note, so prevention plans should differ by region.
pmc-13625382:
Franziska Keßler and co-authors test a plasma-treated liquid against ovarian cancer cells grown in the lab. Cold atmospheric plasma loads a culture medium with reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, unstable molecules that stress cells. The team dosed three established ovarian cancer lines, plus tumor cells taken from patients' abdominal fluid. They then measured survival, death signals, DNA damage, and cell cycle shifts. The energy chemistry of mitochondria completed the panel.

Stronger doses killed more cells in every line, switched on the executioner enzymes of programmed death, and left clear marks of DNA breakage. Imaging of energy molecules showed mitochondria faltering, with the balance of free and bound fuel carriers shifting hard. Cell shapes changed as their inner skeletons thinned. Plasma-treated liquids may thus attack ovarian tumors on several fronts at once.
pmc-13626082:
Chaojie Wang and co-authors demonstrate a compact way to run multiport quantum interference when the optics are lossy. Most quantum interference theory assumes perfect, lossless beam paths, described by tidy unitary mathematics, yet real devices leak light, and the math changes. Their experiment implements transformations that can be nonunitary on purpose, and they probe the setup with Hong-Ou-Mandel interference, the classic test where twin photons bunch together.

Both the familiar bunching and an anomalous form tied to the lossy transformation appeared, each exposing the hidden phase the photons pick up when they swap paths. The tool gives physicists a handle on complex light-matter interplay inside imperfect hardware. That matters for scaling quantum simulation and computing, where loss cannot be wished away and must instead be understood and used.
pmc-13629282:
Mi Young Kim and Yujeong Kim explored parents' experiences of safety incidents during their children's hospital stays in South Korea. Past work centred staff views, leaving parents' lived experience thin. Their qualitative study interviewed seven parents whose hospitalised children had experienced safety incidents between August and December 2023.

Six themes formed three clusters: indelible pain from incidents, limits of the child-health system, and the need for integrated child-safety management. Parents wanted child-centred services, honest disclosure, support after incidents, and genuine engagement in safety. Kim and Kim call for family-centred safety programs in paediatric care.
pmc-13631882:
Soroush Masrouri and five colleagues published this 2026 study testing a new way of defining obesity in Tehran. A recent Lancet Commission definition counts body measurements beyond body mass index, the usual weight-for-height score. The team used a long-running Tehran health study to ask whether the new definition better predicts heart and blood vessel disease. They followed thousands of adults for first cardiovascular events and deaths.

Under the new definition, about two thirds of adults counted as having obesity, far more than under the old rule. Over roughly twenty years of follow-up, obesity by the new definition was linked to higher risk of cardiovascular disease. The link was stronger in women than in men, including for deaths from cardiovascular causes. Even people flagged only by body measurements, not by the mass index, carried extra risk.
pmc-13632182:
Parents who have survived cancer often worry about their young children, and Zhou and three colleagues built a questionnaire to measure those worries in China. Existing tools did not capture this burden well, leaving clinicians without a reliable way to spot parents who need support. The team therefore created a parenting concerns scale through literature review, expert consultation, and interviews with patients about how each draft question read.

They tested the draft with 165 survivors who had minor children, then checked the refined version with 200 more survivors. The final scale kept twenty-one items across three dimensions, with strong internal consistency and acceptable structural validity in confirmatory testing. Zhou and colleagues offer it as a practical instrument for identifying parenting worries early, so support can reach survivors who are coping with both illness and child-rearing.
pmc-13632382:
Balance help from wearable robots could rest on a single, body-based rule, according to Jakubowski and two colleagues. Exoskeletons aim to steady people and cut fall risk, but most controllers have only been tested in one plane of motion, either while standing or while walking. The authors tested a controller that adjusts torques at several joints based on how far the body's centre of mass has shifted from its steady position.

In nine healthy young adults, a model trained on one kind of standing push predicted joint torques well across push directions and sizes, with strong accuracy for every joint tested. When the same model was applied to rhythmic, walking-like motion, it transferred well for hip and knee bending but poorly for ankle and hip sideways motion. Jakubowski and colleagues conclude that centre-of-mass feedback generalises partly, not fully, across movement types.
pmc-13638482:
Humam Emad Rajha and six colleagues published a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2026 on iron chelator drugs in chronic kidney disease. People with kidney disease often build up excess iron from transfusions and iron treatment, and the drugs that remove iron are well studied in other settings but not in this one.

The authors pooled eleven studies covering 206 patients in total. Chelation lowered ferritin, transferrin, and serum iron, and hemoglobin rose, while stomach and bowel side effects were common and serious events were rare. Because the studies were small and varied a lot, the authors say larger trials are needed before routine use.
pmc-13638982:
Scott E Allen and six colleagues offer a 2026 framework that makes implementation science practical for schools. New teaching methods often fail in predictable ways when they move from research into real classrooms, yet existing guidance is complex and hard to apply.

Their simplified protocol helps educators plan a rollout, name likely problems in advance, and keep evidence-based practices intact during adoption. The authors draw on examples such as frequent low-stakes quizzing, a technique known for decades but adopted slowly. They argue that a usable plan can close the gap between what research shows and what students actually experience.
pmc-13639082:
Adrien Sarlet and three colleagues report a 2026 study of why bacterial biofilms wrinkle. Biofilms are microbe communities wrapped in a self-made matrix, and their folds reflect the mechanics of that material.

The team grew Escherichia coli films from two strains, each making one of two complementary matrix fibers, an amyloid protein or a treated cellulose. The strains sorted into separate sectors, and wrinkles formed both inside regions and where sectors met. Adding bacteria-attacking viruses mixed the strains more and produced thicker, taller wrinkles. The work shows how matrix makeup and mixing shape the physical form of a living film.
pmc-13644382:
Maria Karolaynne da Silva led a 2026 computer-based design of a multi-epitope vaccine against Trypanosoma cruzi, the parasite that causes Chagas disease. No effective vaccine exists, treatment works mainly in the acute phase, and the parasite's two life stages demand both antibody and T-cell responses. The team built a joined protein from 38 selected T-cell and B-cell fragments drawn from the surface proteins ASP-2 and gp82, joined with immune boosters and steady linkers.

The construct predicted strong immune recognition, good solubility, and safety, with no allergy risk or toxicity, and coverage near 62 percent in Latin America. Docking predicted strong binding to immune receptors TLR2 and TLR4, motion tests over 300 nanoseconds supported complex stability, and immune models predicted innate, antibody, and cell responses across doses. Vaccine researchers get a solid early candidate on paper, with animal and human testing still required before any efficacy claim.
pmc-13645782:
Fei Yang and six colleagues compare two antibiotic-based treatments for chronic inflammation of the womb lining in women who have had repeated reproductive failure. The condition, chronic endometritis, is diagnosed here by a tissue marker test. Their forward-looking cohort held 330 women, split evenly between doxycycline alone and doxycycline plus a hormone drug called medroxyprogesterone acetate. The main measure was whether one course cleared the inflammation on tissue testing.

Cure rates were somewhat higher with the added hormone, yet the gap was too small to rule out chance. Pregnancy, though, was clearly more common in the combined group, while side effects were mild and equal in both groups. The authors read the pattern carefully: the hormone may aid conception without clearly curing the underlying inflammation. They offer the regimen as an option worth weighing for women in this difficult situation.
pmc-13646882:
Clara Delaroque and five colleagues review how diet, gut microbes, and the immune system interact at the gut lining in food allergy, in a 2026 paper. The gut surface is where food, microbes, and immune cells constantly negotiate what is safe. When that negotiation fails, tolerance breaks and allergy follows. The review pays special attention to the mucus layer as an active go-between, not a passive coat.

The authors trace how microbe products and food-derived molecules teach the immune system, and where those lessons go wrong in allergic sensitization. Diet change, microbial therapies, and food-based treatments are weighed as ways to restore calm at the surface. Knowledge gaps are flagged plainly, above all the exact chain from surface disruption to allergy. The review aims to give researchers and clinicians a shared map of a crowded, fast-moving borderland.
pmc-13647382:
Aydin Bordbar-Khiabani and Michael Gasik soak three implant metals in fluids mimicking inflamed tissue for a full year to see which corrodes least. The contenders were pure titanium, the standard titanium alloy, and a newer alloy mixing titanium with niobium, zirconium, and silicon. The year-long bath was never refreshed, imitating a stagnant pocket around an implant. Afterward the metals faced electrical corrosion tests, and the fluids were analyzed for escaped elements.

The newer alloy held the most stable surface, the lowest corrosion current, and the toughest protective layer in every fluid strength. Total metal release rose as the fluids grew more aggressive for all three. The standard alloy shed aluminum and vanadium, elements doctors would rather keep out of patients, while the new alloy released less overall and none of the worrying kind. The pair present it as the safer long-term implant candidate under inflammatory conditions.
pmc-13649482:
Rui Zhang and three colleagues asked if routine biopsy reports, written before treatment starts, can predict which breast cancers will vanish fully under drug therapy. Their study covered 171 patients at one Chinese hospital from 2016 to 2026, of whom 64 reached that full response.

The team turned 361 report files into coded traits and text features. Models built on report traits and report text each sorted outcomes fairly well, and joining them did a bit better. Standard clinical and lab facts alone sorted poorly, and adding them did not help. Fancy language models also failed to beat the plain text method. The core lesson is that the biopsy report itself holds most of the signal.
pmc-13649682:
Jia Zhou and five colleagues tested a fast-track care path for children having keyhole surgery to tie off a hernia sac. The trial enrolled 120 children from March 2023 to April 2024 and split them by chance into routine care or routine care plus a team-based recovery path.

Children on the fast-track path left hospital about two days sooner on average. Their bowels woke sooner, they passed gas sooner, and they ate sooner too. Problems in hospital struck far fewer of them, and parents rated the care higher. Some extra measures, such as pain and sleep scores, were set aside as purely early looks. The authors back the path for this common child surgery.
pmc-13649982:
Aleksandr Raikov sets out what a photonic artificial intelligence would need in order to help physicists think about the Planck epoch. That epoch is the first instant of the universe, when space and time as we know them did not yet exist. Ordinary digital AI, he argues, lacks both the training data and the energy that direct study of that era would require.

His proposal is a fully analogue machine that skips digitizing the signal altogether. A single holographic plate would stand in for a layered digital network, and one-step Fourier convolution, a way of combining many images at once, would represent states of the early universe. He also expects the design to handle hard tools of the field such as Markov chains and genetic algorithms. The project sits at an early stage, with method, principles, and design laid out rather than hardware built.
pmc-13650282:
Alexander Muacevic and five colleagues report a 31-year-old woman who lost much of her sight during a pregnancy that nobody knew about. She had received no prenatal care, and she arrived with three days of blurred central vision in both eyes and newly found severe pre-eclampsia, a dangerous blood pressure disorder of pregnancy.

Eye examination showed swollen optic discs, a star-shaped pattern at the center of the retina, and widespread pale patches from blocked small vessels, a condition called Purtscher-like retinopathy. Scans confirmed severe swelling with fluid lifting the retina. High-dose steroids given by vein, followed by weeks of tapering tablets, did not restore her sight, and she later missed follow-up care. The authors argue that the fluid separation marks an unusually severe breakdown of the retinal barrier, and that missing prenatal monitoring let the underlying vessel spasm destroy the central retina beyond rescue.
pmc-13651482:
Geoffroy Solelhac and fourteen colleagues follow a Swiss population cohort to test whether having insomnia and sleep apnea together, a combination called COMISA, predicts future cardiovascular events better than either condition alone. Both disorders individually carry heart risk, yet their overlap had rarely been tracked prospectively in the general public.

Nearly nineteen hundred participants underwent full overnight sleep studies and sleep quality questionnaires. They were then sorted into four groups and followed for a median of about eight years while an expert committee verified heart attacks, strokes, coronary disease, and cardiovascular deaths. The combined group carried a clearly higher event risk than the no-disorder reference group, while insomnia alone and apnea alone showed no significant increase. A statistical interaction between the two conditions supported treating their overlap as its own high-risk state. The authors urge prevention programs to screen for the pair together.
pmc-3096582:
Michie, van Stralen, and West present the Behaviour Change Wheel, a method for designing programmes that change habits. Improving evidence-based practice depends on interventions that truly shift what people do. Planners lacked a shared method for describing efforts and linking them to a close study of the target behaviour.

Many competing frameworks existed, which the authors call a vast plenty. The wheel brings them together around skills, chances, and motivation as drivers of behaviour. Planners can then match each barrier to suitable effort types, making health and policy programmes more planned.
pmc-3120982:
Austin studies the best caliper widths for propensity-score matching in observational research. The propensity score is a person's chance of receiving one treatment, given their measured background traits. Matching treated and untreated people with similar scores helps estimate treatment effects without a randomised trial.

A caliper sets how close two scores must be to count as a match. Too wide leaves bias; too narrow drops too many people. Austin tests widths for estimating differences in both averages and proportions. His results give applied researchers a practical rule for cleaner comparisons.
pmc-3310682:
Nordmann, Naas, and Poirel review the global spread of carbapenemase-producing gut bacteria that defeat last-resort drugs. These bacteria make enzymes that break down carbapenem drugs. Their resistance traits have been identified in infections caught both in hospitals and in the community.

Spread outside hospitals is most alarming, since it removes the last setting where control seemed possible. The authors survey where these organisms have appeared and how they travel. Their warning helped frame this resistance as a worldwide emergency needing joint tracking and new treatments.  Care teams were urged to screen patients moved between countries and hospitals.
pmc-3532182:
Houseman, Accomando, Koestler, and co-authors show that DNA methylation arrays can serve as surrogate measures of cell mixture in blood samples. Biomedical research long needed a way to quantify the mixture of white blood cell types in a sample. Direct methods such as flow sorting are limited by fragile cell surface markers.

Methylation patterns differ by cell type, so array data can estimate proportions without fresh cells. That trick lets analysts adjust studies for cell mix, a major hidden confounder. Their approach is now routine in epigenome-wide association studies using stored blood.
pmc-3648782:
Colović, Krstić, Lazarevic-Pasti, and co-authors review acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, covering pharmacology and toxicology. The enzyme acetylcholinesterase ends nerve impulses by rapidly breaking down the messenger acetylcholine. It acts along cholinergic pathways throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems.

When inhibitors inactivate the enzyme, acetylcholine builds up, with effects that range from therapeutic to lethal. The review spans drugs that exploit this action and poisons, such as some pesticides and nerve agents, that abuse it. Understanding both sides guides safer medicines and better antidotes.  Poisoning treatment also depends on the same enzyme science the review explains.
pmc-4702882:
Huerta-Cepas, Szklarczyk, Forslund, and their team updated eggNOG in 2016 with version 4.5. EggNOG is a public resource of orthologous groups, sets of proteins that descend from one ancestral protein. Groups are given at several taxonomic levels, each with summarized functional notes.

Changes since the last release improved how the groups are built across taxa. Coverage spans eukaryotic, prokaryotic, and viral sequences. Users can look up a protein's group to infer its function from better-studied relatives. A hierarchical frame helps because the right level of grouping depends on the question, from close strains to distant kingdoms.
pmc-4989882:
Rambaut, Lam, Carvalho, and their co-authors described TempEst in 2016, a tool for sequences sampled over time. Gene sequences taken at different points in time can reveal phylogenies on a timescale of months or years. That works only if the sequences change measurably between sampling times.

TempEst, formerly called Path-O-Gen, explores whether a dataset has that temporal structure. It checks if genetic distance grows with time, which signals a usable molecular clock. Virus outbreak studies depend on this check before dating origins and spread. A clear test early saves researchers from building time-scaled trees on data that cannot support them.
pmc-5339682:
Öhlund, Handly-Santana, Biffi, and their team studied the tissue around pancreatic tumors in 2017. Pancreatic cancer grows inside dense scar-like tissue, called stroma, whose role was unclear. The team grew mini tumors in the lab next to the cells that make that stroma.

In the shared dish, two distinct types of fibroblast emerged. One type drove inflammation; the other made the tough scar matrix. They sat in different places and sent different signals to the tumor. That split shows the stroma is not one block but a mix of cell types with opposed roles. It changes how labs think about drugs aimed at the tumor's surroundings.
pmc-6597582:
Haley Amemiya, Anshul Kundaje, and Alan Boyle defined the ENCODE blacklist in 2019. High-throughput assays light up some genome regions for artifactual reasons. Those regions can fake results in any experiment that counts DNA reads.

The blacklist lists problem regions for human, mouse, worm, and fly genomes. It flags zones with odd, unstructured, or extreme signal across many data sets. Filtering them out prevents classic false peaks in binding and accessibility studies. Pipelines across functional genomics now apply the list as a routine early step. Separate lists are maintained per species, since problem regions do not line up across genomes.
pmc-7751482:
Yangteng Pan and co-authors reviewed in 2020 the part played by tumor-associated macrophages, immune cells that settle inside tumors and shape how cancer and immunity interact. These macrophages are one of the main immune cell types found within tumors. They are usually sorted into two opposing camps, one that attacks and one that tends to help the tumor by calming immune defenses and feeding growth.

The authors explain how tumors recruit these cells and push them toward the helpful camp. They also survey attempts to turn the cells back into attackers, block their recruitment, or remove them. Because these macrophages are so plentiful in many tumors, learning to reprogram them could widen the reach of cancer immunotherapy.
pmc-9467582:
Inga Zerr presents the collected abstracts of the Prion 2022 conference, a meeting devoted to prion diseases, the fatal brain disorders caused by misfolded prion protein. The collection gathers work on the animal and human forms of these diseases. Including chronic wasting disease in deer and elk, BSE in cattle, and human conditions studied by labs around the world.

One featured study tracks chronic wasting disease spreading through Alberta deer and asks which genetic variants in the prion protein might protect caribou. A food source for northern and Indigenous communities. Other contributions span detection methods, transmission risks, and disease mechanisms. Conference abstract volumes serve as a field's snapshot in a single year: what researchers feared, measured. Argued about, preserved in short form for anyone who needs the state of prion science at that moment.
priestley-corruptions-christianity-1782: The opening of this record holds no page of the book itself. What survives at the front is the standard wrapper Google Books placed on its public-domain scans. The notice explains that the volume was copied from a library shelf copy whose copyright had expired. The record is Joseph Priestley's History of the Corruptions of Christianity, dated 1782 in the record's title. Beyond the wrapper, nothing of Priestley's text is visible in this record, so his arguments cannot be described from it.
rheims-new-testament-1582:
English Catholics in exile produced their own New Testament at Rheims in 1582, translated from the Latin Bible. The Rheims New Testament was the first Catholic version in English. Its scholars worked at the English College, driven abroad by the religious settlement at home.

The translation served Catholics cut off from the Protestant Bibles of their own land. Its learned, Latin-flavored style sounds stately, sometimes strange, to modern ears. Even so, its wording left marks on the King James translators who came after. Notes in the margins argue the Catholic case against Protestant readings. The book stands as evidence that the hunger for English scripture crossed every party line of the age.
rowlandson-captivity-1682:
Mary Rowlandson wrote her captivity account after Native warriors seized her in a raid on Lancaster in colonial New England. The title page calls the work a display of God's rule and care, written by her own hand. It opens on February 10, 1675, with houses burning at sunrise and neighbors killed or carried away.

Rowlandson spent about eleven weeks as a prisoner before ransom freed her. Grief for her dead child runs through pages shaped by deep Puritan faith. Printed in 1682, her book was the first by an Englishwoman in America. It sold widely and set the pattern for the captivity narrative.
rubaiyat-khayyam-whinfield-1882:
E. H. Whinfield published his Quatrains of Omar Khayyam in 1882, in Trubner's Oriental Series, with the Persian text and English verse on facing terms. Where Fitzgerald had chosen and reshaped a hundred quatrains into a famous poem, Whinfield gives all five hundred. His version is the full scholarly alternative, with introduction and notes.

Wine, roses, brief life, and the turning heavens fill quatrain after quatrain. Some praise pleasure; others mock the learned and the pious alike. Readers can watch Khayyam's thought range wider than Fitzgerald's selection suggests. Whinfield, an Indian civil servant and Persian scholar, translated closely rather than freely. Students still set his completeness beside Fitzgerald's art.
saint-martin-tableau-naturel-1782:
Saint-Martin published his Tableau naturel in 1782, seven years after his first book made him the Unknown Philosopher. Its full subject is the natural relations among God, man, and the universe. The work is the mature statement of Martinist theosophy, the cornerstone of the French esoteric revival that followed him.

Man stands between God and nature in Saint-Martin's scheme, able to read both. Signs in the physical world answer to truths in the spiritual one. His tableau sets those correspondences in plain order. The book ripens the thought of Des Erreurs into a system. Generations of French occultists studied it as a master text of their tradition.
sarva-darsana-samgraha-cowell-gough-1882:
E. B. Cowell and A. E. Gough translated Madhava's Sarva-Darsana-Samgraha in 1882, a learned review of India's systems of thought. Madhavacharya, a fourteenth-century scholar and minister, surveys sixteen schools in rising order of truth as he sees it. Materialists, Buddhists, Jains, and the great Hindu systems each get a fair, careful statement of their claims and proofs.

The survey climbs toward the author's own Advaita Vedanta, which the last chapter crowns above the rest. Few books let a reader compare Indian philosophies in their own terms so compactly and so clearly. The translation remains a standard guide to the darsanas, the viewpoints that shaped India's intellectual history for centuries.
sbe-17-vinaya-texts-2-1882:
Book Seventeen of the Sacred Books of the East came out in 1882. It holds Part Two of the Vinaya Texts in the dress of Rhys Davids and Oldenberg. The Vinaya is the rule book of the monks of the Buddha. Part One gave the core rules and the first books of the Mahavagga.

Here the Mahavagga runs from Book Five to Book Ten. The Kullavagga then starts, with Books One to Three in this part. Rules deal with dress, food, the rains rest, and strife in the host. The book is a dry text with rich worth for the tale of the faith.
scientific-american-supplement-no-315-ja: Supplement No. 315, dated New York, January 14, 1882, in Volume XIII, lists a watchman's detector, an integrating apparatus, and a canal boat propelled by air at the head of its contents. Head linings of passenger cars and an improved mortar mixer follow. J. P. Davies contributes practical notes on plumbing, with figures running from 37 to 53, They cover tinning iron pipes and soldering irons to lead. They also cover pipe bending by water, sand, balls, and windlass, plus set-offs, bad bends, and bends made into traps.
scientific-american-supplement-no-324-ma: Machine tools for boiler makers, with an improved radial drill and a bending roller, lead Supplement No. 324, dated New York, March 18, 1882, in Volume XIII. Colonel Maitland on modern ordnance follows, covering rifled cannon, built guns, steel castings, breech loading, long guns, slow burning powder, projectiles, and destructive power. Shaw's oscillating cylinder locomotive, C. W. Siemens on gas motors and producers, and the Bazin system of dredging complete the first section.
scientific-american-supplement-no-344-au: Volume XIV, Number 344, dated New York, August 5, 1882, leads with Manuel Eissler on the Panama Canal. Eissler gives notes on Spanish finds in Central America, early explorations, Nicaragua projects, and the Panama railway. An improved averaging machine, Borsig's compound beam engine in four figures, Daniel Longworth on power hammers with movable fulcrum, and the Bicheroux furnace system for puddling iron follow. Cloth pressing, ring spindles, and woolen carding engines round out the first section.
scientific-american-supplement-no-358-no: A hydraulic filtering press for treating oily seeds, with fifteen figures on construction and handling, opens the contents of Supplement No. 358, dated New York, November 11, 1882, in Volume XIV. Laurent and Collot's automatic injection pump, an improved one ton bucket dredger, a history of the fire extinguisher, and advice on how to tow a boat follow. Railways of Europe and America, John S. Atwater on locomotive painting, crackle glass by a new process, and how marbles are made complete the first section.
scientific-american-supplement-no-360-no: Soaking pits for steel ingots lead Supplement No. 360, dated New York, November 25, 1882, in Volume XIV. John Gjers explains rolling steel ingots with their own initial heat by means of the soaking pit process, in six figures. Tempering by compression by L. Clemandot's process, William Barnet Le Van on economical steam power, and Mississippi River improvements near St. Louis follow.
scientific-american-supplement-no-362-de: Recent improvements in textile machinery head the contents of Supplement No. 362, dated New York, December 9, 1882, in Volume XIV. Harris's revolving ring spinning frame, a new electric stop motion, and a new positive motion loom appear in six figures, with a companion piece on spinning without a mule. New binding machines, flumes and their construction, and Chuwab's rolling mill for dressing and rounding bar iron follow. Burning of town refuse at Leeds, with sections of destructor and carbonizer in six figures, closes the first section.
scientific-american-supplement-no-363-de: The New York canals, their history, dimensions, and commercial influence, lead Supplement No. 363, dated New York, December 16, 1882, in Volume XIV. Cottrau's locomotive for ascending steep grades, Bachmann's steam drier, and H. S. Parmelee's patent automatic sprinkler follow. An instrument for drawing converging straight lines in ten figures, a feed water heater and purifier by George S. Strong, paper making down East, and Goulier's tube gauge come next. Soldering without an iron and working copper ores at Spenceville close the first section.
scientific-american-supplement-no-365-de: Louis Favre, constructor of the St. Gothard Tunnel, heads Supplement No. 365, dated New York, December 30, 1882, in Volume XIV, with a portrait and a monument at Turin marking the tunneling of the Alps. The new harbor of Vera Cruz follows, with Captain Eads's plan shown in one figure. Cost of power to make flour, driving gear mechanism for lift hammers, a machine for cutting annular wheels, and recent hydraulic experiments on flow of water in the Ganges Canal come next.
shufeldt-treaty-1882:
Commodore Robert Shufeldt negotiated the 1882 treaty between the United States and the Kingdom of Korea, then called Chosen. Korea had long limited contact with the outside world and was known in the West as the Hermit Kingdom. Signed in May 1882, with ratifications exchanged at Seoul a year later, it was Korea's first treaty with a Western nation.

The articles promised lasting peace and friendship, opened Korean ports to American trade, and set rules for ships and merchants. One clause said the United States would use its good offices if another power treated Korea unjustly. Within decades Japan took control of Korea anyway, but the treaty marked America's first formal step onto the peninsula.
skeat-etymological-1882:
Walter Skeat published his Etymological Dictionary of the English Language in 1882, the fruit of a life's work on word origins. Skeat, a Cambridge philologist, had edited Chaucer and founded the English Dialect Society. His dictionary traced English words back through French, Latin, Norse, and the old Germanic tongues to their roots.

Each entry gives the word's history in order, showing how its form and meaning changed on the way to modern English. Skeat worked by the new scientific rules of sound change, which let him dismiss many charming but false derivations. The book became the standard English etymology for half a century. Where our words came from is authoritatively told here, and later dictionaries, the Oxford included, built on the ground Skeat cleared.
st-osyth-true-just-recorde-1582:
A True and Just Recorde gives the full account of the witch trials at St Osyth in Essex in 1582. Fourteen people faced charges there, in the largest witch case of Queen Elizabeth's reign. The pamphlet prints the charges, the witness statements, and the confessions at length.

Because the record is so full, readers can follow how each charge was built. Neighbors tell of lost beasts, sick children, and sudden deaths blamed on hidden malice. The court sorts the claims and sends some of the accused to the gallows. No Elizabethan witch case left a richer paper trail.
stanton-history-woman-suffrage-vol-2-188:
Volume 2 of History of Woman Suffrage appeared in 1882, edited by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B Anthony, and Matilda Joslyn Gage. The volume covers 1861 to 1876, years when the movement split and reorganized. The editors again built the history from speeches, letters, and reports.

War work by women, the fight over the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, and the founding of rival suffrage groups fill the record. The editors' own National Woman Suffrage Association stands at the center of their telling. State campaigns and early votes, including women voting in western territories, get full documentation. The volume preserves the words of a movement arguing with itself and with the nation.
stephen-science-ethics-1882:
Leslie Stephen wrote The Science of Ethics in 1882, bringing Darwin's theory to bear on moral life. Stephen was a leading man of letters and a frank agnostic. He asked whether ethics could rest on science rather than on church command. The book was his most sustained work of philosophy.

Stephen traces moral rules to the health and survival of the social group. Feelings of right and wrong, he argues, grow as societies grow. He tests his view against rival schools, including the utilitarians he partly followed. The result is a calm, tough piece of Victorian thought. It helped set terms for later ethics.
stevenson-new-arabian-nights-1882:
Robert Louis Stevenson modeled The New Arabian Nights on the old tales of Harun al-Rashid wandering Baghdad in disguise. He published the stories in magazines, then as his first book, in 1882. The setting is not Baghdad but gaslit Victorian London.

Prince Florizel of Bohemia roams London at night hunting adventure, with his loyal colonel at his side. In The Suicide Club he infiltrates a society where tired men draw cards for death. A second cycle follows a diamond stolen and passed from hand to hand. Stevenson mixes danger with wry humor and polished style. The book launched his career as a teller of tales.
strindberg-lucky-pehr-1882:
August Strindberg wrote Lucky Pehr in 1882, an allegorical five-act fairy play, here in Velma Swanston Howard's translation. Howard's authorized translation carried Strindberg's most performed early play to English-speaking stages and readers in print. The play mixes folk tale, satire, and dream in a form all Strindberg's own at twenty-three.

Pehr, a church verger's son, finds a ring that grants wishes and rides luck up the world. He tries wealth, fame, and love, and each gift sours in his hands by the tale's logic. A cathedral tower, a talking statue, and a chorus of townsfolk frame his rise and fall in life. At last he renounces the ring and chooses honest work and love without magic's false ease and shine. The fable's charm hides a sharp moral on ambition that Strindberg never outgrew in art.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Richmond Palace, taken from a very old drawing, fills the Mirror's No. 336, dated Saturday, October 18, 1828. Richmond draws few antiquarian visitors despite its court associations and the hallowed names of Pope and Thomson, the article complains. Most visitors fly to the Star and Garter and its well-stored cellars. The engraving shows the palace as Henry VII built it, on the manor of Sheen by the river.

Sheen became a royal palace under Edward I, and Edward III died there in 1377. His successor Richard, grieving Queen Anne's death there in 1394, had the palace thrown down and defaced. Henry V restored its magnificence, and Henry VII held a grand tournament there in 1492. After a fire in 1499 Henry rebuilt it and gave it the name Richmond. Wolsey often resided there afterward. Readers get a lost palace rebuilt on paper from chronicles.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, January 31, 1829, No. 354, illustrates the Colosseum in Regent's Park from outside. An earlier number had guided readers through the interior of this stupendous building. The structure is a polygon of sixteen sides and 130 feet in diameter. Double square Doric pilasters strengthen each angle and carry an entablature around the whole edifice.

An attic and blocking course add height, crowned by a majestic cupola on three receding steps. The cupola's upper part is glazed under fine wire-work, its lower part covered in sheet copper. The portico is considered among the metropolis's best specimens of Graeco-Doric, copied from Rome's Pantheon. Its proportions, the article claims, surpass every temple on earth in the quoted judgment. Readers get London's panorama palace measured like a classical temple, angle by angle.

Dated June 27, 1831, No. 496 of volume 17 carries an engraving of Baron Brougham and Vaux, Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain. Only that issue heading, the portrait caption, and the volume title page are present here, so no article text appears. The title page names the magazine The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction.

On that title page the magazine promises original essays, historical narratives, and biographical memoirs. It also lists sketches of society, topographical descriptions, novels and tales, anecdotes, and poetry both original and selected. Extracts from new and expensive works, discoveries in the arts and sciences, and useful domestic hints round out the stated fare.
the-phrenological-magazine-volume-3-1882: Volume III of The Phrenological Magazine, dated 1882, carries the subtitle of a journal of education and mental science. Its editor was Alfred T. Story. The title page names him as author of a manual of phrenology and of a work on woman in the Talmud. L. N. Fowler published the volume in London, and George Wilson printed it. Only the title page appears here, so none of the year's articles are present.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-31:
Headed volume thirty-three in its own pages, though the record calls it volume thirty-one, this portion covers 1580 to 1582 in chapter four. La Noue sits captive, Groningen is besieged, Hohenlo is beaten on Hardenberg Heath, and Orange stands isolated as Count John departs dissatisfied.

Holland and Zealand offer Orange sovereignty, Granvelle drafts the Ban against him, and Orange answers with his Apology, both documents analyzed in the summary. A declaration of independence by the United Provinces closes the movement. Outlawry and statehood arrive in the same chapter, which is Motley's dramatic point.
tob-4282:
Apollodorus of Athens gets credit for the Library, the ancient world's own handbook of Greek mythology. Gods, heroes, and their tangled families march in order from the first beings to the Trojan War and the heroes' returns. James George Frazer translated it for the Loeb series in 1921, with rich notes.

A student who needs to know how Heracles ties to Perseus, or which king fathered which monster-slayer, finds the answer here in plain prose. The Library lacks poetry; it offers system instead, which scholars crave. Verified from the 1919 edition record, Frazer's Apollodorus remains antiquity's one-stop reference for its own myths.
tolstoy-confession-1882: Leo Tolstoy's A Confession and What I Believe appears in a badly garbled Oxford title page, in the World's Classics series from Oxford University Press. Aylmer Maude translated the work and wrote an introduction, as the page states despite broken lettering. A line below gives Tolstoy's birthplace as Yasnaya Polyana, Tula, though the birth year is cut off in what is present. Library stamps and shelf marks crowd the opening page. The damaged title page is what is present here, so Tolstoy's confession itself does not appear.
travels-in-england-in-1782:
C. P. Moritz, a young Prussian clergyman, walked through England in 1782 and wrote his trip up as letters to a friend. The 1886 Cassell edition reprints the account, first published in English in 1795. Its introduction presents Moritz as a calm enthusiast for freer citizenship.

Moritz arrived with little money and a copy of Paradise Lost in his pocket. He spent seven weeks in England, three of them in London. From the capital he walked to Richmond, Windsor, Oxford, Birmingham, and Matlock. The introduction contrasts his admiration for English liberty with the military system of Berlin he knew at home.
un-ga-res-a-69-82:
Germ and toxin arms are banned by a pact that still lacks some states, and Resolution A/69/82, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, presses for its full reach. The Convention on Bacteriological and Toxin Weapons bars the making, holding, and storing of such arms, and calls for their destruction. One hundred seventy states had joined the pact by the time of this vote, among them all five permanent members of the Security Council.

States that signed but have not yet ratified are called to do so without delay. States that have not signed are urged to join at the soonest date. A full, world-wide ban, the Assembly holds, is the only fit end for arms of this kind.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/82 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns the Convention banning bacteriological (biological) and toxin weapons. With 170 states parties, it presses for universal membership. It calls on parties to file their annual confidence-building information by 15 April. It notes the 2012-2015 round of expert and states parties meetings. It looks ahead to the Eighth Review Conference, due in Geneva by 2016.
un-sc-res-1382:
The Security Council's Resolution 1382 on Iraq's oil-for-food program was adopted on 29 November 2001. The program let Iraq sell oil to buy food and medicine for its people. Sanctions were then eleven years old. A plan for smarter sanctions would screen only goods that might serve war.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the program for 180 days from 1 December 2001. It adopts a Goods Review List to take effect on 30 May 2002. Goods on the list, like night vision gear and special electronics, need committee approval before export. Inspectors must judge whether each item could be diverted to military use. All other civilian goods would flow freely under the new plan.
un-sc-res-1482:
Two Rwanda tribunal judges needed to finish their trials past their terms in 2003. Cases before them were close to judgment when their time ran out. On 19 May 2003 the Security Council let both judges complete the work they had begun. One would finish the Cyangugu case, due by February 2004. The other would finish a second trial on the same terms. Three more cases were set to end by December 2003.

The tribunal's president had to report on progress three times. The dates were August and November 2003 and January 2004. The step bent the court's normal rotation rules. Losing a judge mid-trial would have forced costly restarts. The text keeps justice moving without wasting years of testimony.
un-sc-res-1582: Security Council Resolution 1582 is held here as a record transcription, sourced from English Wikisource. The Council's resolutions form the backbone of UN action on conflicts, sanctions, and missions. This one follows the common pattern, grounding its decisions in stated findings first. The preservation of the exact phrasing is the point of the entry.
un-sc-res-1682:
More troops and police for Côte d'Ivoire were authorized by the Security Council on 2 June 2006. The Council voiced serious concern that the crisis and the blocks on peace and reconciliation persisted from all sides. The Secretary-General had recommended reinforcements in his January and April reports. The country stayed split between the government south and the Forces nouvelles north.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council raised the strength of the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire by up to 1,500 staff until 15 December 2006. The increase allowed at most 1,025 extra military personnel and 475 civilian police. The Council said it would keep the mission's proper size under review as events unfolded in the country and the subregion. The build-up aimed to give the peacekeepers weight to protect civilians and back the road map toward elections that kept slipping.
un-sc-res-1782:
Côte d'Ivoire sanctions are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1782, adopted on 29 October 2007. The Ouagadougou peace deal had been signed that March. First steps had begun, but voter listing, disarmament, and army reform all lagged. An expert group had also reported fresh breaches of the diamond rules.

The text renews the arms embargo and related bans until 31 October 2008. The ban on rough diamond exports from the earlier sanctions round stays in force too. A review will come by 30 April 2008 at the latest, or after free elections. The expert group keeps its mandate for the same full year.
un-sc-res-182:
Apartheid's arms supply lines were widened as a target on 4 December 1963. The Secretary-General's report on states' replies lay before the Council. South Africa's foreign minister had confirmed in October that Pretoria would not comply with resolution 181 (1963). The General Assembly's October text on apartheid had won overwhelming support.

The Council appealed to all states to honor resolution 181 (1963), the first arms embargo text. South Africa was urgently asked to stop its discriminatory and repressive measures at once. Its refusal to comply was condemned. All who were jailed or restricted for opposing apartheid were to be freed. States were solemnly called to halt the sale of gear and materials for making and maintaining arms and ammunition in South Africa. A small group of recognized experts would be set up under the Secretary-General to study ways of settling the race conflict in peace.
un-sc-res-1882:
Children in war gained wider grounds for the Council's name-and-shame lists on 4 August 2009. The Council restated its line of texts from 1261 (1999) to 1612 (2005). Monitoring under 1612 had freed children and opened talks with armed groups, it noted. Yet parties still broke the law shielding children without penalty in too many places.

The Council strongly condemned every breach of the law protecting children in armed conflict. Recruiting child soldiers, killing and maiming them, and rape and other sexual violence all counted. The monitoring and reporting mechanism would run on. The Secretary-General was asked to list in his report annexes the parties guilty of killing, maiming, or sexual violence against children, not only recruiters. His working group machinery and country task forces were backed. States bore the duty to end impunity and prosecute those who commit grave crimes against children.
un-sc-res-282: Council action recorded as Resolution 282 appears in this catalog under the year 1963. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-582: United Nations record keeping gives this text the number 582, and the catalog dates it 1925. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-82:
North Korean troops crossed the 38th parallel on 25 June 1950. The Security Council met the same day in New York. It recalled that South Korea's government had been found lawful by the General Assembly. That government rested on elections watched by a United Nations commission. The Council then determined that the attack was a breach of the peace. Few findings in its history carry more weight.

Hostilities had to stop at once. North Korea's authorities had to pull their forces back to the 38th parallel. The United Nations Commission on Korea had to help apply the resolution. It also had to report on the facts. All member states were told to aid the United Nations and to give North Korea no help.
un-sc-res-982: Council action recorded as Resolution 982 appears in this catalog under the year 1995. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The situation in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia is the business of the Security Council's 3982nd meeting, held in February 1999 and kept in this verbatim record. The Council had before it a report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Preventive Deployment Force, a small mission posted on Macedonia's borders to deter spillover from wars nearby.

Delegates debate the force's future as its mandate nears its end. The record keeps each statement as delivered, with Canada's ambassador in the president's chair. Weeks later the Kosovo war would test the region. The file is a full primary record of the Council at work.

Iraq's oil-for-food programme is extended and its import controls redesigned in Resolution 1382, adopted on 29 November 2001. The humanitarian programme under Resolution 986 (1995) was again expiring. The Council had before it a proposed Goods Review List. The list was meant to focus controls on military and dual-use goods while speeding civilian imports.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council keeps the Resolution 986 (1995) arrangements in force for a new 180-day period beginning 1 December 2001. It adopts the proposed Goods Review List and its application procedures, subject to any refinements agreed in further consultations, for implementation from 30 May 2002. The annexed list covers dual-use categories such as advanced materials, electronics, computers, telecommunications, sensors and lasers, navigation equipment, and propulsion, plus specified items from night-vision systems to missile test equipment. States are pressed to process applications quickly so urgently needed humanitarian supplies reach Iraqis fast.

Four judges at the Rwanda war crimes court faced a time trap in 2003. Their terms were about to end. Their trials were not done. A change of bench mid-case could force a fresh start. The court's head wrote to ask for a fix in March. Resolution 1482 passed with no dissent on 19 May 2003.

Each named judge could stay to close a case. Dolenc and Ostrovsky would end the Cyangugu trial. Maqutu would end two trials, Kajelijeli and Kamuhanda. Pillay would end the famed Media case. Set end dates were named: most by the close of 2003. The Cyangugu case had to February 2004. Progress notes were due in August, then November, then January.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended on 28 January 2005, and the Abkhazia parties are pressed to negotiate yet again. The pattern of earlier texts holds: Geneva meetings kept the process alive, no settlement was in sight, and the 2001 helicopter attack remained unsolved. A fresh report from the Secretary-General informed the renewal.

Both sides are urged to enter constructive talks toward a political settlement and to take concrete steps to revive the process. Calls to settle the division of powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi on the basis of the agreed principles paper are repeated. The Abkhaz side is pressed in particular to improve law enforcement in the Gali district and to allow teaching in the Georgian language there.

Extra troops and police for a stalled peace process are authorized by Resolution 1682, adopted on 2 June 2006. Côte d'Ivoire remained split after its civil war, and the Council voiced serious concern at obstacles thrown up by all sides. Reports from the Secretary-General in January and April had recommended reinforcing the UN operation there, known as UNOCI.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized an increase in UNOCI's strength until 15 December 2006. The reinforcement drew on the Secretary-General's recommendations, which were repeated in his April report. The decision shows how the Council used temporary surges to protect a peace process it feared was sliding backward, while keeping the extra deployment on a fixed clock.

Côte d'Ivoire's sanctions are renewed by Resolution 1782, adopted on 29 October 2007. The Ouagadougou Political Agreement was being put into effect, but voter identification, militia disarmament, and restoring state authority all lagged. An attack in Bouaké on 29 June 2007 against the Prime Minister had killed several people, and the Group of Experts reported breaches of the diamond measure.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo, travel ban, asset freeze, and diamond measures from Resolutions 1572 (2004) and 1643 (2005) until 31 October 2008. It demands that the Ivorian authorities end violations at once and give the Group of Experts, UNOCI, and the French forces unhindered access. Blocking their freedom of movement counts as a threat to the peace process and can trigger targeted measures. The Group of Experts is extended to 31 October 2008, with a midterm report by 15 April 2008.

On 4 December 1963 the Security Council took up the race conflict in South Africa, created by the apartheid policies of the South African government. Members were troubled that South Africa had refused to follow Resolution 181 from earlier that year. The Council said the situation was seriously disturbing peace and security around the world.

Resolution 182 condemns South Africa for ignoring UN appeals and for keeping harsh, race-based measures in force. It again asks South Africa to free everyone jailed, held, or restricted for opposing apartheid. It calls on all states to stop selling equipment and materials used to make or maintain arms in South Africa. It also asks for a small group of experts to study peaceful ways to win full human rights for everyone in the country.

Resolution 1882, adopted on 4 August 2009, widens the net used to shame armies that harm children. The monitoring system built since 2005 had listed parties mainly for recruiting child soldiers. Progress was real in places, the Council noted, with children released and action plans agreed, but violations continued with impunity in several conflicts.

The Council expanded the listing criteria. Parties that engage in patterns of killing and maiming children, or in rape or other sexual violence aimed at children in war, could now be named in the Secretary-General's annexes as well. National governments were reminded that protecting children is their job first, and that UN task forces exist to support, not replace, that duty.

South Africa's apartheid system is the target of Resolution 282, adopted in 1970. Forty member states had brought the question of race conflict in South Africa before the Council. Earlier Council calls for an arms embargo, from 1963 and 1964, were being broken.

The Council restated its total opposition to apartheid. It condemned the violations of the arms embargo. All states were called on to strengthen the embargo by applying it fully. No conditions or reservations were to be attached, and the embargo had to be strictly obeyed. The text warned that South Africa's military build-up was a threat. It endangered the security and independence of African states that opposed South Africa's racist policies.

The war between Iran and Iraq had run for nearly six years when the Council adopted Resolution 582 on 24 February 1986. The vote was unanimous. Both countries were bound by the 1925 Geneva Protocol, which bans poison gas in war. The fighting had spread to attacks on cities, shipping, and civilian aircraft.

The Council deplored the acts that had started the conflict and the way it had grown. The bombing of purely civilian centers was named in particular. Iran and Iraq were called on to observe an immediate cease-fire. It had to cover land, sea, and air, and all forces had to pull back to the recognized international borders. A full exchange of prisoners of war was urged soon after the fighting stopped. The Red Cross would help with that exchange. Both sides were also told to put their dispute to mediation at once.

War came to Korea on a Sunday in June 1950. North Korean troops swept south at dawn on 25 June. The Council met that same day in New York. The Soviet team was away, in a boycott of the body. That gap let the West act fast. Resolution 82 passed by nine votes to none. Yugoslavia held back.

The attack was ruled a breach of the peace. Guns had to fall still at once. North troops had to pull back to the 38th parallel, the line that split the land. UN men in Korea would watch the pull-back. They would send word of what they saw with all speed. All states were told to back the UN's work. None could give aid to the North's chiefs. Two days on, the Council would urge states to fight for the South.

Bosnia's war paused under a fragile cease-fire agreed in December 1994. The Bosnian government had accepted a peace plan put forward by the Contact Group of major states. The United Nations Protection Force, UNPROFOR, was working in Bosnia and in Croatia. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 22 March 1995, set out new arrangements. Resolution 982 was adopted unanimously on 31 March 1995.

The Council extended UNPROFOR's mandate in Bosnia until 30 November 1995. It approved the arrangements in the Secretary-General's report. Most of the force's people and equipment had to leave Croatia by 30 June 1995. Those needed for the new, separate Croatia operation, called UNCRO, could stay. The force's support structures in Croatia would remain in place. The parties were reminded of one duty in particular. The safety of UNPROFOR was their responsibility.
weyer-de-lamiis-latin-1582:
Johann Weyer, the Dutch physician whose De praestigiis daemonum first pleaded for accused witches, published De lamiis in 1582. The shorter Latin book gives his focused treatise on lamiae alone, the harmful women of classical and popular fear. It is Weyer's other witch book, distinct from the famous work the library also holds.

Weyer argues that the supposed witches are mostly ill, melancholy, or deceived. Their confessions describe dreams and delusions, not deeds. Mercy follows from medicine in his careful Latin. He urges judges to send such women to doctors, not to fires. The tract distills the outlook that made Weyer the accused witch's first great defender.
yusuf-zulaikha-jami-griffith-1882:
Ralph T. H. Griffith translated Jami's Yusuf and Zulaikha into English verse in 1882, for Trubner's Oriental Series. Jami, the last great classical poet of Persia, retold the story of Joseph and Potiphar's wife in the 1400s. The Quran and Persian tradition had already made Zulaikha's love a figure of the soul's longing for God.

Griffith follows Jami through Joseph's beauty, his trials, and Zulaikha's long, refining passion. In Sufi reading, her desire is purified until it becomes devotion itself. The Victorian rendering became the classic English dress of the poem. Griffith, known for his Ramayana and Rigveda versions, brought the same care here. The romance remains the crown of Jami's seven poems.
zola-piping-hot-1882:
Vizetelly issued Piping Hot in London in 1887, rendered from the sixty-third French edition. Sixteen page engravings from designs by Georges Bellenger illustrate the book. The French title, Pot-Bouille, names a bubbling stewpot in common slang.

Behind the grand front of a Paris apartment house, Zola finds a stew of vice. Adultery, false piety, and social climbing simmer on every floor. Young Octave Mouret charms his way upward from room to room. Bourgeois morals rot from within while faces stay smooth in public. Sharp and often funny, the 1882 novel may be Zola's most savage comedy of middle-class manners.
